News.title: Russell Brand was a 'sexual predator', prosecution alleges as rape trial begins
News.content:
On Wednesday, the jury heard details of the alleged offences.

The first complainant says she met Brand before he was famous in 1999, the jury was told.

She had attended the Labour Party conference and went to a fringe event where she spoke to Brand. He later allegedly raped her.

The prosecution said when Brand was questioned by police about this allegation of rape, "he said if it happened, he didn't remember the incident".

He added that he did not remember the first complainant's name and that he "had never engaged in non-consensual activity".

The second complainant worked for MTV at the time when she says Brand indecently assaulted her.

She said Brand asked her where the toilets were and the woman offered to show him.

When they reached the toilets, prosecutors say, Brand asked the woman to "come in" before grabbing her forearm.

She resisted by struggling and pulling back. He had what she described as a desperate, wild-eyed look on his face, as he said: "Please please come in â oh go on."

The third complainant says Brand orally raped her in a toilet after meeting her at a party in 2004.

Within a minute of meeting, in the middle of a conversation, he lurched forward and grabbed her breasts and squeezed them with both hands, the jury was told.

The prosecution said the woman remembered he had a "big, weird grin" on his face as he did so, then grabbed her arm and pulled her towards the toilets.

The same woman said that as they were driving to another venue, Brand exposed himself, the court heard.

"He said, 'Come on, come on, suck it' â to which she just said, 'No no'," the prosecution added. "He simply laughed but appeared to accept her refusal."

News.title: Burnham careful as he meets Zelensky but promises Ukraine won't leave 'empty handed'
News.content:
For the prime minister there was the tricky but now familiar diplomatic task of needing to show solidarity with Zelensky without appearing to criticise Trump.

Burnham's answer was to say and announce as much as he could without exposing himself to questions from journalists asking about Trump's latest betrayal of Kyiv.

So Downing Street issued an embargoed press notice overnight with warm words of support for Zelensky.

It said Burnham would promise to go "further and faster" in helping Ukraine with financial and military aid.

Specifically, the prime minister would pledge to speed up the delivery of lightweight multirole missiles that can help bring down fast jet-powered Russian drones.

There was a military honour guard in Downing Street to greet Ukraine's president, followed by a controlled photo opportunity showing the start of the meeting between the two men.

Crucially, as is common with most of Zelensky's visits to the UK, there will not be a full and open press conference where he and the prime minister will answer detailed questions at length.

In the House of Commons, at the start of his weekly question time, Burnham used the opportunity to offer what he called his "unwavering" support for Zelensky and promise greater military and financial aid in the future.

But it fell to the Liberal Democrat leader, Sir Ed Davey, to ask the question journalists might have asked if they had the chance.

Sir Ed said the prime minister had studiously avoided commenting on Trump's decision to rip up international sanctions on Russia.

"This House does deserve to know his position, as does frankly President Zelensky and our brave Ukrainian allies," Sir Ed said.

"Doesn't he agree this is yet another shameful Trump betrayal of the Ukrainian people and European security?"

In reply, Burnham admitted it was a "very dark and difficult moment" for Zelensky, who was "carrying the heaviest of weights" right now.

But Burnham eschewed the chance to criticise Trump and told MPs this: "What I have to do in my role is try and repair bridges so that the support comes back and therefore I should, at this moment in time, be careful in terms of laying the ground to bring people back together."

"That is the role I intend to play - it's the right role for me to play - in this moment. I will listen to President Zelensky carefully but he won't be going away from Britain today empty handed."

In other words, do not expect the prime minister to join in the widespread European criticism of Trump.

After the now infamous falling out between Trump and Zelensky in the Oval Office in February 2025, the UK played a key role in calming the row and bringing both sides back together.

A key player was national security adviser Jonathan Powell, who shuttled between Washington and Kyiv pouring oil on troubled waters. It seems Burnham hopes the UK can play a similar bridge-building role now.

For millions of Ukrainians facing a grim winter potentially with less US support than before, the task could not be more urgent.

News.title: Family pays tribute to 'warm and engaging' man killed in tiger attack
News.content:
The family of a man who was killed by a tiger after he entered its enclosure at a wildlife park has paid tribute, describing him as "bright, warm and engaging".

William Chapman, 23, visited Yorkshire Wildlife Park near Doncaster on Saturday and was attacked after going into the animal's pen. He was pronounced dead at the scene.

In a statement, his family said that he had suffered from "significant mental illness" over a number of years and had been prescribed "strong medication".

His family added: "It will be for the coroner to decide what part this played in his death. We would ask everybody to respect that process."

City of Doncaster Council has launched a health and safety investigation into Chapman's death.

The park remains closed and a reopening date has not yet been confirmed.

"William was a bright, warm and engaging young man whom his family dearly loved - and William loved them back," a statement released on Tuesday evening said.

The family also asked for privacy, saying "the publication and circulation of deeply offensive media content is causing them severe distress at an exceptionally vulnerable time".

"The family are utterly devastated by their loss and are struggling to come to terms with what has happened," the statement continued.

"The family are hopeful that the relevant authorities will do their upmost to get to the bottom of why our amazing son did what he did."

News.title: One stolen every four minutes - inside the police battle against vehicle thieves
News.content:
It is 01:00 on a Thursday and we are in the back of an unmarked police car on the hunt for vehicle thieves in east London.

A call comes in over the radio about a stolen Ford Transit van. Within 25 minutes officers have found it, chased it down and arrested a suspect.

Officers tell us the night has been successful, with further arrests made, yet across the UK a car is stolen every four minutes.

Despite a recent drop, vehicle thefts are up almost 50% in England and Wales compared with a decade ago, according to Home Office data. Last year, just 3% of vehicle theft offences resulted in a charge or summons.

As well as spending time on the front line in London and Sussex, we have privately spoken to 20 police officers from six forces.

They told us while they have the skills and experience to tackle vehicle crime, they are overstretched, under-resourced and struggling to keep pace with increasingly sophisticated criminal networks.

Thieves are becoming more confident. A man who claims he receives stolen vehicles and breaks them into parts at a so-called "chop shop" told the BBC he does not fear the authorities, because they "couldn't catch a cold".

Once the preserve of joyriders and opportunists, vehicle theft is now a lucrative global criminal business. Cars are stolen to order, and moved across the country or dismantled within hours, say police, making them difficult to recover and suspects hard to track. Many vehicles are sent overseas to places like the United Arab Emirates, The Democratic Republic of Congo and Jamaica.

Victims of car theft have told us they feel frustrated and helpless. One woman said it took car thieves just 35 seconds to steal her BMW, yet police only began investigating a day later. Another man said he feared for his life when masked thieves broke into his home demanding his car keys.

The success criminals are having is also hitting motorists more widely, with insurance quotes having risen by 82% since 2021, according to security think tank the Royal United Services Institute (Rusi).

News.title: What we know about the Pope's lung cancer diagnosis
News.content:
Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer but had a successful surgery to remove part of his right lung, the Vatican has confirmed.

The Pope, 71, underwent a 90-minute surgery on Tuesday at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, where he is expected to stay for about a week.

BBC Southern and Eastern Europe Correspondent Sarah Rainsford is in St. Peter's Square in the Vatican as people sent their well wishes to the pontiff.

News.title: Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Man City chairman, deleted records show
News.content:
Andy Burnham had two hospitality dinners with Manchester City football club's chairman while mayor of Greater Manchester, it has emerged.

The PM dined with Khaldoon Al Mubarak at matches in 2017 and 2018 - but this was not detailed in a statement on Monday by the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) about his meetings with the club.

Burnham has been under pressure to clarify his previous discussions with Man City since the club was found guilty of having "systematically" broken Premier League rules, which it will appeal.

The PM, who was mayor until June, sparked widespread controversy when he said last month he would be "really concerned" if the club's owners now sold up.

On Monday, the GMCA released a statement about Burnham's meetings with Man City in his role as mayor for the region for almost a decade.

The statement said he had a formal meeting with Al Mubarak in October 2021 at the UK Government's Global Investment Summit, arranged by the Department for International Trade; and that he met the club chairman "informally in the stands" at a testimonial match in 2019 for former player Vincent Kompany.

It also said that "in his capacity as mayor, he was a guest of Manchester City at home matches on a small number of occasions".

But the statement did not specify that this referred to, external two hospitality dinners he had with the Manchester City chairman at separate matches.

A previous GMCA register of declarations for Burnham, seen by the BBC, detailed a "dinner with [then-Manchester City Council leader] Richard Leese and Chair of Man City" for an Everton match at the Etihad stadium in August 2017, valued at Â£300 for hospitality.

Below is another entry for "dinner with the Chairman at the Man City/Man Utd derby at the Etihad" in April 2018, valued at approximately Â£699.

Burnham previously declared those dinners, alongside a Â£150 pair of tickets to see Ed Sheeran perform at the stadium in May 2018.

But the register of declarations has since been deleted from the GMCA website, as first reported by The Sun. The BBC understands it is the authority's policy to only publish entries from the current mayoral term.

News.title: Civil servant faked illness with make-up to juggle five jobs, court hears
News.content:
A civil servant is accused of earning almost Â£350,000 by juggling five full-time public sector roles - using sick notes and working from home to cope with the workload.

Kashim Chowdhury allegedly held multiple government jobs between February 2020 and September 2023, earning Â£350,000 overall.

The jury at Southwark Crown Court has been told he wore white make-up during a video call with his boss to try to look ill, but the make-up began peeling off his skin.

Chowdury, a 55-year-old from east London, is on trial accused of nine counts of fraud, which he denies. He denies acting dishonestly or intending to make a dishonest gain.

The jury was told that Chowdhury got jobs by making ''false representations'' about his employment status whilst applying. Over three years he held overlapping jobs at Tower Hamlets Council in east London, the Home Office, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), the UK Health Security Agency and the Department of Health and Social Care.

The jury was told that in 2023 his manager at the Health Security Agency, Aleesha Adams, organised a video call with him to discuss his sick leave.

Ms Adams claims Chowdhury was wearing make-up on his face to appear ill - and that during the meeting the make-up started to separate on his forehead showing his real skin underneath. At the time of the call he is alleged to have been paid for five full time jobs.

Lucy Organ, for the prosecution, told the court: "There could be no doubt about it, the defendant had applied make-up to his face for this Teams meeting to try and pretend to his line manager that he was unwell.

"This almost laughable incident demonstrates, we say, quite how far the defendant was willing to go in his deceit."

Prosecutors say Chowdhury "exploited" the work from home culture that began during the Covid pandemic. The court was told that Chowdhury had told his employers that he had to work from home to care for his "unwell" mother.

But the prosecutor, Ms Organ, said his workload eventually became "too much to cope with" and his performance suffered.

The court heard that he was signed off work from some jobs due to "mixed anxiety and a depressive disorder", but he did not hand his sick note to all his employers.

Jurors heard that the alleged fraud came to light after the National Fraud Initiative alerted Defra to them.

The trial continues.

News.title: Davina McCall says memory loss after brain surgery was like 'advanced Alzheimer's'
News.content:
TV presenter Davina McCall has said she experienced symptoms similar to "advanced Alzheimer's" following brain surgery.

Speaking on Paloma Faith's podcast Mad, Sad and Bad, the 58-year-old described suffering from memory loss while recovering from an operation to remove a benign brain tumour in 2024.

"After I'd had my brain tumour taken out, I had advanced Alzheimer's, so I couldn't remember anything," the former Big Brother host told singer and Celebrity Traitors star Faith.

"When I came out of the operation, I didn't know I'd had an operation," she recalled. One regular member of staff would ask McCall every day if she could remember their name. "And I'd go, 'I don't know'."

The Masked Singer judge had surgery in November 2024 after a colloid cyst was found in a health check-up as part of her menopause advocacy work.

In November last year she revealed she had also undergone surgery for breast cancer.

She called 2025 the "hardest year" for both her and her partner.

Speaking about the recovery from her brain surgery, she said: "Michael would come and visit [hospital] for two hours, and he'd go to the loo and come back, and I'd go, 'Oh my God, you're here', and I didn't know he'd been there.

"I couldn't watch a movie for six months because I couldn't remember what had happened in the movie 15 minutes before. [When reading] a book I couldn't remember the page before."

A year ago, for the first time since the surgery, she noted, she woke up and could remember what she had done the previous day.

News.title: Driving test waits fall to two-year low - but still average 20 weeks
News.content:
Waiting times for driving tests have dropped below 20 weeks for the first time since November 2024, according to official figures.

But learner drivers in September still had to wait an average of 19.7 weeks, or around five months, for a practical test.

The Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA) has been trying to cut waiting times and clear a backlog which began during the Covid pandemic in 2020.

Commenting on the agency's progress, one driving instructor told the BBC: "I don't think this is anything to boast about."

The DVSA initially had hoped to reduce the average waiting time to seven weeks by the end of last year.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander pushed the target back to summer 2026, but subsequently admitted even that would not be possible - with waits not expected to fall to seven weeks until next autumn.

The DVSA conducted 191,682 practical driving tests in September, with more than half of those passing.

Learner drivers have repeatedly told the BBC how a lack of access to driving tests has limited their freedom, education and job prospects.

Until earlier this year, many learner drivers chose to pay inflated prices to access driving tests being resold by third party providers who'd used automated programmes, or bots, to block book tests before learners could access them.

But a number of changes were made to the test booking system earlier this year by the DVSA to stop the system being exploited. Now, only the learner driver is able to book their driving test.

News.title: Mechanic who falsified MOT before crash that killed three given community order
News.content:
The car had been sold at auction to a friend of victim Rafel Jeanne, who was driving on the night of the fatal crash. The car had previously been involved in a crash in Scotland.

It failed an MOT carried out on 9 February 2023 with the warning system light on, indicating a fault with the seatbelt, air bag, or both, and with the mileage recorded at about 98,000.

Lewis retested the car two weeks later, telling police in interview when he did so "the seatbelt and warning light were now off and the rear seatbelt was now working", so he "passed it with some advisories" and it was collected by Jeanne.

He sent a text starting with a grin emoji which read: "Car is done. It's 560 you have to sort the seatbelt and the airbag light. I've passed the car though."

The seatbelts on the car had not ever been replaced and were defective.

Abigail Jackson, prosecuting, said she was not asking for the fatal crash to be treated as an "aggravating" factor to the offence.

Jon Lewis, defending, said Lewis had been in the motor industry for 30 years "with no prior criticism or complaint".

He said Lewis's decision to pass the MOT was "baffling" and it was unclear why he chose to ignore the standards "that had become the very foundation of his professional business".

Judge Charlotte Murphy said choosing the "harm" levels in the case was "not straightforward", saying she was able to consider the "wider impact" of the defendant's actions.

She said his actions represented a "dereliction of his duty" as an MOT tester but she accepted it was a "one-off offence" and "not motivated by financial gain".

Lewis was ordered to do 100 hours of unpaid work, and pay a Â£185 court surcharge and Â£114 costs.

News.title: Burnham says he wants to 'repair bridges' between Ukraine and US
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will try to "repair bridges" between Ukraine and the United States, ahead of a meeting with President Volodymyr Zelensky at Downing Street.

The Ukrainian president was welcomed by a military ceremonial guard outside Number 10 as he arrived for the meeting, in what is thought to be a first for a foreign leader.

It comes after President Donald Trump said he had struck a deal with Moscow to import Russian diesel.

Asked about Trump's move during Prime Minister's Questions, Burnham resisted criticising the US president, saying he wanted to "be careful in terms of laying the ground to bring people back together".

However, he stressed that Zelensky would not be leaving the UK "empty-handed", as he said further military and financial support would be drawn up in the coming weeks.

Burnham is expected to use the visit to promise further sanctions against Russia, while also announcing the UK will accelerate its delivery of air defence missiles to Kyiv.

The UK will also urge allies to step up pressure on Russia, with Chancellor John Healey using International Monetary Fund meetings to call for a ban on Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG).

It is Zelensky's second visit to the UK since Burnham became prime minister.

While other world leaders have received military welcomes, Number 10 said it could not find a record of one taking place on Downing Street.

News.title: 'Dark day for Lewis' as one fisherman dead and two missing
News.content:
Police say a body has been found in the search for three men who were onboard a fishing boat that has gone missing off the Western Isles.

The Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) said the alarm was raised at about 21:20 on Tuesday when it emerged the boat was overdue from Lewis.

A plane, two helicopters, two lifeboats and volunteers were making searches off the Port of Ness in north Lewis. Police have warned the public not to make their own searches due to bad weather.

Local councillor Kenneth Macleod said it was a "very dark day" for islanders, and their thoughts were with the families of the three men.

Police Scotland said the man's body was found at about 02:45, but the remaining two men and their boat remained unaccounted for.

News.title: Woman died after suffering 55% burns when paint can exploded in fire
News.content:
A woman died three months after suffering severe burns when a paint canister exploded in a garden fire.

Katie Louise Marshall, 32, of Vaughan Williams Drive, Newport, died at Bristol Royal Infirmary on 24 September.

In June, she put a black bin bag containing rubbish and a paint canister on the fire she had lit in her garden, Gwent Coroner's Court heard.

The canister exploded, and a neighbour raised the alarm. Marshall was initially taken to the Grange Hospital in Cwmbran but then moved to Morriston Hospital, Swansea, after suffering 45-55% burns.

Marshall was transferred to Bristol where she died from bacterial pneumonia caused by inhalation and burns.

Senior coroner for Gwent Caroline Saunders said Marshall's death was "unnatural" and adjourned the hearing.

Saunders said her investigation would look into "the circumstance of the fire and how she obtained her injuries and a narrative of the treatment thereafter".

A full inquest will be held on 9 June 2027.

News.title: Semenyo 'froze' after alleged racist abuse, court told
News.content:
Footballer Antoine Semenyo "froze" after he was allegedly racially abused by a Liverpool fan during a Premier League match at Anfield, a court has heard.

The Manchester City winger, who was playing for Bournemouth at the time, was preparing to take a throw-in when Mark Mogan, 47, allegedly shouted a racist insult at him on 15 August 2025.

Prosecutors said Semenyo was "clearly hurt and upset" and reported the incident to referee Anthony Taylor when the ball next went out of play.

Mogan, of Dovecot, Liverpool, denies racially aggravated behaviour.

Liverpool Magistrates' Court heard Mogan, who uses a wheelchair, shouted an offensive slur about 30 minutes into the opening match of the Premier League season.

Prosecutor Simon Jones said: "Mr Semenyo briefly froze as he couldn't believe what the male had said."

News.title: Gales and heavy rain to impact UK as yellow wind warning issued
News.content:
A weather system containing the remnants of Hurricane Isaias is forecast to send gales, heavy rain and a surge of warm air to parts of the UK this week.

The centre of the low, and its most significant impacts, will stay hundreds of miles from UK shores but north-west Scotland will see a spell of gales.

A Met Office yellow warning has been issued for parts of the Highlands and Western Isles with the risk of gusts touching 70mph (113km/h) in places.

Heavy rain will also affect parts of Scotland and Northern Ireland but much of England and Wales will remain largely dry with spells of sunshine.

The area of low pressure will also send a renewed surge of warm air across the country bringing above-average temperatures for many.

News.title: Hundreds of Royal Mail staff quitting each week under new efficiency plans
News.content:
About 400 postmen and women are leaving Royal Mail per week, according to the Communication Workers Union (CWU), who claims this number has gone up since the company introduced a new delivery system earlier this year.

The CWU says the firm had been losing about 330 postal staff a week from a workforce of 83,000 before it rolled out DM26, which reorganised routes to improve delivery performance.

The union claims the new system is not working in hundreds of offices, and BBC Your Voice has heard from staff warning of a "nightmare" Christmas ahead as the number of parcels increases.

Royal Mail says the reforms are part of its plan to deliver a more "efficient and financially sustainable" service.

Over the last year we've been in touch with more than 30 postal staff in all four nations of the UK, as they have switched over to DM26.

It allows for second class post to only be delivered every other weekday, and is supposed to guarantee first class mail and parcels are delivered every day, by putting workers into groups of three and changing the walking pattern of rounds.

But posties speaking to us anonymously say parcels are still being prioritised, letters left behind, and time wasted in sorting and dividing mail into first and second class.

"I didn't take any first class mail out on my last shift because I was on a road that's been behind for weeks," a worker in the West Midlands told me. "But I'm sure a manager would have ticked a box to say all first class mail went out."

A Royal Mail spokesperson said the company always worked to ensure all mail - both letters and parcels - were delivered on time.

News.title: Celine Dion immortalised as Barbie doll complete with iconic Titanic look
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A new signature Barbie doll has been created in the likeness of Celine Dion.

The doll's outfit recreates the navy, long-sleeved dress Dion wore for her performance of the Titanic theme song “My Heart Will Go On” at the Academy Awards in 1998.

A blue necklace is also part of the design, inspired by the “heart of the ocean” jewel, which plays an important role in the 1997 blockbuster.

The doll's hair is styled into an updo. It also wears a pair of silver earrings.

open image in gallery The appearance of the doll pays tribute to the navy, long-sleeved dress Dion wore when she performed Titanic theme song 'My Heart Will Go On' at the Academy Awards in 1998 ( PA )

Dion said: “It is a true honour to join the Barbie legacy with a doll inspired by one of the most meaningful moments of my career.

“I hope this doll inspires everyone to express themselves with confidence, follow their dreams and believe in the power of their own voice.”

She is the latest star to have her likeness used for a Barbie doll, following the likes of Mariah Carey and Tina Turner.

Margot Robbie, who played Barbie in the 2023 blockbuster film, also had a doll made in her likeness.

Dion has sold nearly 260 million albums worldwide.

That makes her one of the best-selling and most decorated artists in pop music history, known for hits including My Heart Will Go On and Because You Loved Me.

Last month, the singer was brought to tears on stage during her emotional comeback concert in Paris, telling fans she had kept her pledge to return following major health struggles.

Dion’s break from performing came in 2022, when she revealed that she had been diagnosed with stiff person syndrome (SPS) diagnosis and cancelled her Courage world tour.

open image in gallery The blue necklace the doll wears is inspired by the necklace known as the "heart of the ocean" that plays an important role in the 1997 blockbuster ( PA )

On stage, the five-time Grammy winner was filmed crying during her emotional return to the stage before delivering a speech to tens of thousands of fans in the crowd.

“It’s amazing we are all together,” Dion addressed the cheering audience.

“I made a promise; I made a promise to come back and to be back on stage. Here I am singing for you, and singing for me. Thank you so very much for your support, your patience. I am everything I am because you love me.”

The Barbie Signature Celine Dion Doll is available for sale now for £69.99.

News.title: Instagram’s Threads has made an important change – and it could help explain why social media feels different
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Instagram’s Threads says that it has made a change that might have altered how people’s social media looks.

The Meta-owned social media platform recently made a change to its algorithm that aims to show people more posts that they might actually want to read, according to its boss. The app appears to have changed its algorithm so that it will show more posts from accounts that users actually follow.

The announcement comes shortly after a theory swept Threads, X and other platforms that suggested that the number of automated accounts across social media had dramatically reduced. Users have rejoiced in the fact that they were seeing more posts from people they actually wanted to interact with.

Many pointed to an attack on Russian internet company Yandex that took down a large number of its servers. That led to suggestions that the same incident could have removed automated traffic from the internet.

Data does suggest that the incident dramatically reduced bot traffic from Yandex, and from Russia more generally. But there is nothing clear to indicate that it meaningfully reduced the number of automated accounts posting online, since that automated traffic can be used for a range of different purposes.

But there may be other reasons that the range of posts across different social media platforms feels like it has increased in quality in recent times. Threads said that it had recently made a change intended to “show you what we think you'll be interested in”, which includes making tweaks that mean the feed will show more posts from accounts that users actually follow.

“On Threads, we're always trying our best to show you what we think you'll be interested in,” wrote Connor Hayes, the head of Threads at Meta. “This involves a mix of posts from profiles you already follow, as well as some you may not have discovered yet.”

“We recently made a change that could increase the posts you see from those you follow. For creators, this should mean you see on average more reach to your followers. For everyone, this should hopefully mean you get a better feed filled with more of what you want.”

Mr Hayes did not confirm exactly when the change had gone into effect.

News.title: Liverpool led by surprise new captain amid Virgil van Dijk absence and Alisson ruling
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Kostas Tsimikas will captain Liverpool for the first time as the Reds play Austrian side LASK in the Champions League on Tuesday.

The Greek left-back, who scored the winning penalty in the 2022 FA Cup final but spent last season out on loan with Roma, wears the armband with Virgil van Dijk on the bench.

Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola confirmed before the season that he had named Alisson Becker his vice-captain following the departures of Mohamed Salah and Andy Robertson.

But Iraola explained that the goalkeeper would never actually wear the armband on the pitch due to rules that mean only the captains can talk to the referee on the pitch.

“I explained to Alisson especially that it’s not going to be possible that he wears the armband because with the new rule I think there is a big limitation if a keeper wears the armband,” Iraola said in August.

“Because if something happens in the opposition box the referee has to explain to the captains what’s happening, all the decisions.

“I had one season with [goalkeeper] Neto [as captain] in Bournemouth and then you have to start every game to say a different player that can act as a captain, and this is not viable.

“But I wanted him to feel like we value him. I’ve had enough time and we will have more time to know each other, but I had to explain also the decision about the armband to Ali because he is a keeper and, unfortunately, they are putting the rules in a way that there is a lot of disadvantages to having a keeper as a captain.”

open image in gallery Alisson is technically Liverpool’s vice-captain but will not wear the armband ( Getty )

The 30-year-old Tsimikas joined Liverpool in 2020 and is the longest-serving outfield player starting for the Reds in Austria.

Iraola confirmed before the start of the season that Dominik Szoboszlai and Joe Gomez were also among his vice-captains, but Gomez is on the bench while Szoboszlai remains injured.

Tsimikas wore the armband in pre-season, taking the captaincy from Gomez after the defender was forced off with an injury in the game against Sunderland.

Liverpool XI: Alisson, Frimpong, Jacquet, Araujo, Tsimikas; Gravenberch, Nyoni; Ngumoha, Wirtz, Barcola; Koumas

Subs: Mamardashvili, Woodman, Gomez, Van Dijk, Kerkez, Mac Allister, Munoz, Chambers, McConnell, Danns, Sonni-Lambie, Lucky.

News.title: EU ‘satisfied for now’ on AI regulation, says justice commissioner
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Europe is “satisfied for now” that it has appropriate regulation in place for artificial intelligence, the justice commissioner has said.

Michael McGrath said the EU is trying to achieve a balance between “exploiting all of the enormous potential” of AI with ensuring there are “appropriate guardrails” in its development to ensure trust in the technology.

He was speaking at the Irish Government’s AI summit in Dublin on Wednesday, which came weeks after highly publicised incidents involving “rogue AI agents” which have broken into servers and also accessed private data on an Australian government website.

Mr McGrath, the European Commissioner for democracy, justice, the rule of law and consumer protection, told reporters that regulation of AI is on an implementation phase through the EU and national regulators.

“I think what is needed globally is for more coordination: What we want to see is proper global dialogue on the issue of AI, because the EU cannot deal with this on its own.

“AI doesn’t respect or stop at any international border, inside or outside of the European Union.”

Mr McGrath said the UN has “done good work in this space” but said the EU is open to further discussions with “like-minded partners” such as Canada, the UK and others.

“The truth is that everybody is still feeling their way through this – but at the same time, the technology is developing at an extraordinary pace, and we have to make sure that humans remain in control and that we do not allow the technology to outstrip our capability to control it and to regulate it, and I think that is the fundamental message.”

Mr McGrath he added: “We are satisfied for now. We have an appropriate system of regulation in place.

open image in gallery Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence Niamh Smyth and Taoiseach Micheál Martin speak to the media during the Government’s International Artificial Intelligence Summit at the RDS in Dublin (Cillian Sherlock/PA) ( PA Wire )

“It is in the relatively early days and it is now about implementation and ensuring then that we see enforcement at an EU level, but also at a national level.”

Pressed on how the EU could be satisfied that regulatory guardrails are effective given emerging issues around AI this year, Mr McGrath said: “The truth is that this is a rapidly evolving situation.

“AI is developing so quickly; the technology is advancing, but we do have the regulatory guardrails in place.

“The focus now is on the implementation and the enforcement of them in Europe.

“Bear in mind, we cannot enforce law beyond the jurisdiction of the European Union.

“But in the European Union, I am satisfied that both at an EU level and also at a national level, that the appropriate tools and powers are now in place.”

News.title: New report of alleged sexual assault at University of Chicago frat house after Cornell 7 ‘gang rape’ case
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A group of men cheered as a 21-year-old woman was sexually assaulted in the bathroom of a University of Chicago frat house this past weekend while her two friends frantically tried to pick the lock to rescue her, according to reports.

The woman, 21, reported that she was sexually assaulted by a man at the Alpha Epsilon Pi house at 5625 S. University Ave., around 2 a.m. Sunday, the Chicago Police Department confirmed to The Independent.

Two of her friends told police that a group tried to stop them from entering the bathroom after the men were seen “cheering and appearing to encourage the activity inside,” according to a police report obtained by the Chicago Sun-Times.

University of Chicago, one of the U.S.’s top colleges, told The Independent that “a person of interest has been identified.” No arrests have been reported, and the individual has not been publicly identified.

There has been a nationwide reckoning over sexual assault on college campuses after a civil lawsuit was filed last month by a Jane Doe alleging that she had been gang-raped by seven fraternity members at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York, in October 2024.

open image in gallery A woman reported that she was sexually assaulted at the Alpha Epsilon Pi house at the University of Chicago (pictured) over the weekend ( Google Maps )

According to the new Chicago police report, a group of men outside the bathroom at Alpha Epsilon Pi told the woman’s friends that she was not inside, according to the police report.

Her friends continued to push and try to enter the bathroom. A man grabbed one of the women by their hair as the other picked the bathroom lock, the report said. When her friends finally made it into the bathroom, the woman was “not fully conscious” and both the man and woman were partially undressed, the report noted.

The report says that when one of the women’s friends told the man to get off her, he “responded that everything was ‘cool,’ as though nothing had occurred.”

The woman and her friends confronted the man outside the frat house who said they “had identified the wrong person.” He pointed them in another direction and ran off, per the report.

One of the friends tried to chase him, but ran into a police officer and reported the alleged assault, according to the report. The 21-year-old was then hospitalized, police confirmed to The Independent.

The woman is not a student at the University of Chicago, according to the Chicago Sun-Times. She did not return the newspaper’s request for comment, but one of her friends told the paper she was “obviously shaken up” and worried about her name getting out.

open image in gallery The woman’s friends told police that they picked the bathroom lock to save her during the alleged assault ( Getty )

The Chicago Maroon, the university’s student newspaper, published an article Tuesday describing a video shared to TikTok that appears to show the alleged perpetrator.

Police said the man is 5 feet 7 inches tall with curly hair. He was wearing a black, short-sleeve shirt with black pants at the time of the alleged assault, according to the police report.

An alert from the University of Chicago said the suspect is not affiliated with the school. He was not named in the alert because he has not been charged with a crime.

“This identification has been corroborated by key witness statements and video evidence from University cameras and license plate readers, all of which has been shared with [the Chicago Police Department] by the Department of Safety & Security,” the university alert said.

The university’s chapter of Alpha Epsilon Pi said in a statement on Instagram that no one affiliated with the fraternity was “involved or complicit with this incident.” The chapter says it is working with authorities.

open image in gallery University of Chicago’s Alpha Epsilon Pi said in a statement that no one in the fraternity was involved in the incident ( Getty )

The Independent has contacted the fraternity’s national chapter for comment.

Cornell’s Jane Doe lawsuit alleges she was drugged and gang-raped by seven members of the now-defunct Chi Phi fraternity house in Ithaca, New York, in October 2024. None of the men have been criminally charged. All have denied wrongdoing.

Cornell announced this week that it has banned fraternity parties for the rest of the year.

Earlier this month, the Ivy League school appointed former Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates to lead an independent investigation into how the school handles sexual assault cases. New York Governor Kathy Hochul has also assigned state Attorney General Letita James to the case as special prosecutor in a criminal investigation.

After Doe reported the alleged rape in 2024, Cornell began an investigation, which involved multiple hearings and resulted in the suspensions and expulsions of some of the students involved. The Chi Phi fraternity was also shut down.

“Any suggestion that the University did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false,” the university said in a previous statement. “A continuation of the false narrative that there were minimal consequences in this case is irresponsible, will make survivors feel less safe and supported, and will perpetuate the underreporting of sexual assault.”

News.title: New York to ban Central Park's horse-drawn carriages after teen's death
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

New York City lawmakers plan to ban horse-drawn carriages from Central Park, ending their more than 150-year run as an iconic, old-timey tourist attraction, following decades of opposition from animal welfare activists and the death of a teenage tourist last spring.

The City Council is expected to approve a bill next week that would end the rides by 2028. Three consecutive mayors had called for an end to the carriage rides because of safety concerns, only to have lawmakers yank back the reins.

A spokesperson for Julie Menin, the council speaker, confirmed the incoming vote and said the proposal had enough support to pass. Mayor Zohran Mamdani's office said he had reached a deal with the speaker on the legislation.

“The horse carriage industry is coming to an end in New York City,” Mamdani said in a social media post.

Teen's death reignited debate over carriage rides

The latest push for a ban started in June, when 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan, visiting the city from India, died after jumping from a runaway horse carriage during a ride with family members. His death, which appeared to be the first fatality in a horse carriage accident since they were introduced in Central Park, reignited the debate over whether carriages, a romantic throwback to the city's past, have a place in a modern metropolis.

Mahajan's family has appeared at City Hall, in person and through videoconference calls from India, begging the city to finally end the rides.

“We are shattered, our whole family shattered. The pain does not go away,” his father, Deepak Mahajan, told city council members via a videocall during a hearing for the bill last summer, saying his son leapt from the carriage to try and help his mother, who was flung from her seat, after the horse bolted. “Every morning we wake up and think of nothing but the loss of our son.”

For decades, animal welfare activists and other critics have decried the carriage industry, arguing horses shouldn't be hauling tourists around busy streets and Central Park while having to navigate bustling traffic and gawking passersby. In the past, horses have collapsed, gotten startled and run off, hitting cars or other objects, with each accident resulting in fresh calls for a ban.

“The tragic and preventable death of 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan made clear that the status quo is no longer acceptable. Horse-drawn carriages have long been part of New York City’s history, but in an increasingly busy Central Park, this tradition has become a growing public safety liability,” Menin said in a statement.

The industry and its supporters have long cast the rides as a way for visitors to experience the New York they know from classic movies and television.

Fred Astaire and Cyd Charisse danced into one of the carriages in “The Band Wagon.” Robert Redford and Jane Fonda rode one in “Barefoot in the Park.” Macaulay Culkin escaped bandits in a carriage in “Home Alone 2: Lost in New York.”

“Taking a horse and carriage ride in New York City is one of the most iconic things to do in New York City and people from all over the world know about us and travel to New York to go to a carriage ride in New York,” Conor McHugh, a longtime carriage driver, told the Council earlier this year.

Mayors have faced pushback in efforts to ban rides

Efforts to close down the industry have been met with pushback from unions and influential supporters, often resulting in tiresome political fights that have seen mayors throw up their hands over nagging worries about putting carriage drivers out of work and what to do with the horses if they can no longer work.

Transport Workers Union International President John Samuelsen said the Council's bill has “no meaningful economic relief for workers” and that Menin “used the tragic death of a tourist to contrive a public safety crisis.”

“This is disgraceful political opportunism, and Zohran should not simply go along with it, particularly when immigrant families’ livelihoods are being destroyed. This entire situation is reprehensible,” he said in a statement.

The proposal as written would require the mayor's office to develop a workforce transition plan for drivers, and includes a measure that would allow the city to consider some kind of compensation for industry workers. Carriage owners could not sell their horses off for slaughter, according to the bill's language, which requires that horses be disposed of in a “humane manner.”

The mayor's predecessor, Eric Adams, called for ending the industry during the waning days of his administration, but the proposal went nowhere. The mayor before that, Bill de Blasio, had pledged to eliminate the rides on day one of his administration but abandoned the crusade after heavy opposition from unions and a media blitz involving actor Liam Neeson.

Over the years, the city has placed various safety regulations around the industry, including a requirement that the horses get at least five weeks of vacation a year outside of city limits with daily access to a pasture. The horses are inspected by a veterinarian twice a year, and the maximum age they can work at is 26, according to city regulations. And they don't work when it is hotter than 89 degrees.

News.title: Kenya confirms second Ebola case, a relative of first patient
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Kenya’s Health Ministry confirmed the country’s second Ebola case Wednesday, saying a relative of the man who died two days after arriving from Congo had tested positive while in quarantine.

The ministry said the 39-year-old man had been identified as a close relative of Kenya's first Ebola case and developed symptoms Tuesday.

The first patient, a 40-year-old Kenyan, had been living in Congo, where he fell ill and was treated at two health facilities. He traveled through three Ebola-affected provinces before leaving the country and arriving in neighboring Uganda on Oct. 1. He flew to Kenya, where a relative picked him up at the airport and drove him to a hospital. He began receiving treatment and tested positive for Ebola on Oct. 5. He died that day.

Health officials identified about 128 contacts linked to the first case, and placed 108 of them in quarantine. Five of the contacts are outside Kenya, and authorities in those countries have been notified, according to Kenya’s Ministry of Health.

The second patient was among those quarantined. The health ministry said early detection of the infection “improves his chances of recovery.”

The ministry said the two cases were linked and there was “no evidence of spread in the community".

Kenya has tightened screening at border crossings and airports since detecting its first Ebola case and urged the public to take precautions and report suspected infections through an emergency hotline.

News.title: I tried Apple’s new smart home hub – the brand faithful will love it
News.content:
HomeView can control smart lights, heating, security cameras and video doorbells via touch or voice, but devices must support Matter – the cross-brand smart home standard. That means you aren’t confined to Apple-approved gadgets, but you are still limited – Ring video doorbells, for example, aren’t Matter-compatible, so they won’t work with HomeView, which could be a deal-breaker for even the biggest Apple fan.

But for anyone put off by the complexity of setting up a smart home, Apple is trying to simplify things. It has partnered with LG on Home Collection – a range of devices, including security cameras and a video doorbell – that connect with a single tap, just as AirPods do with an iPhone. They won’t be available until later in the year, but they could mark a major step towards making smart home set-up less complicated.

My early verdict

HomeView is built for the Apple faithful: set-up requires an iPhone or iPad, personalised AI features need a recent Apple Intelligence-capable iPhone, and some apps work only when your phone is nearby. In a household split between iPhone and Android, Android users will get a much thinner experience, and Apple’s own services come first at every turn.

Still, HomeView is the most polished smart display I have seen. Face recognition makes it both a great shared and personalised device; the sound quality is excellent; and Siri AI is finally worth talking to, especially when it can draw on your personal context. I’ll need to live with it for a few weeks before giving a final verdict, but so far it’s a beautifully designed device I’d be happy to invite into my home.

News.title: Ed Miliband calls for ‘new deal on debt’ as developing countries face spiralling borrowing costs
News.content:
Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, has called for a “new deal on debt” as spiralling borrowing costs force developing countries to spend more on interest payments than on education or health.

In a speech in Bangkok on Wednesday, Mr Miliband warned that the global financial system is failing emerging markets, and promised to use the UK’s diplomatic heft to push for urgent reform.

He said: “The short-term repayments are crippling, and while many are not defaulting on their payments they are being forced, if you like, to default on the lives and prospects of future generations.

“So we need a new deal on debt, a deal that supports countries to repay over longer time horizons and, crucially, refinancing with better rates to give developing countries precious fiscal space.”

Although public debt is not inherently problematic, servicing costs are at a 25-year-high – squeezing government coffers just as conflict, climate change and a ‘Godzilla’ El Niño push food and fuel prices ever higher.

Emerging economies in particular have little headroom: according to the Rockefeller Foundation, average interest payments now exceed 10 per cent of revenue in developing nations, while UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) analysis found 3.7 billion people live in countries where debt servicing costs exceed spending on health or education.

At the same time, overseas development aid (ODA) spending from wealthy countries has plummeted – hitting social, infrastructure and humanitarian projects, and disaster response.

The mounting global debt pile has dominated discussions in Bangkok this week, where some 15,000 people have descended for the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank annual meetings.

This included the first meeting of the newly formed Borrowers’ Platform on Monday. A group of finance ministers and central bank governors from some 30 countries, it was formed to exchange ideas about how to deal with debt burdens – and how to avoid pitfalls.

News.title: Trump backs down in Zambia mineral and data-sharing row
News.content:
Zambia has signed a five-year health financing agreement with the US government after the US dropped demands for access to sensitive health data and separated the deal from negotiations over the country’s mineral resources.

The agreement follows months of negotiations over a $2.49 billion health aid package, with Zambia pushing back against US demands to share medical data and give preferential access to the country’s rich mineral reserves in exchange for money to provide lifesaving healthcare.

Under the final agreement, Zambia will not be required to hand over individual patient records or biological specimens, which the US had previously argued was important for global disease surveillance.

Data sharing will be restricted to monitoring and evaluating US-funded health programmes.

A separate agreement covering US access to Zambia’s critical minerals has also been decoupled from the health financing deal, it was confirmed last week.

“The government will not be sharing any specimens with the United States because we removed all those aspects that raised concern,” Zambian Health Minister Roma Chilengi said last week as the agreement was signed.

Zambia’s Foreign Minister Mulambo Haimbe also confirmed that the health and mineral agreements had been separated.

“There was this [memorandum of understanding] on health and another on critical minerals, and we were saying that these need to be decoupled, and this has been done,” he said.

News.title: Progress against HIV stalls in South Africa, research shows
News.content:
South Africa’s progress in tackling the Aids and HIV crisis has stalled in one of its most populous provinces, new research has found.

The number of new cases of the infection in KwaZulu-Natal province, centred around the eastern port of Durban, have stopped falling after years of steep declines.

Data from a long-running study following thousands of people also showed those with detectable levels of virus in their blood had risen slightly despite years of medics prescribing antiretroviral drugs.

Researchers said the peer-reviewed study published in The Lancet HIV medical journal “provides a stark warning on prevailing HIV trends in rural South Africa, where ground is being lost in the fight against the HIV epidemic”.

The researchers, led by scientists at Durban’s Africa Health Research Institute (AHRI) and Stellenbosch University’s South African Centre for Epidemiological Modelling and Analysis (SACEMA), used a 20-year study which has tested nearly 60,000 people.

Analysis showed that after steep reductions in HIV incidence from 2013 to 2018, incidence rates for both males and females showed little or no decrease from 2019 onwards.

Incidence rates had continued to fall for young people under 35, but that had been offset by a lack of progress for those in middle age.

News.title: Carrick’s United are in crisis and now spotlight is on Wilcox
News.content:
They seem to lack players who can play on the front foot, who have the athletic dynamism required in this league and too many self-indulgent forward players who either can’t be bothered to help out their team-mates or cannot concentrate long enough to do so. Spooked by their lack of pace in defence and midfield, they are hidebound by caution, dropping ever deeper, ever more reliant on counter-attacking despite the blatant disconnect between the front four and back six. If they drift through this match and Sunday’s trip to Elland Road, Carrick may join the long list of Ineos-driven managerial mis-steps.

Atlético have won six of eight in La Liga and have been defeated only once. They are five points behind Barcelona in second and have score 18 goals and let in eight, which may seem a curious thing to include in a preview but it is done to emphasise that many fans’ perception of Diego Simeone’s team are out of date. Back in the days of Diego Godín, Gabi, Juanfran et all, six wins a draw and a defeat would have had goals for of about 10 and goals against of maybe three.

Simeone is a martinet about attitude not systems or styles and his team have evolved, with the World Cup-winner Alex Baena, who has scored four goals so far, driving them on. He has reintegrated Julián Alvarez, too, after his brazen attempt to force a move to Barcelona so incensed Atléti fans that it seemed they would drive him out of the club. Simeone refused to let Alvarez get his own way and he is now buckling down. Ten years ago Simeone would have bitten his head off.

News.title: Arsenal’s big guns blow Lille away after the second string flop
News.content:
The Arsenal players wore black armbands to mark the passing, aged 94, of Ken Friar, the club’s life vice-president. He had served the club from 1945 to 2014 and was variously club secretary, managing director and a driving force in building the stadium in which they now play. Even Arteta, no sentimentalist, insisted on beginning his press conference with a tribute.

For Arteta’s players, there will be a much bigger test than this one in Munich next week against Bayern. Arsenal have already won in Naples but a victory at Bayern would be significant beyond that. Arsenal have won all but one of their 10 games this season – that big defeat at the Amex Stadium, almost one month ago. They clearly have another gear to go to when required although ideally, Arteta would not always have to ask it of the same players. The club have spent too much on this squad not to be able to trust the understudies.

Madueke did at least end the game with an assist. Of Saka’s understudy, Arteta said: “When you talk about players being clinical – what is clinical? Clinical sometimes means that they score one in every 500. It’s about generating volume and more actions and getting him into the good position because he will decide matches.”

No goals for Gyokeres this season and a general acceptance that the time for persevering with him has passed. It could be ever-dwindling returns for him in terms of game-time as the season goes. Coming off the bench for Lille in the second half was the unmistakable Olivier Giroud, now 40 and more than 14 years on since he signed for Arsenal from Montpellier. He was given a warm welcome by the home fans and, later, an equally warm farewell despite the Chelsea years in the interim. He was a much better player than Gyokeres in an era when Arsenal were in decline.

Guimarães had two chances in the first half. Lille’s Japan international Ayase Ueda had a goal disallowed for offside. Guimarães would have a further penalty appeal before the hour as Arteta began to consider the substitutions.

News.title: Lionesses take step closer to World Cup but do not look like they can win it
News.content:
England may have edged a step closer to booking their place at next summer’s Women’s World Cup but they do not yet look like a team who can win it.

This two-legged qualifying play-off with Greece was always going to be somewhat academic. Greece are ranked 58th in the world and have never qualified for a major tournament. But they could – and should – have taken the lead before England eventually broke the deadlock through Georgia Stanway just before half-time.

The goals flowed more freely in the second half, but Greece deservedly found the net themselves and are not yet out of the tie. There is every chance of the Lionesses winning the second leg in Leicester on Tuesday more comfortably, but not being able to put teams to the sword is exactly why they ended up in the play-offs in the first place.

The best teams are ruthless and unforgiving – and England did not display those traits here. They snatched at chances, and several players were guilty of firing wide. There were also defensive problems. Greece got in behind England’s back line too often and the goal they scored was far too easy for them.

“I think we made it [the game] a bit harder,” England manager Sarina Wiegman said. “Greece were very well prepared. They were very well organised and well disciplined. Of course I’m happy with the 3-1, I’m not happy with the one.

“We could have scored more goals, we should have. The final stage, the final pass needs to be better. I think we were a little bit in moments really good on the ball and in other moments not so good, and we could have made better decisions too. Lots of things to take from today.

News.title: Donkey prices in Gaza skyrocket from $1,000 to $30,000
News.content:
The price of a donkey in Gaza has jumped from about $1,000 before the war to $30,000 today, according to one of the embattled enclave’s most senior vets.

The surge in the value of the pack animals is due to the virtual elimination of motorised private transport in the strip and the emergence of a small group of black marketeers who have become hugely rich trading in intercepted aid.

The donkeys, whose number has been halved in the past three years, are also now in comparatively short supply.

“It’s a little bit crazy and people keep asking me ‘are you sure about that number?’”, Dr Ahmed Thabet, a Gazan veterinary surgeon told the Telegraph.

“They say ‘do you mean $3,000?’ but I tell them ‘no’. The average price of a donkey before the war was between $1,000 and $1,200. Recently it was $20,000 and last week I witnessed one that was sold for $30,000”.

Sports.title: Shakhtar Donetsk are football’s ultimate survivors from sleeping in bunkers to epic 20-hour journey to Stamford Bridge
Sports.content:
Next

THEY are football’s ultimate survivors.

A club that was forced to climb through the rubble of their country, after most of the team was lost by a Fifa decision that still rankles.



But when Shakhtar Donetsk walk out at Stamford Bridge to face AEK Athens in the first of four Champions League “home” matches to be staged in London, they will have an entire nation watching.

Even fans of rival clubs like Dynamo Kyiv now see Shakhtar as the symbol of Ukraine’s resilience and refusal to bow to Russian aggression.



More than a decade after the first Russian incursion forced Shakhtar to flee their home city, domestic matches are frequently interrupted by missile and drone attacks, while more than half the squad sleep in underground bunkers.

Yet through it all, the club has been rebuilt, continued to play, against the odds, against Europe’s elite.

The reward this season is a “home” game against Real Madrid in January.

It will give thousands of Ukrainian refugees of the war who came to the UK a chance to see the orange and black shirts pitted against Jude Bellingham, Kylian Mbappe, Vinicius Jr and the rest of Jose Mourinho’s team of superstars.

Shakhtar’s sporting director, former Croatia wing-back Darijo Srna, who has spent more than two decades in the country, recalled: “We lost everything in 2014. For us, that was when the war started.

“We lost our beautiful stadium, our fans, our training camp and had to start a new life.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

“Then in 2022, when we started to feel at home in Kyiv, the war for the whole of Ukraine started.

“Now we are based in Lviv but we are the only Ukrainian club in European competition this season.

“So we are playing for the whole Ukrainian people, for the army, who will be watching our games on their mobile phones, sending them good emotions for 90 minutes in the middle of a war for our country.”

Following the start of that Russian offensive, Fifa ruled that Shakhtar’s foreign players could declare their contracts suspended.

Srna’s anger towards Gianni Infantino remains incandescent. He added: “Fifa destroyed us. We lost a lot of money, a lot of players.



“Like Manor Solomon, who went to Tottenham, Tete, who joined Lyon, Dodo, now at Fiorentina, players who are now worth £200million-£300m.

“So we had to build a team for 2022/23 with Ukrainian players, in two weeks.

“Now we are back, with some of the best young Brazilian players, the model this club has had for 20 years.

“Isaque Silva, the attacking midfielder, Gabriel Carvalho on the right wing, Luca Meirelles and Alisson up front all play for Brazil Under-20s, Ryan Roberto and Bruninho too.”

Funding from Ukraine’s richest man, Rinat Akhmetov, whose SCM holdings company operates in 30 countries including the UK – with businesses in the energy, metals, minerals and tech industries – make it all possible.



SCM’s Natalya Yemchenko, very proud that the company’s steel helped construct Everton’s Hill Dickinson Stadium, explained: “When the club plays, now, everyone watches.

“Ukrainians need some victories and good stories and hope. Our vision for the future of Shakhtar is one of the big parts of this.

“Nobody was born ready for war but we are fighting for what Europe stands for and believes in – for freedom, for democracy, independence, equality.”



Yet even Akhmetov’s billions cannot hide from the ongoing reality – which is Turkish coach Arda Turan’s squad living in the steel bunkers built by SCM in the bowels of major cities.

Srna added: “The president has invested so much in football, so much in Ukraine, to help the people.

“It’s a unique thing and we are all with him. He only saw his club for the first time in 12 years a few months ago because of what has happened.

“We don’t have our stadium, we haven’t had fans for many years, none are allowed in the grounds and when a match starts it might stop because of the bombing and not finish for four hours.

“The Russians have been attacking every day so we have to go down to the shelter during matches and then come back to finish them.



“Our Brazilian players sleep in the shelters. Even Arda sleeps in the same place sometimes, to check with them. It would be funny – but it’s not funny.”

Nor was Shakhtar’s journey for tonight’s game.

Friday’s 3-0 win at Veres Rivna, keeping them top of the domestic table, was the start of an epic 20-hour plus trek to London, via coach, train and a flight from Warsaw. AEK flew direct from Athens.



But it will feel worth it with Shakhtar hoping for a huge crowd of UK-based fans inside the Bridge for the four games.

Srna added: “We have played in Poland and Germany before but we wanted to come to London – and not just because Arsenal are the only team from there playing in the Champions League this season.

“It may not be our home but it will feel like home. Fans with the flags, including English people who have supported us so much.

“We have lost our home but we have not lost our cause. We cannot lose that. We will always fight for Shakhtar and Ukraine.

“I still find it incredible that the Ukrainian people are so brave, so strong, so united. We are winners already.”

Sports.title: Vincent Kompany blasts ‘stupid’ Michael Olise red card with Bayern Munich star now suspended for Arsenal clash
Sports.content:

BAYERN MUNICH boss Vincent Kompany blasted Michael Olise for the “stupid” red card that will see him miss next week’s clash with Arsenal.

The winger was sent off with 17 minutes left of Bayern’s 3-3 draw at Norwegian side Viking FK on Tuesday night.

Olise got two yellow cards in a matter of seconds after tugging the shirt of winger Zlatko Tripic and then throwing the ball in his face.

Sports.title: Gianni Infantino ready to DOUBLE money given to every national association as he targets Fifa presidential re-election
Sports.content:
Next

GIANNI INFANTINO will propose more than DOUBLING the money given to every national association – in a further move to underpin his re-election campaign.

Infantino’s opponents, led by Uefa, say the move is proof there was NO need for his World Cup sell-off plan.



But it is a further sign that the Swiss, 56, is increasingly confident he will be voted in for a further four-year term in March without any opposition.

In a proposal to be put before Thursday’s meeting of Fifa’s ruling Council in Zurich, the world body will offer all 211 member nations an extra £11.3million over the next four years.



That is on top of the £7.5m over the same period that they currently receive.

And while Uefa will lead the criticisms on Infantino’s stewardship of the global game, using the figures as evidence to underpin their claims the failed World Cup plan was never required, it will be another victory for the president.



As part of his efforts to force through the Fifa Forward Enterprises plan, Infantino told national bodies they would be able to expect £30m in total funding.

Half of that figure would be up front, if they accepted the sell-off by a mid-September deadline.

Infantino was forced to withdraw the proposal after a global backlash, with Uefa, backed by Asia and Concacaf, demanding immediate payments of £7.5m per nation from the central funds.

But the Fifa chief has used Uefa’s own public argument – that the world body did not need the proposed private investment to meet its global obligations – against them.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

Under his latest plan, almost certain to be voted through, the funding for the new pay-out will come straight from Fifa’s £4.5billion cash reserves after the financial success of the 2026 World Cup.

Around £2.65bn of that residue will be used to support the new scheme.

The proposal mandates that 40 per cent of the total pay-out should go on operational costs, the same on specific projects and the remaining £3.8m on women’s and youth football.

It adds: “Member Associations would continue to define their own individual priorities with some criteria added to the purpose of the funds being disbursed.”



And while anger towards Infantino remains widespread, led by Europe, the inability of his opponents to find a challenger leaves him barely a month away from being able to claim victory without a vote.

Sports.title: How Lisandro Martinez’s astonishing blasts sent shockwaves through Man Utd as legends have their say
Sports.content:

LISANDRO MARTINEZ’S blast at Manchester United chiefs has caused a stir after he was slammed by a number of ex-players.

The Argentine defender, 28, risked the wrath of the club’s hierarchy by slating their work in the transfer market.



Speaking after the team’s 2-0 defeat to Atletico Madrid in the Champions League, Martinez turned the focus on United supremos.

He said: “We had a fantastic season last season and now we expect more from the top, more players to compete because many teams bring many players as well.



“Atletico have an amazing team and they deserve to win today. I expect more [investment]. One hundred per cent. I expect more from our technical director (Wilcox).“

But Martinez’s future at Old Trafford is now in doubt after reports his team-mates confronted him on the flight home from Spain.



Club legends aren’t happy with them either as a number of them scolded for his comments.

Wayne Rooney

The iconic former striker wasn’t pleased with the centre-back’s public criticism of the United board and felt it should have been said internally.

He told TNT Sport: “Something like that will rip that dressing room apart. I disagree. I thought that the performance was okay. I thought it was better, so there were some positive signs.

“It’s a difficult one because I always used to feel that I was outspoken as a player and you want to have your opinion.

“He’s maybe gone a bit too far, and that should have stayed internal.”

Rooney admitted he went through a similar situation after initially refusing to sign a new deal at Old Trafford in 2010 over a lack of quality signings.

But he added that Martinez’s comments were actually disrespectful to his fellow team-mates as he had suggested the squad wasn’t good enough.

Rooney added: “I think in some ways he’s right in terms of the club needing to invest more at the top end of the pitch and the defence.

“But I think it looks like it was a bit of an agenda and he wanted to say that because it doesn’t reflect the performance I thought the performance was better.”



“It’s disrespecting his team-mates as well, saying they are not good enough. So it’s disrespectful. I think only Bruno has any right to come out and say something. But it should be kept indoors.

“That interview there is not going to help. The situation the club are in at the minute. The noise. That is not going to help at all.”

Ashley Young

Rooney’s former United team-mate Young agreed the interview had the potential to cause “fractions” within the squad.



He claimed Martinez had only added to “pressure that’s building” ahead of their trip to Leeds United this weekend.

Young told TNT Sport: “We spoke before the game about how the club needed to invest more, but what does he want? For them to buy a whole new team?

“They’re not going to do that. There’s going to be no change now until January and that transfer window

“Other players will see that interview and think, ‘What’s he talking about? We need to stick together’.

“With an interview like that, that could have fractions throughout the squad and derail what this performance was tonight, which was a good performance.



“It’s not needed at all. The pressure that’s building, going to play Leeds away, you don’t need it.

“I don’t feel like he’s got the right to be saying anything like that in that way.”

Rio Ferdinand

SEVERAL Manchester United players believe Lisandro Martínez challenged the board to shield Michael Carrick and ensure blame fell on the right heads.

A dressing room source dismissed claims that the defender acted on raw emotion, insisting he merely voiced similar frustrations felt by other players.



Multiple United stars are concerned the club squandered Champions League momentum and fear another managerial upheaval, despite Carrick not having the tools.

Speaking to Amazon Prime moments after Tuesday’s 2-0 defeat at Atletico Madrid, Martinez tore into sporting director Jason Wilcox, placing the majority of the blame on the board for United’s poor start.

Wilcox was appointed technical director of United in April 2024, but rose to director of football in June 2025 following the shock axing of Dan Ashworth as sporting director six months earlier.

Sources close to insiders say United will likely call a meeting between Wilcox and the squad once tensions have cooled.

It seems inevitable that Martinez will be fined for publicly dismissing the top brass and his future is uncertain given his contract ends next summer.

Sports.title: From Set Piece FC to Second Half FC, how Arsenal have rebranded thanks to their elite ‘finishers’
Sports.content:
Next

ARSENAL were labelled Set Piece FC last season – but it is time for a rebrand.

Mikel Arteta’s side must surely now be referred to as Second Half FC after the way they have started the current campaign.

Tuesday’s win continued the theme of the Gunners clicking into gear after the break as they struck three times to down Lille.



It takes Arsenal’s tally of second-half goals this season to 14 – double their total from the opening 45 minutes of games.



Midfielder Mikel Merino said: “Mentality is the main concept when you score late in the game.

“When you get tired physically you get tired mentally. This team is proving that they don’t.

“It is not only the guys on the pitch who are always focused – but the guys who come on for the last couple of minutes, they come ready to make an impact.”

Arsenal have now not scored in the first half during any of their last five matches in the Champions League or Premier League.

And the Gunners blitzing teams after the break has come at the same time as their set-piece goals drying up.

Just one of their 21 goals in the opening 10 games of this season was a set-piece, and that was Bukayo Saka’s penalty at Sunderland last month.

BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS



It is hard to pin down exactly why that drop-off has happened, but it is far easier to understand how the Gunners are finishing games strongly.

Arteta has always been a big believer in players having a role off the bench.

When he was hired in December 2019, the Spaniard changed the name of substitutes to ‘impactors’.

They are now called ‘finishers’ – and this season they are stronger than ever.

The cavalry against Lille involved Kai Havertz, Martin Odegaard and Saka coming on as a triple sub with 25 minutes to go.



Jurrien Timber opened the scoring just before they were brought on, yet once the trio were introduced they killed the game.

Saka set up Eze for Arsenal’s second goal, before combining with Havertz to score a third.

All of that came in seven second-half minutes and any memories of a turgid first half were forgotten.

It was a similar story against Leeds last weekend, when Bruno Guimaraes came off the bench to smash home the winner.

The Brazilian was rewarded with a start against Lille and it was a reminder to Arteta’s players how the ‘finishers’ could change each game.



Merino added: “It’s the key of this squad – everyone is ready when they have the chance.

“There is no chance we could have a small squad. You need the biggest squad possible with the most quality possible.

“I’m a perfect example of this, the finishers are crucial. I’ve had the opportunity to show it with club and country. We’re all ready to play our part.”

Arsenal leaned into their set-piece threat last season, and they should do the same with their second-half blitz tactic.

It is not quite rope-a-dope, as the Gunners give their opponents so few chances to hurt them.



But sides do seem to tire late on at the same time that Arteta’s men are able to find their stride.

Taking advantage of that is key and Arsenal started last season in a similar fashion.

After the opening 10 games of last term, they had scored seven first-half goals and 13 after the break.

By the end of the campaign, that split had levelled out to 53 before half time and 68 after it.

Arteta has revamped his fitness and medical department since then, hiring a string of new staff this summer.



That may well be having an impact now as they have brought in new methods.

After a win at Ipswich in the Carabao Cup last month, players did a mini weights session in the tunnel of Portman Road before getting the bus home.

Asked about changes to fitness work, Merino said: “There’s a new style absolutely.
