“That’s very personal, some players might like something and some players might like other things.

“I do like a lot what we’re doing, you can see the squad is fresh and ready to play at the highest level with the highest rhythm to the last minute. That’s good news.”

Sports.title: Fans say ‘I need to see Roy Keane react to this’ after Man Utd nutritionist coach’s Instagram post
Sports.content:

FOOTBALL fans were quick to comment after Manchester United’s nutritionist posted a series of matchday pictures of himself on Instagram.

Filipe Sousa shared some images of himself at Old Trafford earlier this month, captioning the post: “Unposted bits.”



However, some rival fans were quick to make a joke about it – with one person even questioning how legendary United hard man Roy Keane would react.

One person wrote: “Nutritionist doing gameday dumps is ridiculous.”



Another joked: “I need to see Roy Keane react to this.”

However, many jumped to the defence of Sousa, who has been working at the club since last summer.



One fan responded: “Man working what could be a dream job posts about it. Some of you aren’t normal.”

While another said: “In what way is it ridiculous? He has a job just like you do and he is posting about his life. Whats the problem?”

Sousa previously worked as a nutritionist in Portugal before joining United in July last year.

The Red Devils have endured their worst start to a league season in 40 years.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

They currently sit 13th in the Premier League table with just six points from six games.

Defender Lisandro Martinez took aim at the United board on Tuesday following a 2-0 Champions League defeat against Atletico Madrid, accusing them of failing to invest.

He said: “Really poor. Really poor. I have to control myself a lot, but sometimes it is a reflection of the mirror of how our club is at the moment.

“We had a fantastic season last season and now we expect more from the top, more players to compete because many teams bring many players as well.

Sports.title: Pep Guardiola volunteered to lead Man City’s public fightback against guilty verdict as he jets in for PSG clash
Sports.content:
Next

PEP GUARDIOLA is set to spearhead Manchester City’s public fightback as he flies in for their first home game since being found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules.

The highly respected Spaniard, who remains the face of the club despite leaving his role last summer, has volunteered to return to the Etihad following the damaging verdict.



Guardiola is well aware of his global influence and sources say he had always wanted to be at the helm when the verdict was delivered.

But after waiting and waiting for a decision that never came, he eventually departed in the summer.



Since the guilty verdict, Guardiola has already issued a statement and told close friends he wants to stand by his beloved City every step of the way.

SunSport understands the 55-year-old will fly into Manchester on Wednesday afternoon before holding talks with City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak and his long-time friend Ferran Soriano.



He is then expected to sit alongside Khaldoon in the directors’ box for the clash against Paris Saint-Germain, with City determined to present a united front.

SunSport has also been told the club have printed cards bearing the letters ‘CTID’- standing for ‘City Till I Die’- for supporters sitting in the Pep Guardiola Stand.

After the game, Guardiola is expected to meet City boss Enzo Maresca and PSG manager Luis Enrique before making a swift departure from Manchester.

Sources close to Guardiola told The Sun he had not planned to return to City so soon after leaving last summer.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

But given the club’s current predicament and his unwavering belief in the people running it, he is determined to stand by them throughout the battle.

City have appealed against the verdict over 114 charges and vowed to continue fighting to clear their name.

There is also a feeling within the club that they could receive greater backing from across Europe than from their Premier League rivals.

That was underlined by comments from PSG boss Luis Enrique, who played alongside Guardiola at Barcelona and insisted City’s achievements on the pitch had not been tainted by the verdict.

Speaking ahead of the Etihad showdown, Enrique said: “When I heard [the decision] for the first time, it was a surprise, but we need to respect the process and wait for the [appeal].



“I hope everything works out well for Man City because I think what they have done on the pitch has been incredible and they certainly deserved to win on the pitch what they won.”

City captain Ruben Dias also insisted the dressing room remains firmly behind the club and confident in its appeal.

He said: “I really feel like I speak for the whole group, we’re very calm, we trust the club and we’re very focused on enjoying football.”

Sports.title: Six Kings Slam tournament in Saudi Arabia postponed until December
Sports.content:
Tennis' big-money Six Kings Slam tournament in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia has been postponed from October to December due to unrest in the Middle East.

The tournament, which is in its third edition and awards £1.2m per competing player and an extra £3.5m for the winner, was originally scheduled for October 21-24, but has now been moved to December 27-30.

The six players included for 2026 are Carlos Alcaraz, Novak Djokovic, Alexander Zverev, Taylor Fritz, Alex de Minaur and Learner Tien.

The decision to postpone follows continued unrest in the Middle East and the recent bombing of the international airport in Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh.

"The decision ⁠reflects Riyadh Season's commitment to ‌delivering sporting events to the highest ‌standards, following an assessment of the organisational and logistical challenges ⁠associated with hosting ​the tournament ​and their potential ​impact on the ⁠quality of the audience experience," ⁠organisers said in ​a statement.

Italy's Jannik Sinner, currently out injured due to a knee complaint, clinched victory at the Six Kings Slam in 2024 and 2025, beating Alcaraz in the final on both occasions.

Sports.title: Feyi-Waboso expected to be fit for England's Nations Championship campaign
Sports.content:
Immanuel Feyi-Waboso is expected to be fit for England's Nations Championship campaign this autumn after receiving a positive update on his hamstring injury.

The explosive wing hobbled off in the second half of Exeter's 34-28 victory over Newcastle last weekend.

Chiefs director of rugby Rob Baxter insists Feyi-Waboso is expected to return sooner rather than later, suggesting he should be available for the opening Nations Championship fixture against Australia on November 8.

Baxter said: "Manny's got some awareness there. The scan doesn't show up too much and on testing he's very good.

"We're hopeful that we can treat the symptoms he's showing and see where he gets to over the next week or so.

"Looking at how he's reporting post-game and (Monday), there's nothing I'm hearing from our physios saying there should be a long-term issue now.

"Seeing that he's reporting so well and he's functionally so good, there may not need to be too much intervention."

Image: Feyi-Waboso is one of 25 centrally-contracted players

Feyi-Waboso has been limited to 16 caps since making his debut two years ago due to a series of injuries including shoulder, hamstring and concussion.

The 23-year-old is one of 25 centrally-contracted players, giving England control over his medical arrangements, and he has already been assessed by one of their physios.

Baxter added: "England like players to go and see certain specialists and we're in a delicate time for both parties.

"We're desperate for Manny to play because we've got some important games and England want him to be able to feature in the autumn.

"Hopefully there won't be any dispute based on where Manny feels he is."

Ann Li sealed the biggest win of her career by upsetting Aryna Sabalenka on her 10th match point after Britain's Sonay Kartal secured another huge win at the Wuhan Open.

American Li upset the world No 2 and three-time champion in China 3-6 6-4 7-6 (7-5) to reach the last 16.

It was another contest where Sabalenka appeared in control only to falter, with the top seed leading by a set and 4-2 then trailing 5-2 in the decider and saving nine match points before Li finally took her 10th opportunity.

Kartal continued her impressive comeback from long-term injury against world No 12 and former Olympic champion Belinda Bencic in the second round in China, claiming a 6-0 7-5 victory.

The British star missed six months of the season with a stress fracture in her back, returning last month at the Billie Jean King Cup Finals in Shenzhen before reaching the third round in Beijing last week.

Bencic is the highest-ranked player she has beaten since then world No 5 Mirra Andreeva in the Chinese capital last year.

Kartal, who plays Jasmine Paolini next, told a press conference: "I trusted that I would be able to get my level back, I just didn't know how quickly. I did a lot of things right today but I still think there's a long way to go.

"I can produce the level, but can I sustain it? I think that's going to be the hardest challenge. I'm happy to be back, I'm feeling good."

Sports.title: NFL player Hill found liable for two counts of battery
Sports.content:
Tyreek Hill found liable for two of 10 counts in battery civil trial; Hill, 32, ordered to pay estranged wife $500k in damages; former Dolphins and Chiefs player's timeline to return to NFL still unclear

Tyreek Hill: NFL free agent receiver found liable for two counts of battery as jury awards estranged wife $500k

Tyreek Hill was most recently with the Miami Dolphins before being released in February

A Miami jury has found Tyreek Hill liable for two counts of battery but not liable for the eight remaining claims made by Lakeeta Vaccaro, ending the high-profile civil trial involving the NFL wide receiver and his estranged wife.

Hill, who has played for the NFL's Kansas City Chiefs and Miami Dolphins, was found liable for two counts of battery - one stemming from an incident in January 2024, and another from April 2025.

The jury awarded Vaccaro $500,000 (£377,000) in compensatory damages but did not award her punitive damages.

The jury found Hill, 32, not liable for eight other counts that included battery, assault and continuing domestic violence.

The trial involved allegations of abuse made by Vaccaro, 30, who on the stand described instances in which Hill allegedly pulled her hair and "treated me like I was, just, a man."

Hill took the stand last week and mostly denied what he called "false allegations" made by Vaccaro, while saying in one instance he shoved her and "created a hole in the wall."

Hill, wearing a dark polo shirt on Tuesday, embraced one of his attorneys and shook hands with others following the verdict before leaving the courtroom by himself.

It is not immediately clear what the verdict means for Hill's return to the NFL.

He is still working his way back from a dislocated knee and torn ligaments suffered in September 2025 while he was with the Dolphins, but his agent, Drew Rosenhaus, has indicated he could be ready to play by November.

Sports.title: Saka struggling? He’s more of a threat than ever
Sports.content:
Mikel Arteta challenged Bukayo Saka to start scoring "two or three goals per game" before Arsenal's meeting with Lille. The winger clearly was listening. He only needed six minutes to find the net. And that was after providing an assist with his first touch.

The Arsenal boss was asked if his comments had served as motivation. "If that's the case, I'm very happy and I welcome it," he said with a smile, before revealing he had joked to Saka about "killing him" in his press conference before Tuesday's game.

Arteta was acknowledging that he had set Saka a borderline impossible target but the 25-year-old's game-changing appearance from the bench showed he is at least willing to have a crack at it.

Saka's focus appears streamlined to one thing: goals.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Gary Cotterill and Nick Wright give their player ratings for Arsenal against Lille

His 71st-minute strike against Lille was his fourth in all competitions this season. There have been another two on international duty with England. And his overall total could easily be higher. Saka missed one-on-one chances against both Napoli and Leeds.

"If he misses the chance, so be it," Arteta said after the win over Leeds. "In the end, the more volume we generate, the bigger the probability of him scoring more goals. He is doing well and he could have had another four or five goals by now, easily."

Image: Saka has scored three goals from in or just outside the six-yard box

His goal against Lille, swept home from Kai Havertz's cut-back, was his third this season to have been scored from either in or just outside the six-yard box. There has been a focus on getting him into more dangerous goalscoring positions and it is paying off.

The underlying data supports Arteta's comments about Saka's increased volume of chances. In the Premier League this season, he is averaging nearly twice as many open-play expected goals per 90 minutes as in any previous season for Arsenal, at 0.50.

The result of the adjustments is that only two players, out-and-out strikers Thierno Barry and Erling Haaland, have generated more expected goals in the Premier League this season.

Image: Saka's attacking numbers reflect his goal threat

Saka is actually creating less than in previous years but he ranks in the top three for shots on target and penalty-box touches. He has also made the most fast breaks of all Premier League players.

Among some fans, though, there is a perception that he is struggling to regain his best form after the injury issues that interrupted the previous two seasons. Saka did look some way below his best against Leeds before his explosive cameo against Lille.

Saka is held to higher standards than most but the numbers throw up little cause for alarm. Quite the opposite, in fact.

According to Gradient Sports, whose data grades players based on quality of execution rather than raw outcomes, Saka ranks as the best performer in the Premier League this season.

His overall grade of 88.5 puts him ahead of Joao Pedro, Elliot Anderson, Lewis Hall and Rayan Cherki.

His Arsenal team-mates Declan Rice and Odegaard are just outside the top five with overall grades of 87.3 and 84.9 respectively.

Image: Saka has a league-high Gradient Sports execution grade of 88.5 out of 100

Saka's outstanding grade reflects the quality of his decision-making and his ability to execute in the moment. He may not be as eye-catching in style as some other wingers. He rarely over-elaborates on the ball. Instead, the efficiency of his actions is unrivalled.

Consider the fact that he only needed one touch to provide an assist against Lille on Tuesday. By contrast, Noni Madueke, the player he replaced, made 14 unsuccessful crosses before finally setting up the opener, despite getting into good areas repeatedly.

Saka also brings a level of completeness few can match and continues to contribute in all areas. "The reason he's graded so highly is that he's executing well across so many different categories," Rob Berwald of Gradient Sports tells Sky Sports.

The graphic above shows he has scored comfortably above the average for Premier League wingers this season in passing, shooting, crossing, ball carrying, duels and even one-vs-one defending. On top of everything, Saka always helps out his full-back.

Another area in which he excels, according to Gradient Sports, is in tackle resistance. Saka's ability to retain possession under pressure is another attribute which becomes invaluable in central zones as well as out on the right flank, facing up defenders.

His transformation into a penalty-box goal-getter continues a gradual evolution under Arteta, who told Sky Sports he needed time to "figure him out" back in 2021, moving him from left-back to left wing before he eventually flourished as a right winger.

Now he is becoming something else. A right winger, yes. But one with a narrower focus and a different mindset. The hope for Arsenal is that they will continue to reap the rewards of channelling his immense quality into the business of scoring goals.

Sports.title: England Women's World Cup half-back dilemma
Sports.content:
England Women have three outstanding half-back options for the upcoming Rugby League World Cup, with Jenna Foubister, Izzy Rowe and Georgia Roche all vying for a place in the side; their campaign gets under way against Wales on October 17 with Izzy Rowe and Georgia Roche starting

If there is one position that highlights the growth of the women's game in England, it is the competition for the half-back spot at the Rugby League World Cup.

Two Wigan stars provide one option, with Woman of Steel Jenna Foubister joined by her best friend and Warriors half-back partner Izzy Rowe. Then there's NRLW star and former Woman of Steel Georgia Roche, who has been tearing it up on the other side of the world.

It is a selection headache that England Women head coach Stuart Barrow welcomes as he prepares his side for three pool games, with a place in the semi-finals at stake.

Sports.title: Lask v Liverpool: Champions League – live
Sports.content:
The only previous time that Liverpool have visited Lask, in the Europa League back in 2023, Jürgen Klopp was still manager of the club and the German put out a largely second-string XI, with Caoimhin Kelleher, Kostas Tsimikas, Harvey Elliott, Steven Bajcetic, Ben Gannon-Doak, Wataru Endo, Darwin Núñez all part of the starting line-up.

At half-time, Lask were 1-0 up and although Núñez scored a penalty early in the second half, it was only after the hour mark – when Klopp brought on Dominik Szoboszlai and Alexis Mac Allister – that Liverpool finally wrestled control of the match. Two minutes after those subs, Luis Diaz put Liverpool ahead before another late substitute, Mohamed Salah came off the bench to seal a 3-1 win.

Nearly all of those players (and manager) are unavailable today, either having left the club or sidelined with injury, and Andoni Iraola will surely pick a much stronger XI this time around. Not only because the Spaniard can ill afford a slip up in Austria, but also because Lask are stronger since that last Liverpool visit, with the Linz-based club winning the Austrian Bundesliga last season for the first time since 1965. Absences of key personnel – including Alexander Isak, Cody Gakpo and Dominik Szoboszlai, his three leading goalscorers – means that Iraola will surely play his strongest team elsewhere. Some players, including Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola (the latter without a goal or an assist in six appearances since his £123m arrival from Paris Saint-Germain, or even win possession in the final third) desperately need to play themselves into form if the Reds are to play again in the Champions League next season. Iraola has said he trusts the £100m+ pair, which is at least something.

Liverpool should be wary of striker Christoph Lang, who has started this season like a train with five goals in eight league matches. It would be a big blow for Lask if Moses Usor is not fit – the winger topped both the club’s scoring and assists in their double-winning season last year and scored on his Nigeria debut during the recent international break but is a doubt for this match. Melayro Bogarde, nephew to former Ajax, Barcelona and Chelsea defender Winston Bogarde, is another important cog at the base of Lask’s midfield.

View image in fullscreen Christoph Lang (centre) celebrates after scoring for Austria against Kosovo earlier this month in just his second international appearance. Photograph: Georgi Licovski/EPA

An intriguing kick-off at 5.45pm BST for an intriguing match-up. And one that Liverpool should not take lightly.

Sports.title: Football Daily | Martínez lets rip as United’s dirty laundry gets a very public airing
Sports.content:
LISANDR … OH!

As ringing endorsements from the punditocracy go, not being quite as terrible as they were against Spurs was just about the best Manchester United could hope for after Atlético saw out a fairly routine 2-0 Bigger Cup win in Madrid on Tuesday night. In the opening minute, though, United were every bit as terrible and more as they had been on Saturday, as they allowed their hosts to steal an early march when Pablo Barrios’s shot beat Senne Lammens, only for the ball to squeeze under Leny Yoro, wipe its feet and trundle over the line. For the benefit of our reader who can’t be bothered with Bigger Cup until the knockout stages, United went on to create chances they didn’t take, Atlético had a goal ruled out by VAR for handball, both sides hit the woodwork and the game more or less ended as any kind of meaningful contest when Yoro was shown a rough red card. When your luck’s out, your luck’s out, and Ademola Lookman made sure of things for Atlético with a follow-up strike after Lammens saved from Jonathan David.

While we’re prepared to concede we’ve probably made all that sound far more exciting than it actually was, it was just a prelude to the real entertainment. That began after the game when somebody from the United media team made the ill-advised and potentially career-damaging decision to allow Lisandro Martínez to run the obligatory post-match interview gauntlet. For a man who hasn’t been delivering much on-pitch bang for the generous buck he’s been paid so far this season, Martínez had plenty to get off his chest. Amazon Prime’s pitchside reporter Gabriel Clarke thought all his birthdays had come at once as the Argentinian started spitting home truths. “Tonight it is easy to say the coach, easy to say the players but also we have to see other areas,” he harrumphed, pointing in a direction generally accepted to have been ‘upstairs’. “I expect more [investment], 100%. I expect more from our technical director [Jason Wilcox]. Last season we did everything, we created the base to create an amazing team. You can’t keep changing, changing, changing the manager. What about other areas? I can’t say more.”

Except he could. Moments later, the centre-half cut loose again, embarking on a follow-up torching of Wilcox and United’s transfer policy in an interview with Peter Schmeichel for the CBS Bigger Cup B@nter Show. The former Manchester United goalkeeper, a global ambassador for the club, looked visibly flustered as Martínez vented but couldn’t shut him down despite repeated attempts to change the subject. Opinions on Martínez’s post-match tirades were mixed, with some saying a man caught red-handed in close proximity to so many on-pitch crime scenes this season has no right to belittle his teammates. Others were of the view that any club dirty laundry should be washed behind closed doors. Meanwhile, Big Website’s Jamie Jackson has it on good authority that Martínez was simply airing an opinion shared by most of his teammates.

As for their spokesman? One suspects Martínez could pay a heavy price for running his mouth off in such a public fashion, with a hefty fine and an indefinite spell training with the kids potentially just the start of any punishment that may be coming down the pike. Having spent the early part of the season defending with all the poise and assurance of a deckchair flapping in a gale-force wind, he is far from indispensable and may well be angling for a January exit from an increasingly listing United ship. If the club’s technical director is still around by then, the best revenge might well be to force the mouthy mutineer to remain on board until his contract expires in June.

Sports.title: Gianni Infantino faces grilling at potentially ‘explosive’ Fifa council meeting
Sports.content:
Gianni Infantino will be questioned by Fifa council members over his involvement in the aborted World Cup sell-off plan, the Folarin Balogun affair and the decision to award Donald Trump the inaugural Fifa peace prize at what is expected to be a heated meeting at the world governing body’s headquarters on Thursday.

The Fifa president rejected repeated calls for an extraordinary general meeting of council during the summer after the emergence of the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposals, but will meet his critics for the first time since in Zurich with one attender predicting that the talks could be “explosive”.

Aleksander Ceferin, Victor Montagliani and Sheikh Salman Bin Ibrahim al-Khalifa, the presidents of Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation respectively, all of whom have all called for Infantino to resign, will be in attendance to press home demands for an independent review of Fifa’s governance.

Quick Guide How do I 

In response to letters from Ceferin, Montagliani and Salman sent last month Infantino pledged to commission an external review of Fifa’s future governance, but no details have been forthcoming and there remains scepticism over whether it will be truly independent.

In addition to FFE, Balogun and the peace prize, which featured on an agenda circulated by Fifa last month, Infantino is also likely to face questions about a report in the Times this week that he received a “second salary” of about £1.3m in 2024 on top of the £3.9m declared in Fifa’s accounts.

US Internal Revenue Service filings show a Fifa subsidiary in charge of running last summer’s World Cup paid Infantino $1.76m, which was not mentioned in Fifa’s annual report, where his salary is recorded as 4.27m Swiss francs (£3.88m).

Fifa statutes state that “the individual compensation of the Fifa president … shall be made public”. The governing body has denied wrongdoing.

“Fifa does not pay a second salary to the Fifa president and complies with all reporting requirements in relation to compensation,” it said. “The Fifa president’s annual compensation, as well as other contractual benefits, are decided by the independent compensation subcommittee.

“Fifa strongly rejects any claims that it has failed to disclose any financial information and has violated Fifa’s statutes. Fifa accounts are independently audited, and all declarations are in line with tax regulations in Switzerland, the United States and elsewhere.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Despite these controversies, and the public opposition of the European, Asian and North and Central American and Caribbean confederations, Infantino is on course to be re-elected unopposed in March’s election.

Montaglini has rejected calls to stand against Infantino to focus on being re-elected as Concacaf’s president and Uefa has yet to find an alternative candidate despite tentatively sounding out high-profile footballing figures including Arsène Wenger and Michele Kang, who owns clubs including London City Lionesses.

The deadline for candidates to declare their intention to stand is 18 November, with the election to be held at Fifa congress in Rabat on 18 March.

Sports.title: Sunderland hope to enjoy warmth in Portugal after 53 years away
Sports.content:
There is a pleasing symmetry about Sunderland’s Europa League trip to Portugal to face Torreense on Thursday night. The club’s last competitive venture on European soil, 53 years ago, was the second leg of a European Cup Winners’ Cup second-round tie against Sporting in Lisbon for the FA Cup holders, then in the Second Division.

In a striking parallel, second-tier Torreense prompted widespread surprise by beating Sporting in the Portuguese Cup final last season. The reward was a place in the Europa League’s initial phase and their chances of reaching next spring’s sudden-death rounds were boosted when they beat Lillestrom 2-1 in Norway last month.

Torreense are struggling in LigaPro, where they sit 15th with six points from seven games. They face a side who have made an underwhelming opening to the Premier League campaign featuring one win, against their fellow strugglers Fulham.

With a visit to Bournemouth, who are 18th, a place and a point below Sunderland, on Sunday, Régis Le Bris is expected to rotate his squad. Even so, it would be a minor shock if Sunderland fail to beat Torreense.

Torreense’s home ground, the Estádio Manuel Marques in Torres Vedras, 31 miles north of Lisbon, holds 2,431 spectators, dictating it does not meet Uefa capacity regulations. This has prompted the match being switched to the medieval town of Leiria, an hour’s drive north of Torres Vedras and almost two hours from the luxury Lisbon hotel where Sunderland are basing themselves after failing to find suitable accommodation elsewhere.

Almost 4,000 Sunderland fans are travelling to the 23,888-capacity Estádio Dr Magalhães Pessoa, normally the home of second tier União Leiria. With a limited supply of local hotel rooms, some are staying in Lisbon or Porto, while others have found lodgings in nearby towns and villages, including Fatima. Very much a pilgrimage town, Fatima is one of the most important shrines in the Catholic world and attracts more than six million tourists every year. As visitors from Wearside sightsee in forecast bright sunshine and 25C, they may be tempted to pray for respite from a harsh north-east winter at the Stadium of Light.

Although Sunderland have played well at times this season, the failure to sign a specialist right-winger during the summer has led to Régis Le Bris frequently fielding two natural right-backs in Trai Hume and Thomas Meunier. Hamstring injuries to Brian Brobbey and Dan Ballard have caused problems at both ends of the pitch and the previously reliable Robin Roefs has suffered a few untypical goalkeeping wobbles.

View image in fullscreen Sunderland’s keeper, Robin Roefs, has slipped from his usual high standards at times this season. Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Ed Sykes/Sportsphoto

Context is required though. Sunderland’s first six league fixtures have been against the present top four – Manchester City, Arsenal, Brighton and Brentford. Nonetheless, quiet concern will segue into downright panic should the next two domestic games – at Bournemouth and then at home to Leeds – fail to produce at least one win. There is also anxiety that Malick Fofana, the £30m left-winger signed from Lyon on deadline day who is struggling to displace the erratic Nilson Angulo, may be too lightweight for England’s top tier.

On Tuesday evening, Sunderland announced that their set-piece coach, James Brayne, had left and would be replaced by Thor Herdal. The 34-year-old arrives from Nordsjælland, where he was head of dead balls and analysis. He has also worked with Denmark’s national team.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Given that Sunderland also travel to Poland to face Lech Poznan next Thursday, minimising travel and the attendant fatigue has become a priority. It explains why they will fly straight from Lisbon to Bournemouth on Friday.

Not that Torreense intend to merely make up the numbers. Back in the club’s home town, locals are preparing for an annual national day of celebration on 20 October. It commemorates the role played by an imposing series of forts and military defences built in 1809-10 and known as the Lines of Torres Vedras in defending Lisbon from French invaders during the Peninsular war. Torreense are hoping to demonstrate similarly stout resistance against a team led by a Frenchman and staffed heavily by French-speaking players.

Sunderland have reason to be wary of Stopira, Torreense’s influential 38-year-old captain and left-back, who played for Cape Verde at this summer’s World Cup, and their gifted playmaker João Marques and Ghanaian striker Malik Abubakari. The challenge for Sunderland is to use this last blast of southern European warmth to revitalise a season in danger of unravelling.

Sports.title: Joining Shakhtar as they make base in London: ‘We’re here to show the world that we are alive’
Sports.content:
The morning has thinned out into low, wispy cloud. Beneath it, Shakhtar Donetsk’s players are going through their paces. It is a light session for those who did not start against Veres Rivne the previous day; that means Arda Turan observes from the side, watching with the director of football, Darijo Srna. A stray ball zips towards them and Srna, after juggling it up, bends it into the goal with a familiar right-footed arc. “Modric!” exclaims Turan. But the two men are football legends in their own right and, as they continue to joke before Srna dashes away to take another phone call, the thought occurs that this happy scene could be played out almost anywhere else. Nearby, just beyond the team’s accommodation, a lake shimmers under the emerging sun.

It masks the fact that, around dawn, air raid sirens disrupted the peace for everyone in view. Even here, in Shakhtar’s bucolic spa hotel base 15 minutes outside Lviv, nobody is safe from the threat of Russian rockets and drones. In Rivne, three hours’ drive to the north-east, another alarm had sent the players and staff down to the stadium’s shelter. The second half was delayed by 20 minutes and that, no matter the corner of the country or the vividness of the autumn colours, is a weekly reality.

So is a travel schedule any other Champions League club would recoil at. Shakhtar are about to hit the road yet again, because there remains no chance of playing European games in Ukraine. This season they will host matches in England for the first time, Stamford Bridge the winner in a beauty contest of three venues in the capital. If the border crossing into Poland is unforgiving, the journey could take anything up to 18 hours. The Guardian has been invited to join their trip to London for Wednesday’s game “at home” to AEK Athens.

“It has good feelings for me and inshallah it will for our players too,” a beaming Turan says, a few hours before making a journey that starts via a convoy of people carriers. He has wrought a transformation at Shakhtar since his appointment as head coach in May 2025 and has been reminding anyone who will listen of his semi-final goal against Chelsea in 2014, when an Atlético Madrid side at the peak of their powers produced a classic away performance. Alisson, one of Shakhtar’s forwards, was unaware of Arda’s heroics and has been made to learn quickly. But there is always a serious point. “It’s an iconic stadium but it’s not our home,” Turan says. “If you don’t have a home stadium at this level it’s very difficult, ask any other club. But we have a dream and inside we have great power.”

They will need all of it for the trip. Shakhtar have become used to packing up, regrouping and taking their roadshow to locations in Poland, Germany and Slovakia for their “home” matches on the continent. But it does not become easier and, with parts of Ukraine under intensified attack from Russia, there is no immediate prospect of a happy ending.

View image in fullscreen Newertton, one of Shakhtar’s many Brazilians, is unfazed by the journey at Rzeszow airport. Photograph: Courtesy of Shakhtar Donetsk

“In the first year playing games away we felt more enthusiastic,” says Vitaliy Khlivnyuk, Shakhtar’s director of sports management. “And we continue, but with each year it becomes harder and harder for everyone. It’s like if you didn’t sleep for one day, you can recover. You didn’t sleep for two, you already feel worse. The third, it’s something else. It accumulates. Physically you can get over it but mentally it’s really tough.”

Khlivnyuk half-jokes that his office has become a “panic room” for the endless last-minute hitches and logistical challenges of running a club in wartime. Today’s quandary is a case in point: Shakhtar need new residency permits for their foreign players and staff, but the application system has been taken offline by Russian bombs in Kyiv. According to the rules, there is little time for a workaround.

Kyiv, where Shakhtar were based more regularly until three years ago, is an increasingly dangerous place. “Now it has the kind of atmosphere where the birds don’t sing,” says Khlivnyuk, drawing an unhappy parallel with the early days of the invasion of Donetsk in 2014. Domestic matches are still played in Kyiv but the entire league may soon need relocating to the country’s west.

At lunch one of Shakhtar’s bus drivers, Oleksandr, readies himself for the task ahead. He has long since lost count of the miles accrued during two and a half years on the payroll, but remembers travelling 930 miles to Slovenia for a Conference League game last season. On one trip, Shakhtar were held up at the border for eight hours. He has set today’s departure time for 1pm. Three of the squad play-fight by the dessert buffet and then, realising time is tight, hurry downstairs to collect their belongings.

The players and coaching staff travel in a group of smaller vehicles, four or five to each. Shakhtar introduced that extra concession to comfort a year ago, receiving a favourable response. Other club employees follow on a larger coach, the vehicles winding through low‑slung villages and past glinting domed churches. Crumbling Soviet signs are reminders of a complex past; a couple of modest cemeteries bring the present starkly into view.

Passengers’ names are taken before arrival at the Krakovets border crossing, which is reached in just under two hours. Many of the players leap out to stretch their legs. Kauã Elias, among the brightest talents in Shakhtar’s modern crop of exciting Brazilians, has been playing Fifa video games with a carload of his compatriots. “Before I came here I didn’t know about this travel situation, but it’s just something we have to do,” he says. “It’s normal now. My friends always want to know how it is for me playing in a country with a war, but this bus travel is the only real difference. Having so many other Brazilians for company helps a lot.”

In Lviv they all meet once a week to cook churrasco; Marlon Gomes has the best knack for it, according to Elias. The prospect of Stamford Bridge is plenty to chew on. Wednesday’s match is, at least in part, the culmination of a lifelong ambition. “Since I was a kid I dreamed of playing there for Chelsea,” Elias says. “So going there with Shakhtar is a dream in the same way. We’re very happy to play in London this year.”

Border formalities on the Ukrainian and Polish sides take an hour and a quarter. It rarely gets smoother on this particular crossing. On one occasion, an overenthusiastic young immigration official demanded that all of Shakhtar’s vehicles were emptied and their contents searched one by one. The buses begin coursing through the corn fields of south-east Poland; 10 minutes later a vast snake of lorries, led by a police escort, passes in the opposite direction. All of life, and life support, must take the slow road to enter Ukraine now.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Shakhtar’s head coach, Arda Turan, says of the club: ‘I feel 100% part of this family and this story.’ Photograph: Courtesy of Shakhtar Donetsk

Shakhtar arrive at Rzeszow airport four hours after leaving Lviv. There are shirts to sign with a handful of fans who have caught wind of their presence. As usual, late administrative dramas have materialised too. One player has discovered that his electronic travel authorisation to enter the UK did not work; the system had seemingly misread the name on his passport. A rushed reapplication later, and his safe passage is ensured with half an hour to spare before boarding.

Turan makes a video call while waiting for the flight; one of his assistants is watching Chelsea play Bournemouth and another is clipping up action from the 3-0 win at Veres. “There’s time to do it all on these trips,” Turan says. He is working through episodes of Mobland when downtime is called for.

This magnetic, emotional figure has thrown himself into Shakhtar. “I feel 100% part of this family and this story,” Turan says. “Sometimes when I see children smiling at us I can tell they have home, and if I feel I’ve helped that then it’s the greatest thing for me. It’s something more important than football. I want to raise the voice of the people here. We live in war but we will never accept it and I will always continue bringing it up. Football is sometimes everything in life, but sometimes it’s nothing.”

London, or at least Gatwick airport, is only two and a half hours away when Shakhtar’s chartered plane departs. Srna sits across the aisle from Turan in row one. “We now have nine games in 29 days, three of them in the Champions League, and have to travel home too,” he says. “It’s a very difficult thing to understand if you don’t experience it with us.”

Shakhtar hope at least 25,000 fans will attend the AEK game, perhaps the lowest-profile home match of a quartet that will conclude with Real Madrid’s visit in January. The club’s connections with London extend beyond football: Metinvest, its sister company, provided 5,000 tonnes of steel that built the Shard, the capital’s tallest building. On the pitch, they will wear shirts highlighting the “Invest in Ukraine” campaign driven by their owner and sponsor SCM.

There is hope of progress to the playoff round after a useful draw at PSV Eindhoven on the opening matchday. “If you come along and support Shakhtar, you’re supporting Ukraine,” Srna says. “This team need support and need emotion, because we are living under sirens and bombs. We’re here to show the world that we are alive, strong, united and will fight to the end.”

At the back of the plane, Shakhtar’s Ukrainian contingent are playing cards. “On some of these long trips I feel like a squished lemon by the end of the day,” says the midfielder Dmytro Kryskiv, turning away from the pack. “But there are others that are easier and this feels like one of them, travelling to Stamford Bridge for the Champions League.”

Kriskiv thinks there is “something special connecting the team”, driven by the mercurial Turan. They disembark after a nine-hour expedition and, within 90 more minutes, will be settled into their west London hotel. For modern-day Shakhtar it gets no easier than this. On Thursday they must make the return journey before preparing for Saturday’s league game with Kolos Kovalivka.

“But we have to continue to play,” Khlivnyuk concludes. “Many of our citizens are struggling more than us. When you know that a win or draw can be a spot of light in this darkness, you will always do it.”

Sports.title: Hong Kong club hope David Silva can be their hero – but just for one day
Sports.content:
Hong Kong, China (as is the official football name), has long tried to follow the advice of Han Solo in Return of the Jedi: keeping their distance from China while trying not to look like they are keeping their distance. It is all about maintaining an independent football association and the trappings and privilege that come with it. There was some talk a few years ago about getting a Hong Kong team in the Chinese Super League, when the spending was in full flow, and although that did not happen the local Premier League has belatedly got in on the act – kind of.

This glittering city is not known as a football hotbed but has a long history in the sport that started when it was a British colony and has continued since it became a special administrative region of China in 1997. George Best, Peter Shilton, Arie Haan, Bobby Moore, Diego Forlán, Nicky Butt, René van de Kerkhof, Tony Morley, Gordon McQueen and Craig Foster have played in the territory and soon David Silva will too.

Shortly after the trophies Silva helped Manchester City to win between 2011 and 2018 were tainted by the findings of the Premier League’s independent commission, the 40-year-old picked up the boots that thrilled the Etihad Stadium for so long and is returning to action, though there is confusion as to how long he will be in action for.

Last week it was announced that Silva had joined the Hong Kong Premier League club Supreme Sha Tin, more than three years after retiring owing to an anterior cruciate ligament injury picked up during pre-season training for Real Sociedad. There had been three seasons in San Sebastián after his decade with City, with whom he won four Premier League titles, two FA Cups and five League Cups. Add 125 caps for Spain, the 2010 World Cup triumph and the Euros on either side and it was quite the career – and it is not quite over.

Supreme Sha Tin were promoted last season and tried to sign Juan Mata but have landed a bigger name. “I am very happy to join Supreme Sha Tin for this experience,” Silva said. “I am really looking forward to going to Hong Kong to enjoy the culture, the people and the food.”

That was the video posted on the club’s Instagram account with Silva’s introduction. “Our founders struck it big with this deal!” was the reaction and there were promises made to fans of special perks of behind-the-scenes access to training.

“We are officially announcing that the legendary Spanish No 21 midfielder, David Silva, has officially joined Supreme Sha Tin!” The post then added: “David Silva will be in Hong Kong soon to settle in, link up with squad training, and build up to peak match fitness before making his pitch debut. Stay tuned!”

View image in fullscreen David Silva playing for a World Legends XI in Hong Kong in 2025. Photograph: Yu Chun Christopher Wong/Eurasia Sport Images/Getty Images

It sounded as if Silva would be with the club for the remainder of the season, 17 games for the team to try to climb the table after a slowish start. It made headlines around the world, much to the confusion of the player. “I am surprised because in the end it is only to play one match,” Silva said. “The news made it look like I had signed for a season and it has kept me busy all afternoon. It is a league match, but it is still just one match.”

Whether it is good for Hong Kong football to bring a 40-year-old out of retirement for only one game is not a question for Silva to answer. He is not doing it for the money either.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Silva said: “It is in Hong Kong, a city I love very much … Some have expressed concern about the financial side for me … But that is not the case here. Thanks to my father and my adviser, with whom I have been investing well for years, I have achieved great success.”

Investing well and achieving success are precisely what the ambitious Sha Tin owner, Jim Wong Chi-chuen, who also plays for the team, wants after taking over three years ago. Along the way, the club have been rebranded and before this new season he appointed the girl group Collar as club ambassadors.

A change of image was necessary because the coach who delivered promotion, Lo Kwan-yee, a former Hong Kong footballer of the year, was reportedly arrested in June in relation to match-fixing allegations. Local media reported that the allegations relate to the period before Lo joined Sha Tin but Wong said the club had been affected. “We’ve lost some sponsors and, financially, they haven’t been replaced,” he told the South China Morning Post. “The financial pressure on me is greater than I expected, but I want to push this forward and make it work. I’m trying to do something very pure.”

When scandals and sham contracts are making the headlines, the sight of Silva in full flow is as pure as it gets. If he can be a hero, even if for just one day, it could be the talk of Hong Kong for years to come.

Sports.title: Have any footballers ended their career with more own goals than goals? | The Knowledge
Sports.content:
“How many professional players have ended their senior careers with more own goals than goals for their own team?” wonders Peter Clark.

In the past we’ve looked at the players with the most own goals, but we haven’t looked at those who ended their professional career in debit. “Southampton cult hero Francis Benali scored only one ‘positive’ goal in his career and was legendary for banging in goal-of-the-month contenders at his own end, most notably a bullet header against Oldham in the 1993-94 season,” writes Daz Pearce. We could only find a couple of OGs for Benali, the other being against Manchester United in 1999-2000. But we were unable to find a comprehensive Southampton database, so there’s a chance we’ve missed some beauties.

Another unsentimental defender, Riccardo Ferri, the formidable stopper in Internazionale’s title-winning side of 1988-89, scored six goals and eight own goals in Serie A. He may be in credit overall – he scored three more goals in cup competitions, but we only have his OG data for Serie A. “Jamie Carragher finished his career with four goals and seven own goals,” writes Dean Whearty. “He even managed to score two in one match against Manchester United in 1999!”

And another in the FA Cup final of 2006, though that had a happier ending for Liverpool. Some sources credit Carragher with five goals at the right end, including an equaliser against Middlesbrough in August 2008. But the official Premier League site puts that down as an Emmanuel Pogatetz own goal.

“Sven van Beek is the all-time leading own-goal scorer for the Eredivisie, with eight in a career at Feyenoord, Willem II and Heerenveen, over the course of 12 seasons and 193 matches,” writes Rob de Hair. “He only managed to score five goals for his own team in those matches. ESPN provided a ‘highlight’ reel here.” Van Beek is still playing in Qatar, and appears to have netted five goals at the right end for Al-Shahania.

Another player on minus three is Luigi Zannier, a defender who played for several Italian clubs, including Milan, in the 1950s and 1960s. In Serie A matches, he scored three and put in six at the wrong end.

Zannier and co have nothing on Everton’s Billy Balmer, however. “At the turn of the 20th century he netted eight goals during open play; all, unfortunately, at the wrong end of the pitch,” writes Gavin Buckland. “In more than 300 appearances for the Toffees his only goal at the right end was a single penalty in 1899.”

Un-Brescia-dented

“What is the earliest point in a season a team in the top flight has been confirmed as having a trophyless season?” asks Matt Walker.

The concept of a trophy has changed in the last 15 years, particularly since Arsène Wenger referred to fourth place – and Champions League qualification – as a trophy. But this is The Knowledge, not La Vibe, so we are only referring to actual shiny things you can lift above your head in triumph.

In England, the flicker of a trophy is often extinguished at the start of January, when Premier League teams play in the third round of the FA Cup. Tom Reed cites the example of Bournemouth last season. “They were knocked out of both domestic cup competitions by 10 January. Despite having a good season, they had no realistic expectation of winning the Premier League, and weren’t in Europe either.”

But, as Tom points out, Bournemouth were not mathematically out of the title race at that time. Tom has calculated that Derby County, who finished the 2007-08 season with only 11 points, are the earliest case of an English top-flight team being mathematically unable to win a trophy. “They were knocked out of the League Cup on 28 August and the FA Cup in the fourth round on 26 January. Their inability to win the Premier League was officially confirmed in their 26th league match of the season, on 9 February, when a 3-0 defeat by Tottenham – coupled with a victory for the leaders Arsenal – made the gap between top and bottom insurmountable.”

View image in fullscreen Derby County’s Roy Carroll is put under pressure by Olof Mellberg resulting in the first of six Aston Villa goals at Pride Park in April 2008. Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA

Other countries start their main cup competition earlier in the season, which means many clubs have been forced to embrace their trophyless-ness before Christmas (realistically, if not mathematically). “The early rounds of the Coppa Italia are played at the start of the season,” writes Daz Pearce, “and therefore the weaker Serie A teams could easily crash out of it in September. That’s what happened to Lecce in 1993-94 and Brescia in 1994-95. They were never in contention for the title – Lecce won one of their first 23 games, Brescia none of their first 14. They also tumbled out of the Coppa Italia in round two, the earliest possible stage for a Serie A club at the time. I’m sure at some point, they would have clocked that the Scudetto was probably beyond them.”

We’ve looked into it and think that Lecce and Brescia were both mathematically out of contention after 22 of the 34 Serie A games. In Lecce’s case, that was 6 February 1994; in Brescia’s, 5 March 1995.

Bum luck (part II)

In last week’s Knowledge, we looked at players who ended their scoring droughts with a goal off their backside. Tom Clarke has one more to add to the list.

“I think there is in fact a case of a usually prolific striker enduring a barren run with a goal off their bum, at least partially,” he writes. “Late in the 2023-24 Championship season, Leeds’ automatic promotion push was stumbling due in part to Patrick Bamford’s goals drying up. He needed one to go in off his derrière, which is pretty much what happened during a 4-3 win at Middlesbrough. You could say it’s partly hip, partly backside, but surely it’s sufficiently rear-end to count! I recall saying to a fellow Leeds-supporting friend during the match how funny it was that he’d literally got one to go in off his backside and fulfilled the cliche.”

Knowledge archive

“Where and when was the term ‘shithousery’ first used, and do other languages have a word for it?” asked Brian in 2022.

Before we consider the contemporary phenomenon, we should probably look at how the word from which it is derived became part of the English language. According to our own John Ashdown, who wrote about the S-word during the 2018 World Cup, it can be traced back to Scouse slang used in the 1960s. The Concise New Partridge Dictionary of Slang has an entry for “shithouse”, with definitions “an extremely unpleasant individual” and “a coward”.

It had certainly reached the east Midlands by the 1970s. In Duncan Hamilton’s wonderful book Provided You Don’t Kiss Me, he talks about Brian Clough’s penchant for using the word. “The phone rang. ‘Where are you, shithouse?’ asked Clough. (He used the word ‘shithouse’ as frequently as other people use ‘please’ and ‘thank you’. ‘It’s an affectionate term,’ he’d explain – though he didn’t always use it that way)”. It also appears in most of the Clough stories told by Mark Crossley in his hilarious Undr the Cosh interview.

Jack Charlton was equally fond of the phrase. In 1990, during a prescient observation about how the media might ruin Paul Gascoigne, he said: “Journalists … they’re all shithouses, them”. A couple of years earlier, he said during an interview there was no room for “shithouses” in his Republic of Ireland squad.

View image in fullscreen Jack Charlton issues a few choice words to his Republic of Ireland team at the 1994 World Cup. Photograph: Peter Robinson/Alamy/PA Images

John Hartson, then at Arsenal, was sent off against Middlesbrough in January 1997 after calling the referee, Mike Reed, “a shithouse”. But the neologism of shithousery only emerged in the 21st century. “The word does not (yet) feature in the Oxford English Dictionary,” writes the lexicographer John Williams, “but taking the ever-excellent Jonathon Green’s Dictionary of Slang as a baseline, we see that his earliest citation is from 2014, with Nicolás Otamendi as the alleged culprit.

“As this is a Twitter citation, I looked back further. The first football personality accused appears to be Arsène Wenger in 2011, the accusation coming from the Guardian’s own Daniel Harris.”

It started to become a wider part of the football lexicon in the 2010s, most notably when, according to one Arsenal fan, Crystal Palace “bantered us off for 90 minutes with shithousery”. Arsenal actually won 2-1, so goodness knows what he’d have said had they lost.

Can you help?

“AIK and Brommapojkarna contested an 11-goal thriller in the Allsvenskan league, with Brommapojkarna winning 6-5. Remarkably, all goals came in the second half. Is this the highest-scoring match where every goal was scored in the same half?” asks Kári Tulinius.

“As a Maidenhead United fan (National League South, the sixth tier of English football, since you ask), I was delighted when our marauding wing-back Jordon Ragguette recently received an international call-up for Saint Vincent and the Grenadines,” writes Adie Bradshaw. “Jordon was on the winning side in all four of their recent Concacaf Nations League games, which gives him a 100% win record in international football. This made me wonder: are there any players with 10 or more international caps who have a 100% win record?”

“In a Vietnamese league match against Nam Dinh in 2022, the home side Hai Phong had a goal ruled out for handball by video replay – even though VAR wouldn’t come to Vietnam until 2023. There was a giant TV screen in the stadium, and the referee happened to see an instant replay of the goal. Has there ever been another situation like this, where the referee didn’t have VAR, but another source of video replay helped them to reverse a decision?” asks Duc Tran Anh.

Sports.title: Tottenham’s forgotten man Richarlison scores for under-21s: ‘I was missing it’
Sports.content:
Tottenham’s forgotten man Richarlison has been hailed for his attitude after he scored for the under-21s on Tuesday. Richarlison has not played for the first team since an opening-day defeat at Brentford on 22 August after he was left out of the 25-man Premier League squad list, having been told he was not part of the plans for this season.

Failed moves to Trabzonspor and Vasco da Gama, after talks with Everton collapsed in the final days before the transfer window in England shut, have left Richarlison in limbo for the first half of the campaign. However, the Brazil international made a surprise appearance in the Jersey Mike’s (EFL) Trophy tie at Cheltenham. He scored after 56 minutes in a 2-2 draw and converted a spot-kick in a 7-6 penalty shootout loss.

The Cheltenham manager, Steve Cotterill, told Gloucestershire Live: “We weren’t expecting it. When I found out he was on the team sheet, I was actually chuffed with that. It gives our lads a glimpse of what it’s like at that top level.

“Richarlison’s attitude was immaculate tonight. He was really, really good and his attitude was great. He could have easily come down here and thought: ‘I am not too bothered about tonight.’

“We had a decent crowd here, but he’s used to playing in front of 60,000 every week – when he gets picked anyway. It was great for our lads to play against someone of his stature. I really enjoyed tonight.”

After Richarlison’s fine first-time finish in the 56th minute, Tottenham’s academy players joined him in performing his pigeon celebration. He later posted on Instagram: “Happy to do what I love the most in life. I was missing it!”

Sports.title: William Saliba absent from Arsenal squad photo as reason given
Sports.content:
William Saliba absent from Arsenal squad photo as reason given

William Saliba was a notable absentee as Arsenal shared their 2026/27 first-team squad photo on social media.

In the annual image, Gunners boss Mikel Arteta could be seen posing behind the Premier League and Community Shield trophies at their London Colney base.

3 Saliba, who is yet to feature this season due to injury, missed out on Arsenal's squad photo for the 2026/27 season Credit: Getty

Eagle-eyed fans quickly noticed that Saliba does not feature alongside his manager and team-mates, though, amid his injury absence.

The France defender has been sidelined since July with a back injury.

Saliba was forced off during his nation's World Cup semi-final defeat to Spain in the summer.

Despite not requiring surgery on the issue, he has yet to return to action with Arsenal.

Why is Saliba not in Arsenal squad photo?

His absence from the new squad photo had caused concern from supporters online.

However, the club have now explained the reason behind his non-appearance.

Writing on X, Arsenal said: "Due to a medical appointment, William Saliba was not available this afternoon."

It comes as the 25-year-old steps up his recovery ahead of a long-awaited return.

Saliba is back training on grass as he eyes a comeback in November.

In his absence, summer signing Ezri Konsa has formed a partnership with Gabriel Magalhaes in central defence.

3 Saliba has not featured since picking up a back injury at the World Cup Credit: Getty

Meanwhile, Arteta can also call upon Cristhian Mosquera and Piero Hincapie in the position.

How long has Saliba been at Arsenal?

Saliba has been a key part of the Gunners' improvement in recent seasons under the Spaniard's stewardship.

He first joined the club as an 18-year-old in 2019, signing from boyhood club Saint-Etienne in his native France.

Having returned to his former side on loan, subsequent stints with Nice and Marseille also followed.

However, Saliba has established himself in the first-team since making his Premier League debut in August 2022.

He has also been named in the PFA Premier League Team of the Year in every season since making his top-flight bow for Arsenal.

3 Saliba helped Arsenal end their 22-year wait for a Premier League title last season Credit: Getty

Across all competitions, Saliba has made 184 appearances as well as scoring eight goals from defence.

Last season's Premier League triumph added to a pair of Community Shield victories during his time in north London.

Saliba's current Gunners deal runs until the summer of 2030 after he penned a new five-year contract in September last year.

Sports.title: Simon Jordan: Man United have a weakling in charge, Jose Mourinho was last true leader
Sports.content:
Simon Jordan believes Michael Carrick looks weak and under further pressure at Manchester United after Lisandro Martinez's outburst.

Martinez called out the United board, including sporting director Jason Wilcox, in a furious post-match rant after they lost their fourth match this season in a 2-0 defeat to Atletico Madrid.



3 Martinez took aim at the United board after losing to Atletico in a shock post-match outburst for a club in a mess Credit: Getty

talkSPORT understands that senior players share his frustrations with the hierarchy after an underwhelming summer window, during which key areas in need of improvement were overlooked for midfielders.

United are winless in five matches across all competitions and Carrick, who impressed as head coach during the second half of last season before taking on the job full-time, faces uncertainty in the dugout.

Martinez's comments have only added to the chaos at Old Trafford, and Jordan believes it has impacted his boss amid a tough spell.



Martinez rant makes Carrick look 'weak'

The former Crystal Palace owner was asked on White and Jordan for what he would do with Martinez if he was in charge at United, and said: "That's an irrelevance. What do you do?

"You fine him, who cares? You fine him because you can make sport of it, but what does it achieve? You look at the overall position that you've created, you put people in there."



He added: "What it does, it makes Michael Carrick look like a twerp, it makes Michael Carrick look weak. He doesn't need his players to speak for him."

Jordan later confirmed: "It puts more and more pressure on Carrick.

"He looked like a stuttering weakling on the weekend (the 1-1 draw vs Tottenham), with respect to him.



"He's a very nice character from what I understand.

"I told you from the outset that I don't think he wanted the job and really wanted to be a manager, you're seeing the comments come out from players that know him."

Nicky Butt previously said Carrick told him before taking the United job that management is 'too much'.

3 Jordan believes Carrick looks weak as the United head coach as a result of Martinez's rant and faces increased pressure Credit: Getty

3 He has also cited Mourinho, who left eight years ago, as the most recent manager to show true leadership at United Credit: Getty



Mourinho was last 'top-drawer' leader

It has been 13 years since Sir Alex Ferguson retired as United manager after a legendary spell that brought 13 Premier League titles, as well as two Champions Leagues, five FA Cups and four League Cups.

The club have struggled to appoint anyone capable of delivering such success, with David Moyes, Louis Van Gaal, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, Erik ten Hag, and Ruben Amorim falling way below past standards.

However, former Chelsea boss Jose Mourinho won the Europa League and League Cup during his stint from 2016 to 2018, and Jordan claims he is the last manager with any authority to take the United hotseat.

"United lack leadership, they lack real top-drawer leadership. They had it previously, they didn't know what it looked like.



"They had it - you might not have liked Mourinho's style of football, you might not like his attitude, but they would bite their arms off at the shoulder for Mourinho to be back in charge of Man United, delivering outcomes he did five or six years ago.

"At that time, it was considered not good enough because the proximity to what Ferguson had had was too close. Now you're 13 years down the line, and they're grateful now for getting into the Champions League."

Sports.title: Why LASK vs Liverpool is in early Champions League slot as Andoni Iraola looks to bounce back
Sports.content:
Why LASK vs Liverpool is in early Champions League slot as Andoni Iraola looks to bounce back

Liverpool are in Austria to face LASK in the Champions League this evening as Andoni Iraola looks to hit back from their loss to Manchester City.

Following a highly anticipated matchup against Enzo Maresca's City, the Reds will hope for better against LASK, who currently sit third in the Austrian Bundesliga.



3 The loss against City was Iraola's first as Liverpool manager Credit: Getty

The Merseyside-outfit heads into the clash off the back of Ryan Gravenberch being sent off before Erling Haaland, Jeremy Doku and Rayan Cherki scored to sink Liverpool.

Iraola had become the first manager since Joe Fagan to avoid defeat in his first five league games in charge of Liverpool.

However, their top-flight form of two wins, three draws and now a defeat shows the difficulty the ex-Bournemouth boss has faced at Anfield.



Liverpool did win their first Champions League fixture of the season, beating Diego Simeone’s Atletico Madrid 2-0 last month.

Despite that win, Liverpool have been warned by European football commentator Kevin Hatchard not to misjudge LASK.



On talkSPORT's Trans Euro Express, Hatchard said: "This is one of those where LASK have done brilliantly to get there.

"We saw what they did to Celtic over two legs in the play-off. They came back from 4-0 down on aggregate.



"This is one of those classic games where if Liverpool are even slightly off it, they could come unstuck."

3 Liverpool fans are still waiting for Wirtz to fully click into gear Credit: Getty

How to follow LASK v Liverpool

This Champions League league phase tie will take place on Wednesday, October 14.

The match has been picked for the early slot so will kick off at 5:45pm UK time.



It is being held at the Raiffeisen Arena in Linz, Austria.

talkSPORT will have commentary from Joe Shennan and former England striker Dean Ashton.

Listen talkSPORT through the website or find us on DAB digital radio through your smart speaker and on 1089 or 1053 AM.

Download and listen to all our live commentaries via the talkSPORT app, whilst talkSPORT is also available to watch on Samsung TV Plus.

Subscribe to the talkSPORT YouTube channel for news, views and analysis plus our regular goals show and for more, 



For the latest odds and bet boosts for every big event, visit talkSPORT BET.

You can watch on TNT Sports 1, TNT Sports Ultimate and HBO Max - coverage will start from 5pm.

3 Virgil van Dijk was the only remaining member of Liverpool's 2025 title-winning backline on the pitch against Man City Credit: Getty

LASK v Liverpool team news

Regarding injured players such as Dominik Szoboszlai, Cody Gakpo, and Alexander Isak, Iraola was unable to confirm whether they would be fit enough to return for the Champions League fixture.



After the City loss, he said: "It'll be difficult because it's two days. You never know."

On Szoboszlai's fitness specifically, Iraola said: "Dom came from the national team with tightness, an overload.

"We put him as a floater in the training and tried to protect him but he was feeling something very small.

"It's true that now we play four games in 10 days, so it's going to be difficult because we fly to Austria in two days. I think it's going to be difficult to recover any of the players.

Sports.title: Man City v Paris Saint-Germain LIVE commentary: Pep Guardiola set for Etihad return in Champions League
Sports.content:
Manchester City will take on reigning European champions Paris Saint-Germain tonight in their first home game since their guilty verdict.

Enzo Maresca will hope to build on the weekend's 3-0 victory over Liverpool by taking on the French giants.

2 Maresca won seven matches in a row in all competitions heading into the international break Credit: Getty

The Citizens have had an incredible start in the Premier League, winning all six games this season and sitting top of the table.

Meanwhile, Luis Enrique's PSG have had a slow start to their Ligue 1 campaign but they have managed to win a third game in a row with a comfortable 3-1 success over Le Mans last time out.

Both teams won convincingly in their European openers, with the French champions beating Slovan Bratislava 6-1 and City securing a 2-0 victory over Porto.

However, the upcoming PSG encounter will be overshadowed by off-field drama as it will be City's first home game since an independent commission found the club guilty of the majority of the 115 charges brought against them by the Premier League.

The Citizens, who remain adamant of their innocence and have submitted an appeal regarding the decision, played up to their role as pantomime villains against Liverpool, waving inflatable bananas and performing the poznan.

Additionally, this fixture is set to have all eyes on it as Pep Guardiola is will attend the Etihad for the first time since leaving the club last summer.

His decade in charge yielded six Premier League titles - including a record four in a row from 2020/21 to 2023/24.

In the aftermath of the publication of the independent commission's findings, Guardiola released a statement in support of his former club.

He posted on social media: "I want every single Manchester City fan across the world to know I am here more than ever.

"I am, always have been, always will be behind my club, my owner, my chairman, Ferran [Soriano], the players, staff, Enzo [Maresca] and you, our unique supporters.

"Let me be clear: we will get through this together. I love you all."

2 PSG will seek to win the Champions League for a third consecutive season Credit: AFP

How to follow Man City v PSG

The game will take place on Wednesday, October 14.

Kick off is at 8pm (UK time) at the Etihad Stadium in Manchester.

talkSPORT will provide commentary from Adrian Durham, alongside Jim Proudfoot and former Scotland striker Andy Gray.

Listen talkSPORT through the website or find us on DAB digital radio through your smart speaker and on 1089 or 1053 AM.

Download and listen to all our live commentaries via the talkSPORT app, whilst talkSPORT is also available to watch on Samsung TV Plus.

Subscribe to the talkSPORT YouTube channel for news, views and analysis plus our regular goals show and for more, 

For the latest odds and bet boosts for every big event, visit talkSPORT BET.

Additionally, you can watch Man City v PSG will be live on TNT Sports 1, TNT Sports Ultimate and HBO Max.

Man City v PSG team news

Man City have no injury or fitness concerns heading into Wednesday’s contest.

Erling Haaland, Antoine Semenyo and Nico O'Reilly all recovered from minor issues over the international break to start against Liverpool, and the trio will be available for selection once again against PSG.

PSG also have a completely fit team ready to face Mareca's side.
