The 71-year-old pontiff is recovering in Rome’s Gemelli hospital after surgery to remove a cancerous growth on his lung.

Share Pope Leo recovering well after cancer surgery, Vatican says on social media

Pope Leo XIV is out of bed, walking, eating and has undergone respiratory physiotherapy, according to a doctor’s note published by the Vatican a day after his lung cancer surgery.

A blood test and chest X-ray revealed “normal post-operative” progress, doctors Luigi Carbone and Stefano Margaritora said, adding that values were “within the expected range for the type of procedure performed”.

“The Holy Father underwent respiratory physiotherapy and has begun walking in his room”, they said, adding that “he resumed his regular diet and had breakfast and lunch.”

“Recovery is proceeding as planned,” the doctors said.

Part of lung removed

The 71-year-old pontiff was diagnosed with cancer after an operation to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, according to a medical bulletin published by the Vatican on Tuesday.

Tests confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican added, noting the diagnosis had been suspected by preoperative tests. It did not provide details on the recovery outlook or course of treatment.

The Vatican said the procedure lasted 90 minutes and that the surgery “was successful, and there were no complications”.

A medical statement shared by The Holy See’s press office, following the surgery, noted the “radical” removal of the lobe as an indication that doctors removed all suspect tissue in the hope of eliminating any lingering traces of the cancer.

After the procedure, Pope Leo returned to his room at Rome’s Gemelli hospital, where he is expected to recover for a week, with all his audiences through October 20 cancelled.



The Vatican said doctors are not currently discussing chemotherapy or other therapies pending the results of other tests.

World.title: Renewed fighting risks ‘humanitarian catastrophe’ in Yemen, aid groups warn
World.content:
Almost one million people are on brink the of starvation as health infrastructure is overwhelmed by the war-wounded.

The humanitarian groups the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) and the World Food Programme (WFP) have sounded the alarm over the worsening humanitarian situation in Yemen amid ramped-up fighting.

An estimated 800,000 people have been cut off from life-saving food assistance as front lines have rapidly shifted between Saudi-backed forces of the internationally recognised government and the Iran-aligned Houthis, according to the WFP.

“This is the kind of situation that can rapidly spiral into a humanitarian catastrophe,” said El-Khidir Daloum, WFP’s country director in Yemen.

The crisis is worst in Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, where an estimated 600,000 people have no access to food assistance, including 200,000 women and children, the United Nations agency said in a statement.

Taiz has been the focus of recent clashes and is hemmed in by Houthi forces, imperiling aid deliveries.

The WFP said that the loss of access is especially alarming given that Taiz has some of the country’s highest levels of food insecurity.

Across Yemen, more than 18 million people do not have enough to eat, it added, while the latest monitoring shows a record 74 percent of households in accessible areas cannot meet their daily food needs.

Casualties flood hospitals

Meanwhile, “overwhelmed” health facilities in Marib, Taiz and along the Red Sea coast were bearing the brunt of the fighting in those areas, according to a statement released by the ICRC, with some receiving more than 700 cases in a single week,



Firas Abu Samra, the ICRC’s health services coordinator, said only a handful of facilities operating in Yemen can provide comprehensive care for the injured.

Front-line hospitals are taking in large numbers of wounded while running short of surgical supplies, anaesthetics, oxygen and medicines, he said.

“Additional pressure on hospitals can mean fewer beds, fewer supplies and less capacity to treat people with conditions unrelated to the conflict”, said Eduardo Toro, an ICRC surgeon at Marib General Hospital.

Christine Cipolla, the ICRC’s head of delegation in Yemen, said the country’s battered health system is ill-prepared to cope with any more fighting.

“Our concern is that the system may have little capacity left to absorb a major surge in casualties,” she said.

World.title: Saudi national charged with planting a listening device at OpenAI offices
World.content:
US FBI said Abdulrahman Alfozan was engineer at the tech giant from June 2025.

United States federal agents have arrested a Saudi national and charged him with planting a hidden audio recording device in a conference room at the California offices of OpenAI, where he was working as an engineer.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, had been working at the AI company since ⁠July 2025, the US Department of Justice said in a statement on Tuesday.

OpenAI discovered the device plugged into a USB port behind a television in an executive conference room at one of its San Francisco buildings on September 30, according to a criminal complaint filed by the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI).

Following the discovery, the company placed a camera in the room, which captured Alfozan entering last week and checking behind the television where the listening device had been installed, the FBI alleges.

The case highlights growing security concerns around sensitive AI research as companies and governments compete for the best talent and technology with the potential to alter regional economic and strategic dynamics.

Who is Abdulrahman Alfozan and what is he charged with?

Alfozan has been a legal permanent resident of the US since September 2020.

According to a LinkedIn profile in his name, he studied at ⁠the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and the University of California, Berkeley. He previously worked at Meta and Microsoft, it said.

Before he joined OpenAI, he was a venture partner at Raed Ventures, headquartered in Riyadh in Saudi Arabia, which invested “in seed and early-stage startups in Saudi Arabia and MENA”.



Al Jazeera could not independently verify the details mentioned in this LinkedIn profile.

Alfozan made his first court appearance on Tuesday on a charge of “using or endeavouring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications”.

It was not immediately clear if he has legal representation. He is expected to return to court on October 19.

If convicted, Alfozan faces up to five years in prison, a $250,000 ⁠fine, and three years of supervised release.

What happened at OpenAI?

The FBI says a thumb-sized device with a microphone, and which ‌could connect to a camera, had been concealed in toilet paper and placed behind a television set in the conference room. It was installed around September 28, the FBI said. Its stored data was encrypted and inaccessible. Investigators later found a similar device in Alfozan’s personal bag.

In a post on X, OpenAI said it had evidence that the employee intended to place other listening devices throughout sensitive areas of its offices to secretly record meetings.

“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was ⁠terminated,” the company said.

The FBI complaint also alleges that Alfozan used an AI productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about the company’s building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars, despite not having the authority to access these spaces or participate in meetings there.

“This alleged attempt by a Saudi national to steal sensitive communications from OpenAI was taken extremely seriously. Theft of intellectual property involving cutting-edge super intelligence technology poses a serious threat to our national security,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement on X.

Hasn’t OpenAI been accused of helping to spy on civilians?

In an X post by OpenAI explaining how its own systems were used to trap Alfozan, the company said: “Our security program is designed to protect against a wide range of threat actors, from insider risks to cybercriminals to nation states, and this case is an example of how AI can help address these sophisticated security threats.”

But AI technology is used not only to catch spying, but conversely, to engage in it as well.



In February 2025, an investigation by The Associated Press found that US tech giants had enabled Israel to track and kill people in Gaza and Lebanon through AI and computing services. The AP reported that the Israeli military had bought advanced AI tools from tech companies including OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, through Microsoft’s Azure cloud platform, to assist with surveillance.

OpenAI denies having a relationship with the Israeli military.

But OpenAI also faced criticism when it signed a deal with the US Department of Defense in February this year to supply its technology to the US military for use in classified settings, including intelligence gathering. OpenAI’s competitor, Anthropic, refused to sign the same deal unless the Pentagon barred mass surveillance of Americans.

There have been several incidents in which OpenAI models have gone “rogue” by independently breaking out of a testing environment and then hacking into other organisations and even government sites, leading to calls for stronger regulations against unchecked AI surveillance.

World.title: Law of the Sea comes to life in the hunt for sanctioned Russian oil
World.content:
Share Law of the Sea comes to life in the hunt for sanctioned Russian oil on social media

Until US President Donald Trump reversed the thrust of his sanctions policy of Russian oil on Friday, Ukraine’s Western allies had been ramping up the use of international law.

Countries sanctioning Russian oil have for the first time enforced boarding and inspection rights under the Law of the Sea this year, experts told Al Jazeera.

“The whole idea now is to disrupt, deter and make it more expensive and costly for Russia to logistically get their oil to market on these ships, and that’s definitely happening,” said Michelle Bockmann, an analyst at maritime intelligence company Windward.

Some Russian officials believe worse is to come.

“Western countries are trying to organise the interception of our vessels. London and Brussels are drawing up plans to blockade the Baltic Sea and the straits leading into it. Other key shipping routes are also under threat,” Russian Maritime Board chairman Nikolai Patrushev told officials during a visit to China on October 12.

Western sanctions not only ban Russian oil purchases in the sanctioning territories. They forbid Western-insured tankers from selling Russian oil to third parties except at below-market prices, which leaves Russia with little or no profit.

Since sanctions were imposed in 2022, Russia has been exporting about half of its crude oil through a “shadow fleet” of tankers that are not owned or insured by Western institutions, and often do not comply with environmental and safety standards.

It is the right to enforce these standards that allows the United States, United Kingdom and European Union to step up compliance inspections using Article 110 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which allows coastal states to inspect vessels.



That has decreased Russia’s room for manoeuvre in its cat-and-mouse game of circumventing oil sanctions 45 months after the EU, US and other Group of Seven (G7) states imposed them.

“A lot of these ships were using fraudulent registries, and they were stateless,” said Bockmann. Under UNCLOS, she said, “Instead of just hailing them, ‘Hey, what’s your flag? What’s your insurance?’ and then letting them merrily go on their way under the right of innocent passage … they now had a legal basis to board them.”

Shadow tankers have engaged in various illegal practices that exposed them to suspicion and boarding. They have transferred Russian oil from one vessel to another on the high seas to disguise its provenance. They have turned off their trackers to avoid monitoring, falsified their positions, evaded insurance obligations, and flown false flags.

The catalyst for using Article 110 against these practices was the US, which invoked it late last year to board vessels evading US Department of the Treasury sanctions against the export of Venezuelan oil in Operation Southern Spear.

With help from the UK, US Marines seized the Russian-owned Bella I, sanctioned for carrying Iranian and Venezuelan as well as Russian oil, in the North Atlantic last January.

The UK and France have since boarded several other vessels under UNCLOS rules. Although these inspections are few compared to the hundreds of shadow tankers afloat, they have put pressure on the shadow fleet, experts said.

“Article 110 had just been sitting there, not really getting any traction,” said Kristina Siig, a professor of economic law at Aalborg University in Denmark. “The tool has always been there, but it just never got pulled out of the drawer.”

This new adherence to law has had knock-on effects in the shipping industry.

“Due diligence has become the biggest headache in ship management,” said George Xiradakis, a maritime consultant who sits on the boards of several shipping companies in Piraeus, Greece.

Ship charterers and buyers “have to check thoroughly that a ship is in compliance with international standards”, he told Al Jazeera, noting, “The time requirement compared to 2025 has gone up by a factor of several times manyfold.”

The sanctioning nations have pursued the shadow fleet relentlessly.

After being evicted from Western fleets, Russia turned to flags of convenience. The EU, UK and US approached those registries and persuaded them to oust the shadow vessels.

“St Kitts and Nevis were the very first ones in early 2024 … Palau, Gabon, Gambia, Cook Islands, San Marino, Barbados, Comoros, Guinea-Bissau, Sao Tome – they’ve all stopped,” said Bockmann.



Russia reacted this year by bringing many of those tankers onto its own registry.

TankerTrackers.com lists 340 dark or shadow tankers as Russian-flagged. Sanctioning states have responded by using UNCLOS.

Zelenskyy’s ‘sanctions’

Ukraine wants to see all of Russia’s export revenue from fossil fuels dry up, and its President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that Trump’s rapprochement with Moscow will prolong the four-and-a-half-year Russia-Ukraine war.

Kyiv has this year struck at least 26 of Russia’s 30 refineries, causing headaches on the global market.

Russia saw an initial windfall of 31 billion euros ($35bn) this year, after the crisis over the blockage of the Middle East’s Strait of Hormuz raised oil and gas prices worldwide, the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) calculated.

That windfall temporarily bucked a trend of constantly falling Russian oil and gas revenue since the Ukraine war began in 2022. Month-on-month revenues shot up by 52 percent in March.

But Russia’s August revenue from crude oil, refined products and gas all fell by eight percent, following a 12 percent drop in July and a one percent drop in June.

The binary weapon of UNCLOS and national law

The official rationale for inspections is safety, and under UNCLOS “we have a right, we actually have a joint obligation, to try to help each other to police that”, said Siig.

But the agenda that drives these inspections – stopping Russia’s war of aggression in Ukraine by interdicting the Russian oil trade – is not enforceable under UNCLOS, she said.

“We are not allowed to tell certain states that they can’t export goods. The only entity that can do that is the UN,” she said. “To enforce sanctions, you have to have state jurisdiction.”

That combination of national and international law makes Denmark and Sweden extremely important.

Together, they control the narrowest chokepoints in the Baltic, where shipping has to pass to enter the North Sea and the Atlantic. So tankers loading crude oil and petroleum products at the Ust-Luga and Primorsk refineries in the Leningrad region have to pass through Danish and Swedish territorial waters, where national laws fully apply, to reach global markets.

The Danish Maritime Authority recorded 292 Russian shadow tanker transits through the Baltic in 2025, and it has progressively tightened its inspection regime. In February 2025, Danish authorities began compliance inspections on tankers anchored off Skagen, and in April detained the Vietnamese-flagged shadow tanker Vigo after finding its fire safety lax.

In October, Denmark broadened inspections to include ballast systems, fuel quality, emissions, waste management and certificate verification.

“The Danish approach has been to throw the book at [Russia],” said Siig, as Danish authorities now ask for an oil insurance certificate, a sail plan through the Danish Straits and safety documents in addition to an insurance certificate, she said.

Russia ‘acting aggressively towards NATO’

Conscious of the danger of being bottled into the Baltic, Russia has reacted with fury.



On September 14, a Russian frigate fired two flares at a Danish helicopter that was inspecting it in international waters south of Gedser, in the Danish Straits.

“Russian forces are increasingly acting aggressively towards NATO military units in the Baltic Sea region,” said a recent Danish Defence Intelligence Service report. “Russia is under more pressure than it has been at any other point during the war against Ukraine. Ukraine’s sustained long-range attacks are causing still more extensive damage deep inside Russia … The Russian economy is on the brink of a major crisis, driven by military expenditures, international sanctions and Ukrainian strikes.”

Denmark is treading carefully as it flexes these provisions of international law for the first time, said Siig. Danish authorities may now be asking for an oil insurance certificate, safety documents, a sail plan through the Danish Straits, and an insurance certificate, but closing off the Strait is not on the cards, she said.

“I have seen no public evidence that such a measure is being considered. Under the ordinary Law of the Sea regime, the Danish Straits are international straits subject to transit passage, and the Kingdom of Denmark has a strong interest in preserving that rules-based system,” Siig said.

“Russia has lost the Baltic,” she noted. “Everybody seemed to be getting along just fine. Then Ukraine happened, and suddenly they got boxed in, geopolitically.”

Ukraine has asked its allies to enforce sanctions even more forcefully. That, said Siig, “might stop the Ukrainian war, and it might start a new one”.

World.title: What is potash, and why is the US importing it from Belarus?
World.content:
Share What is potash, and why is the US importing it from Belarus? on social media

The United States is preparing to receive its first shipment of Belarusian potash in four years, as President Donald Trump seeks cheaper fertiliser for American farmers amid rising costs linked to the Iran war and a trade dispute with Canada.

A 30,000-tonne shipment of potash is expected to arrive at the Port of New Orleans on Wednesday, according to data from Kpler. The shipment follows Washington’s decision to lift sanctions on major Belarusian potash producers in March, opening an avenue for trade to resume.

Although this shipment from Belarus accounts for only a fraction of the 5.6 million tonnes of potash the US imported last year, it signals a tentative opening of relations between Washington and Minsk.

Trump has said the US is working on a larger agreement to buy Belarusian fertiliser at prices substantially below what it pays Canada, its dominant supplier. But analysts have questioned whether Belarus can compete with Canadian producers on price and expand exports enough to significantly change the US market.

What is potash and why does the US need it?

Potash is a potassium-rich mineral that is a primary fertiliser element. Potassium, an essential plant nutrient, has no substitutes, and potash is widely used in agriculture, including in the cultivation of corn and soybeans.

The US depends heavily on imports to meet its potash needs. Canada accounts for almost 80 percent of US potash imports, according to the US Geological Survey’s 2026 Mineral Commodity Summaries. Russia accounts for 12 percent, the second-largest share of US potash imports.



That reliance has made fertiliser supply an economic and political concern, particularly as farmers face rising production costs. In recent months, US farmers have reported higher fuel and fertiliser costs, putting pressure on already tight profit margins.

Trump has reportedly been concerned that financial strain may cost Republicans some of the US farmer vote in this year’s midterms. In 2024, Trump won 78 percent of the vote in farming-dependent counties. At an agriculture roundtable in Wisconsin in June, Trump promised fertiliser prices would “go way down” as the US emerged from the Iran conflict.

Disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have added to pressure on global fertiliser markets, particularly for nitrogen-based products. Potash, however, is less directly exposed to the crisis, with the US relying heavily on supplies from Canada.

Trump has argued that buying Belarusian potash could reduce those costs. An additional supplier could also give US buyers more options in a market dominated by Canadian imports.

For farmers, the immediate benefits remain uncertain. Fertiliser is one of several major expenses facing agricultural businesses, alongside diesel fuel and machinery. Even a reduction in potash prices would not necessarily offset increases elsewhere.

Can Belarus offer cheaper fertiliser?

In September, Trump boasted on social media about striking a potential potash deal with Belarus.

“The United States is working on a massive Deal with respect to the purchase of Potash from Belarus,” Trump said in the post. “The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada, very good news for our Farmers and Ranchers.”

Trump promoted Belarusian potash as a less expensive alternative to Canadian supplies, but the economics of delivering it to American buyers complicates that plan.

Belarus is landlocked, and EU restrictions are affecting its export routes, forcing potash shipments to take a more circuitous path through Russia. The incoming cargo was loaded at the Russian port of Bronka near St Petersburg, according to reporting by the Financial Times.

Those logistical challenges could raise transportation costs and make Belarusian supplies less competitive, even if the product itself is cheaper.

The scale of the exports also matters. A single shipment shows that trade between the US and Belarus has resumed, but it does not mean Belarus can replace a substantial share of Canadian potash or drive down prices across the US market.



However, access to an alternative supplier could give Washington greater leverage in negotiations with Canadian producers, potentially helping US buyers secure more competitive potash prices.

Could Belarus replace Canada as the main potash supplier in the US?

Relations between the US and Canada have been strained since Trump’s second term began, when he unleashed a volley of tariffs on most trading partners, including Canada. His administration initially imposed a 25 percent tariff on many Canadian imports in March 2025, including potash, but reduced that to 10 percent following pushback from agricultural groups and lawmakers. Potash that meets the requirements of the USMCA trade agreement – the trade deal between the US, Mexico and Canada – is exempted. Most Canadian potash imports qualify under the USMCA and remain duty-free.

Trump has maintained that Washington would continue buying from Canada, even as Belarus offered to sell potash at a lower price.

But the viability of Belarus as a major supplier remains unlikely. In September, Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko said the country could not supply large volumes of potash fertiliser to the US.

“Even if we wanted to supply [potash] to other, Western markets, we simply do not have those volumes – everything is contracted,” Lukashenko said.

Whether this October shipment becomes part of a much larger deal will depend on the ability to sustain exports and the durability of the diplomatic opening between Washington and Minsk.

Why did the US impose sanctions on Belarus, and why are they being lifted?

The planned shipment marks a significant step in the restoration of trade between Washington and Minsk, which have spent years being at odds over Belarus’s human rights record and its support for Russia’s war against Ukraine.

The US, under former Democratic President Joe Biden, imposed increased sanctions on Belarus in 2021 after Lukashenko’s authoritarian government cracked down on mass protests against its disputed 2020 presidential election. Belarus has also faced Western sanctions for allowing Russian forces to use its territory in the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

But since Trump returned to the White House in 2025, his administration has pursued direct negotiations with Lukashenko. Those talks have led to the release of political prisoners in exchange for lifting US sanctions, creating a pathway towards renewed economic ties.

In March, Belarus released 250 political prisoners under a US-brokered agreement. Washington subsequently lifted sanctions on major Belarusian potash producers and eased restrictions on several financial institutions. In September, US special envoy John Coale announced a further agreement under which Belarus would release 25 prisoners in exchange for sanctions relief.

The rapprochement has opened the door to proposals for deeper commercial cooperation.



On September 29, Lukashenko said he had agreed with Russian President Vladimir Putin that Russian state-controlled energy company Gazprom would participate in a project to build a nitrogen fertiliser plant in Belarus. He proposed inviting the US to join the project using American technology, according to the Reuters news agency.

Before this agreement, exiled Belarusian opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya said that a deal with Lukashenko comes with risks.

“Our position is that it is not time to trade with the regime while all the income from potash goes to repression, goes to support of the Russian war machine,” Tsikhanouskaya told AFP in September.

The proposal has not established that Washington will participate in the project. But alongside Trump’s stated interest in buying Belarusian potash, it illustrates how Minsk is seeking to turn improved political relations into broader commercial opportunities.

World.title: Colombia inaugurates embassy to Israel in Jerusalem
World.content:
Palestinian officials condemn move by Colombia’s new government that marked a major shift after former President Petro had severed ties with Israel.

Colombia has opened its embassy to Israel in Jerusalem, joining a small group of countries in taking the controversial step of backing Israel’s claim to sovereignty in the contested city.

Palestinian officials swiftly denounced the inauguration on Wednesday that came as Israel is facing mounting international pressure over the genocidal war on Gaza, where three years of attacks have killed more than 74,000 people.

The move by the administration of new Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella is a major shift from his left-wing predecessor Gustavo Petro, who in 2024 severed ties with Israel over the war on Gaza.

De la Espriella, who was sworn in in August, has also restored a free trade agreement between Israel and Colombia that Petro terminated.

Colombian Minister of Foreign Affairs Omar ‌Bula Escobar said on Wednesday that relations between the two countries “should ⁠never have been broken” and that Bogota was taking “taking a concrete step towards ⁠restoring diplomatic relations”.

“Israel is a strategic partner. It always has been, and from now on, it will be an even stronger one,” he said during a ceremony that marked the embassy’s opening.

The opening made Colombia the 10th country to establish its embassy in Israel in Jerusalem – most countries keep their formal diplomatic missions in Tel Aviv.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar welcomed the move during the ceremony. “This is an important date for the State of Israel. It’s also an important date for the city of Jerusalem,” he said while signing the Colombian embassy’s guest book.



Colombian Ambassador Tania Gilinski said Israel had always been a “strategic partner” and that moving forward it “will be so with even greater determination and strength”.

‘Violation of international law’

The Palestinian Authority condemned Colombia’s embassy move, calling it “a violation of international legitimacy resolutions” that undermines “the international consensus on the legal status of the holy city”.

Jordan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs also criticised the move as a “violation of international law and relevant international resolutions”.

United States President Donald Trump moved the US embassy to Israel from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem during his first term in 2018, angering Palestinians and sparking international condemnation. Previous US presidents, as well as nearly every other country, refrained from opening embassies in Jerusalem, arguing that the city’s final status should first be resolved in negotiations between Israelis and Palestinians.

The status of Jerusalem remains one of the core unresolved issues of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, with Israel claiming the undivided city as its capital while Palestinians view occupied East Jerusalem as the capital of a future Palestinian state.

Israel occupied East Jerusalem and annexed it in 1967, in a move not recognised by the vast majority of the international community.

Since Trump relocated the US embassy to Jerusalem, only a handful of small, US-aligned countries have followed suit, namely Fiji, Guatemala, Honduras, Papua New Guinea, Paraguay and Nauru. Kosovo and Somaliland, which are not member-states of the United Nations, have also opened what they consider their embassies in Jerusalem.

World.title: Starlink restrictions in Ukraine war linked to political situation, Zelensky aide says
World.content:
New restrictions on the speed at which some of Ukraine's weapons can travel and stay connected to the Starlink internet network have disrupted Ukraine's battlefield "missions", President Volodymyr Zelensky's adviser has warned.

Serhiy Beskrestnov said Ukraine had not been told about speed limits set overnight at 100mph (160km/h) by Elon Musk's SpaceX company.

Starlink is a vital tool allowing Kyiv to effectively guide drones to Russian targets and also protect Ukrainian skies.

Beskrestnov said SpaceX's move "cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation". The firm has not commented.

In Wednesday's post on Telegram, Beskrestnov said that SpaceX had "implemented overnight a speed limit on Starlink terminals" and this had already resulted in "the disruption of a number of missions".

In a follow-up post, the adviser stressed that Starlink was the most effective tool for enabling interceptors to shoot down Russia's newly developed jet-propelled drones.

It comes as at least 600,000 people across Ukraine were left without electricity after deadly overnight Russian missile and drone strikes, Zelensky said. Pictures from Kyiv showed residents, some dressed in their pajamas, with bloodied faces.

He added that "critical" energy infrastructure had been hit in Kyiv and the capital region, and in the north-eastern city of Kharkiv â despite US President Donald Trump's claim on Sunday that an "energy ceasefire" was in place between Russia and Ukraine.

Three people were killed in Kyiv, local officials reported. Russia said its "massive" strikes had hit communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military.

Later on Wednesday, at least six people were killed in a Russian drone strike on a warehouse in the north-western city of Lutsk, local officials said.

Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

World.title: Pope walking and recovering 'as expected' after surgery, doctors say
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV's recovery from surgery to remove a lower lobe of his lung is "progressing as expected", his doctors have said.

The 71-year-old pontiff has started to walk and has "resumed a normal diet" following the roughly 90-minute procedure, the medics said in an update shared by the Vatican.

The Pope was diagnosed with lung cancer after the surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, which the Vatican said had been "successful" and proceeded without complications.

Blood tests and an X-ray early on Wednesday showed his recovery was "proceeding normally", the doctors said, and he has also undergone respiratory physiotherapy.

The whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical", the Vatican said following the surgery.

"After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room," it said earlier, before spending a "peaceful night" at the hospital.

The pontiff is expected to remain there for about a week as he recovers.

World.title: US inflation rises more than expected - here's what is happening with prices
World.content:
US inflation rose by more than expected in the year to September, according to official figures, in the final data release before the midterm elections next month.

The pace of price rises increased to 3.7%, up from 3.4% in the 12 months to August.

Inflation was above forecasts, driven by higher gasoline prices which have risen following disruption to Middle East energy supplies due to the US-Israel conflict with Iran.

The elections are being fought over cost of living pressures across the US.

World.title: Germany puts Ukrainian on trial accused of blowing up Nord Stream pipelines
World.content:
A Ukrainian man has gone on trial in Hamburg accused of blowing up Russia's Nord Stream gas pipelines to Germany, four years after one of the most dramatic acts of sabotage in modern European history.

Prosecutors say Serhii Kuznetsov played a leading role in a team of saboteurs that destroyed the pipelines, accusing him of a war crime. His defence has called for the case to be dismissed.

The case is highly sensitive in Germany, one of Ukraine's closest allies since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, seven months before the attacks took place.

Extradited to Germany last year, Kuznetsov denies the charges, as does a second suspect who is fighting extradition from Croatia.

Kuznetsov became the first suspect to go on trial for the blasts on Wednesday morning, and a packed public gallery looked on as he entered the courtroom, appearing relaxed.

He even smiled at times, including during initial exchanges where he spoke to confirm personal details such as his name and place of birth.

He had previously only been identified by German prosecutors as Serhii K and pictured with his face blurred, before the court lifted an anonymity order on Wednesday.

Kuznetsov, 50, wore a pair of headphones and appeared to listen intently to a translation of proceedings in Ukrainian, as the prosecution read out the charges against him of ordering divers and an explosive expert to attack civilian infrastructure.

The defence outlined their case, telling the court that only circumstantial evidence had emerged in the four years since the Nord Stream blasts.

"[Prosecutors] made a thorough investigation of four years," Italian defence lawyer Nicola Canestrini told the BBC outside the courtroom. "They did not find one single witness, they did not find no forensics, no DNA, no fingerprints - nothing!"

World.title: Australia's first-ever Michelin stars go to 11 restaurants in one state
World.content:
Australia has been awarded its first Michelin stars, with 11 restaurants in the state of South Australia receiving the distinction.

Magill Estate Restaurant in Adelaide was the only venue to receive two stars, while 10 others were awarded one star each.

South Australia's government paid for incognito inspectors to visit the state, according to national broadcaster ABC, which is why no spots have been recognised in other parts of the country.

The announcement comes more than a century after the Michelin Guide was first published in France and following years of unsuccessful attempts to bring it to Australia.

Michelin has approached the national tourism board several times about bringing the guide to the country with no success.

South Australia decided to go it alone and pursued its own deal. The state government has not disclosed how much it paid, but Tourism Minister Emily Bourke defended the investment in an interview with ABC News.

"It is enabling us to create a tourism destination and put us on the world map," she said.

The move follows Michelin's expansion into New Zealand, which became the first destination in Oceania to feature in the guide in July, agreeing to pay NZ$6.3m (Â£2.7m; $3.5m) over three years for its inclusion.

World.title: Turkish police raid opposition TV station, halting live broadcasts
World.content:
Turkish police have raided the headquarters of one of the country's most-watched news channels, halting its live broadcasts.

Reports in Turkish media said financial crimes police were searching the building of Halk TV, a pro-opposition channel, and that 11 people had been taken into custody in a raid linked to the channel's owner. The government also appointed a new administrator to run the channel.

It is the latest in a series of crackdowns on news sources deemed to be critical of Turkish President Tayyip ErdoÄan and his government.

Halk journalists were initially unable to get into the building, although they later were allowed in, several reporters said on X.

There was a heavy police presence in the building, they said.

Halk's news channel and live broadcasts on its YouTube page were both offline early on Wednesday.

The channel has been seen by many in the country as being close to the opposition Republican People's Party (CHP). It often voices criticism of ErdoÄan's ruling AK party.

Prosecutors said arrest warrants had been issued for 17 people as part of the investigation into Halk chairman Cafer MahiroÄlu on allegations of bribery, rigging tenders and money laundering, Turkish media reported.

MahiroÄlu, who was reportedly not in the country during the raid, wrote on social media that seven members of his family were among those detained.

"Today is a dark day for Turkey," he said in a video message. "The public's right to information is being seized for political reasons."

The Istanbul Bar Association denounced the move, which it noted came hours before Ekrem ImamoÄlu, widely seen as ErdoÄan's biggest political rival, was due to begin his defence against corruption charges in court, for which he has been in prison for over a year.

World.title: Hundreds of thousands of workers on strike across Republic of Ireland
World.content:
More than 300,000 workers, including nurses, doctors, teachers and civil servants, are on strike across the Republic of Ireland.

It comes amid an ongoing pay dispute between public sector workers and the Irish government, with a further strike planned on 21 October.

It is expected schools could be closed with hospital appointments cancelled and picket lines formed across the country during the 24-hour strike.

At the end of September, more than 100,000 workers, including nurses, school staff and civil servants, moved to work-to-rule measures.

At the start of October, primary and secondary school teachers in the Republic began work-to-rule action.

Previously almost 97% of FÃ³rsa members, who voted in an industrial ballot, did so in favour of action. It is the Republic's biggest public service union.

World.title: World's oldest shipwreck found off coast of Turkey
World.content:
The world's oldest shipwreck has been discovered off the coast of Turkey, archaeologists say.

They have dated it to between 4,400 and 4,700 years old, which is the Early Bronze Age, and is around the same time that the Great Pyramid was being built.

The ship's wooden structure has not survived, but the ceramic storage pots it was carrying were lying on the sea floor and, remarkably, some still contain traces of what they held inside.

The archaeologists who found the ship say it was about 10m in length and was a trade vessel carrying cargo across the Mediterranean Sea.

"The shipwreck is a time capsule at the bottom of the sea," said Prof Hakan Ãniz, from Akdeniz University in Turkey, who led the Mediterranean Archaeology Association expedition.

World.title: How ex-minister Hadi Sirika secured ‘Nigeria Air’ contract for his friend  – Witness
World.content:
The Federal Capital Territory (FCT) High Court in Maitama, Abuja, heard from a crime investigator on Wednesday that former Minister of Aviation Hadi Sirika allegedly imposed his friend on the ministry to be engaged for a failed Nigeria Air-related contract in 2023.

Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) investigator Christopher Odofin said this in his testimony as the 12th prosecution witness in Mr Sirika’s corruption trial.

Mr Sirika is facing prosecution alongside two family members and a firm on six corruption charges that partly centre on an alleged N1.3 billion contract the aviation ministry awarded in 2023 to Gabriel Tilmann, a professor.

EFCC alleged that Mr Sirika corruptly awarded the consultancy services contract for the start-up of the failed Nigeria Air national carrier to a firm belonging to Mr Tilmann, whom the prosecution described as the former minister’s friend.

The then-outgoing administration of President Muhammadu Buhari unveiled the national carrier days before handover in May 2023, only for the public show to be later found to be a ruse.

Mr Sirika allegedly disguised an Ethiopian Airlines aircraft as Nigeria’s national carrier, Mr Odofin previously said in his testimony which he started over a year ago on 30 June 2025.

On Wednesday, the witness fielded questions during cross-examination by defence lawyer Kanu Agabi, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN), which centred on the propriety of the contract awarded to Mr Tilmann.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The questioning touched on a voice note which the prosecution believed belonged to Mr Sirika.

When it was played in court in July, the voice note, ascribed to Mr Sirika, was heard instructing another person the EFCC believed to be the then-Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Aviation, Enitan Abel, to award a contract to Mr Tilmann.

“Do the right thing. Generate the necessary contract and give it to his company. In that way, we can be paying for his services,” the voice note was heard saying.

It added, “Whatever we can get, he’s quite resourceful and very energetic…So he has what it takes.”

Referencing the voice note on Wednesday, Mr Agabi asked Mr Odofin if an “energetic person” was not fit for the job.

The witness insisted that Mr Sirika imposed his friend on the ministry.

“The man was imposed by the first defendant (Mr Sirika) on the ministry,” Mr Odofin said.

Responding to another question from Mr Agabi, the witness said Mr Tilmann was not questioned by the EFCC because he was not in the country during investigations.

“We made an effort to reach him to no avail,” the witness said.

He maintained that due process was not followed in awarding the contract to Mr Tilmaan.

But he added that the former minister only followed due process “after the contract had been awarded.”

Mr Agabi expressed surprise at the line of testimony and asked the trial judge, Slyvanus Oriji, for an adjournment of the proceedings.

Following no objection from EFCC’s lawyer, Rotimi Jacob, also a SAN, the judge adjourned the matter until Thursday.

Charges

The EFCC is prosecuting Mr Sirika, alongside his daughter, Fatima Sirika, her husband, Jalal Hamma, and the couple’s firm, Al Buraq Global Investment, on six counts, including a N1.5 billion contract fraud and N1.3 billion gratification proceeds.

The prosecution accused Fatima, who works at the Nigerian National Petroleum Company (NNPC) Limited, and her husband, Mr Hamma, a staff member of the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission, of holding “indirectly private interests in the contract for the Apron Extension at the Katsina Airport” for almost N1.5 billion.

One count accused the former minister of “criminal breach of trust by being dishonestly connected with the illegal award” of the contract for the Apron Extension at Katsina Airport for the benefit of his daughter and son-in-law’s company, Al Buraq Global Investment Ltd.

EFCC charged them with possession of N1.3 billion allegedly traced to Mr Sirika as “proceeds of criminal conducts” in the form of gratification.

A count dedicated to the contract awarded to Mr Tilmann accused Mr Sirika of conferring unfair advantage on Mr Tilmann’s Tianaero Nigeria Limited by using his position as the aviation minister to award to the firm a consultancy contract for the Nigerian Air start-up to the tune of N1.3 billion. Mr Sirika allegedly did this between April 2022 and March 2023.

Yet another count accused the former aviation minister of being dishonestly connected to the “illegal” award of the N1.3 billion consultancy contract for the Nigerian Air Start-up to Mr Tilmann’s company, Tianaero Nigeria Limited.

The defendants denied all six charges.

The prosecution case so far

The prosecution has called 12 prosecution witnesses so far.

Since Mr Odofin, the 12th prosecution witness, started taking the stand on 30 June 2025, he has testified extensively on the botched Nigerian Air national carrier and the contract awarded to Mr Tilmann.

He said Mr Sirika allegedly disguised an Ethiopian Airlines aircraft as Nigeria’s national carrier during the former President Muhammadu Buhari administration.

He testified that the aircraft was loaned to Nigeria for just three days, from 27 to 29 May 2023. He testified that the plane was flown back to Ethiopia immediately after being passed off as a Nigeria Air national carrier.

In May 2023, then-aviation minister Mr Sirika promised that Nigeria Air would commence operations before he left office; a promise he delivered on a mere three days before his departure.

The purported unveiling was fraught with concerns. First, in June 2023, the Nigerian Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA) rejected an application from Nigeria Air seeking certification to proceed to “phase two” in the process of obtaining an Air Operator’s Certificate (AOC).

According to the NCAA’s rejection letter, there was no adequate preparation for the airline’s operation.

Also, the former minister had disclosed earlier in 2022 that Ethiopian Airlines emerged as a core investor in Nigeria Air with a 49 per cent shareholding.

This did not sit well with local airline operators who claimed they could manage Nigerian Air better than a foreign airline.

During the unveiling, only one aircraft belonging to Ethiopian Airlines was unveiled at the ceremony.

In June this year, the witness testified that Mr Sirika split a contract the Nigeria Air-related contracts to evade the Bureau of Public Procurement (BPP) and the Federal Executive Council (FEC) in the contract approval process.

World.title: 2027: Men have failed Nigeria – Presidential candidate
World.content:
The presidential candidate of the National Rescue Movement (NRM), Esther Okereke, has urged Nigerians to give a woman a chance to lead the country, arguing that years of male-dominated leadership have failed to deliver the desired results.

Mrs Okereke said her candidacy should not be judged simply on gender, but on what she described as her “blueprint, a plan and a framework” for governing Nigeria.

She made the remarks on Wednesday during an appearance on Sunrise Daily, a Channels Television programme, while discussing her campaign ahead of the 2027 presidential election.

Mrs Okereke said she had encountered people who questioned whether a woman could lead Nigeria.

She said she responded by questioning why Nigerians should continue with male leadership.

“Do you think a man who has failed for over 20 years should continue? If you don’t think so, then give this woman a chance,” she said.

Nigeria has never elected a woman as president. The 2027 election will again be contested predominantly by men, with only two women among the 18 presidential candidates cleared by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC).

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mrs Okereke represents the NRM, while Ada Okwori is the National Democratic Party’s presidential candidate.

The two women are seeking the presidency against candidates including President Bola Tinubu of the All Progressives Congress, former Vice President Atiku Abubakar of the African Democratic Congress and former Anambra State Governor Peter Obi of the Nigeria Democratic Congress.

“By the way, I’m not here for gender politics. I’m here with accountability. I’m here with a blueprint, a plan, a framework to rescue,” she said.

Energy first

Mrs Okereke identified electricity as one of the first areas she would address if elected, arguing that unreliable power supply undermines businesses, technology adoption and economic activity.

She said small and medium-sized businesses often lose customers because of power failures and the cost of relying on generators and other alternatives.

She said reliable electricity is also necessary for the country to benefit fully from technology and smart monitoring systems.

Tackling insecurity

The NRM candidate also identified insecurity as another immediate priority, saying it discourages Nigerians living abroad from returning to invest in the country.

“I have lots of friends that want to come back home to invest, not as charity, but as partners, for us to build Nigeria,” she said.

“But when you tackle the insecurity, you would have lots of people coming home, you know, peacefully.”

Mrs Okereke also criticised the practice of repairing roads shortly before political leaders visit, arguing that infrastructure should be maintained as part of normal governance rather than to impress visiting officials.

“If you have decided to go into public office, just have it at the back of your mind that you’re a servant. You’re here to serve the people, and that’s how it should be,” she said.

Grassroots partnership

Mrs Okereke said her campaign is built on a grassroots structure and argued that citizens should be treated as partners in governance, not merely voters.

“You don’t just need the grassroots for votes. You need them for partnership,” she said.

“After the election, you need to answer questions from them. You need to give them updates.”

She said her proposed governance framework would prioritise areas including housing and healthcare, particularly healthcare services for people at the grassroots.

World.title: Jigawa partners presidential CNG initiative to expand alternative energy infrastructure
World.content:
The Jigawa State Government has pledged to deepen its collaboration with the Presidential Initiative on Compressed Natural Gas and Electric Vehicles (Pi-CNG & EV) to expand alternative energy infrastructure and promote the adoption of compressed natural gas (CNG), particularly in the agricultural sector.

Governor Umar Namadi disclosed this on Tuesday, when the Chairman of the Presidential Initiative, Ismaeel Ahmed, led a delegation on a courtesy visit to the Governor at Government House, Dutse.

Governor Namadi said the state’s interest in CNG extends beyond its use in transportation, saying that affordable energy for irrigation is critical to reducing farmers’ production costs and sustaining agricultural activities.

He stated that energy costs currently account for more than half of farmers’ operating expenses, a situation he said was discouraging some farmers from returning to their farms.

“As of today, energy costs constitute more than 50% of the operating expenses of our farmers,” the governor said.

He also said that the state had resolved to undertake the conversion of irrigation pumps from conventional energy sources to CNG as part of measures to lower production costs, alongside other subsidies on agricultural inputs.

“On this initiative, the state government is ready to bear the cost of conversion for the targeted farms. For us, going into CNG is a matter of necessity,” he said

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The governor said the proposed intervention was particularly important to the state’s dry-season wheat and rice production programmes, as he reiterated Jigawa’s target of cultivating 500,000 hectares of wheat by 2030 and producing four million metric tonnes of rice annually within the same period.

He said the government was ready to provide land and other necessary support to facilitate the initiative, including collaboration with private-sector investors.

Earlier speaking, Barrister Ismaeel Ahmed described Jigawa as an important location for the expansion of CNG infrastructure because of its strategic position between Kano and the Northeast, as well as its land availability and the state government’s interest in alternative energy.

He said the presidential initiative was in discussions with private-sector investors to explore opportunities for establishing a major alternative energy hub in Jigawa, which could serve vehicles and heavy-duty transport operating along major routes.

The chairman also disclosed that the initiative was working towards expanding the number of CNG conversion centres in the state, saying that the target was to have at least 30 centres by December 2026, subject to the willingness of local investors to participate.

He added that the initiative would also explore collaboration with the state government to establish electric vehicle charging infrastructure as part of the wider alternative energy programme.

The governor welcomed the proposals and reaffirmed Jigawa State’s readiness to work with the Presidential Initiative, investors, and other relevant partners to advance the development of alternative energy infrastructure.

He said the proposed collaboration would complement the state’s investments in irrigation and agricultural mechanization while supporting efforts to reduce the cost of food production and improve farmers’ livelihoods.

World.title: Soroman’s pioneering involvement in Dangote Consortium propels first loading milestone
World.content:
Soroman Nigeria Limited, a leader in the oil and gas industry and a key player in Nigeria’s evolving energy landscape, marked its entry into the consortium with the successful loading of 20,000.00 metric tonnes (MT) of Premium Motor Spirit (PMS) aboard the vessel African Marvel. The cargo is destined for the Soroman Depot in Calabar, Cross River State, signaling an important step for the company’s strategic initiatives in petroleum distribution and coastal logistics.

The Vessel African Marvel’s movement under this consortium arrangement not only underscores the company’s commitment to operational excellence but also reinforces its role as a pioneering participant in a new era of petroleum refining and distribution led by industry heavyweights.

In an environment where market dynamics and commercial partnerships are continually evolving, Soroman’s breakthrough cargo operation stands out as a testament to the company’s agility and strategic foresight.

The Dangote Petroleum Refinery consortium arrangement represents a structured commercial framework through which qualified downstream operators lift refined products directly from the refinery for distribution across Nigeria’s domestic market.

Soroman’s ability to secure its first loading under this arrangement places the company among the early participants in a model that is expected to reshape how petroleum products flow from refinery gate to end-user, reducing the country’s long-standing reliance on imported fuels and strengthening the domestic supply chain.

Commercially, the transaction is structured on a dollar-referenced product rating, with payment settled in naira in accordance with the specific terms agreed upon for this loading. It is worth noting that the applicable conversion basis, quotation validity and payment timeline are governed by the relevant transaction documents between the parties. These terms are specific to the transaction and should not be construed as a general pricing policy applicable to all consortium participants or future liftings.

The choice of Calabar as the discharge destination carries its own strategic weight. Situated in Cross River State along Nigeria’s south-eastern coastline, Calabar has historically served as a gateway for maritime commerce in the region.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

By directing the African Marvel cargo to Soroman Depot in Calabar, the company is reinforcing the city’s relevance as a petroleum distribution hub and positioning itself to serve the commercial fuel needs of buyers across the South-South geopolitical zone. The coastal routing from the Dangote Refinery in Lagos to Calabar demonstrates the viability of maritime logistics as an efficient channel for moving large petroleum volumes to regional markets that have traditionally depended on road-based haulage and imports.

Soroman’s achievement in the petroleum space is amplified by the company’s broader industrial footprint. While oil and gas remain a core business line, Soroman Nigeria Limited operates across multiple sectors, including engineering, procurement and construction, mining, manufacturing and production, and fertilizer, agriculture and food value chains. This diversified portfolio means that the visibility and credibility generated by the consortium milestone extend beyond petroleum, introducing the Soroman brand to a wider audience of potential customers, commercial partners, investors and industry stakeholders who may find value in the company’s capabilities across these adjacent sectors.

The company has also made deliberate investments in digital platforms to ensure that increased brand awareness translates into accessible commercial engagement. Soroman’s corporate website offers a detailed overview of its operations and service offerings. An online ordering portal provides a direct channel for customers to place product orders and submit business enquiries.

For mobile users, the Soroman application is available for download on both the Apple App Store and Google Play, extending the company’s digital reach to smartphone users across Nigeria. Additionally, a WhatsApp ordering channel offers a familiar, conversational interface for customers who prefer to transact and communicate via messaging. These platforms collectively ensure that prospective clients can discover, contact and do business with Soroman with minimal friction.

As Nigeria’s petroleum landscape continues its historic shift toward domestically refined supply, companies that position themselves early within the new distribution architecture stand to gain a lasting competitive advantage.

Soroman Nigeria Limited’s pioneering first loading under the Dangote consortium arrangement is precisely such a positioning move — one that combines operational execution with strategic ambition. The Vessel African Marvel, carrying 20,000.00 metric tonnes of PMS toward Soroman Depot in Calabar, is not merely a vessel in transit; it is a visible marker of the company’s readiness to play a prominent role in the next chapter of Nigeria’s energy distribution story.

ABOUT SOROMAN NIGERIA LIMITED

Soroman Nigeria Limited is a Nigerian multi-sector company with business interests spanning oil and gas, engineering and procurement, construction, mining, manufacturing and production, and fertilizer, agriculture and food value chains.

World.title: African security chiefs strategise to tackle exploitation of social media, digital technologies by terrorists
World.content:
African security chiefs are worried about the increasing use of digital technologies and social media platforms by terrorist groups that hold sway over ungoverned territories across the Sahel and West Africa region.

The security leaders, according to Punch, expressed their concerns on Tuesday at a three-day regional conference on detecting and disrupting terrorists’ exploitation of information and communication platforms as well as emerging technologies.

Participants were drawn from across the volatile region, including representatives from the African Union (AU), the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) and the Multinational Joint Task Force (MNJTF), among other regional and international bodies.

Idriss Lalalli, the acting director of the AU Counter-Terrorism Centre, acknowledged the expanding digital footprints of Islamic State and al-Qaeda affiliates in the region.

PREMIUM TIMES reports that Islamic State Sahel Province (ISSP), Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), Boko Haram and other terror groups are consolidating their presence in the Sahel and Lake Chad basin states, deploying new technologies in an unconventional war already overstretching state and regional forces.

JNIM, for instance, has conducted several drone attacks in the Sahel since its first AI-enabled aerial assault on military positions in Bandiagara, Mali, in 2023. The ISSP also deployed a drone for the first time in its attack on Niamey airport earlier this year.

Also, these groups continue to exploit many digital platforms for propaganda and recruitment, gaining territory control and winning hearts and minds beyond their physical strongholds, a trend Mr Lalalli said poses threats faster than security agencies could respond.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Across West Africa and the Sahel today, ISWAP, Boko Haram and JNIM are extending their reach through technology,” Mr Lalalli said. “They recruit on social media platforms, move and conceal funds via mobile money, gift cards and cryptocurrencies.”

The regional defence chief alleged that these terror groups purchase weapons on “darknet marketplaces,” fly drones, communicate over satellite links, and use AI “to tailor propaganda and evade detection.”

“What makes this difficult is speed and cost,” he continued. “A [terror] cell with a modest budget can now reach audiences far beyond its physical presence and move faster than our procedures can respond.”

Mr Lalalli called for specialised training, regional coordination and stronger collaboration with private sector operators.

In his remarks, Nigeria’s National Security Adviser (NSA), Nuhu Ribadu, noted that emerging technologies further complicate Africa’s security landscape.

Represented by Adamu Laka, the coordinator of the National Counter Terrorism Centre (NCTC), Mr Ribadu said AI-created content, drones and autonomous systems “can expand operational capabilities,” noting that these assets can pave the way for new terror financing channels.

“We must, therefore, strengthen our ability to anticipate, detect, analyse and disrupt threats before they materialise,” the NSA advised.

Beyond acquiring sophisticated equipment, Mr Ribadu said the continent needs technical knowledge, institutional coordination and cooperation among security agencies.

He also urged West African and Sahelian countries to strengthen cross-border intelligence cooperation and share actionable cyber threat information promptly.

“Nigeria recognises that no institution, country or sector can defeat terrorism alone,” he said.

The NSA added that Nigeria was working with the African Union Counter-Terrorism Centre to secure accreditation for the NCTC as a regional centre of excellence for counterterrorism in West Africa and the Sahel.

He said the initiative followed President Bola Tinubu’s declaration at the High-Level Africa Counterterrorism Summit in April 2024.

Conference expectations

Mr Lalalli said the conference would train participants in cyber threat intelligence, open-source intelligence, digital forensics and blockchain analysis to help them track online recruitment networks, preserve digital evidence and trace cryptocurrency transactions.

He said the skills needed to be integrated to strengthen investigations and prosecutions.

The AU official also urged stronger collaboration with social media companies, telecommunications operators and financial service providers, noting that terrorist groups often exploit privately owned infrastructure.

“You leave as this continent’s first cohort of trainers in this domain. You will leave here not just carrying home a certificate, but a responsibility. The Centre will stand behind you. But the multiplier is you,” he said.

World.title: AI won’t decide outcome of 2027 general election – INEC Chairman
World.content:
The Chairman of the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), Joash Amupitan, has said Artificial Intelligence (AI) must not be allowed to determine the outcome of Nigeria’s 2027 general election.

Mr Amupitan said this on Wednesday in Abuja while delivering a keynote address at the AI and Democracy Forum 2026, organised by Yiaga Africa in partnership with INEC, Microsoft, TikTok, the Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development (CJID), Dataphyte, the MacArthur Foundation, the International Foundation for Electoral Systems (IFES), the German Agency for International Cooperation (GIZ) and other partners.

The two-day forum, themed “Safeguarding the 2027 General Elections in the Age of Artificial Intelligence,” brought together representatives of electoral commissions from Senegal, Kenya, Gambia, Liberia, Sierra Leone and Togo, as well as security agencies, civil society organisations, the media, technology companies and students.

Mr Amupitan said the forum was aimed at moving discussions around artificial intelligence beyond identifying risks to developing practical responses ahead of the 2027 elections.

“Will algorithms decide the 2027 votes?” he asked.

“I consider our gathering here today not merely as an academic exercise or a routine policy consultation. This is a strategic imperative.”

He answered the question himself, saying the choice of who leads Nigeria must remain with the electorate.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“No, algorithms will not and must never decide the 2027 vote.

“2027 votes must be decided by the sovereign people of Nigeria,” he said.

According to him, AI would nevertheless have a significant influence on the information environment in which voters make decisions and on the administration and security of elections.

“AI will undeniably shape the information environment in which citizens form their choices, influence the speed and security of electoral logistics, and alter the tactics of both democratic actors and anti-democratic actors,” he said.

He urged INEC and its partners to ensure that AI was deployed to strengthen the electoral process rather than undermine it.

“Our task, therefore, at this forum and within the commission, is to ensure that AI remains a servant of democracy, not its master,” he said.

AI to support election logistics

Mr Amupitan said the scale of Nigeria’s electoral process made the use of technology increasingly necessary.

He said INEC was preparing to manage more than 100 million registered voters across 176,846 polling units in 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory.

The presidential and National Assembly elections are scheduled for 16 January 2027, while the governorship and state Houses of Assembly elections are scheduled for 6 February.

The chairman said INEC would have to deploy personnel and sensitive materials to difficult terrains across 774 local government areas, including remote and riverine communities and areas affected by insecurity.

He cited Kabi Ward in Kuje Area Council of the FCT as an example of the logistical difficulties faced by the commission.

According to him, reaching the area could take about three hours and there was limited network coverage.

Mr Amupitan said AI could help the commission overcome some of these challenges through predictive modelling, geospatial analysis and dynamic routing.

“Machine learning algorithms can analyse historical traffic patterns, weather forecasts, road conditions and security incidents to generate optimal deployment routes for logistic vehicles across the terrains,” he said.

He added that AI-powered systems could also help INEC predict demand for non-sensitive materials, monitor warehouse stock and identify supply-chain bottlenecks before they affect election-day operations.

Mr Amupitan said INEC had tested some of these systems during elections conducted since he assumed office, adding that there had been improvements in the early deployment of election materials and commencement of voting.

AI deployed in voter registration, results management

The INEC chairman also listed several areas where the commission had incorporated technology into the electoral process.

He said the commission had digitised its candidate nomination process through the INEC Candidate Nomination Portal, which he said had processed more than 15,000 nominations from 22 political parties ahead of the 2027 elections.

He also said INEC had introduced online voter registration, allowing Nigerians to begin the registration process remotely using digital devices.

Mr Amupitan said the commission had also experimented with downloadable voter cards, including during the Osun governorship election, for voters whose cards had been lost or damaged and who were unable to receive replacements before the election.

He said AI could also assist with detecting anomalies in election results.

According to INEC boss, algorithms could identify mathematical inconsistencies, unusual patterns and image-quality problems in uploaded polling-unit results before they were accepted into INEC’s results management system.

He said this would complement, rather than replace, human oversight and the statutory processes for declaring election results.

Mr Amupitan also said AI was being used to improve the voters’ register by helping the commission identify duplicate biometric records.

“With over 13 million records in our national register of voters, AI-enhanced automated biometric identification systems drastically accelerate deduplication processes, detecting facial and fingerprint duplicates with unprecedented speed and accuracy,” he said.

INEC establishes AI unit

The chairman disclosed that INEC had established an AI unit within its Information and Communication Technology department.

He said the commission was also finalising a governance framework for the use of artificial AI in elections, with support from IFES and other partners.

He said the framework would be guided by principles including integrity, transparency, human intervention and public auditing.

Mr Amupitan warned that the same technology that could strengthen elections could also be exploited to attack electoral systems and manipulate public information.

He said INEC’s digital infrastructure, including its results management and candidate nomination platforms, could become targets for malicious cyber actors.

“Every day we check, working with experts in this area, to detect faults and threats to our systems,” he said.

He added that AI-powered cyber-security systems could help detect denial-of-service attacks, brute-force attacks and other threats to electoral infrastructure.

Yiaga Africa warns against opaque AI result platforms

The Executive Director of Yiaga Africa, Samson Itodo, said rebuilding public confidence would be one of the major challenges ahead of the 2027 elections.

Mr Itodo said Nigerians’ distrust of the electoral process remained high, partly because of the role technology played in the 2023 election.

“Just last week, Yiaga Africa issued a national voting intention survey report, where it is obvious that Nigerians doubt the credibility of the process, and that their votes will not count in 2027,” he said.

The survey was designed to assess voter interest and participation and identify factors that could encourage or discourage Nigerians from taking part in the elections.

He said the deployment of technology alone would not guarantee credible elections, stressing that the integrity of those managing the systems was equally important.

“It is one thing to deploy technology; it is another thing for the personal integrity of those managing those technologies to deliver,” he said.

Mr Itodo also raised concerns about the growing number of AI-powered platforms being developed to aggregate election results ahead of the 2027 elections.

He said only INEC had the legal authority to declare election results and winners, although other organisations could independently aggregate results for monitoring and oversight.

“We encourage stakeholders to continue to use different tools and platforms to keep an eye on the results process,” he said.

He urged organisations deploying AI for results aggregation to ensure that their systems were accurate, transparent and auditable.

“For us, as an organisation, we’re very open and transparent about the methodologies that we use,” he said.

Mr Itodo said organisations using AI in elections should be guided by the principles of integrity, transparency and auditability to prevent the technology from becoming a source of political instability.

The forum is expected to develop practical recommendations for governing the use of AI in Nigeria’s electoral process ahead of the 2027 general elections.

World.title: ‘Agbara Nla: The Return’ remake records biggest non-December Nollywood opening
World.content:
Nollywood faith-based film ‘Agbara Nla: The Return’ recorded the biggest non-December opening for a Nigerian film, earning about N170.6 million across its preview screenings and first weekend in cinemas.

The film generated about N71.4 million from preview screenings ending on 1 October and added approximately N99.2 million between Friday, 2 October, and Sunday, 4 October.

The performance also makes it the highest-grossing October opening for a Nigerian film and the strongest opening recorded by a faith-based Nollywood production.

Non-December Release

This non-December distinction matters because Nigerian cinemas usually record their strongest traffic during the festive season. Major Nollywood productions are often scheduled for December to benefit from public holidays, family outings, increased consumer spending, and the “Detty December” entertainment rush.

As a result, many of Nollywood’s biggest opening records belong to December releases, including Funke Akindele’s ‘Everybody Loves Jenifa’ (2024) and ‘Behind the Scenes’ (2025).

By earning N170.6 million in October, ‘Agbara Nla: The Return’ achieved blockbuster-level numbers without the advantage of the Christmas holiday season.

In this context, the “biggest non-December opening” refers to the highest opening gross recorded by a Nollywood film released between January and November, based on available Nigerian box-office figures.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

‘Agbara Nla’ was originally produced by Mike Bamiloye in 1993. The story returned to cinemas on 1 October 2026 as ‘Agbara Nla: The Return’, directed by his sons, Damilola Mike-Bamiloye and Joshua “Jay Mikee” Mike-Bamiloye.

Box-office performance

Before its first full weekend, ‘Agbara Nla: The Return’ generated approximately N71.4 million from 12,134 admissions during its preview screenings.

The film then recorded about N99.2 million from 16,223 admissions between 2 and 4 October, bringing its four-day gross to about N170.6 million.

The opening places the faith-based production among Nollywood’s strongest cinema debuts, although Funke Akindele’s December releases remain ahead in the overall opening-weekend rankings.

‘Everybody Loves Jenifa’ recorded an opening-weekend total of approximately N206 million, while ‘Behind the Scenes’ earned about N205.5 million.

Agbara Nla began with N5,000

Speaking in a video about the film’s history, Mike Bamiloye recalled that production of the original Agbara Nla began in 1993 with only N5,000.

“In 1993, we wanted to shoot Agbara Nla. We started the film with N5,000. People were bringing yam and corn; we were eating corn in the forest just to shoot Agbara Nla,” he said.

The filmmaker said the production had neither a manager nor a promotional team when it was completed, although several marketers later competed to distribute it. He recalled that the filmmakers continued to struggle financially even as the film became popular across Nigeria.

“We were hungry, we were suffering, we had no food to eat, but our name was everywhere,” he said.

Mr Bamiloye also recounted approaching a marketer for financial assistance after the production, “We approached one marketer and said, ‘Give us money, please give us money, even if it is N10,’ and the marketer said, ‘Mount Zion people, you are becoming lovers of money; you are pursuing money.’

“But he is the one advertising the thing and selling. You can take all the money; you can’t take the anointing. You can take all the money; you can dupe us, but you can’t carry the grace. If you steal our movie, another one will rise from inside.”

The filmmaker said the difficult experience eventually shaped his understanding of the film’s impact, “I went to God and said, ‘Lord, we are suffering.’ You know what God said? He said, ‘I never told you that I would make you rich through Agbara Nla, but I will give you a name through the movie,’” he recalled.

Mr Bamiloye said the promise became evident as the film attracted a following and audiences increasingly associated him and his colleagues with Mount Zion Faith Ministries.

Making of Agbara Nla

Although the film became widely known through television broadcasts and home-video circulation in the 1990s, Mr Bamiloye traced the story’s origin to the National Festival of Christian Drama, HARVEST ’87.

Mount Zion Faith Ministries organised the festival at the GOFAMINT International Gospel Centre in Ojoo, Ibadan.

The project was initially titled Agbara To Ju Agbara Lo. It involved drama ministers from churches and tertiary institutions, including the University of Lagos, University of Ibadan, Ogun State University and the College of Education, Ilesa.

The first production attempt collapsed after filming at Apete Village in Ibadan. According to Mr Bamiloye, the cameraman disappeared with the recorded tapes, and repeated attempts to find him failed.

The project was subsequently abandoned before Mr Bamiloye rewrote the script and restarted production at Badeku Village in Ibadan.

Members of the Christian community helped to keep the production alive. A Foursquare Gospel Church pastor contributed N5,000 toward a camera deposit, while the late Idowu Animashawun of World Hope Mission accommodated crew members.

The completed film was eventually broadcast on television, introducing the story to audiences across the country.

An English-language adaptation, ‘The Ultimate Power ‘, followed in 1994, extending its reach beyond the predominantly Yoruba-speaking audience of the original production.

The original story
