World.title: Kenya: Kenya Confirms Second Ebola Case
World.content:
Nairobi — Kenya has confirmed a second case of Ebola (Bundibugyo virus disease), involving a 39-year-old man who is a close family member of the first patient who died, the Ministry of Health has announced.

The man was already in quarantine under daily monitoring when he developed fever, fatigue and joint pains on October 13.

Health officials isolated him immediately and collected samples that tested positive at both the National Virology Reference Laboratory and the KEMRI-CDC laboratory.

He has since been transferred to a designated treatment centre, where he is receiving supportive care.



The Ministry said early detection and isolation had helped limit the risk of further transmission, adding that both confirmed cases were linked, with no evidence of wider community spread.

Contact tracing is ongoing, with 128 people identified as contacts of the first patient. By October 13, authorities had traced 113, including 108 who are in quarantine in Kenya and undergoing daily clinical and temperature checks for 21 days.

The remaining five contacts are outside the country, and relevant health authorities have been notified. Efforts to trace the other 15 contacts are continuing.

Health teams are also assessing people who may have come into contact with the second patient since his symptoms began, including quarantine personnel and health workers.

The Ministry said infection prevention and control measures had been strengthened at quarantine and treatment facilities, while health workers had been provided with protective equipment.

It urged anyone experiencing fever, unusual fatigue, muscle or joint pains, vomiting, diarrhoea or unexplained bleeding to seek medical attention promptly.

The Ministry clarified that Ebola is not airborne but spreads through direct contact with the blood or body fluids of an infected person who is sick or has died from the disease.

Kenya remains open, with no restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings, as the government continues coordinating the response with relevant health authorities and the World Health Organization.

The public has been urged to rely on official Ministry of Health updates and respect the privacy of the affected family. Members of the public can call the toll-free number 719 for information.

Principal Secretary for Public Health Dr Patrick Amoth said the response was being coordinated under the Public Health (Declaration of Formidable Epidemic Disease) Order, 2026, and the Public Health (Ebola Disease) Rules, 2026.

World.title: Mozambique: Mondlane's Appeal Regarding Live Broadcast of His Trial Rejected
World.content:
Maputo — Mozambique's Supreme Court has rejected an appeal filed by defendant Venâncio Mondlane, a former presidential candidate, seeking to have his trial broadcast live on television and social media.

During the trial, scheduled for November 17, the Supreme Court had also refused recording of sound and images. However, media outlets would be authorized to cover the hearing and produce written records of the proceedings. The decision also grants the public access to the courtroom.

In a statement released on Tuesday, the Supreme Court claims that it had dismissed Mondlane's appeal in a ruling issued on 12 October, explaining that the type of decision he was challenging cannot be appealed under the country's Criminal Procedure Code.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The Supreme Court's ruling maintains the restrictions on live broadcasting and audiovisual recording without overturning the principle that the trial is open to the public.

Mondlane, leader of the National Alliance for a Free and Autonomous Mozambique (Anamola), is accused of five criminal charges related to post-election mass demonstrations. The mass demonstration he called to protest against the alleged fraudulent results of the general elections held in October 2024 started peacefully but then degenerated into rioting.

Mondlane is accused of having committed the following crimes: public apology for a crime, incitement to collective disobedience, public instigation to crime, instigation and incitement to terrorism. Recently, the Council of State, the advising body to the Mozambican President, decided to lift Mondlane's immunity in order to allow him to stand trial.

The Supreme Court had also argued that a live broadcast could lead the public to form premature conclusions regarding guilt or innocence before a final verdict is reached. This is the most highly anticipated moment in the country, given that Mondlane is effectively the leading opposition figure, as a result of his political prominence and the crowds that attend his rallies across the nation.

World.title: Libya: Libya's Arsenals Are a Blind Spot in the Tripoli Agreement
World.content:
analysis

Disbanding militias is key to Libya's reunification, but could lead to weapons stockpiles being trafficked into neighbouring countries.

An agreement signed in Tripoli on 30 August between rival eastern and western Libyan camps could pave the way for national elections within two years. It could also restore political stability and territorial unity, which have remained elusive since the 2020 ceasefire that ended large-scale fighting in the country.

The African Union (AU) and United Nations (UN) Security Council welcomed the electoral agreement, and Hanna Tetteh, the UN Secretary-General's Special Representative for Libya, considers it an important step towards breaking the political and institutional deadlock. The deal has revived Libyans' hopes of emerging from a long crisis, but scepticism about its prospects remains.



While eastern Libya's House of Representatives approved the agreement, the western faction's advisory body, the High Council of State, rejected it. The council argued that electoral changes should go through Libya's established constitutional mechanisms, and that the agreement bypassed earlier understandings between the two chambers.

The latest rapprochement also raises other complications. For Niger and Chad, which share nearly 1 400 km of border with Libya, and indeed for the Sahel as a whole, a reunifying Libya could paradoxically increase regional insecurity in the short term if the weapons issue remains unaddressed.

For the past 15 years, several Chadian and Tuareg rebel movements and terrorist groups have used southern Libya as a rear base to resupply with weapons and ammunition. South-eastern Libya is also a transit zone for equipment destined for the Rapid Support Forces, the paramilitary group that has been fighting Sudan's army since 2023. This supply line, which runs through Kufra, is already operational and could simply change clients.

Reunifying the army means disbanding the militias, integrating their fighters and recovering their arsenals, which have continued to grow despite the 2020 ceasefire. Without strict controls, these stockpiles - along with the surplus weapons accumulated during the second civil war (2014-2020), which was largely fuelled by foreign powers - could be diverted to trafficking networks in neighbouring countries.

A community leader from Agadez in Niger told the Institute for Security Studies (ISS) that some factions linked to these networks could encourage the resale of weapons on the cross-border black market. The natural outlets for this trade would be in the Sahel, a transit zone where many Nigerien and Chadian intermediaries facilitate arms smuggling.

A flood of Libyan weapons like the one following the fall of Muammar Gaddafi's regime in 2011 is a major concern, even if the circumstances differ. At that time, the state's collapse left weapon depots open to looting; today, the negotiated dismantling of the militias could release their stockpiles.

After 2011, looted weapons flooded the Sahel and Lake Chad Basin via the Salvador Pass in Niger's far north and Chad's Tibesti region. These flows contributed to the outbreak of the Malian crisis in 2012, the strengthening of Boko Haram and the expansion of terrorist groups from 2015.

A resumption of such trafficking could channel Libya's surplus weapons into the Lake Chad Basin, the Sahel and coastal states, fuelling insecurity there. In the hands of non-state armed groups, large quantities of mortars, rocket launchers and drones could shift the balance of power on the ground with devastating consequences for national armies and civilians.

The actors in this cross-border trade - local transporters and intermediaries - also traffic in fuel, drugs, gold and migrants along the routes linking Niger and Chad to Libya. With their intimate knowledge of the desert areas straddling these countries, they can easily move large quantities of arms and ammunition to various buyers, including terrorist groups.

Unless precautions are taken, the groups destabilising the Sahel, Lake Chad Basin and Gulf of Guinea countries risk becoming over-armed, a Tuareg community leader from Mali told ISS. Countries south of Libya, and the UN and AU, which sponsored the 30 August agreement, must act quickly to minimise this risk, rather than wait until the political crisis is resolved before intervening.

The first step is for Libyan parties to attach a mechanism to the political agreement that governs the collection and control of arsenals. The mandate of the UN Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL), which is mainly political, should be expanded without delay to include a dedicated disarmament component.

Working with Libyan actors, UNSMIL could, within six months, design a process for collecting, inventorying, marking and registering weapons as a prerequisite for integrating militia members into the unified army. Implementation could start before the end of 2027.

Close 

Closer military cooperation between Algeria, Niger and Chad should be encouraged. This could involve intelligence sharing and joint border patrols.

The UN and AU should also help Alliance of Sahel States (AES) countries and the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) tackle weapons proliferation through national commissions on small arms and light weapons. Ideally, this should be regionally coordinated, but the AES' withdrawal from ECOWAS may prevent that.

The AU could draw on its Strategy on the Control of Illicit Proliferation, Circulation and Trafficking of Small Arms and Light Weapons, and its Silencing the Guns initiative, to encourage countries to join forces against a resurgence of arms trafficking.

If nothing is done before a unified executive is installed in Libya, the militias' weapons will have headed south long before the polls.

For permission to re-publish ISS Today articles, please email us. In South Africa, News24 has exclusive rights to republish ISS Today articles. In Nigeria, Premium Times has exclusive rights to republish ISS Today articles.

Hassane Koné, Senior Researcher, ISS Regional Office for West Africa, Sahel, Lake Chad Basin and Central Africa

World.title: Nigeria: Special Report - Insecurity Exposes Zamfara Communities to Recurring Cholera Outbreaks
World.content:
Zamfara has been one of the states hardest hit by the insecurity that has spread across north-western Nigeria over the past decade.

It started with a sharp pain in Musa Saidu's stomach.

The 20-year-old initially thought little of it. But the pain was soon followed by fever, vomiting and frequent watery stools. Within hours, his condition had deteriorated.

This was August 2025, during a cholera outbreak in Bukkuyum Local Government Area of Zamfara State, where Mr Saidu and his family were living after fleeing their home in Dan Bago village following attacks by bandits.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Like thousands of people displaced by years of insecurity in the state, the family had already lost the stability of home. Now, as Mr Saidu became increasingly ill, they faced another problem: getting medical care.

His parents first tried what they could afford. They gave him some medicines and mixed a local herbal remedy with water, hoping his condition would improve. But it did not.

With the health facility serving their community no longer functional, the family eventually took Musa to the Orphan and Less Privileged Clinic (OLPC) in Bukkuyum town, where he was diagnosed with cholera.

But reaching a health facility did not immediately end their difficulties.

The clinic was struggling with an influx of cholera patients. Only three health workers were on duty, while essential medicines were unavailable.

Many residents affected by the outbreak were brought to the same facility, while some had to seek treatment elsewhere because of shortages of staff, medicines and space.

For displaced families such as Mr Saidu's, the outbreak exposed a problem that went beyond cholera.

Years of insecurity have displaced many communities across Zamfara, forced health workers away from some rural areas and disrupted access to healthcare, safe water and disease surveillance. These are services that become particularly important during an outbreak of a disease that can kill within hours if severe dehydration is not treated.

When insecurity becomes a health crisis

Zamfara is one of the states hardest hit by the insecurity that has spread across north-western Nigeria over the past decade.

What began largely as cattle rustling has evolved into organised violence by armed groups commonly referred to as bandits. Communities have been attacked, residents killed or abducted and thousands forced from their homes.

The armed groups have also imposed levies on some farming communities, stolen livestock and harvests and carried out kidnappings for ransom.

Data obtained from the Mass Atrocities Tracker show that 28,974 people were killed across Nigeria between 2021 and 2025. Borno recorded the highest number, with 4,539 deaths, followed by Zamfara with 3,936 and Kaduna with 2,811.

Zamfara recorded the highest number of abductions during the same period, with 5,447 people kidnapped. Kaduna recorded 4,050 and Niger 3,331.

But deaths, abductions and displacement are only some of the consequences.

In Bukkuyum LGA, residents and health workers told The ICIR that insecurity has also weakened access to healthcare. Some communities have been deserted, while health workers have stopped providing services in areas they consider unsafe.

Reports in 2025 indicated that only about 200 of Zamfara's more than 700 Primary Healthcare Centres (PHCs) were functional, with persistent insecurity blamed for the closure or abandonment of many facilities.

For residents of affected rural communities, the closures mean illness can require travelling several kilometres, sometimes through unsafe areas, before reaching a health worker.

For people displaced by violence, the risks are compounded by overcrowding, poor sanitation, poverty and limited access to safe water.

During a cholera outbreak, those conditions can become deadly.

Displaced, then confronted by cholera

Buba Muhammad had already fled his home in Sadawa with his family because of repeated bandit attacks when his son began vomiting and passing frequent watery stools.

The 40-year-old farmer and his family were living as displaced persons in Bukkuyum, where several families shared limited space and sanitation facilities.

Mr Muhammad immediately tried to find medical help.

There was no functioning health facility close to where they were staying.

"My first attempt when my son was affected was to go to a hospital, but there was no facility nearby," he said. "I had to take him to a medicine shop."

The medicines he obtained there did little to improve the boy's condition.

As the vomiting and diarrhoea continued, Mr Muhammad decided to take him to General Hospital Bukkuyum, the nearest facility where he believed the child could receive appropriate treatment.

But another problem awaited them.

The hospital was struggling with patients arriving from communities affected by the outbreak.

"We didn't receive the proper care we expected immediately because there were not enough staff," he recalled.

"There was no bed space. We even kept our patient on the floor before a staff member later found us a bed."

The illness also placed a financial burden on a family already displaced by insecurity.

Mr Muhammad said they spent heavily on transportation and medicines, including drugs they had to buy outside the hospital after receiving prescriptions.

"The only solution to ease the hardship of such unwanted incidents or outbreaks is to provide facilities in our local communities," he said.

But he said restoring healthcare without addressing insecurity would leave another part of the problem unresolved.

"We need security in our locations because we are not safe; there are attacks every day and night in our locations. The government needs to double its efforts to end the problem."

A preventable disease finds fertile ground

Cholera is an acute diarrhoeal disease caused by consuming food or water contaminated with the bacterium Vibrio cholerae. Without prompt treatment, severe cases can lead to rapid dehydration and death.

It is also largely preventable through access to safe water, adequate sanitation and good hygiene, while prompt administration of oral rehydration solution and other appropriate treatment can substantially reduce deaths.

Yet cholera has repeatedly affected communities in Zamfara State.

In 2023, a World Health Organisation (WHO) report recorded 907 suspected cholera cases in the state, representing about 28 per cent of Nigeria's suspected cases during the period covered.

The state was affected again in 2024. WHO reported more than 700 cases and over 30 deaths across Zamfara and neighbouring Sokoto during the period covered by its report.

By 9 July 2025, Zamfara had recorded 1,619 suspected cases, six confirmed cases and 31 deaths across 12 of its 14 local government areas, according to a UNICEF situation report.

UNICEF said suspected cases increased by 30 per cent within one week, with children and young people accounting for 62 per cent of reported cases.

The crisis continued.

In August 2025, an outbreak in communities in Bukkuyum LGA killed at least eight people and affected more than 200 across 11 communities, according to residents and local officials cited by Reuters.

For residents already dealing with displacement, unsafe water and weakened healthcare services, the outbreak exposed how insecurity can magnify an otherwise preventable public health emergency.

The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) identifies unsafe water, inadequate sanitation and poor hygiene as major factors driving cholera transmission.

In parts of Bukkuyum LGA, insecurity has made addressing those risks more difficult. Residents have been displaced into congested settlements, some health facilities are non-functional, and health workers say reaching remote communities for surveillance and other services can be dangerous.

For some patients, simply reaching treatment presents another risk.

For rural residents, treatment can mean a dangerous journey

In Masu community, Salihu Bello returned home one afternoon to find his two sisters seriously ill.

"They had stomach pain, and became very weak," he recalled. "Later we realised it was cholera."

With no health facility in the community, the family initially relied on local remedies.

But the sisters' condition continued to worsen. Seeking treatment meant undertaking a difficult journey to Bukkuyum town. Before reaching the town, they had to cross a river, a challenge that has become even more dangerous since insecurity forced many healthcare workers to stop visiting remote communities.

"Sometimes health workers used to come to our community, but because of security problems they stopped," Mr Bello said.

As night fell, the family began the trip. Fear of bandits lingered throughout the journey, but Mr Bello said concern for his sisters outweighed every other worry.

"At that moment, we were not thinking about insecurity. We only wanted to save them. It took about three hours before we received attention because we arrived very late at night," he said.

When a health worker eventually prescribed medicines, he had to wake a medicine vendor before dawn to obtain them.

His sisters remained under observation for about 24 hours before their conditions improved.

For Mr Bello, the experience showed the cost of having no functioning healthcare facility nearby.

"If we have a health facility in our community, things will be easier, considering how quickly the disease can affect the human body," he said.

"Before a patient from our community gets to the hospital, they suffer a lot. Having our own health facility would make access to treatment much easier."

But the health facility is only part of what residents say they need.

In Masu and other communities around Bukkuyum, preventing cholera begins with something even more basic: clean water.

Unsafe water keeps the risk alive

In communities around Bukkuyum, residents said access to clean water remains a major challenge.

Some depend on streams for drinking, cooking and other household needs. In Dan Bago, residents said people and cattle sometimes rely on the same water sources.

For a community already vulnerable to cholera, such conditions increase the risk of transmission.

Nigeria's 2021 Water, Sanitation and Hygiene National Outcome Routine Mapping (WASHNORM) report highlighted the scale of the country's water and sanitation challenge.

The report, based on a survey of more than 24,600 households, estimated that approximately 179 million Nigerians, about 87 per cent of the population, lacked access to safely managed drinking-water services.

The situation was particularly difficult in northern Nigeria. The Northeast had the lowest access rate at just two per cent, compared with 29 per cent in the Southwest.

Although 67 per cent of the population had access to basic water supply services, about a quarter of Nigerians still relied on unimproved or surface water sources.

Muhammadu Sadawa, a community leader, said insecurity has made the situation worse by forcing residents from their homes and concentrating displaced families in already strained settlements.

"Another major challenge we have in our community now is insecurity," he said. "Most of our people left the community because of banditry. Where we are now living is too congested and very dirty. That congestion helped the disease spread among us."

Mr Sadawa said access to healthcare had also deteriorated.

Although there is a health facility in his community, he said it is no longer functional.

"We have a facility, but it is not in existence. There are no staff, no drugs. The building is dilapidated and almost collapsing," he said.

During the cholera outbreak, residents therefore had to look elsewhere for treatment.

He said some families struggled to obtain care before outside assistance arrived, while others faced delays because of distance and the cost of treatment.

"Many people died, and it took a long time before we received any intervention. Some people were treated, some were not. I have a relative who spent over N50,000 on treatment. Many families went through the same thing," he said.

For critically ill residents, reaching another health facility can itself be difficult.

Mr Sadawa said residents must cross a river to reach Bukkuyum town, where they can get more comprehensive medical care.

"When someone is sick, we have to cross a river before reaching the hospital. We need the facility renovated, and we also need a bridge or canoes to help us cross," he said.

He estimated that more than 50 people in and around his community were affected during the outbreak, with some becoming ill in displacement settlements before being taken to Bukkuyum town for treatment.

Health workers struggle to reach vulnerable communities

At General Hospital Bukkuyum, Abdullahi Salihu remembers the pressure as cholera patients arrived from communities across the local government area.

"At the time of the outbreak, it was very tense and hectic considering how patients were being brought to the hospital," he said.

"Some survived, some were quarantined, and unfortunately some died."

According to Mr Salihu, insecurity complicated the response.

Patients who could leave affected communities were brought to the hospital. But health workers had limited options for people trapped in settlements that were difficult or unsafe to reach.

"As health workers, we faced a lot of challenges because of insecurity," he said.

"Some people managed to bring patients from their communities because they had no other option. But for those who could not come out, there was little we could do for them."

Mr Salihu said government officials, politicians and humanitarian organisations provided intravenous fluids, antibiotics, rehydration supplies and other support during the outbreak.

But insecurity was not the only challenge.

Many of the patients were displaced people who had lost livelihoods and struggled to afford transportation, food and other necessities.

"Most of them were displaced from their communities with nothing to eat," he said. "Then the outbreak added another difficulty to their lives."

Zaharadeen Abdullahi, a health worker at the Women and Children Welfare Clinic in Bukkuyum, also described insecurity as a major obstacle to preventing and responding to outbreaks.

"Insecurity is a major contributing factor to outbreaks like this," he said.

"We have services, vaccinations and awareness programmes, but because of security challenges many health workers cannot reach vulnerable communities."

Some affected settlements are more than 10 kilometres from health facilities, Mr Abdullahi said. In some areas, insecurity has also limited the transportation options residents can use.

"Some communities cannot use motorcycles because of security threats," he said. "People have to walk long distances or use donkeys. Because cholera requires urgent treatment, these delays can lead to deaths."

He said displacement had created additional risks.

"Most of the affected people are internally displaced persons living in congested conditions," Mr Abdullahi said. "Many rely on unsafe water sources, and stagnant water is still being used for drinking and household activities."

He acknowledged support from the Zamfara State government, UNICEF and other organisations during the outbreak but said greater investment was needed in health facilities, medical supplies and outreach to vulnerable communities.

Insecurity weakens disease surveillance

Shakir Balogun, an epidemiologist, said recurring cholera outbreaks in conflict-affected parts of Zamfara should not be viewed simply as a disease problem.

He said they also expose weaknesses in healthcare access and disease surveillance created or worsened by years of insecurity.

Mr Balogun said insecurity had affected the health system's ability to reach some communities even before recent cholera outbreaks.

"When insecurity makes communities difficult to reach, children can be missed by immunisation programmes, cases of Acute Flaccid Paralysis (AFP) can escape surveillance, and cases of acute watery diarrhoea can similarly go undetected or reach treatment late," he said.

"The pathogen changes; the health-system vulnerability does not."

Mr Balogun said these weaknesses became particularly evident during the 2025 cholera outbreak.

According to him, the African Field Epidemiology Network (AFENET), with technical and financial support from the US Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, deployed eight Field Epidemiology Training Programme residents and a graduate to support Zamfara's response between 11 September and 2 October 2025.

The team worked with state authorities in four high-burden local government areas.

Mr Balogun said the response identified cases in inaccessible and insecure settlements. It also identified under-reporting linked partly to weak active case searches and insecurity, as well as delayed reporting and incomplete records.

Other challenges included transporting stool samples to the state reference laboratory, shortages of essential supplies outside initially prioritised LGAs and inadequate personnel in some health facilities.

The findings suggest that insecurity can affect almost every stage of outbreak control, from identifying a sick person and reporting a suspected case to testing samples and getting treatment to patients.

Mr Balogun said strengthening community-based surveillance could help close some of those gaps.

Close 

Trusted residents and community structures, he said, can help identify and report suspected cases when conventional health teams cannot safely reach affected settlements.

Treatment also needs to be brought closer to vulnerable communities.

"If insecurity means a severely ill patient has to travel several hours or cross an unsafe area before receiving ORS or intravenous fluids, geographical access itself becomes a determinant of survival," he said.

He recommended establishing oral rehydration points and treatment units close to vulnerable communities, backed by reliable referral systems for patients who develop severe disease.

Authorities should also use surveillance and previous outbreak data to identify communities repeatedly affected by cholera and position essential supplies there before outbreaks escalate, he said.

"You do not want to begin moving ORS, IV fluids, chlorine and other essential supplies into a hard-to-reach community only after an outbreak has accelerated," Mr Balogun said.

"We should use surveillance and historical data to identify recurrent hotspots and position supplies before the rainy season."

Treatment alone will not stop recurring outbreaks

Bringing treatment closer to affected communities could save lives, but Mr Balogun said it would not eliminate the conditions that allow cholera to return.

He said safe water and sanitation remain fundamental.

Vaccination and effective case management can reduce infections and deaths during outbreaks, he said, but communities will remain vulnerable if they continue to depend on unsafe water and inadequate sanitation.

Mr Balogun recommended strategic use of oral cholera vaccines among high-risk populations and in communities with recurring outbreaks, particularly where insecurity makes immediate improvements to water and sanitation infrastructure difficult.

But he cautioned against treating vaccination as a replacement for those investments.

"Vaccination is an additional layer of protection, not a substitute for water, sanitation, surveillance and access to treatment," he said.

Government turns to community-based response

The Zamfara State government said it has adopted community-based measures to maintain disease surveillance and provide basic cholera support in areas where insecurity makes conventional healthcare difficult.

The state Ministry of Health, working with the World Health Organisation (WHO) and other partners, has also begun developing a Multi-Hazard Incident Action Plan to strengthen preparedness and response to public health emergencies, including cholera.

Ahmad Muhammad, the Zamfara State epidemiologist, acknowledged the difficulty of reaching communities affected by insecurity.

He said one strategy has been to identify community health workers from insecure areas, bring them to safer locations for training and then send them back to support residents.

"We train them, particularly the community health workers there. So we train them and then allow them to go back to their community and support them," he said.

Mr Muhammad said trained workers are provided with available medical supplies and asked to report suspected cases so health officials can track whether infections are increasing or declining.

He said the approach forms part of the state's risk communication and community engagement strategy, under which people with health-related roles in affected communities are trained to support local outbreak response.

Patients who can safely be evacuated are moved to accessible areas for further treatment, including general hospitals and the treatment centre at the Infectious Disease Hospital in Gusau, he said.

He attributed the state's reduced cholera burden this year, compared with the previous year, to interventions including community sensitisation, improved hygiene, and oral cholera vaccination.

"Community sensitisation and improvement of hygiene, oral cholera vaccination campaign last time. The burden of the disease has reduced this year compared to last year," he said.

He said the government had also intensified water, sanitation and hygiene interventions, including measures aimed at reducing open defecation.

"So I think those strategies have really gone a long way in mitigating the impact," he said.

But for residents of communities where health facilities remain closed or poorly equipped and safe water remains difficult to obtain, the conditions that make cholera dangerous have not disappeared.

This reporting was supported by the Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development (CJID).

World.title: Kenya: Gachagua Accuses Ruto of Using Fuel Price Hikes to Fund 2027 Campaigns
World.content:
Nairobi — Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua has accused President William Ruto of exploiting fuel price increases to raise money for political bribery ahead of the August 2027 General Election, escalating his attacks on the government's economic management.

Gachagua, who leads the Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP), alleged that the President was facing growing public rejection over abductions, alleged extrajudicial killings, corruption, poor policies and the rising cost of living.

In a statement, Gachagua alleged that the President had ordered an increase of Sh12 per litre of petrol and Sh9 per litre of diesel to generate funds for political mobilization.

"Desperate to raise more cash, last evening, he ruthlessly ordered an increase in the price of diesel by Kshs. 9 and petrol by Kshs. 12, to be processed through Gulf Energy for political bribery.



Gachagua claimed the proposed increases would be processed through Gulf Energy and alleged that Energy and Petroleum Cabinet Secretary Opiyo Wandayi had been instructed to defend the adjustment by citing global oil prices.

He dismissed the anticipated explanation as dishonest, insisting that the alleged price increases were politically motivated rather than driven by international market conditions.

However, the statement did not provide evidence to substantiate the allegations of political bribery or establish a link between Gulf Energy and the alleged scheme.

Gachagua further claimed the government was increasingly relying on cash handouts to win public support, alleging that demands for money had followed Ruto even in the Rift Valley, his political stronghold.

Gachagua also launched a personal attack on Ruto, portraying the President as frustrated by mounting political pressure and accusing his administration of mismanaging the economy and failing to address public concerns.

He said the approaching August 10, 2027, election was increasingly weighing on the President, whom he accused of attempting to regain public support through financial inducements.

The latest remarks add to the political confrontation between the former deputy president and his former boss as the country moves towards the next general election.

Gachagua has increasingly positioned himself as a critic of the Ruto administration, with economic management, the cost of living and allegations of state-sponsored abuses forming part of his attacks on the government.

World.title: Malawi: Malawi Urged to Build Economic Resilience As World Economy Wobbles
World.content:
Malawi cannot afford to rely on external demand or donor support as the global economy slows, according to a senior Reserve Bank of Malawi economist, who has warned that the country is underperforming even by regional standards and must accelerate reforms to strengthen economic resilience.

Analysing the implications of the latest World Economic Outlook projections, economist Kisu Simwaka said the expected moderation in global growth to 3.1 per cent from 3.5 per cent signals a more challenging external environment for African economies, particularly those dependent on commodity exports and foreign aid.

"The message is clear: the world economy is slowing down. But Africa must not slow down. Africa must accelerate. And Malawi must accelerate," Simwaka said.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

He argued that weaker global growth, coupled with sluggish expansion in Europe, was already being reflected in Malawi's export performance.

Tobacco earnings, the country's largest foreign exchange earner, reached US$287.1 million by early October 2026, down sharply from US$526.2 million during the same period a year earlier.

According to Simwaka, the decline reflects weakening global demand as major economies lose momentum.

"When the world economy slows, small open economies such as Malawi cannot depend on external demand to drive growth," he said, adding that slower expansion in advanced economies could also translate into tighter aid flows.

Particular concern, he said, lies in Asia, where growth is projected to ease from 5.6 per cent to 4.9 per cent.

As a major engine of global commodity demand, a slowdown in the region could put further pressure on export prices and Africa's terms of trade.

"Weakening growth in Asia is a headwind for Africa because it affects commodity markets and export earnings," he said.

Simwaka also pointed to volatility in the Middle East and Central Asia as a source of uncertainty for fuel-importing countries such as Malawi.

Fluctuating oil prices could either worsen inflationary pressures or provide relief to the country's import bill, depending on exchange-rate stability.

"If oil prices fall, Malawi only benefits if the exchange rate remains stable enough for those gains to be passed through to domestic prices," he said.

While Sub-Saharan Africa is forecast to expand by around 4.5 per cent, Simwaka argued that the figure masks a deeper problem.

With population growth estimated at about 2.6 per cent, the region's per capita growth rate remains too low to achieve meaningful reductions in poverty.

Close 

"Four-and-a-half per cent growth for three consecutive years is effectively stagnation when population growth is taken into account," he said.

Against that backdrop, Malawi's projected growth of 2.7 per cent appears particularly weak. Simwaka noted that neighbouring economies such as Zambia, Tanzania and Rwanda are expected to outperform Malawi, underscoring the need for a stronger domestic growth strategy.

"Malawi is underperforming an underperforming region. The country must catch up," he said.

The economist argued that the policy response should focus on building internal resilience rather than hoping for a stronger global cycle.

He identified the accumulation of foreign exchange reserves, addressing fiscal imbalances and removing structural constraints to productivity as key priorities.

"In a global economy growing at only 3.1 per cent, countries such as Malawi cannot rely on exports and donor assistance alone," Simwaka said. "The challenge is to strengthen domestic foundations for growth and reduce vulnerability to external shocks."

His assessment comes as policymakers grapple with persistent foreign exchange shortages, inflationary pressures and subdued economic growth amid an increasingly uncertain global outlook.

World.title: Iowa Dem Senate candidate says he's too busy campaigning to attend all state House votes
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Democratic Iowa State Rep. Josh Turek defended his attendance record after being called out by his opponent, Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, during a Tuesday night debate for the state's open Senate seat.

Hinson remarked on Turek's absences while responding to a question posed to both candidates about Iowa's rising cancer rates.

"You have to show up to vote for things like pediatric cancer research, and I've invested in legislation to make sure that we're redirecting those resources to get to where it needs to go to help get to the bottom of this cancer crisis," Hinson said.

As Fox News Digital first uncovered, Turek missed 261 votes in Iowa's state legislature from Jan. 12, 2026, through May 3, representing nearly 58% of the total votes during that time.

The debate's moderator asked Turek directly why he missed the votes.

DEM SENATE HOPEFUL RIPPED AS 'ABSENTEE LEGISLATOR' AFTER MISSING NEARLY 60% OF VOTES

"I have gone out there, and I have met with Iowans all over the state, all 99 counties, hundreds of public forums," Turek responded.

FOX NEWS POLL: TUREK, HINSON IN CLOSE IOWA SENATE RACE

"Meanwhile, Ashley Hinson, since she's decided to run for U.S. Senate, has not done one in-person town forum. Also, in my first three years in the legislature, [I had] more than a 90% attendance record," Turek continued.

"I want to ask again, though, why did you miss those votes?" the moderator repeated.

MEDIA NARRATIVE PREDICTING BLUE WAVE IN KEY BATTLEGROUND STATE NOT MESHING WITH LOCAL REPUBLICANS: 'FIRED UP'

"I'm out campaigning. I'm out meeting Iowans all over all 99 counties. I've done hundreds of in-person town halls. Meanwhile, Ashley Hinson, since she's running for the U.S. Senate, has not done a single in-person town hall," he said.

Hinson objected to the notion that she hasn't done any town halls during the campaign cycle.

World.title: African nations on ‘knife’s edge’ as US embassy warns Americans of long-range attacks

The entire Horn of Africa region is said to be on a knife’s edge. As explosions reportedly claimed to be caused by drones hit Ethiopia's capital city in early October, the U.S. Embassy in Addis Ababa warned U.S. citizens of the danger of "long-range attacks."

Analysts say there’s a high probability that Ethiopia and Eritrea are about to erupt in a new war, with worrying regional backing for both sides.

Former CIA analyst and National Security Council Africa Director Cameron Hudson says the Trump administration needs to become more involved. He told Fox News Digital, "Regional leaders will say privately that they don’t want a regional war. But with so many armed actors and so much meddling going on in each other’s countries, a regional conflagration becomes increasingly likely. It is this kind of miscalculation that the Trump administration needs to be working now to guard against."

EXCLUSIVE: TRUMP ENVOY BLASTS SOUTH AFRICA OVER HATEFUL ‘KILL' CHANT, SAYS COUNTRY IS DRIFTING TOWARD US FOES

The U.S. Embassy in Addis Ababa took to its website to caution Americans in Ethiopia that it "is aware of reports of possible long-range attacks directed at Ethiopian military installations on several instances in October of this year. U.S. citizens should accordingly exercise caution and follow the advice of local authorities."

The Embassy also hit out at reported disinformation, "some social media accounts contain false and misleading reports about the security situation in Ethiopia. U.S. citizens are urged to verify information using multiple sources or reliable information."

Indeed, although explosions in and around Addis Ababa, mainly at military installations, can be confirmed as having taken place, it cannot be established that the frightening spectacle of drones crashing into buildings in a major African city which houses the headquarters of the African Union happened.

Requests for comment to the Ethiopian government were not returned.

TRUMP GETS MAJOR WIN AGAINST CHINA IN AFRICAN RARE EARTH MINERALS RACE

Dr. Jalale Getachew Birru, regional expert of the U.S.-based Armed Conflict Location and Event Data research group, told Fox News Digital this is potentially a worrying development. "If identified as an aerial or drone attack, they exceed the capabilities of Ethiopia’s domestic insurgent groups, confirming Ethiopia's allegation of foreign state involvement."

The rebel groups opposing Ethiopia’s government have joined together to form the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival. This coalition claimed responsibility for the Addis Ababa attacks, stating they used drones.

Blen Mamo, executive director of the Ethiopian Horn Review thinktank, is also concerned about a new phase of conflict using drones. Mamo told Fox News Digital, "should the Alliance for Survival possess drone capabilities, it could fundamentally alter the dynamics of the conflict, refocusing strategic control on aerial dominance."

In early October, Ethiopian troops pushed out rebel groups who had occupied the Tigrayan capital, Mekelle. This operation ended a four-year-long ceasefire between Ethiopia and Tigray, the northernmost province of Ethiopia.

Last week, reports claimed Eritrean troops had entered Ethiopia. Although the allegations have not been independently verified, Fox News Digital has seen multiple videos showing what appears to be large convoys of trucks carrying uniformed soldiers passing through the Ethiopian city of Adigrat. Addis Ababa is said to have subsequently launched drone attacks and pushed the Eritreans back over the border.

The latest fighting was sparked principally by Ethiopia’s statements that it wants to get access to Red Sea ports. The country became landlocked when Eritrea became independent in 1993. In a speech as he was sworn in for a new five-year term Oct. 5, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed said sea access was "of vital importance to Ethiopia’s civilization."

He added, "Based on the principle of give and take, we will work diligently to ensure that Ethiopia has an outlet to the sea."

US VISA CLASH EXPOSES SUDAN’S FORGOTTEN WAR AS FOREIGN POWERS COMPETE FOR STRATEGIC FOOTHOLD

Possible regional expansion of any conflict also comes from the creation of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. Egypt and Sudan are at odds with Addis Ababa, after it built the dam across the Blue Nile, affecting access to water to these countries which are downstream. Egypt this month took up a formal position against Ethiopia, when it created a coalition with Sudan, Eritrea and Somalia.

The State Department has been active diplomatically to try and resolve the situation. A spokesperson told Fox News Digital that Undersecretary of State for Political Affairs Allison Hooker met this month with Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh and spoke with Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timotheos.

Also, Assistant Secretary for African Affairs Frank Garcia met with Minister Saleh. The spokesperson added, "Both U.S. officials underscored the importance of respecting the sovereignty and territorial integrity for all countries in the Horn of Africa."

Following these discussions, State Department spokesman Thomas "Tommy" Piggott released a statement, saying, "Increasing cross-border tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea have the potential to affect the entire region. The Horn of Africa cannot sustain another military conflict and humanitarian crisis. A conflict jeopardizes ongoing U.S. collaboration on shared interests with both countries."

Piggott added, "We strongly urge Ethiopia and Eritrea to respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of their neighbors, exercise maximum restraint and return to dialogue and cooperation as agreed in their 2018 peace framework. Peace through dialogue is the only path toward sustainable security, economic growth, and prosperity."

The Horn Review’s Mamo told Fox News Digital the reality on the ground is "increasingly pointing toward a conflict that may prove impossible to avoid," and warned of Egypt’s motives: "Parallel military and technical cooperation with Asmara (the capital of Eritrea) also adds strategic depth along Ethiopia’s northern frontier, while Egypt’s expanding role in Somalia and Red Sea port initiatives extends its regional influence."

"The situation in Ethiopia and in the region is extremely dynamic," analyst Cameron Hudson told Fox News Digital. Hudson added, "The question remains, given the weakness of the internal (rebel) coalition, will external forces attempt to step in and exert greater leverage against Abiy."

He continued, "We are seeing Eritrea begin to move forces into Ethiopia, while a coalition of regional states including Somalia, Egypt, Sudan and Eritrea have issued a statement that amounts to a veiled threat against Ethiopia and its regional ambitions to establish a Red Sea naval presence and expand a series of hydroelectric dams on the Nile. The entire Horn of Africa region is on a knife’s edge and it is being made only more complicated by Houthi efforts to shut Red Sea shipping and the war in Iran."

"The risk of regional conflict remains high," Hudson said. "Egypt would be happy to see Ethiopia bogged down in internal conflict and unable to pursue its ambitions on the Nile and in the Red Sea. Similarly, Sudan hopes that internal conflict in Ethiopia distracts Addis from its support of the rapid support forces militia in Sudan’s war."

"Local disputes can quickly become regional and international disputes with global consequences very quickly in this corner of the world," Hudson added, "Closure of the Bab el Mandab Strait, owing to unchecked tensions and violence across the Red Sea, will quickly be felt in the U.S."

World.title: Social Security recipients will receive a 3.6% cost-of-living increase in 2027
World.content:
Social Security recipients will receive an annual cost-of-living adjustment next year of 3.6%, one of the largest increases this decade. But advocates say it’s still unlikely to go far enough for many struggling seniors.

It’s the largest adjustment since 2022, and will amount to an additional $75.15 per month on average, according to the Senior Citizens League, an advocacy group for older Americans.

Elevated inflation continues to bedevil the U.S. economy, with rising energy and gas prices sparked by wars in Iran and Ukraine as the primary culprits. Yet even without the added cost of gas, so-called core inflation — which excludes volatile energy and food prices — has remained stuck at about 2.5%, well above the Federal Reserve’s 2% target.

For senior citizens, who are the majority of Social Security retirement benefit recipients, next year’s increase will be welcome, but it will still come up short given rising costs, said Shannon Benton, the league’s executive director.

“Seniors have spent years watching their expenses outpacing their benefits,” Benton said. “This provides a little breathing room but won’t undo the damage of what we’ve seen this decade.”

The league found in a survey that 89% of older Americans thought the cost-of-living adjustment that kicked in this year, 2.8%, was inadequate given rising costs in the economy. About 44% of seniors draw all their income from Social Security, the survey found.

The annual adjustment is typically calculated using inflation data from July, August and September. But it uses an obscure inflation index that advocates say doesn’t accurately reflect seniors’ spending priorities, which include more medical and prescription drug costs, as well as a greater likelihood that they will pay rent and generally higher home energy costs.

Those categories have historically outpaced headline inflation, though the rate of medical-cost increases has slowed recently. One reform proposal would index the annual adjustment to more precisely reflect seniors’ needs — but Benton said it is unlikely to be adopted until all of Social Security is overhauled.

“They need Social Security benefits to cover the cost of living, and it’s just not happening,” she said.

World.title: Jon Ossoff says he won’t run for president in 2028 during heated Georgia debate
World.content:
Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., said Tuesday night during a debate that he will not run for president in 2028.

Ossoff made the statement in response to a question as he faced off with his Republican challenger, Rep. Mike Collins. Ossoff is seeking a second six-year term in Georgia and said he would serve the full term.

“I have zero interest in running for president,” Ossoff said when he was asked directly by one of the moderators. “I’m not running for president. I’m running for re-election to the Senate.”

Ossoff has been regularly discussed as a potential Democratic contender in 2028. If he were to win the presidency, he would have to give up his Senate seat, which he stressed Tuesday night that he would not do.

After the brief remark, Ossoff quickly transitioned to pressing Collins about why he has supported President Donald Trump’s tariffs, a main focus of both his campaign and a debate the two held last week. Tuesday was the second debate in the nationally watched Georgia Senate race, this one organized by the Atlanta Press Club.

Collins quipped that Ossoff was actually trying to run for president and will be “your DSA candidate,” a reference to the Democratic Socialists of America.

The exchange came at the beginning of the hourlong debate, which covered ground including data centers; the economy under Trump, whose approval rating is at record lows; the war in Iran; and the issue of Collins’ son-in-law’s promoting white nationalist posts on social media.

Ossoff asked Collins directly whether he considered himself a “white nationalist.”

“I condemn any sort of hate speech,” Collins said. “Antisemitism, hate of any kind. It’s abhorrent.”

The exchange continued when Collins again asked Ossoff to denounce Reid Hoffman, a major donor to Democratic causes — including Ossoff-aligned political committees — whose name appeared in the Epstein files. Collins brought up Hoffman several times last week and did so again during the second debate.

Ossoff did not directly respond, and he again pointed to the fact that those close to Collins amplified white nationalists’ posts.

“How weak a person do you have to be to be unable to stop someone under your own roof from disseminating neo-Nazi propaganda while you run for Senate?” Ossoff said. “The paper reported it’s still going on today.”

Given a chance to respond, Collins did not address it directly. But he said rhetoric like Ossoff’s had motivated a New York man who is accused of making death threats against him.

“I’m a little tired of this, Jon,” Collins said. “This crazy person is in jail right now because of your rhetoric.”

Neither candidate directly answered the other’s charges.

Collins also, once again, did not answer questions about whether or not Joe Biden won the 2020 presidential election. He was asked about audio of a call Trump made after the 2020 election asking Georgia Republican Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger to “find 11,780 votes” to help overturn the 2020 election.

“You know, Joe Biden went into office, and boy, Georgians paid for it,” Collins said.

World.title: Ukraine accuses SpaceX of restricting Starlink, disrupting military as it reels from intel gaps
World.content:
Ukraine has accused Elon Musk’s SpaceX of disrupting its military operations by limiting Starlink internet services, as the country reeled from a pair of intense Russian missile attacks that it said came without the usual advance warning from allies.

Facing pressure from President Donald Trump to halt strikes on Russia’s energy industry, Kyiv and its backers have worried Washington could cut off battlefield support to try and force it into concessions at the negotiating table.

Ukrainian officials and their European partners were already scrambling to understand the status of U.S. intelligence sharing after the lack of alert ahead of two Russian ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv this week caused confusion, two Ukrainian and two European officials told NBC News.

Trump insisted the U.S. was still sharing intel, but with relations spiraling Ukrainian officials and military units were on Wednesday accusing SpaceX of throttling a technology essential to their battlefield communications and drone operations.

It was not immediately clear what might be behind the Starlink interruptions, though some Ukrainian officials said the timing could not be a coincidence given that Musk is a close Trump ally.

Drone disruptions

SpaceX had introduced speed limits on the operation of its Starlink satellite internet terminals overnight, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s defense tech adviser, Serhii Beskrestnov.

“Our defence forces received no warning of such a restriction, and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” Beskrestnov said on Telegram. “It is obvious that this action cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation,” he added.

An army unit fighting in the southeastern Zaporizhzhia region said Wednesday it had been forced to cancel some planned operations.

The 7th Rapid Reaction Corps of the Ukrainian air assault forces said it began “noticing Starlink connectivity problems caused by data transfer speed limits” overnight, adding that the changes directly affected drones that use the service for in-flight control.

“The drones kept flying, but the interruptions made them harder to control,” it said in a statement.

Beskrestnov said that restrictions were specifically put on the operation of the military-grade version of Starlink at speeds above 100 mph.

Starlink was also key for Ukraine’s aerial defenses as it was used to intercept the jet-powered drones that Moscow has unleashed on Ukrainian cities in recent months, he added. Asked about the importance of the technology, Ukraine’s Charge d’Affaires to the U.S. Denys Sienik said “the technology helps us save the lives of civilians and prevent more destruction in Ukraine caused by the Russian side.”

World.title: Texas DA says ICE intentionally hit immigrant with a car and may have withheld evidence
World.content:
HOUSTON — Videos collected by local investigators make it “pretty obvious” that an ICE officer intentionally ran over Miguel Parra Hernandez during an immigration stop Saturday, which could lead to assault charges, the district attorney said Tuesday.

“This was an intentional striking and running over of the person by the vehicle, and in that case, that is an aggravated assault with a deadly weapon in Texas,” Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare told NBC News.

Teare said the federal government is not cooperating with the investigation conducted by his office and the Harris County Sheriff’s Office. He also said ICE may have allowed the erasure of critical data in the vehicle involved in striking Parra, who was on foot.

Teare said that in his seven years as a Harris County vehicular crimes division chief, he has reviewed video from a number of other auto-pedestrian collision cases. He said the video his investigators have gathered in Parra’s case “goes above” the video that was posted online and obtained by NBC affiliate KPRC of Houston.

“My viewing of it, and many other investigators that have viewed it, as well, it’s pretty obvious that this was an intentional striking and running over of the person by the vehicle, and in that case, that is an aggravated assault with a deadly weapon in Texas,” he said.

Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare. Raquel Natalicchio / Houston Chronicle via Getty

Parra, 48, was left with multiple breaks and fractures in his body, according to his attorney and an advocate who has been speaking on his behalf. He had surgery on one leg and faces multiple additional operations, said Cesar Espinosa, co-founder and executive director of FIEL, an immigrant civil rights group.

Video obtained by KPRC shows a white truck headed in the opposite direction of traffic on a busy roadway. It shows a vehicle jumping a yellow median and heading in the direction that Parra is running.

It then appears to show the vehicle, which is not marked, swerving left toward Parra’s path, in front of a truck stopped in a shopping center. The parked truck leaves, and a man can be seen on the pavement behind the ICE vehicle, the video shows.

An ICE spokesman said over the weekend that officers were pursuing the fleeing men and that “Miguel Parra Hernandez ran in front of an ICE vehicle and was struck.”

Teare, a Democrat, announced late Monday that his office had launched an independent investigation.

On Tuesday, an ICE spokesperson who was not identified said in a statement that “allegations that ICE struck Miguel Parra-Hernandez intentionally are RECKLESS and FALSE. The men and women of ICE are entrusted with upholding the rule of law and are held to the highest standards of professionalism, integrity, and ethical conduct.”

ICE said the allegations are “disgusting smears” that are “peddled by the media,” leading to more than a 1,600% increase in assaults and a 3,300% increase in vehicle attacks against its law enforcement officers. It did not offer data behind those numbers.

ICE has said that Parra was not the target of the attempted stop but that he was in the country illegally. Parra’s attorney and family have said he has no criminal record and was on his way to work applying stucco.

Teare said his office and the sheriff’s office determined that the vehicle that struck Parra was a Jeep Cherokee and that it potentially had evidence, including a data crash recorder. He said his office wanted to know whether the vehicle locked in information at the time of the collision that could be downloaded, such as speed, steering and braking. Teare said the way to preserve data from the car would have been to “put it on a flatbed trailer and you take it to forensically download it.”

But he said he believes any data on the recorder related to the incident could have been erased when ICE drove the car away.

He and the sheriff’s investigators told ICE the information needed to be downloaded, but ICE refused, Teare said.

ICE did not respond to questions about a data crash recorder, the erasing of any potential data or any refusal to download it.

“Our office began drafting a search warrant that we were in the process of drafting when the ICE agent in question, the one that had been driving, we believed, at the time of the collision, jumped back into the car and drove it away from the scene,” Teare said. “In my 20-year career, I’ve never heard of anything like that.”

Teare also said two people from “an entirely different operation” were in the back seat of the ICE vehicle when it struck Parra. Those two people are also in ICE custody, along with Parra. Teare said his office is working to ensure all three remain in the country as material witnesses.

“I’ve taught for years at the Houston Police Department Academy, Harris County Department Academy. I’ve worked with law enforcement for 20 years. There is not a single agency in the United States that would teach that once you put people in custody in your car, you then begin to pursue other people,” he said.

Doing so puts “every single person out there in danger again,” he said.

According to Teare, the ICE vehicle should have activated its emergency equipment, such as its lights and siren, as it jumped a median and crossed into oncoming traffic.

A senior official at the Department of Homeland Security told NBC News on Tuesday that multiple ICE officers on the scene at the time were wearing body cameras. ICE is reviewing video of the scene as part of an internal investigation, the official said.

Espinosa said Parra told him that he fled because it was unclear whether there were officials in the vehicles, which he said were unmarked, did not use sirens and had dark, tinted windows.

ICE has said it was targeting another man, Jose Mendoza Cervantes, who was in the country illegally and had committed several crimes. Espinoza and Parra’s attorney Kim Bruno said neither Parra nor the man who was with him when ICE stopped their vehicle has any association with Mendoza.

Miguel Parra Hernandez. Noticias Telemundo

In previous encounters between ICE and targets of its arrests in vehicle stops, including some who have been killed, such as Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston, ICE has alleged the people it tried to arrest weaponized their vehicles.

Parra was struck less than two weeks after the Trump administration issued guidance setting tighter rules for vehicle stops.

The guidance says only agents who have completed specific training should make vehicle stops. The memo also says that vehicles used for traffic stops must have lights and sirens and that all officers on the scenes of vehicle stops must wear and activate their body cameras.

The Harris County District Attorney’s Office has been asking witnesses and people who may have photos or video of the incident to contact it. Teare said that there is a secure portal that goes directly to the district attorney’s office and that no one is asked about citizenship or immigration status.

“All we are interested in is getting the truth, and any shred of cellphone footage, anyone that saw something and really can point us in the right direction, it would be wonderful,” he said.

World.title: Joni Mitchell becomes an American citizen after more than 60 years
World.content:
Joni Mitchell can see both sides of the U.S.-Canada border freely now.

The famed Canadian singer-songwriter shared a major milestone with fans on Tuesday, posing with an American flag to reveal she is officially a U.S. citizen. She also shared a clip of her citizenship ceremony in the Instagram post.

“A journey that began 62 years ago,” Mitchell’s caption said.

Mitchell, 82, was born and raised in Canada before moving to the U.S. with her then-husband in the 1960s. She lived in Detroit and New York City before eventually settling in the Laurel Canyon area of Los Angeles.

Her fans might say that Mitchell is synonymous with California, considering her hit song named after the state on her beloved 1971 album “Blue.”

“Oh, California, I’m coming home,” Mitchell sang in the song. “Oh, make me feel good rock ‘n roll band. I’m your biggest fan. California, I’m coming home.”

Joni Mitchell outside The Revolution club in London in 1968. Hulton Archive / Getty

And although Mitchell has not been a U.S. citizen until now, that hasn’t stopped her from speaking out about American politics.

She wrote “The Fiddle and the Drum” in 1969 in protest of the Vietnam war. Mitchell’s lyrics urged America to find peace as the world had “all come to fear the beating of your drum.”

Mitchell also lashed out at tax exemptions for religious institutions in the 1980s in the song “Tax Free.” She called out the United States in the lyrics as well as religious leaders who call for large donations while “preaching love like hate.”

Most recently, Mitchell was on stage at the Hollywood Bowl in 2024 when she made her current political opinions clear. She was performing with singer Brandi Carlile, according to Billboard, when she told the crowd, “‘F--- Donald Trump.’ I love that song.”

World.title: Romance scammers are getting harder to catch. The consequences are costly.
World.content:
For people looking for love online, a match with a scammer could cost them their life savings.

A congressional investigation, which began in September 2025 and lasted about a year, found that Tinder’s scam detection systems struggled for years to keep fraudulent accounts off the dating app. Parent company Match Group has since moved to address the shortcomings with new verification requirements and upgraded detection technology.

Romance scams have become a leading form of financial fraud in the U.S., costing Americans nearly $1.5 billion in reported losses last year, according to the Federal Trade Commission.

Sens. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., and Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn. Getty

“There’s a lot of stigma to being a victim to scams,” Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., who launched the investigation alongside Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., said in an interview last week. “People should understand that really sophisticated people who are doing all the right things are still getting scammed because of the level of technology and resources that these criminal enterprises now do.”

Scammers today can realistically pose as representatives from familiar organizations like the local YMCA or a bank, and the accessibility of AI tools makes it easier than ever to research family members and mimic their voices. But romance scams, Hassan said, can be particularly emotionally devastating.

That was the case for Pennsylvania resident Sue Nuss, who told Congress’ Joint Economic Committee about her experience turning to Tinder in search of companionship after she lost her husband. There, she met a man who claimed to be from New Jersey.

I fell prey because of my personality and because I was lonely. And I was very ashamed of what happened. -Sue nuss, who spoke to Congress’ Joint Economic Committee about her experience turning to Tinder in search of companionship.

Nuss told NBC News that, over a month and a half, he won her trust with words that made her feel like he really “sees” and “understands” her.

The committee’s report, published Tuesday, stated that the man duped Nuss with a series of “fabricated” crises: job problems on an oil rig, an arrest in Mexico, his mom’s stroke and even her funeral — all excuses to ask Nuss, 77, for money. When the scammers behind the profile tried to trick her into believing the man she was dating had died, she said, she realized it was all a scam.

“I have always been a very giving person my entire life, and I’ve always been a caregiver,” Nuss told NBC News last week. “And I fell prey. I was very vulnerable. I fell prey because of my personality and because I was lonely. And I was very ashamed of what happened.”

Days after what she thought was a budding online relationship fell apart, Nuss’ scammer showed back up on Tinder with the same profile, she said in an interview.

Soon, another group approached her claiming they could recover what she had lost. Then, through an elaborate cryptocurrency scheme, that group managed to scam even more money from Nuss. She believes both scammer groups were connected, the report stated. It added that, in total, she lost more than $700,000.

“I struggle. Some days are really bad days and some days are good days. I do get therapy. I’m starting a very special therapy next week called EMDR because it’s a trauma,” Nuss said. “I don’t trust my decisions now.”

Congress last month passed the Romance Scam Prevention Act, which would require online dating service providers to notify and warn any users who get messaged by potential scammers. The bill awaits President Donald Trump’s signature.

This summer, Hassan also introduced legislation with Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., to create a central reporting portal for victims of scams, an initiative that she said could give the federal government the tools to detect patterns in scams to shut them down more effectively.

Scammers stole more than $1 trillion globally in one year, according to a 2024 report from the Global Anti-Scam Alliance.

“Enterprises that run scams are now costing the global economy more than the illicit drug trade does,” Hassan said. “This is really important for individuals. It’s really important for our economy. And so, the more people speak up about the need to change the way the federal government handles scams, the faster it’s going to happen.”

The Joint Economic Committee’s investigation sought to combat the prevalence of romance scams on platforms owned by Match Group, the biggest online dating company in the world, with a portfolio that includes Tinder, Hinge, Match and Plenty of Fish.

It found that during the first nine months of 2025, nearly 1.5 million scammers or other bad actors on Tinder and Hinge matched with someone. Nearly 500,000 of those accounts then exchanged contact information with other users.

Internal documents shared voluntarily with the committee noted that most of Tinder’s machine-learning detection scam models hadn’t been updated in years, and Match Group staff members found that scammers could quickly circumvent the company’s patchwork detection rules. Excessive false positives also overwhelmed the human moderators trying to detect dangerous accounts.

The committee wrote that it welcomes the changes Match Group has made to address those concerns.

Match Group deployed new detection models throughout the latter half of 2025 and the first half of 2026 to better catch bad actors, according to the committee’s report. This year, it introduced 169 automated rules and “improved” 108 others aimed at targeting and removing inauthentic actors.

One of its key rollouts is a mandatory biometric face check for all new users on Tinder and Hinge, meant to prevent users from making multiple accounts and ensure banned users can’t make new accounts.

Yoel Roth, Match Group’s senior vice president of trust and safety, told NBC News the company is “grateful the Committee recognized our significant advancements to protect our users against romance scams.”

“That said, the report mischaracterizes both the historical scale of our investment and the work already completed. Alongside our engagement with the Committee over the past year, we’ve made the largest safety advancements in Match Group’s history,” Roth wrote in a statement. “Trust and Safety is a foundational priority, and we intend to continue leading the industry in building tools that promote authentic, safe connections.”

Much of that safety work, including the face checks, was already underway before the committee’s investigation, according to Match Group. It reports having seen a roughly 60% reduction in exposure to bad actors in every market since the face checks began.

Hassan similarly said those measures have “already been successful in dramatically reducing the number of matches that their customers have with a scammer.”

“They need to do more, though, because there are still gaps in their systems,” she added. “And they are going to need to stay vigilant in new ways, because the criminals are always changing their technology and their tactics, too.”

World.title: Netflix cutting workforce as its revenue growth slows
World.content:
Netflix said it is laying off roughly 6% of its workforce, according to a memo to employees obtained by CBS News.

The cuts will impact the company's product, technology, legal and human resources departments, Netflix co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters wrote in the memo.

"Our business is strong and growing, and we remain on track to deliver our full-year forecast," Sarandos and Peters said. "We'll continue to invest aggressively in high-impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation. Doing that means making focused choices across the business so we can keep delivering for our members, partners, employees, and investors."

Netflix declined further comment on the planned layoffs.

The news was first reported by the Wall Street Journal. The news outlet said Netflix's job cuts will impact roughly 1,000 positions globally, the company's largest workforce reduction since 2022.

Netflix had roughly 16,000 full-time employees as of December 2025, according to a securities filing.

Although Netflix remains highly profitable, its growth has slowed in recent years amid mounting competition from other streaming platforms and a saturated North American market.

Netflix shares, which traded at just below $70 each on Wednesday, have fallen nearly 43% over the last 12 months.
