World.title: Who else besides Danielle Smith is saying 'yes to the nine' in Alberta's referendum?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It’s long appeared that the pro-unity side in Alberta’s referendum would prevail; polling suggests the separatists will lose by a three-to-one margin next week.

Polling is closer on the other nine questions, but Danielle Smith put them to voters, believing she had sure winners.

While she has repeatedly advocated for the “stay” option when asked, she’s focused most of her rhetoric — and the $4 million government advertising campaign — on the referendum’s proverbial undercard, the questions proposing immigration and constitutional reform.

But aside from that taxpayer-funded push, there’s been little public advocacy for Questions 1-9.

Contrast that with the more visible “No to the Nine” campaign that has cropped up alongside maple leafs on many federalist lawns to push against Smith’s questions and the premier herself.

Though Smith designed the questions to be easy wins among her base and the general public alike, they’ve become a target of both the premier’s anti-separatist detractors, as well as prominent separatists, who treat the questions with either scorn or indifference.

Senior officials in Smith’s United Conservative Party privately say they’re concerned that voters could reject at least some of the questions. If it’s a really bad night, they could lose all of them.

Smith announced the nine questions back in February, months before she added the 10th — the referendum to hold a referendum. She’d crafted them based on some of the most popular ideas from her Alberta Next panel in 2025, which was created to suggest future referendum topics that weren’t stay-or-leave.

Opposition to the nine immigration and constitutional questions has become a central part of some pro-Canadian referendum campaigns. (Jason Markusoff/CBC)

In provincially commissioned polls and an online survey last year, the Smith government found wide support for wresting more control over immigration from Ottawa, denying non-permanent residents access to provincial programs, and trying to amend the Constitution to tilt the scales toward the province — and higher opposition to an Alberta-only pension plan, police force or tax collection agency.

“We think we've done that initial culling of the questions to make sure that we found the ones that are likely to get majority support,” Smith told reporters in April.

Translation: the premier crafted these questions because she believed they’d arm her with fresh ammunition against Ottawa, and that voters would rally around her tough-on-immigration stance.

But aside from her own government’s TV ads, billboards and booklets, there have been scant few voices trying to push the nine into the winner’s column. That said, the $4 million spent amounts to more than double the combined $1.8 million raised as of last week by the various pro- and anti-independence groups, according to Elections Alberta disclosures .

Few prominent conservative Albertans, on either side of that stark independence divide, echo Smith’s call to endorse action on immigration and constitutional measures.

The lesser-known group Alberta Women for Independence is one of the few organizations whose blue pro-separation signs also encourage yes votes for the nine questions.

But after its leader Kathy Flett treated a pro-independence town hall in Medicine Hat to a detailed slide presentation on the merits of all nine referendum proposals last week, the more prominent separatist leader Keith Wilson brushed off their importance.

“These other nine questions are — I’m sorry, they’re a political gimmick. They mean nothing,” Wilson said, before later noting he’d vote yes to them, anyhow.

One of the few pro-independence signs that also urges yes votes on the other referendum questions. (Jason Markusoff/CBC)

Some separatists are frustrated because they don’t like the abstract nature of the independence ballot question, or that Smith diluted the referendum with questions that she didn’t have to put directly to voters.

Jeffrey Rath of Alberta Prosperity Project is urging people to “decline the 9” entirely — even as APP itself is trying to educate voters about what those other questions are.

“The nine questions are a deflection from the independence question,” Rath wrote last week on social media . “They are Smith’s built in excuse not to pursue independence!”

Many conservatives have focused exclusively on Question 10, including Alberta’s federal Conservative MPs and former cabinet minister Monte Solberg’s group Vote to Stay.

Former premier Jason Kenney, one of the unity side’s most active conservative voices, has questioned whether the nine questions needed to be referendums, and said some of them even confused him, a former federal immigration minister.

Contrast all that to the array of people pushing against the nine questions, particularly the ones seeking to restrict the social services that non-permanent residents receive.

In a rare show of bipartisan unity, former Progressive Conservative premiers Ed Stelmach and Alison Redford joined NDP counterpart Rachel Notley in a newspaper op-ed Wednesday urging “no” votes on the immigration ballots, warning they’ll harm Alberta’s economy and ability to attract workers.

The Calgary Chamber of Commerce has also been highlighting immigrants’ contributions to society, while its CEO Deborah Yedlin has warned Smith’s suggested $1,900-per-migrant health care fee would be a burdensome “extra cost” for employers.

Christian leaders have taken the unusual step of weighing in , albeit without directly telling parishioners how to vote.

A joint letter from Alberta’s Catholic bishops called on people to “respect human dignity and avoid making any segment of our population the object of resentment or blame," while a letter from Anglican bishops reminded supporters of Scripture’s “call to welcome and care for strangers and sojourners in their midst.”

Labour unions have also argued for “no” votes down the line, including CUPE Alberta’s “no to scapegoating” video that emphasizes how little services for temporary residents cost the provincial treasury.

“It just reinforces that these questions were not wanted by anyone except Danielle Smith,” said Stephen Carter of Alberta’s Voice, the third-party advertising group behind the “No to the Nine” signs.

“She wrote them. She promoted them. And everyone else opposes them.”

Stephen Carter's group Alberta's Voice is behind one of the most visible opposition campaigns against the immigration and constitutional ballot questions. (Sam Martin/CBC)

As much as Smith believed they were winners, the nine questions haven’t been slam dunks in the polls.

Last month’s Janet Brown Opinion Research poll for CBC News said 52 per cent of respondents oppose limiting access to health and education to temporary immigrants, while 45 per cent agree. There was moderately more support for Alberta taking more control over its immigration (54 per cent agree, 42 per cent disagree) and for constitutional changes (49 per cent agree, 45 percent disagree).

A Research Co. survey in late August, meanwhile, found that support for the five immigration questions ranged between 58 and 66 percent, while views on the constitutional questions were more tepid — between 39 and 46 per cent support.

WATCH | Do Albertans know what they're being asked to vote on?: Many Albertans unaware of 9 other ballot questions | Duration closed caption 2:03 Less than three weeks ahead of Alberta's referendum on whether to seek a vote on separation from Canada, many Albertans seem unaware of the nine other questions on the ballot that involve thorny issues around immigration and constitutional reform.

But undermining those numbers is what appears to be widespread confusion and uncertainty about what those wordy questions are asking of Albertans. Brown’s poll suggested that close to half of Albertans didn’t know how they’d vote or weren’t familiar with the referendum ballot’s lesser-known nine.

As if to prove this confusion and lack of familiarity, the United Conservative Party issued its first message last week to its mailing list trying to explain and promote all nine questions. It was 1,708 words long. (It also didn’t tell the party’s backers how to vote on Question 10, perhaps unsurprisingly because of how split UCP ranks are on separation.)

The governing party doesn’t appear to have engaged in any door knocking or get-out-the-vote campaigns on the referendum. The opposition NDP, meanwhile, have been trying to activate pro-unity voters, with flyers that say “Vote to remain. No to the rest.”

The general lack of non-taxpayer-funded, on-the-ground campaigning may have already cost Smith. The Janet Brown poll showed that among Albertans who do know how they’ll vote on the nine, half will follow the “no the nine” mantra, while some will vote no to some and yes to others.

Only about one in 10 planned to fulfil Smith’s request and mark nine yeses.

Given that nearly half of committed voters would choose the UCP, that means a sizable contingent of Smith’s own political backers are not readily following her wishes into the ballot box.

World.title: Father receives life sentence in New York for murder of Montreal girl
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Montreal man has been sentenced to life in prison for killing his nine-year-old daughter and leaving her in a marsh in rural New York.

The sentence comes two months after a jury in Essex County Court convicted Luciano Frattolin of second-degree murder and concealment of a human corpse in the death of Melina Frattolin.

Judge Tatiana Coffinger delivered the sentence after rejecting a motion to set aside the guilty verdict.

Frattolin would not be eligible for parole before 25 years. Coffinger also sentenced Frattolin to one to three years for concealment of a corpse. That sentence will be served consecutively.

The defence issued a notice of appeal following the sentence.

Melina had been living in Montreal with her mother, and had gone on a road trip to the U.S. with her father in July 2025.

On the night they were scheduled to return home, Frattolin called police, reporting that his daughter had been kidnapped after he had stopped the car he was driving on the side of the road.

During the three-week-long trial, the defence argued that local police had not adequately investigated Frattolin's claims that his daughter was kidnapped.

The prosecution called on several police officers and experts, however, who used car location data, cellphone data and surveillance camera footage to recreate Frattolin's movements on the day his daughter died and prove his story was false.

The jury spent an hour deliberating on Aug. 10 at the end of the trial, before concluding that Frattolin had drowned his daughter in a marsh in a rural area of New York.

World.title: Unexpected leader: Lorne Doerkson pitches himself to British Columbians
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Looking out on Williams Lake from his two-storey rancher, his Corgi-cross Jacksy fighting for his attention, Lorne Doerkson is the first person to admit he did not set out to become the leader of the B.C. Conservative Party.

"Of course, it was a little bit of a short notice," Doerkson says, in his signature understated tone.



Doerkson was on a flight home from South Africa when he learned his caucus colleagues tapped him as the safest choice.

It came hours after Kerry-Lynne Findlay resigned as leader, following four months of scandals that led to the departure or expulsion of more than a dozen MLAs..

Those MLAs have since returned to the party fold and are running as candidates.

While people across the political spectrum describe Doerkson, 58, as a nice guy, he's an unelected and largely unknown leader finding his feet amid a snap election.

Andrew Reeve, a former B.C. Liberal communications director who worked alongside Doerkson in that caucus, said that could be a source of strength.

WATCH | Lorne Doerkson pitches himself to British Columbians: Unexpected leader: Lorne Doerkson pitches himself to British Columbians | Duration closed caption 2:58

"There's that old adage of perhaps we should give power to those who don't seek it, and I think that really fits the type of guy that Lorne is," Reeve said. "The person that'll lend you their truck or they'll give you a ride home from the airport."

Several recent opinion polls suggest the B.C. Conservatives are ahead of David Eby's NDP.

"I think that we've got definitely wind in our sails right now," Doerkson said.

Doerkson was first elected as a B.C. Liberal in the Cariboo-Chilcotin riding in 2020.

His predecessor in the riding, Donna Barnett, says she knew Doerkson would be a strong MLA based on his commitment to his community.



He's often found at fundraisers flipping burgers on a customized trailer called the Funchaser.

Lorne Doerkson outside his home with the barbecue trailer he takes to fundraisers. (CBC News)



There hasn't been a premier from B.C.'s Interior since Bill Bennett, who left office in 1986.

Barnett is confident Doerkson is set to break that dry spell.

"You betcha. There's no doubt. The qualities he has, he cares about people of all walks of life."

Doerkson has lived in Williams Lake with his wife Shelley for 25 years.

He has two adult daughters, Miranda and Shelby, and a six-year-old granddaughter.

Born in New Westminster, Doerkson grew up in Salmon Arm.

He had a short-lived fling as a rodeo rider in his early 20s, then moved on to a career in publishing for community newspapers, including the Williams Lake Tribune.

While the B.C. Conservatives insist they are united behind Doerkson, some of Findlay's supporters have accused the party of overturning the leadership election results and installing a former B.C. Liberal into the position.

Doerkson will likely face the same challenges as his predecessors, bringing together social conservatives and more centrist, fiscal conservatives in his caucus.

"I'm a little bashful when it comes to my guitar playing and rodeo career, but I think that's where I do bring some strength. I'm a broad-thinking person ... who is absolutely convinced that we can do better in this province. And I believe those conversations have been pretty robust in our caucus."

In the last three weeks on the campaign trail, Doerkson says a B.C. Conservative government would not raise taxes or introduce new ones, and pledged to slash every British Columbian's income taxes by $1,000 a year.



However, he's offered few details on how much such promises would cost taxpayers, leading to accusations from the NDP that the only way to achieve that is through deep cuts to health care and education.

"A snap election basically forced him into the situation and he's figuring [it] out as it goes," said Reeve, now a senior public affairs consultant with Earnscliffe.

B.C. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson speaks during a Greater Vancouver Board of Trade event on Oct. 13, 2026. (Nav Rahi/CBC)



Doerkson promised to repeal the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA), and co-operate with First Nations across the province to unlock B.C.'s natural resources, which he says have been choked by NDP government red tape.

Doerkson has already had his leadership tested during this campaign.

Within hours, he dropped the party's candidate for Victoria-Beacon Hill, Joachim Agou, after offensive social media posts surfaced.

WATCH | B.C. Conservative Victoria-Beacon Hill candidate dropped after offensive posts: B.C. Conservative Victoria-Beacon Hill candidate dropped after offensive posts | Duration closed caption 2:47



Doerkson now faces calls from a coalition of Muslim associations to fire the party's campaign manager, Katy Merrifield.

Merrifield posted "f--k Islam," in response to a story about an inquiry into gang rapes in the United Kingdom. Merrifield says her post stemmed from her experience as a rape survivor.

Musa Ismail, director of the Unified Muslim Associations of B.C., says no B.C. Conservative candidate will be allowed into mosques until Doerkson removes Merrifield from the position.



Elenore Sturko, who once served alongside Doerkson in the B.C. Conservative caucus but is now leader of CentreBC, says he must show leadership by firing Merrifield.

"Can you really be an appropriate leader for the province when you're not able to stand up for all British Columbians?" Sturko said.

CBC News has not been able to put a question directly to Doerkson in response to the call from the Unified Muslim Associations of B.C.

Doerkson will put forward his vision for B.C. when he faces Eby and B.C. Green Party Leader Emily Lowan during the televised leaders debate on Wednesday.

World.title: Family of Manitoba woman who died after dental procedure says association has 'conflict of interest' issues
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Manitoba is one of the last remaining provinces whose dental associations also regulate the profession and investigate complaints against dentists — a structure the family of a young woman who died after a procedure says raises conflict of interest concerns.

Virginia Blatz, 23, was pronounced dead in hospital after she went to see Dr. Ronald Janz at the Boundary Trails Dental Centre in Morden to have her wisdom teeth removed on Nov. 27, 2024, according to a statement of claim filed by her father, Dulaney Blatz.

In the nearly two years since her daughter's death, Victoria Blatz said the Manitoba Dental Association — which is both the provincial regulator and industry advocacy group — has maintained a "code of silence" about its investigation, and that the family has been "kept in the dark."

The family's former lawyer got a letter from the dental association's legal counsel in September, saying information wasn't being shared with them because the organization's registrar is the official complainant under rules set out in the Dental Association Act.

The family filed a separate formal complaint against Janz this spring. They also filed a lawsuit against the dentist , claiming the care he provided to Virginia led to her death. The lawsuit was filed in Manitoba's Court of King's Bench late last month.

According to the dental association's registry , Janz is restricted in his ability to administer local anesthetic drugs. He is allowed to administer them if he's under supervision.

The family believes the association's two functions — advocating for the interests of dentists and protecting the public — are brushing up against each other.

Blatz's parents say they have been 'kept in the dark' about the Manitoba Dental Association's investigation into her death. (Submitted by Dulaney and Victoria Blatz)

"It's a conflict of interest. You've got too much sympathy for when something like this happens…. It has felt that they have advocated solely almost for the dentist and themselves," Victoria said.

"That whole body really needs to be dismantled, and it needs to be made into a body that reports to the government and to the public, just like they do in other provinces."

Manitoba and New Brunswick are the last remaining Canadian provinces where a single group handles these two roles, Dr. Jack Gerrow, executive director of the Canadian Dental Regulatory Authorities Federation, confirmed in an interview.

Dulaney said he believes there is a serious "conflict of interest" within this dual-role structure, likening the province's dental association to an "Old Boys club," adding the family's interactions with the group left them feeling frustrated.

"It needs to be shut down, and we need to put something better in place for Manitobans," he said.

"Change should have come a long time ago, before Virginia got into that dentist's chair."

University of Toronto bioethicist Kerry Bowman agrees. He says it's "absolutely an inherent conflict of interest" for associations to act as both a professional industry group and a regulatory body.

Bowman believes the two functions largely have "opposite goals" that could cause friction between each other.

"I think it's very naive to think that these things can be merged," he said.

University of Toronto bioethicist Kerry Bowman says there's an 'inherent conflict of interest' when professional associations also act as regulatory bodies. (Craig Chivers/CBC)

The dental association said in an email to CBC News that "having these two functions within one statutory body does not, in itself, mean an investigation is conflicted or that professional advocacy influences its outcome."

Manitoba's Dental Association Act gives the association regulatory authority in the province, and the group says it "has a duty to protect the public" when it receives complaints. Complaint investigations are "kept separate from the MDA's member services and advocacy activities," the statement said.

The association said dentists are involved in investigations because their clinical expertise is necessary to discern whether standards of practice were followed. However, it says conflicts — whether actual or perceived — are "identified and managed through disclosure, recusal and exclusion from decision-making."

Manitoba association an outlier within Canada

Dental associations across Canada have been shifting away from this dual role for decades.

Ontario has long had a separation between the Ontario Dental Association and the Royal College of Dental Surgeons of Ontario. More recently, Alberta's dental association and regulatory college became two distinct groups in 2022, after the government introduced new rules requiring regulators and industry groups to separate.

Blatz's parents filed a lawsuit regarding her death in Manitoba's Court of King's Bench in late September. (Submitted by Dulaney and Victoria Blatz)

Last year, Manitoba's western neighbour, Saskatchewan, saw the College of Dental Surgeons of Saskatchewan start the process of splitting into two independent organizations.

The Manitoba government has slowly been shifting health professions in the province to regulation under the Regulated Health Professions Act, which was proclaimed in 2014.

The province started talks with the dental association last year to bring industry oversight under the act, a provincial spokesperson said in a statement to CBC News.

The legislation doesn't allow regulatory colleges to also serve as professional advocacy groups, the province said.

The act already governs a handful of health professions in the province, including doctors, nurses, registered psychiatric nurses, audiologists, speech language pathologists and paramedics. All health professions in Manitoba will eventually be regulated under the act.

Process of splitting to start next year: association

Health Minister Uzoma Asagwara told reporters on Oct. 7 that shifting regulation of the dental sector to the act is about "enhancing accountability" and "supporting transparency" among health professions, suggesting it will ultimately make care "better and safer" for Manitobans.

"You separate the regulatory body from the more advocacy arm of the organization. So previously, where lines might seem a little blurry, there's clarity that's created," the minister said, adding the move is "modernizing the way that these organizations function."

The dental association said it has informed the province it plans to start the formal transition to the act in 2027. The association expects the process to take between two to three years.

Manitoba Health Minister Uzoma Asagwara speaks to reporters during a media scrum on Oct. 7. Asagwara says shifting regulation of the dental sector is about 'enhancing accountability.' (Randall McKenzie/CBC)

Once it completes the shift, dental regulation and public protection would become the responsibility of a separate body called the College of Dentists of Manitoba. Meanwhile, the association would keep its name and remain a professional organization representing dentists in the province.

Bowman, the Toronto-based bioethicist, said he believes it's "wise" for governments to step in and encourage more division between these roles, particularly at a time when patient trust in medical professionals has been dwindling.

"Patient trust matters. The vast majority of patients …, when they become aware that these two things are merged — regulatory and professional — they're very concerned that this is not a proper assessment of their circumstances at all, and that it's not objective," he said.

Bowman said divorcing the regulatory and advocacy sides of the association will take time and effort to get it right, but he believes the move will buoy public confidence.

"I'm not going to say it's going to solve all problems, but it's going to increase trust," he said.

"They really have to be separated."

Lengthy investigation a 'denial of justice'

University of Manitoba ethicist Arthur Schafer said the investigation into Virginia Blatz's death is taking so long that it "almost passes the boundary of belief," calling the more than 22-month delay a "denial of justice."

Schafer said the family and the wider public are entitled to know what happened and who is responsible. Without these answers, Manitobans will lose confidence in the association, he said.

"Dentists depend upon public trust — all health-care professionals do. They can't practise their profession unless they're trusted by the public. If the dental association is so lacking in transparency when things go wrong …, then it will soon lose the trust of the public," he said.

"Families are entitled to know, and the public is entitled to know what went wrong, whether anyone was blameworthy, whose responsibility — if anyone's — it is for this tragedy."

University of Manitoba ethics expert Arthur Schafer says the public will lose trust in the dental association if they believe it's not being transparent. (Submitted by Arthur Schafer)

The dental association said in a statement that it "recognizes the profound loss Virginia Blatz's family has experienced" and "continues to carry out its responsibilities under the Dental Association Act."

The organization said it's "bound by legal, privacy, and procedural-fairness obligations that limit what it can say before the process reaches its public stage" in order to "protect the integrity of the investigation and the fairness of the process for all involved."

These obligations are "not a means of avoiding accountability," the association said.

If Virginia's case moves on to a formal inquiry, the hearing will generally be open to the public, unless there's any legally required restrictions, the statement said.

The dental association said it will share more information "as soon as it is legally permitted and procedurally appropriate."

World.title: Canada paused Black Hawk helicopter deal over Trump's trade war: sources
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Liberal government quietly ordered a pause on a modest, but important purchase of 16 U.S.-made UH-60M Black Hawk helicopters just before trade negotiations began last summer with the Trump administration, CBC News and Radio-Canada have learned.

The aircraft, which are intended for use by Canada's special forces, are manufactured by Sikorsky, a subsidiary of the U.S. defence giant Lockheed Martin.

The decision to suspend the acquisition is linked to trade and diplomatic tensions with the Trump administration, according to several sources within the government and defence industry.

The purchase had been signed off by the U.S. State Department agency that handles foreign military sales and was headed for congressional approval when the halt was ordered before trade negotiators met in Washington, according to two confidential sources.

The decision, the sources said, was partially related to the trade talks, which ultimately failed. It was also part of a wider effort by federal officials to inventory what the Canadian military planned to purchase from the United States.

U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly questioned Canadian sovereignty since being re-elected. He has also launched a major trade war with Canada, imposing tariffs on key sectors such as steel, aluminum and automotive manufacturing.

As Canada seeks to reduce its military reliance on the United States, the government decided that the timing was not right to purchase American helicopters without a competitive bidding process, several sources said.

CBC News is not identifying the sources because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

Since being elected in the spring of 2025, Prime Minister Mark Carney has made it a priority to boost domestic defence industrial production, establish partnerships with foreign firms operating in Canada and — only as a last resort — purchase directly from abroad.

The pause on the Black Hawk purchase comes as the Carney government continues to review whether it will purchase a full order of F-35 stealth fighters, which are also manufactured by Lockheed Martin.

The government ordered a review of that plan in the late winter of 2025 and has yet to decide whether it will buy all 88 fighters as originally planned.

Canada has committed to buy 16 F-35s, but has also ordered the parts for more than a dozen others.

Government 'continues to evaluate options'

Whenever Canada — or other countries — buy U.S. military gear, the purchaser is required to request permission through the U.S. Foreign Military Sales program.

Once reviewed by officials, the deal is sent to American lawmakers who have 15 days to object before it becomes official.

A spokesperson for Stephen Fuhr, the secretary of state overseeing Canada's military procurement, suggested options other than the Black Hawks could be considered.

"The government of Canada continues to evaluate options to meet the needs of the special operations forces," said Sofiya Sapeha.

"Canada remains in contact with the relevant partners and continues to review all information necessary for decision-making."

A Black Hawk helicopter is seen on display in Kielce, Poland, last month. A defence expert tells CBC News that the U.S.-made helicopter is well suited for Arctic operations. (Kacper Pempel/Reuters)

The Black Hawks are intended to replace the special forces' use of the CH-146 Griffon, which is more than three decades old and significantly inferior in terms of military operations.

One of the reasons Canada's commandos were keen on the Black Hawk was because of its range and robustness for operations over vast distances in the Arctic.

The UH-60 has a typical combat radius of about 595 kilometres, which can be extended by air-to-air refuelling. In that case, its range goes out to 2,250 kilometres. The Griffon's normal combat range is up to 656 kilometres, but can be fitted with external fuel tanks that take it up to 909 kilometres.

Special forces have been using the Griffon since their inception as a separate unit within the Canadian military in the early 1990s. The helicopter is currently flown by 427 Special Operations Aviation Squadron.

Retired major-general Denis Thompson, who commanded special operations troops, said the difference between the two helicopters is stark.

"In some ways you're comparing apples and oranges because a Griffon is a small, agile helicopter better suited for temperate climates and frankly better suited for urban operations than something as large as a Black Hawk," Thompson said.

"Range is important and the fact that it's a military design, a helicopter designed expressly for the military, means that it is just more robust and it can stand up to more punishment than the Griffon."

Thompson questioned the political calculus, but said he understands the way Canadians feel about the Trump administration.

"When we buy a piece of equipment, we're not hanging on to it for the two years that are left in Mr. Trump's mandate," Thompson said. "We're hanging on to them for 20, 30 years. And so what's important is to make sure that we buy the equipment that Canadian Armed Forces need and that we look to the long-term and not short-term political gain."

Low public support for buying American

Earlier this year, Policy Magazine published the results of a poll that indicated that 62 per cent of Canadians disagree with purchasing military equipment from the United States. Similarly, Abacus Data found that 64 per cent support an immediate halt to U.S. military purchases.

"I know it's difficult to explain that to the public, but that's what needs to be done," said Thompson.

He said equipment like the Black Hawk and F-35 weren't selected "for political reasons, at least not from the military standpoint. They were selected because they are the best piece, the most suitable piece, of equipment to fulfil the task that the military believes it might have to fill."

Defence analyst Justin Massie said the government is also clearly grappling with military procurement projects that were set in motion before the trade tensions began.

WATCH | Canada-U.S. trade minister on state of negotiations: Canada not 'desperate' to get a U.S. trade deal 'at any cost,' says minister | Duration closed caption 1:27 Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc says comments from U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer that the Trump administration is not in a rush to make a deal with Canada are 'consistent with the conversations' he's had with his U.S. counterpart. LeBlanc says the government will keep working to reach an agreement, but 'we're not waiting by the phone.'

"What is changing is not so much the strategy as the political discomfort of publicly announcing purchases of American military equipment." said Massie, a political science professor at Université du Québec à Montréal.

A spokesperson for Lockheed Martin highlighted the firm's willingness to continue working with the Canadian Armed Forces, without commenting on the status of the acquisition process.

"We are ready to support international customers wishing to acquire the latest-generation UH-60M Black Hawk helicopter through the Foreign Military Sales program," said the spokesperson, Amanda Hauck.

Other projects stalled

According to government and defence industry sources, Ottawa is hesitating to approve further military purchases from the United States, or even announce contracts already signed with American firms.

For instance, a recent Department of National Defence contract for specialized cloud computing services with California-based Google has not yet been announced. This contract involves storing and protecting classified information related to national security.

Another contract for a ground vehicle crew training system is reportedly slated for the U.S. firm Raytheon but has not been announced, sources say.

Earlier this year, the government waited months before confirming a contract to purchase M142 High Mobility Artillery Rocket Systems (HIMARS) from Lockheed Martin.

World.title: A man's death on a U.S. roller-coaster triggered closures in Canada. Are the rides safe?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canadians can still feel safe riding roller-coasters after Tuesday's death at a Six Flags amusement park in the U.S., experts tell CBC News, because such accidents are "stunningly rare."

Police say a 42-year-old man killed while riding the Goliath roller-coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia, in Mableton, Ga., was thrown from his seat and struck other patrons before landing below the ride. Several others were injured.

Nine similar roller-coasters at six North American parks have been closed "out of an abundance of caution," according to a Six Flags Entertainment Corp. spokesperson, including two at Canada's Wonderland near Toronto and one at Montreal's La Ronde amusement park.

Doug Perovic, a professor in materials science and engineering at the University of Toronto, says he's ridden the same Goliath coaster at California's Six Flags Magic Mountain "many times" with his son and would still feel safe getting back on.

"When you look at the safety record for roller-coasters, I mean, the numbers of these incidents are so, so small," he said.

"There are systems in place, if they're done properly, to inspect and do maintenance on a regular basis. And that is all documented and recorded. So that's why these types of failures are very rare."

What went wrong?

Experts say it's hard to know what might have gone wrong on the Goliath, given how little information has been released, but Perovic says his first thought, from a forensic engineering perspective, is that the restraint system failed.

He says investigators will look at whether there was a manufacturing problem with the restraint that became a defect over time, or a deficiency in the inspection protocols — for example, if someone missed a crack or other problem that was worsening over time.

"There are a number of different possibilities that are going to be looked at," he said.

WATCH | Canadian parks suspend some rides: Wonderland, La Ronde suspend some rides after Six Flags death | Duration 1:54 One man is dead and several riders were injured after a passenger was thrown from a roller-coaster at the Six Flags amusement park in Austell, Ga., on Oct. 12. At least two theme parks in Canada have temporarily shut down roller-coasters similar to the one at the U.S. theme park 'out of an abundance of caution,' according to a Six Flags Entertainment Corporation spokesperson.

Kathryn Woodcock, a professor at Toronto Metropolitan University's School of Occupational and Public Health and director of the Tools for Holistic Ride Inspection Learning and Leadership lab, says these systems are complex and people will have to wait for answers.

Woodcock said in an email that roller-coasters are typically designed to an internationally recognized standard, and manufacturers establish inspection programs for specific things based on how often they fail and how detectable they are.

Plus, "the ride itself has built-in testing, in the automation system, with hundreds of sensors, and considerable redundancy," she said.

"So if any components have failed, it will have required the improbable event that multiple components failed at the same time."

'No competitive secrets'

But accidents do happen. The most infamous roller-coaster accident in Canada was 40 years ago on the West Edmonton Mall's Mindbender when a car derailed, killing three people and injuring 19. It was blamed on design and manufacturing flaws.

In 2013, in an incident similar to this week's death, a woman riding the Texas Giant roller-coaster died after she was thrown from her seat, fell 23 metres and struck a metal beam at Six Flags Over Texas. Six Flags redesigned its restraints before reopening the coaster two months later, and the park and the ride manufacturer settled a lawsuit with the woman's family.

WATCH | CBC coverage of the Mindbender deaths: From the archives: 3 killed in Mindbender derailment | Duration 1:59 It's been 30 years this week since a car on the Minderbender roller-coaster at West Edmonton Mall derailed, killing three.

But while accidents like these dominate headlines, they are extremely rare.

The National Safety Council said in its 2024 report for the International Association of Amusement Parks and Attractions that there were an estimated 118 serious injuries across North American fixed-site amusement rides that year and 1,360 injuries overall, though parks attributed two-thirds of those to guest-related factors, like medical conditions and behaviour.

The association's website pegs the likelihood of being seriously injured in a fixed-site ride at a U.S. amusement park at one in 15.5 million rides taken.

Woodcock says it is "stunningly rare" for someone to be ejected from a roller-coaster, and adds that people can take some reassurance from other Six Flags operators temporarily closing similar rides for safety reviews.

"We should also be aware of the regulatory authorities in Canadian provinces being well connected to each other and to their counterparts internationally to help communicate about safety," she said.

"The attractions industry has no competitive secrets when it comes to safety."

Extreme rides raise risk

Perovic cautions, however, that there could be a growing danger for some riders even when roller-coasters are working properly.

Six Flags Magic Mountain said last month it would retire its famously extreme X2 coaster following multiple lawsuits alleging riders suffered serious injuries — including a wrongful-death lawsuit from the family of a 22-year-old rider who was rushed to hospital in 2022 with severe brain bleeding and died a day later.

Last year, a medical examiner concluded that a man in his 30s — who was found unresponsive after riding Stardust Racers at Universal Orlando Resort — had died from blunt impact injuries, perhaps related to previous injuries. The man's family settled a wrongful death claim with Universal and the park updated its operational procedures and safety signage before reopening the ride two weeks later.

Six Flags has temporarily closed two roller-coasters at Canada's Wonderland, north of Toronto, out of an 'abundance of caution.' (Ken Townsend/CBC)

Perovic says people may want to consult their doctor before jumping on some extreme rides.

"These coaster manufacturers and these operators in the parks, they're all trying to one-up each other. They all want to be higher and faster and so on and keep breaking the world records," he said.

"Well, that comes at a cost. The forces could be too high and excessive. Not everybody's as fit as everyone else."

World.title: Charlottetown police lost the evidence in a P.E.I. cold-case murder. How did it happen?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The case against the man accused of murdering a P.E.I. teacher in 1988 has unravelled after Charlottetown police revealed the evidence crucial to securing a conviction was missing. How did police lose key evidence, and what does that mean for the case?

All charges against Todd Joseph Irving, 59, were dropped on Tuesday. He had been charged with first-degree murder and interfering with human remains in the killing of Byron Carr, a teacher found strangled and stabbed in his home.

According to the P.E.I. Crown Attorney's Office, moving forward with prosecution wasn’t an option because Charlottetown Police Services lost key evidence, leaving no chance of a conviction at the trial that was scheduled to begin in November.

Darren MacDougall, Charlottetown's interim police chief, told CBC News on Tuesday that the agency knew when the cold case was reopened in 2007 — long before Irving was charged in early 2024 — that the knife left at the scene and the towel used to strangle Carr were missing.

“This was 1988. It was a different time in policing, the standards were far different than they are today,” MacDougall said.

“What we did in 2007 was we endeavoured to look at what we had, realize the challenges, and look forward to what was available to us as far as tools were concerned to identify the offender."

Interim Charlottetown police Chief Darren MacDougall, interviewed on Oct. 13, 2026. (Aaron Adetuyi/CBC)

In the 1980s, MacDougall said, evidence was tagged using handwritten notes and logged manually. Now, that's all done in an electronic database.

So police instead built their case on DNA found at the scene and proceeded to charge Irving, even though they already knew key evidence was lost.

"With the evidence that we relied upon, and we had significant forensic DNA evidence, we believed the evidence met the threshold to believe that [Irving] committed the offense," MacDougall said.

"We believe the evidence that we relied upon to lay a charge. We believe in that evidence."

Police hoped forensic evidence would be enough

When police announced Irving’s arrest in early 2024, they said the break in the case came thanks to advances in investigative genetic genealogy that linked Irving to one of the DNA samples found at the crime scene.

At a pre-trial hearing, police said Irving's DNA was found on Carr’s body, on a pair of underwear left at the scene and on an extinguished cigarette butt placed in Carr’s navel.

His DNA was not found on the towel used to strangle Carr, which was processed for DNA before it was lost, nor or on a sock left at the crime scene that police said was likely used as a glove to prevent leaving fingerprints behind.

"I certainly hoped that the forensic evidence would be enough to carry the day,” said former Charlottetown police chief Brad MacConnell, who led the investigation for years and now works as the city's chief administrative officer.

“It became apparent over the last several months as we worked through this that the challenges were too much to overcome."

WATCH | The man police accused of murdering Byron Carr in 1988 is now free. Here's what happened: The man police accused of murdering Byron Carr in 1988 is now free. Here's what happened | Duration closed caption 7:20 Todd Joseph Irving walked into court Tuesday facing charges of first-degree murder and interfering with human remains in the 1988 killing of P.E.I. teacher Byron Carr. After a two-minute hearing, he walked out a free man after the Crown dropped all the charges because the police lost crucial evidence. CBC's Wayne Thibodeau explains.

But the Crown's office said it didn’t know about the missing evidence until July — years after Irving’s arrest and just months before the trial was set to begin.

Crown attorney Christopher White said he’s disappointed the case won’t go to trial.

“This was a matter of personal and public significance,” he said.

“I think that everyone involved viewed that it was important that it be adjudicated in a public venue, so for that not to be able to take place, it’s disappointing and I cannot image what it would be like for Mr. Carr’s family.”

Byron Carr was 36 years old when he was murdered in his Charlottetown home in 1988. This poster was displayed at a 2024 news conference when police announced they'd made an arrest in relation to the case. (Wayne Thibodeau/CBC)

Charlottetown police say they haven’t ruled out a third-party review into how evidence is handled, but MacDougall said he’s confident something like this wouldn’t happen now.

The Crown said it won’t reopen the case against Irving.

Despite the outcome, both police and Carr’s family say they’re confident that while there isn’t enough evidence to bring him to trial, the right person was arrested.

“There’s no justice when someone is killed,” said John Carr, Byron’s brother.

“Nothing he could be sentenced to would ever bring Byron back or give us any more satisfaction. We’re not out to get anyone for it, but you know, he’s the one that’s got to live with himself.”
