World.title: Colombia’s national strike organizers “are instigators of evil,” claims De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called labor unions and social organizations who organized anti-government protests for Wednesday “instigators of evil” who “seek to once again cause chaos.”

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella stressed that the security forces were instructed to allow peaceful protests, but warned the protesters that “if they intend to set Colombia ablaze, they will face the determination of the tiger and his government to do what is lawfully required—which is to defend the lives, honor, and property of all Colombians.”

Wednesday’s protests are a preparation for a national strike that is set to take place in November and is supported by the country’s political opposition to the far-right government.

According to the president, “those who are promoting the strike and seeking to use it to once again cause chaos and destabilize the government are the very same people who left the country bankrupt, on the brink of a blackout, with the healthcare system in intensive care, energy sovereignty compromised, and public resources plundered and looted.”

“They are instigators of evil, not fighter for freedom,” said De la Espriella.

If they intend to set Colombia ablaze, they will face the determination of the tiger and his government to do what is rightfully required—which is to defend the lives, honor, and property of all Colombians. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president stressed that he would be signing a decree that regulates public protests in an attempt to avoid the chaos that erupted during massive strikes in 2019 and 2021 an killed 80 people.

De la Espriella additionally is expected to present an “anti-terrorism stature” to Congress, which could see the prosecution of protest organizers on terrorism charges, according to opposition leaders and security experts.

World.title: Colombia declares official start of El Niño, warns of strong impacts
World.content:
Colombia’s meteorological institute IDEAM officially declared the arrival of El Niño, and warned that the climate phenomenon could trigger water shortages and forest fires.

In a press statement, the IDEAM said that its “confirmation reflects the sustained warm conditions in the Pacific Ocean, which, according to the latest measurement, broke records, reaching a sea surface temperature anomaly of +3.49°C.”

The meteorological institute said it expected that this year’s “Godzilla El Niño” could continue to disrupt local climate patterns until March next year.

Initially, the weather phenomenon is expected to reduce rainfall between October and December, which is normally the rainy season in large parts of the country.

“Given this situation, and in light of the alerts issued since the beginning of the year, the national government launched an interagency response,.. with specific instructions for the responsible agencies to have their contingency plans formulated and activated by November 30 at the latest,” said the President’s Office in a statement.

The National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD) coordinates response capabilities across the country and enhances the monitoring of wildfires using satellite technology. For its part, the Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development is taking steps to protect strategic ecosystems, water sources, and the most vulnerable areas. President’s Office

The Mining Ministry “is implementing an emergency plan aimed at ensuring the country’s energy security by strengthening thermal power generation, securing fuel supplies, and implementing efficiency and conservation measures,” according to the President’s Office.

EPM, the local utilities firm in Medellin, has been testing the effectiveness of water rations as they fear the lack of rain could affect the hydro-electric power plants that provide the northwest of Colombia much of its energy.

Before leaving office on August 7, former President Gustavo Petro ordered the mass purchase of solar panels to reduce the pressure on the electric grid.

World.title: Colombia’s draft counterterrorist statute “creates foundations of dictatorial and inquisitorial regime:” opposition
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella’s antiterrorist statute would criminalize political opposition, social movements, and social protest, and essentially form a dictatorial regime, said opposition leader Ivan Cepeda on Wednesday.

In a video, Cepeda said that the true purpose of the bill that was leaked earlier seeks “to advance in the formation of essentially a dictatorial regime,.. which, moreover, has such a regime prostrate to drug trafficking.”

“The true objectives of this statute are to wage a crusade against the political opposition, social movements, and social protest, which is a legitimate right of citizens,” said the Senator of the Historic Pact party.

“Most of the articles in this draft are devoted to provisions that seriously undermine civil liberties, human rights, and the right to protest—not to illegal armed groups,’ according to Cepeda.

The broad legal definition of the word terrorism would allow the government to prosecute protest organizers on terrorism charges if any clashes occur between protesters and police.

This law could serve to intensify the persecution already underway in Colombia against journalists, judges, students, teachers, union members, peasants, indigenous people, people of African descent, LGBTIQ+ individuals—in short, any person or group that criticizes the citizen Abelardo de la Espriella, his government, law enforcement, or any state institution. Such a person could be taken to prison—without even prior warning—and subjected to abuse and torture. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Furthermore, the creation of a National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors would allow the government to criminalize citizens based on an administrative rather than a legal basis, and “grants extraordinary powers to the president to regulate a statutory judicial procedure, specifically the expedited preventive detention proceeding,” said the opposition leader.

The aim is to criminalize social protest; the alleged crime of “manipulating the civilian population” punishes anyone who promotes, finances, organizes, or leads crowds—this is the language of the draft statute—and this is nothing less than the institutionalization of political persecution and the criminalization of free speech. Senator Ivan Cepeda

The antiterrorism statute will be facing opposition when the government tries to push the legislation through Congress, Cepeda said.

“The Historic Pact rejects this and will do whatever is necessary to ensure that the opposition’s rights and guarantees are respected,” said the opposition leader.

World.title: De la Espriella announces first $309M in aid for earthquake reconstruction
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella announced that his Miracle Fund received COP1 trillion ($309 million) for the reconstruction of western Colombia, which was hit by a 7.4M earthquake on August 10.

The announcement followed announcements by the press, which reported that the Finance Ministry allocated ($192 million) COP625 billion to the fund almost two months after the disaster.

Thank you for your patience, but please understand that the government’s bureaucratic inertia and the situation we’ve inherited are extremely complex. However, we’re working to resolve the issue, and the Milagro Fund is now up and running, thanks to God and the efforts of all the officials in this administration. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“In November, the government will move forward with contracting another COP2.7 trillion ($835 million),” Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo told Caracol Radio.

The money is the first of an estimated COP30 trillion ($9.3 billion) that would be needed to rebuild the damage to airports, roads, hospitals and other public works.

The fund will be managed by De la Espriella’s general secretary, Carlos Rios, and a handful of businessmen with ties to the administration.

The announcement followed increased unrest about the government’s lack of response to the earthquake, which affected more than 400,000 people in the Valle del Cauca and Choco province, and the coffee region.

The government’s initial response was delayed because De la Espriella suspended the process to transfer power a month before he took office on August 7.

World.title: Colombia seeks to expand definition of terrorism in draft “counterterrorism statute”
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella will present Colombia’s Congress with a comprehensive “counterterrorism statute,” which would give authorities enhanced powers to fight designated terrorist organizations.

A 116-page draft bill, which was leaked to Caracol Radio, would facilitate a military approach to combat illegal armed groups and organized crime groups, for example through air strikes.

The Antiterrorism Statute would additionally create a National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors, which would make it easier to freeze the assets of suspected terrorists and their financiers.

Last but not least, the bill creates a presidential Terrorism Commissioner and a special prison regime for leaders of designated terrorist organizations.

Broader definition of terrorism

The bill seeks to change Colombia’s criminal law and define terrorism as any individual or collective conduct that produces “fear, panic or terror, creating risks, threats or the use of violence.”

A technical body of the National Security Council (NSC) will advise the council on the inclusion of organizations or individuals that ought to be included to its public National Registry of Terrorist Organizations and Actors.

Anyone who believes he was falsely put on the terror list can challenge this decision before the NSC and the Council of State, Colombia’s top administrative court.

The bill additionally seeks that “the Council of State shall hear, in the first instance, constitutional protection lawsuits filed against the President of the Republic or against defense authorities for acts or omissions related to operations by law enforcement agencies to preserve national security.”

This would make the suspension of military operations more difficult for citizens, who now can seek legal support to protect their constitutional rights at lower courts.

The bill also creates new crimes and modifies the penalties for conduct related to “terrorism,” such as the use of drones, illegal mining, oil theft, the extraction and sale of gold, kidnapping, smuggling, human trafficking, drug trafficking, extortion, cybercrimes, election crimes, riots, and attacks on critical infrastructure.

In the case of riots, “the penalty shall be increased by up to double when the riot is directed against law enforcement units conducting operations; or is carried out in conjunction with listed terrorist organizations.”

The bill also allows Colombian authorities to investigate and prosecute terrorism, terrorism financing or providing material support for terrorist organizations abroad.

High Counterterrorism Commissioner

The bill additionally seeks to expand presidential powers to create the Office of the High Counterterrorism Commissioner.

The expanded power would additionally give De la Espriella six months to regulate the powers of this new advisory office and to appoint its first commissioner.

World.title: Mayor from Colombia’s north claims De la Espriella’s armed men intimidated him
World.content:
The mayor of Sincelejo claimed Sunday that armed men intimidated him during a meeting with Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella.

In a video message, Sincelejo Mayor Yahir Acuña said that armed men positioned themselves behind him while the president accused the mayor of corruption and threatened to pull municipal funds.

The accusations were partly published on the social media pages of the president, who accused Acuña of being “a person who, like you, faces 13 corruption charges, has a video in which he explains how to embezzle funds from the PAE, and, on top of that, is set to stand trial in the Supreme Court of Justice on charges of illicit enrichment.”

So let’s see what we do with Sincelejo, but I do not work under your scheme of corruption. And if you think you can continue engaging in those practices, know that someone has arrived who is going to prevent it and that I am going to concentrate on it. This money, mister mayor, I will take care of it, and to take care of it I have to keep it away from your control. President Abelardo de la Espriella

In his response, Acuña claimed that De la Espriella’s video “has been edited and digitally manipulated.”

I ask you, please, to show the full video, where you can see how disciplinary and criminal codes are being violated in Colombia, where you can see how a mayor is being intimidated with rifles in the hands of civilians. How can a mayor be constantly flanked—for the entire duration of an event—by a person armed with a rifle, with the sole purpose of intimidating him? Sincelejo Mayor Yahir Acuña

Investigative journalist Laura Ardila said on social media platform X that sources from the province confirmed Acuña’s allegations.

Sources from the department who were present say—fearing they might be named—that they left the scene terrified. They claim that Acuña was indeed surrounded by heavily armed men in civilian clothing, that the president’s office was recording the entire time, and that, based on details like these, they believe it was a scene staged in advance to go viral. Journalist Laura Ardila

The mayor subsequently pointed out that the investigations into his alleged corruption existed before the presidential campaign, during which the De la Espriella campaign may have violated electoral laws, according to Acuña.

Among other things, the mayor said that he had been approached by De la Espriella’s parents to support the far-right president’s campaign and that local print shops may have received unreported campaign funds.

Since this needs to be clarified, mister President, it would be a good idea for the oversight agencies to investigate whether any printing shops in Sincelejo incurred campaign expenses that have not yet been reported to the National Electoral Council, whether there was campaign financing, and where that campaign financing came from, Mister President. Sincelejo Mayor Yahir Acuña

The mayor also pointed out that two members of the De la Espriella administration are being investigated on corruption charges and that the president had ties to the now-defunct paramilitary organization AUC.

The president has repeatedly used corruption allegations to target political enemies.

World.title: Colombia’s top corporate lobbyist resigns over reported tensions with president
World.content:
The director of one of Colombia’s most powerful business associations, Bruce Mac Master of the ANDI, resigned amid tensions with President Abelardo de la Espriella.

In a letter to the ANDI, Mac Master said that “it is time for me to step down from my role as head of the National Association of Entrepreneurs of Colombia.”

According to the former ANDI boss, “unexpected and troubling circumstances” made working for the association “particularly complex” and ‘multiple pressures have affected its ability to act freely and carry out its functions autonomously.”

In recent weeks, unexpected and troubling circumstances have arisen that have made the Association’s operating environment particularly complex, with potential adverse effects on its members and staff. Multiple pressures have affected its ability to act freely and carry out its functions autonomously. In the face of these challenges, I have sought to act with firmness and prudence, always prioritizing institutional channels and placing the interests of the ANDI above any personal considerations, in an effort to resolve this situation. Bruce Mac Master

Mac Master’s resignation followed news suggesting that De la Espriella instructed his cabinet of boycotting the ANDI chief.

According to political news magazine La Silla Vacia, the rift between the ANDI and the government was because De la Espriella’s law firm was never allowed to join the ANDI and the association’s donations in response to the august 10 earthquake bypassed the First Lady’s newly founded and very controversial foundation.

“The General Board of Directors, its Executive Committee, and I did everything in our power to facilitate a solution and create conditions that would allow the Association to fully fulfill its role, seeking to keep channels of dialogue open and to continue contributing,” but “all of those attempts were unsuccessful.”

I deeply regret this, because I have always believed in collective intelligence and in the need for the government, the private sector, and institutions to work together—even in the face of differences—with respect, independence, and a sense of national responsibility. We tried, but we were unsuccessful. Bruce Mac Master

Mac Master said that he hoped that his resignation would restore “collaboration between the national government and the business community—as represented by the General Board of Directors, the members, and the various divisions of the Association.”

The former ANDI chief had been trying to represent the business interests of its approximately 1,600 members since 2013.

World.title: Colombia seeks to tighten checks on public protests
World.content:
Colombia’s government published a draft decree that seeks to tighten regulations on public protests.

The draft was published weeks before labor unions and social organizations plan regional anti-government protests ahead of a national strike that is set for November.

The draft seeks to update the Decree #3 of 2021, which was issued months before a national strike that was violently repressed by the police and the military.

In an attempt to prevent another bloodbath, the decree seeks to regulate authorities’ response to protests and the coordinated use of force in response to acts of vandalism and violence.

The decree regulates dialogue between the protesters and law enforcement authorities to promote the peaceful nature of protests.

The decree additionally limits the use of police intelligence against those organizing and participating in the protests.

Last but not least, the decree seeks the effective prosecution of those arrested during protests through increased surveillance and a permanent police presence.

The decree comes amid social tensions that surged after the far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella took office in August and announced counterrevolutionary measures that seek to undo reforms by his leftist predecessor, former President Gustavo Petro.

Swelling student protests have been publicly accused of being fueled by insurgencies and De la Espriella has warned that police may enter universities if they find evidence they are used to prepare acts of vandalism or terrorism.

World.title: A tornado and an unusual spring hailstorm overwhelm Santiago, Chile
World.content:
A tornado and an unusual spring hailstorm overwhelm Santiago, Chile

14th Wednesday, October 2026 - 07:01 UTC Full article

An electrical storm with hail, unusual in the middle of spring, flooded streets, homes and businesses in Santiago, Chile, on Tuesday and produced a tornado that the Chilean Meteorological Directorate preliminarily classified as EF0, the lowest intensity category. The national disaster prevention and response service declared a red alert in the Metropolitan Region, five days after the mudslide that hit the Las Condes district.

The tornado struck a bus terminal in Estación Central, in the west of the capital, where the gust lifted dozens of zinc sheets into the air. The storm began around 3:30pm, as students and workers were leaving schools and offices, and within minutes flooded avenues, underground car parks and buildings, in some cases with water coming through the roofs. According to regional governor Claudio Orrego, around 20 millimetres fell in about two and a half hours, and districts such as Independencia and Providencia recorded some 18 millimetres in one hour.

Some 22,000 homes were left without electricity, according to the Superintendency of Electricity and Fuels. Classes were suspended at municipal schools in Santiago, Providencia and Ñuñoa, and Las Condes extended its restricted-movement perimeter because of the risk of further landslides. Interior Minister Claudio Alvarado said “all emergency institutions” had been activated and that the rain was expected to ease overnight.

“Because of global warming, weather processes are intensifying. And we have just had an electrical storm like none ever seen in Santiago,” climatologist Alejandro Vial told the newspaper El País, linking the episode to El Niño.

Last week, an atmospheric river intensified by El Niño made this the wettest October on record in the Chilean capital and caused the October 8 mudslide in San Carlos de Apoquindo, which left six people injured and around 2,000 homes damaged.

World.title: Argentina asks the law of the sea tribunal to halt Sea Lion and bar new oil permits
World.content:
Argentina asks the law of the sea tribunal to halt Sea Lion and bar new oil permits

13th Tuesday, October 2026 - 23:03 UTC Full article

The measures are sought pending the constitution of the arbitral tribunal under Annex VII of the Convention, proceedings Argentina launched with a notification to the United Kingdom on September 28

Argentina has asked the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea to order the United Kingdom to prevent the development of the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands and to refrain from granting new permits to exploit the resources of the disputed continental shelf, according to a statement published by the Hamburg-based tribunal. The hearing will be set “at the earliest possible date”.

The request, submitted on October 13 under Article 290(5) of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, lists four provisional measures: that the United Kingdom prevent “the commencement or continuation” of hydrocarbon exploitation through Sea Lion; that it refrain from using information obtained from exploring the disputed areas “to the detriment of the rights” of Argentina; that it stop preventing Argentina from complying with its obligation to protect the marine environment of those areas; and that it refrain from any measure that might aggravate the dispute, “in particular the granting of new permits”.

The measures are sought pending the constitution of the arbitral tribunal under Annex VII of the Convention, proceedings Argentina launched with a notification to the United Kingdom on September 28. Before that tribunal, Argentina asks for a declaration that the United Kingdom, by unilaterally authorising the exploration and exploitation of resources in the waters around the South Atlantic archipelagos, is in breach of its obligation to respect Argentina’s “sovereignty and sovereign rights” over those maritime areas; of the obligation to refrain from unilateral measures in areas subject to a dispute “within the framework of the decolonization process” of the UN; of the obligation to protect the marine environment; and of the obligation to settle disputes by peaceful means.

To prescribe provisional measures, the tribunal must consider that the arbitral tribunal would have prima facie jurisdiction and that the urgency of the situation so requires. In previous cases, such as Chagos in 2015 and Crimea in 2020, tribunals under the Convention have declined to rule on questions of territorial sovereignty.

The United Kingdom has said it will engage with the process and challenge any attempt to use it to settle sovereignty. Overseas Territories Minister Uma Kumaran said on Tuesday that London’s position is that provisional measures are binding on the parties. Sea Lion, operated by Navitas Petroleum with 65% and Rockhopper Exploration with 35%, expects first oil in 2028.

World.title: Pope Leo XIV has lung cancer and underwent successful surgery, Vatican says
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV has lung cancer and underwent successful surgery, Vatican says

13th Tuesday, October 2026 - 23:00 UTC Full article

Leo XIV announced on Sunday, after the Angelus prayer, that a lung nodule had been detected “at a very early stage” and was “well localised”

Pope Leo XIV, 71, has been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma and underwent successful surgery on Tuesday at Rome’s Gemelli hospital, where doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung, the Holy See said in a medical bulletin. The operation comes three weeks before the start of his tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, whose schedule has not been changed.

According to the bulletin, a histological examination carried out during the operation “confirmed the diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, as suspected by the preoperative tests”. To “ensure a radical intervention”, surgeons removed the entire lower lobe using a video-assisted technique. The pontiff spent about three hours in the operating room, though the surgery itself lasted about 90 minutes. “The surgery was successful, and there were no complications,” the Vatican said. After waking normally and a brief period of observation, he returned to his room on the hospital’s 10th floor.

A Vatican source quoted by the AFP news agency said further tests were being carried out to determine whether there were signs the cancer had spread. The Vatican had said the Pope would remain in hospital for about a week, and his schedule has been cleared until October 20.

Leo XIV announced on Sunday, after the Angelus prayer, that a lung nodule had been detected “at a very early stage” and was “well localised”. The Archbishop of Tokyo, Cardinal Tarcisio Isao Kikuchi, who met him on Monday, said the Pope had decided to have surgery as soon as possible because he wants to keep his trip to South America, scheduled from November 6 to 17, with stops in Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, where he served as a missionary and bishop.

“Am I worried? Yes, because I certainly wasn’t expecting anything like this,” said Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Pietro Parolin, who highlighted the pontiff’s “serenity”. It is the first serious health problem publicly disclosed since the start of his papacy in May 2025.

World.title: Miliband: Falklands residents have the right to develop their resources “as they see fit”
World.content:
Miliband: Falklands residents have the right to develop their resources “as they see fit”

13th Tuesday, October 2026 - 19:03 UTC Full article

“We will always stand up for the Falkland Islanders, their right to determine their own future, and their right to pursue legitimate economic development,” he added

British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said on Tuesday that the people of the Falkland Islands “have a right to develop their natural resources as they see fit”, as he announced on X the British government’s measures to protect companies and individuals from Argentine sanctions.

“Today we have announced new measures under Protection of Trading Interests legislation to ensure people and companies are shielded from Argentinian threats. Attempts to intimidate those taking part in legitimate commercial activity are unacceptable,” he wrote. The message was shared by Government House, the governor’s residence in the islands.

The Falkland Islanders have a right to develop their natural resources as they see fit. Today we have announced new measures under Protection of Trading Interests legislation to ensure people and companies are shielded from Argentinian threats. Attempts to intimidate those taking part in legitimate commercial activity are unacceptable. https://t.co/haVKR68nPf — Ed Miliband (@Ed_Miliband) October 13, 2026

In an official statement, Miliband said the UK’s support for the islands is “steadfast” and that companies “should be free to make lawful commercial decisions without the threat of political coercion”. “We will always stand up for the Falkland Islanders, their right to determine their own future, and their right to pursue legitimate economic development,” he added.

The announcement coincided with Argentina’s request for provisional measures before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea to halt the Sea Lion oil project. Argentina claims sovereignty over the archipelago and holds that the licences issued by its government are invalid.

World.title: UK Overseas Territories Minister accuses Milei of using the Falklands for electoral ends
World.content:
UK Overseas Territories Minister accuses Milei of using the Falklands for electoral ends

13th Tuesday, October 2026 - 18:53 UTC Full article

Minister Uma Kumaran and MLA Jack Ford in discussion following her statement to Parliament

British Overseas Territories Minister Uma Kumaran on Tuesday accused Argentine President Javier Milei of a “brazen attempt to use the people of the Falkland Islands as some sort of political prop ahead of Argentina’s elections next year”, in a statement to the House of Commons watched from the gallery by the Chair of the islands’ Legislative Assembly, Jack Ford.

Kumaran set out a four-part response to what she called “economic coercion”. The Minister for Latin America, Chris Elmore, made the British position clear to the Argentine ambassador on September 17; the government is in contact with the Sea Lion operator and its supply chain and has issued letters of comfort to businesses; the Business Secretary will deploy the protection of trading interests legislation; and the diplomatic network is engaging G7 and G20 partners. “The United Kingdom will prepare additional measures if this situation persists. They will be legal, proportionate and robust,” she warned.

Asked about relations with Uruguay and Chile, the minister said the government is in regular discussion with “friends and allies” in the region, whom she described as “important partners” on the issue. Conservative MPs urged the government to use Britain’s position to block Argentina’s accession to the trans-Pacific trade agreement and the OECD; Kumaran did not commit, though she said Argentina’s conduct “raises very serious questions about its reliability as a partner”.

On defence, she said the patrol ship HMS Medway is operating in the South Atlantic and that the Typhoon fighters deployed will be replaced with more modern versions in 2027. She also announced that the Foreign Office and the Ministry of Defence will support commemorations next year of the 45th anniversary of the end of the 1982 war. “The United Kingdom never sought this confrontation with the Argentine Government, and less so with the Argentine people,” she said.

World.title: London says it will abide by any law of the sea provisional measures as it moves to shield its companies
World.content:
London says it will abide by any law of the sea provisional measures as it moves to shield its companies

13th Tuesday, October 2026 - 18:45 UTC Full article

The UK is preparing measures under its Protection of Trading Interests law to stop British firms and individuals being forced to comply with extraterritorial Argentine rules

The British government said on Tuesday that any provisional measures ordered by the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea are binding and that the United Kingdom complies with its international obligations, on the same day Argentina asked that tribunal to halt the Sea Lion oil project in Falklands waters. In parallel, London announced it will use its protection of trading interests legislation to shield British companies from Argentine sanctions.

“The UK’s established position is that provisional measures ordered under the applicable international legal framework are binding on the parties, and that the UK complies with its international obligations,” Overseas Territories Minister Uma Kumaran told the House of Commons. She confirmed that Argentina formally notified the start of arbitration under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea on September 28, that the British embassy in Buenos Aires delivered its formal response on Sunday 11, and that the United Kingdom will engage with the process. She added that the notification is not a judgment, does not invalidate licences issued by the archipelago’s government and does not require activity to stop.

With the two-week deadline set by President Javier Milei expired, the Argentine government said on Tuesday it had asked the Hamburg-based tribunal for provisional measures to “preserve Argentina’s sovereign rights over its continental shelf” and prevent activities it considers “unilaterally and illegally” authorised by the United Kingdom.

In a joint statement, Britain’s Department for Business and Trade and the Foreign Office said they are preparing measures under the Protection of Trading Interests legislation, which allows the government to prevent UK companies and individuals from being compelled to comply with extraterritorial foreign rules. The statement made clear it does not seek to restrict British trade with Argentina. “This makes it clear in no uncertain terms that this Government will act where Argentina seeks to impede lawful UK commercial activity,” said Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds. “Argentina’s attempts to intimidate businesses and individuals engaged in legitimate commercial activity are unacceptable,” added Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband.

According to The Guardian, the United Kingdom has also asked Interpol to reject Argentine requests for red notices against individuals linked to Sea Lion, calling them “politically motivated”. Interpol’s constitution prohibits it from intervening in matters of a political character.

Argentina argues that unilateral exploitation contravenes UN General Assembly resolutions 2065 and 31/49. In previous cases, tribunals under the Convention have declined to rule on territorial sovereignty disputes; Kumaran confirmed London will challenge any attempt to use the procedure for that purpose. In the 2013 referendum, on a 92% turnout, 99.8% of voters chose to retain the status of a British overseas territory.

World.title: Lubetkin warns Flávio Bolsonaro that “it is not easy to leave Mercosur”
World.content:
Lubetkin warns Flávio Bolsonaro that “it is not easy to leave Mercosur”

13th Tuesday, October 2026 - 14:52 UTC Full article

“It is not easy to leave Mercosur. There are too many interrelated agreements in the business sphere, and that would cause major losses for the Brazilian economy,” Lubetkin said

Uruguay’s Foreign Minister Mario Lubetkin has warned Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro that “it is not easy to leave Mercosur”, in response to his criticism of the bloc during the campaign for the October 25 runoff. In the same interview, with the newspaper Folha de S.Paulo, he said Uruguay would not restore diplomatic relations with Venezuela while Delcy Rodríguez governs.

“It is not easy to leave Mercosur. There are too many interrelated agreements in the business sphere, and that would cause major losses for the Brazilian economy. And there are too many mechanisms that prevent such a quick exit,” Lubetkin said. “I hope that, if that gentleman ends up presiding over Brazil, when he starts governing he will realise that many statements made during the election campaign are impracticable once in government.”

The government programme Bolsonaro registered with the Superior Electoral Court does not mention Mercosur. On the campaign trail, the senator has spoken of “freeing Brazil from the shackles of Mercosur”, referring to the constraints the common external tariff places on negotiating its own trade agreements, a phrase some media have interpreted as raising the possibility of leaving the bloc. Uruguay has held the Mercosur pro tempore presidency since July 1.

Lubetkin said Uruguay would work with whoever is elected: “First, let the elections be clean, transparent, democratic and calm. Then, naturally, the Brazilian people will choose whoever they consider best, and we will work with whoever wins, as state policy.”

On Venezuela, the minister ruled out resuming relations: “In no way, and we are not going to resume them.” He argued that from elections Uruguay had questioned “came a president who is now, on top of everything, imprisoned in the United States, and from that president comes a president as illegitimate as he was”. Uruguay will restore ties, he said, when “an independent court confirms” the winner of a democratic election. Caracas withdrew its diplomatic staff from Uruguay and six other Latin American countries in July 2024 after they questioned Nicolás Maduro’s re-election; Maduro has been detained in the United States since January. Rodríguez announced at the UN in September that elections would be held, without setting a date.

World.title: “Falkland Islanders will is to remain British, and we will uphold it”, PM Burnham told Trump
World.content:
“Falkland Islanders will is to remain British, and we will uphold it”, PM Burnham told Trump

13th Tuesday, October 2026 - 09:13 UTC Full article

The Prime Minister believes a UK/EU summit will enhance chances for an open discussion “about our relationship with the EU in the longer term”.

“In my meeting with President Trump I raised the Falkland Islands and the clear and declared will of the Islanders to remain British”, revealed United Kingdom Prime Minister Andy Burnham in an oral statement to the House of Commons this Monday.

PM Burnham also emphasized that the point was made very clear in his speech to the UN General Assembly, “we will also always do whatever it takes to uphold Islanders’s will”.

The oral statement on his 22 September intervention before the UN General Assembly Burnham also reiterated support for Ukraine rejecting Russian aggresion, UK’s commitment with NATO and the proposal for a new National Centre for Information Defense, deepeniong collaboration with Germany, Italy and Japan.

On the Middle East situation he confirmed support for the US and Saudi Arabia, and protective security for shared bases.

“I want to thank our police and military personnel for their swift response. to the incidents at RAF Fairford and RAF Molesworth”, which he said is highly likely to have been coordinated and certainly directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard.

As to relations with the European Union, the PM anticipated a UK/EU summit in Brussels on 20th November, with the purpose of boosting UK growth and controlling illegal immigration. And this includes cutting costs and bureaucracy for sectors like farming and its food trade with EU.

On immigration, “we could link up our law enforcement efforts once again, sharing more data and criminal records of foreign nationals as well as faster electronic evidence from the phones of those behind the gangs”.

And “I believe our chances of doing so will be enhanced by being open to a discussion about our relationship with the EU in the longer term”.

Beyond Europe, a confident Britain is ready to play our part on the global stage as we take up the presidency of the G20 in 2027. “I confirmed in New York that we will place AI centre stage in our presidency, capturing the incredible opportunities it presents while guarding against the risks”.

Finally, the message at the UN and to the world is clear, after a decade of turbulence, Britain is back and can be relied upon as a consistent and stable partner in an uncertain world, always upholding the shared values set out in the UN Charter.

World.title: First migrating monarchs are spotted in Coahuila
World.content:
The monarch butterfly’s annual migration from southern Canada to central Mexico is in full swing, with the first sighting confirmed in the border state of Coahuila last week.

Linabeth Flores with the Mexican NGO Profauna confirmed, “We can now officially say that the migration is here.”

The monarch butterflies undertake a perilous southward migration each year from Canada, through the United States, and to Mexico starting in late August to reach their winter resting spot in the pine forests of Michoacán before the bacchanalian breeding season. New generations then migrate north to the Canadian Prairies for spring and summer.

Sightings so far have been concentrated in the cities of Acuña, Múzquiz, Monclova and Cuatro Ciénegas and are expected to increase in the coming days. At the Higher Technological Institute of Múzquiz, several monarchs were spotted feeding on polocote (Mexican sunflower) and pomegranate blossoms.

Before this year’s migration began, two dozen monarch butterflies were tagged with toothpick-sized radio transmitters in Winnipeg, Canada. The practice of tagging butterflies with tracking devices is common among conservation groups in Mexico, Canada and the United States, as it provides valuable information for the protection of the monarch population, which is endangered by climate change and habitat loss.

The first butterfly tagged in Winnipeg, known by the identifier MB26011, has already crossed the Mexican border, just five weeks after leaving Canada.

“She’s done about 2,300 kilometers in about 40 days,” said Laura Burns, the conservation program manager at the Assiniboine Park Zoo in Winnipeg. “It’s really incredible.”

Conservation researchers and members of the public can track the butterflies’ movements on the Project Monarch app.

Peak migration should occur within the next week, with most monarchs reaching overwintering sites in Michoacán and México state in early November. Profauna has asked the public to share photos and reports of the butterflies to help identify flight routes and locate the sites they use to rest and feed during their passage through Coahuila.

The eastern monarch population has fallen by an estimated 80% to 90% since the 1990s, although the number of butterflies in central Mexico this spring was around 64% higher than in the previous season, according to figures from Mexico’s Ministry of Environment and Natural Resources (Semarnat) and the World Wildlife Fund (WWF).

With reports from El Horizonte and CBC

World.title: I never thought of myself as Hispanic. Then I moved to the US
World.content:
A new Pew Research Center analysis asks who counts as Hispanic. For many Mexicans, the answer only arrives after they cross the border — sometimes shouted by a stranger.

I was on the phone with my mother — in Spanish, of course — when a woman who was clearly having a bad day shouted “f—ing South American” at me. My first impulse was to correct her: North American, actually. But I knew precision was beside the point. She wasn’t pointing at my exact origin; she was pointing at my culture.

And yes, unlike her, I am not Anglo-Saxon. So what am I?

The moment I became Hispanic

It is the question the Pew Research Center asked this month in its survey “Who Is Hispanic?,” published at the start of Hispanic Heritage Month. Pew’s answer suggests that it depends on who is counting.

Mine is that I only became Hispanic when I crossed the border.

It sounds naive, but until then I had no idea how many labels I could carry. It was, on a much smaller scale, a Frantz Fanon moment.

Fanon was a Martinican psychiatrist trained in France in the mid-20th century. In “Black Skin, White Masks” (1952), he recounts how a child in the street pointed at him and cried out, “Tiens, un nègre!” The moment forced him to confront everything his skin color meant in the France of his time. It opened a body of work on how such labels are produced by racial violence — territory I won’t step into here.

Labels and how they’re given

One detail of Fanon’s account stays with me, though. He argues that in Martinique, Antilleans did not think of themselves as Black; the label was waiting for them in Europe. Mine was waiting for me in the United States.

If we’re going by labels, I am North American (the region, not the country). I’m also Latin American, Mexican and chilanga, from Mexico City — and, to be precise, from the south of the city.

I know that people who did not grow up in an urban setting like mine are often far more aware of their ethnic origin, especially where an Indigenous language is still alive. Think of Oaxaca and the Mixe, Zapotec, Mixtec or Triqui peoples. I’ll confess that I was always more conscious of my socioeconomic context than of my ethnicity.

The state that made us Mexican

For those of us raised in cities, that blind spot is largely the legacy of the post-revolutionary state. After a decade of war, it decided that the best way to calm the waters was to insist that we were, above all, proud to be Mexican.

To make that true, the state launched an intense education campaign whose first goal was for everyone to speak Spanish, because once you erase the language that sets people apart, you erase the distinction between them. But the shift had started long before.

Around 1820, as Mexico was becoming independent, an estimated 60% of the population spoke an Indigenous language. By 1900, the figure was 15.4%. In the 2020 census, it was 6.1% of Mexicans aged three and older — and 87% of them also speak Spanish.

The project had a name for what it wanted to produce: a generalized mestizo. Anthropologist Manuel Gamio’s “Forjando Patria” (1916) and former education minister José Vasconcelos‘ “La Raza Cósmica” (1925) turned mixture into national identity.

So when I say I was never aware of my ethnicity, that is not entirely accurate. The state gave me one. I simply never noticed it, because the dominant category never needs to be named.

The painted castes

Mixture is not new in Mexico. Under Spanish colonial rule, a hierarchy of castas gave a name to each combination of Spanish, Indigenous and African ancestry, and that name could limit access to offices, guilds and rights. Historians note that daily life was more fluid than the system suggests, but the categories carried weight.

The independence movement explicitly rejected them. Miguel Hidalgo‘s 1810 decree abolished slavery and the tribute paid by the castes. In 1813, José María Morelos’ “Sentimientos de la Nación” called for abolishing “the distinction of castes.” The Plan of Iguala of 1821 declared all inhabitants citizens, regardless of origin.

From that era we keep the 18th-century casta paintings: picturesque and, to our eyes, a little terrible. Perhaps that is why it unsettles me when a society asks me to identify with a label. In Mexico, those labels still shape a person’s prospects. A 2016 survey by INEGI, Mexico’s national statistics agency, found that among Mexicans who placed themselves in the lightest skin tones, 10% had no schooling at all; among those in the darkest tones, the figure was 20.2%.

Who counts as Hispanic?

In the United States, the category was born as an administrative tool. Fifty years ago, Congress ordered the government to count Americans of Spanish-speaking background with roots in Mexico, Puerto Rico, Cuba, and Central and South America. The criterion is not geographic but linguistic — and, at bottom, colonial. Brazilians, Portuguese, Belizeans and Filipinos are left out.

The state does not always accept what people declare. If someone writes “Mexican” in the race question without checking the Hispanic box, the Census Bureau counts them as Hispanic anyway. If someone checks “Other Hispanic” and writes “Irish,” the bureau recodes them as non-Hispanic.

The race question itself fits poorly. In 2024, 23.4 million single-race Hispanics chose “some other race,” and most wrote in a nationality such as “Mexican” or “Latin American.” For those of us raised on mestizaje as national identity, race and nation are the same answer.

Most revealing is how Hispanics describe themselves. According to Pew’s 2025 survey, 53% use their family’s country of origin, 27% use “Hispanic” or “Latino,” and 18% simply say “American.” Most of the people the category covers prefer not to use it for themselves.

One figure seems to contradict my story: 97% of immigrants with Hispanic ancestry identify as Hispanic. I don’t think it does. The survey measures whether you accept the label when it is offered, not whether it existed for you before you arrived. The question assumes you have already crossed the border.

I also understand why the term exists, and why being counted matters to many. In a 2021 Pew survey, 57% of Latino adults said skin color shapes their daily lives at least somewhat.

A society of societies

I know the United States is a different case: a country made of many societies, with different customs coexisting in the same space. In 2024, its immigrant population reached a record 50.2 million, or 14.8% of residents. The only other time the share was that high was 1890.

The Census Bureau’s own breakdown shows how these labels overlap. Of the 341.8 million people it estimated for July 2025, 72.3% are counted as White alone, 13.5% as Black, 6.9 percent as Asian, 2.1% as American Indian or Alaska Native, 0.3% as Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander, and 4.9% as two or more races. Hispanics, 20.5% of the population, are counted on top of those races rather than beside them, which is why non-Hispanic Whites are only 56.1%. The official estimates carry no “some other race” category at all — the box where millions of Hispanics write in their nationality.

The Hispanic population, now 70.1 million, is itself a federation of nationalities. In 2021, it included 37.2 million people of Mexican origin, 5.8 million Puerto Ricans and 2.5 million Salvadorans, with five other origin groups above 1 million each. “Hispanic” holds all of them in a single box.

Naming is classifying

When someone shouts my origin at me in the street — what a casta painter might have labeled mestiza — I become aware of what my features say, and of everything they tell another person before I open my mouth.

In 1952, the same year Fanon published his book, Jorge Luis Borges wrote in “The Analytical Language of John Wilkins” that every classification of the universe is arbitrary and conjectural. To name something is already to sort it.

So the question is not whether I am Hispanic. By the government’s definition, I am. The question is why it matters to name me that way — and what that classification says about us, and about those who do the classifying.

María Meléndez is a writer and art historian. She works at the Mexican Cultural Institute of the Embassy of Mexico in Washington, D.C.

World.title: San Luis Potosí auto cluster sees potential for Chinese manufacturing investment
World.content:
Could a Chinese automaker open a plant in the state of San Luis Potosí?

The president of the San Luis Potosí Automotive Cluster, an industry group, believes it’s possible.

Alberto Rosales Reyna, the cluster’s president, told the San Luis Potosí-based newspaper Plano Informativo that Asian automakers, including Chinese ones, have considered investing in the state, where BMW and General Motors have plants.

He acknowledged that no new automotive plant projects have been confirmed for San Luis Potosí, but suggested that could soon change.

“A very significant [possible] investment in the production of Chinese vehicles [in Mexico] has been spoken about as part of an effort to increase local content and have Chinese production in our state,” Rosales said.

He didn’t mention the names of any Chinese automakers that could open a plant in San Luis Potosí. However, Rosales asserted that the state has the capacity to welcome an automaker from China or any other country.

The geographical location of San Luis Potosí, the “technical ability” of its workforce, proximity to supply chains and “support that the local government could provide” all make the state an attractive place for automotive investment, he said.

Those things give San Luis Potosí “a great advantage,” Rosales said.

BYD is among the Chinese automakers that have expressed interest in opening a plant in Mexico. But neither that company — the world’s largest electric vehicle manufacturer — nor any other Chinese automaker has opened a plant in the country to date.

(However, a Mexican company, Giant Motors Latinoamérica, does assemble vehicles for Chinese automaker JAC at a plant in Ciudad Sahagún, Hidalgo.)

SLP automotive industry event could generate ‘business opportunities’ worth more than US $100 million

Rosales’ remarks about the possibility of a Chinese automaker investing in San Luis Potosí came ahead of Automotive Connection Potosí 2026, a business-to-business (B2B) networking event that will be held in San Luis Potosí city on Nov. 11 and 12.

The San Luis Potosí Automotive Cluster and the state Ministry of Economic Development are collaborating on the event.

According to the event website and media reports, Automotive Connection Potosí 2026 is projected to generate over US $100 million in “business opportunities” through meetings between automotive sector buyers and suppliers. Thirty buyers are listed on the event website, including BMW and Stellantis.

More than 500 suppliers are slated to attend the event, at which more than 1,500 B2B meetings will take place, according to the organizers.

According to a report by the news outlet Quadratín, San Luis Potosí Economic Development Minister Mario García Valde said that the event “seeks to facilitate local companies’ access to automotive sector buyers and open up opportunities for their incorporation in new productive projects.”

With reports from Plano Informativo and Quadratín San Luis Potosí

World.title: Viva-Volaris airlines merger likely to proceed, Reuters reports
World.content:
Mexico’s antitrust commission is expected to approve the unification of Volaris and Viva airlines before the end of the year, creating Mexico’s largest aviation conglomerate.

Citing six sources familiar with the case, Reuters said the National Antimonopoly Commission (CNA) will approve the planned merger between the popular low-cost carriers and the formation of a new company to be called Grupo Más Vuelos.

Executives from Volaris and Viva (formerly Viva Aerobus) say the self-styled “merger of equals” will respect brand identities and “strive to ensure consumers recognize the individual service models with which they have become familiar.”

The CNA will reportedly require Grupo Más Vuelos to meet specific benchmarks and consumer protection criteria — such as keeping fares low and avoiding widespread layoffs — according to three of the sources cited by Reuters.

Critics have raised regulatory concerns, such as route eliminations — the two companies currently operate 55 identical routes — and diminished market competition. They also point out that the transaction would concentrate 73% of domestic air traffic in a single company.

CNA approval is likely to come with requirements that the conglomerate maintain existing route networks and comply with a low-cost mandate that is aligned with regional budget operators.

Yucatán Magazine reported that the federal government has apparently sought to influence the vetting process, since both airlines “serve as redirection points and primary operators at the state-run Felipe Angeles International Airport on the periphery of Mexico City.”

While the merger, first announced last December and approved by international regulatory authorities last month, aims to increase low-cost air travel and connectivity, media reports suggest it is also a “defensive decision.”

Both carriers have experienced financial troubles since the COVID-19 pandemic. Volaris recorded a net loss of US $103.8 million in 2025 and reported a loss of US $127 million in this year’s second quarter. Viva accumulated US $133 million in losses during the first half of 2026.

According to the business consultancy Antitrust Intelligence, the merger aims to build a competitive advantage centered on cost reductions, fleet efficiencies and balance sheet recovery.

Despite the economic challenges the two airlines have been facing, market analysts and investors are said to view future operational synergies favorably.

With reports from Reuters, Yucatán Magazine and Mexico Business News

World.title: Morelos authorities free alleged criminal leader to secure release of 3 kidnapped police
World.content:
Authorities in Morelos freed an alleged criminal leader just hours after he was captured on Monday to secure the release of three kidnapped police officers.

José David Vergara, an alleged leader of the Pueblos Unidos criminal group, was detained on Monday afternoon on drug possession charges in Totolapan, a municipality in northeastern Morelos on the border with México state.

#Estados | Quema de vehículos y bloqueos carreteros se registran la tarde de este lunes en Totoloapan, Morelos, luego de un enfrentamiento armado entre elementos de seguridad e integrantes de un grupo del crimen organizado. De acuerdo con información preliminar, los hechos de violencia son resultado del despliegue de un operativo para capturar a un líder criminal considerado generador de violencia en la región. Información en desarrollo. 📹 Especial — La Silla Rota (@lasillarota) October 13, 2026

The Morelos Attorney General’s Office (FGE) said in a statement that police detained Vergara, known as “El Güero Gym,” during an anti-extortion operation. It said that “cells” of the Pueblos Unidos criminal group retaliated by detaining “three collaborators of the Eastern Region Prosecutor’s Office” — i.e., state police officers. Those officers were conducting homicide investigations and were not involved in the operation during which Vergara was captured.

After the police were kidnapped, “the protocol for handling kidnapping cases was activated to prioritize the lives of the victims being held against their will,” the FGE said before disclosing that the officers were freed at about 7:35 p.m. Monday after “the person detained hours earlier” was handed over.

“One of our colleagues was hospitalized due to a gunshot wound,” the FGE said, adding that he was in “stable” condition.

“The Attorney General’s Office of the State of Morelos stresses that the lives of our personnel are a priority for the institution and for that reason the necessary actions to protect their physical safety were carried out,” the FGE said, adding that “these criminal acts won’t go unpunished.” The newspaper Reforma reported that criminals threatened to kill the state police officers if “El Güero Gym” wasn’t released. On Tuesday, Morelos Attorney General Fernando Blumenkron Escobar said that the events in Totolapan on Monday “can’t be analyzed in an isolated way or reduced to the assertion that [organized] crime forced authorities to give in.” He said that Vergara was under investigation prior to his arrest, but was not subject to an arrest warrant. Blumenkron said the suspect was arrested for drug possession — not for high-impact crimes (such as murder) for which he is under investigation. Blumenkron also said that “at least 10 people” would be investigated in connection with the kidnapping of the three state police officers.

The capture and subsequent release of Vergara was reminiscent of the capture and release of Ovidio Guzmán López in Culiacán, Sinaloa, in 2019. The capture of Guzmán López, a drug trafficker and son of convicted drug lord Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán Loera, triggered a hostile response from the Sinaloa Cartel, leading authorities to decide to release him in an attempt to quell the violence in the Sinaloa capital. García Harfuch: Decision to release suspect was to ‘save lives’ At President Sheinbaum’s Tuesday morning press conference, Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said that the Morelos government’s decision to release Vergara was aimed at “avoiding a greater confrontation” with criminals. “In effect, it was to save lives,” he said. “There were a lot of civilian people in the streets,” García Harfuch said. Citing “preliminary information” from the Morelos government, the security minister said that the state police operation in Morelos on Monday wasn’t specifically aimed at capturing Vergara. However, when officers saw “this individual in flagrante,” they detained him, García Harfuch said. “It wasn’t an operation specifically to detain this person,” he said. As a result, state police officers had “insufficient” force and backup from federal officers to effectively respond to the violence that ensued, García Harfuch said. He said that the decision to release Vergara doesn’t mean that he will go unpunished. “We’re going to arrest him,” García Harfuch said. Vergara’s arrest triggers narcobloqueos in Morelos

In addition to kidnapping three police officers, the Pueblos Unidos criminal group responded to Vergara’s arrest by setting vehicles and tires on fire to create so-called narcobloqueos (narco-blockades).

Reforma reported that narcobloqueos were set up in four municipalities in Morelos: Yecapixtla, Atlatlahucan, Tlayacapan and Oaxtepec.

Criminals also exchanged gunfire with police officers after the arrest of Vergara. Citing “unofficial information,” the El Universal newspaper reported that at least two police officers suffered gunshot wounds.

Morelos, which borders Mexico City, México state, Puebla and Guerrero, is one of Mexico’s most violent states. It recorded 673 homicides in the first nine months of 2026, according to data presented at Sheinbaum’s Tuesday morning press conference.

4 police officers killed in crash while responding to unrest

A police vehicle in which several officers were traveling crashed on the La Pera–Cuautla highway on Monday as they headed to assist colleagues responding to the unrest that followed Vergara’s arrest.

Two officers were killed at the scene of the crash, while two of three injured officers died while being transported to hospital, according to the Morelos Security Ministry.

With reports from EFE, El Universal, Reforma and El Financiero

World.title: In a first, 2 longtime searchers for missing relatives — mother and daughter — earn official certification
World.content:
After years of searching for missing loved ones, Ceci Flores and her daughter have obtained government certification recognizing their skills, a first for relatives confronting Mexico’s disappearance crisis.

Flores announced last week that she and her daughter, Milagros de Jesús Valenzuela Flores, had received the credentials, issued by Mexico’s National Council for Standardization and Certification of Labor Competencies, an agency affiliated with the Education Ministry.

The certification recognizes expertise developed by families who search for missing relatives while pressing authorities to investigate their disappearances.

Flores, 53, has become a leading voice for Mexico’s searching families since her son Alejandro disappeared in 2015. She later founded Madres Buscadoras de Sonora (Searching Mothers of Sonora) and was named to the BBC’s list of 100 inspiring and influential women in 2022.

Alejandro remains missing, but in March, searchers recovered the remains of another son, Marco Antonio, who disappeared in 2019. DNA testing confirmed his identity earlier this year.

Flores’ daughter, Milagros, leads Jóvenes Buscadores de Sonora, a youth search collective she helped establish with about 15 other young people. She is in her mid-20s.

Mexico had 130,381 people still missing or unlocated as of Oct. 12, according to National Registry of Missing and Unlocated Persons figures reported this week by Conexión Migrante. The total excludes people already located alive or dead by that date.

The credentials fall under Competency Standard EC1542, which evaluates information gathering, preparation of case files, interviews, field and remote searches, and reporting.

Flores credited Guanajuato’s State Training Institute and the forensic and legal consulting firm Forensic and Legal with supporting the training, evaluation and certification, El País reported.

“We want to have more tools to do what no mother should have to learn to do: search for her children,” Flores wrote in an Oct. 7 post on X.

Eight women searching in Guanajuato will also receive certification after meeting the same standard, UnoTV reported last week. The women, who will receive their certificates within two months, UnoTV said, completed nine five-hour training sessions, with state scholarships covering certification costs.

In her post, Flores stressed that certification does not transfer the authorities’ search responsibilities to families or search collectives.

Mexico has about 200 such groups — who look for missing relatives while pressing authorities to investigate their disappearances — according to an Amnesty International estimate cited by ADN40 in March.

Meanwhile, Mexico City’s Cuauhtémoc borough has named its council chamber Madres Buscadoras, or Searching Mothers, according to an agreement published Tuesday in the Official Gazette.

The designation honors mothers and other searching relatives without endorsing any specific organization or political position.

With reports from El País, Aristegui Noticias, Vanguardia and Excélsior

World.title: 4 Mexican bars are among this year’s World’s 50 Best
World.content:
Mexico is home to four of the best bars in the world, according to the 2026 edition of The World’s 50 Best Bars, with two of them ranking in the top 10.

Here are the Mexican bars that made the list.

h

Handshake Speakeasy – Mexico City (No. 6)

Crowned The World’s Best Bar in 2024, Handshake Speakeasy has maintained its high global ranking thanks to its culinary approach to mixology.

Located in the heart of Mexico City’s Zona Rosa, the establishment was founded by Rodrigo Urraca, Marcos Di Battista, and Dutch bartender Eric van Beek, who is responsible for its creative cocktail program.

“Hands down, the legend of Handshake Speakeasy speaks for itself,” The 50 Best Bars said, highlighting the bar’s special take on the classic piña colada.

Bar Mauro – Mexico City (No. 10)

Located in the Roma Norte neighborhood, Bar Mauro secured 10th place and won the Disaronno Highest New Entry Award 2026, which honors the highest-ranking of the bars that enter the top 50 for the first time.

The project belongs to brothers Ricardo and Eduardo Nava and opened its doors in November 2024. Ranking even higher (No. 2) on The 50 Best Bars in North America list, Bar Mauro marks one of the standout venues in Mexico.

The 50 Best Bars highlights the Negroni (named after an Italian count), the basilico (a basil-based cocktail) and the Maurito (a diminutive of the bar’s name) as some of the bar’s most recommended cocktails.

El Gallo Altanero – Guadalajara (No. 28)

The only Mexican bar outside Mexico City to make the top 50, El Gallo Altanero is located in the city’s hip Colonia Americana neighborhood. It was opened in 2018 by Swedish bartender Freddy Andreasson and Alejandra Aguinaga.

Its cocktail menu prioritizes Mexico’s seasonal ingredients, and The 50 Best highlights the Jalisco Old Fashioned and the tuna negra (that’s the Spanish word tuna, by the way, as in the fruit of the nopal cactus).

Tlecan – Mexico City (No. 47)

This mezcalería opened in 2019, founded by Bernardo Serna, Eduardo Panchur and Eli Martínez Bello. Like Bar Mauro, it’s located in the bar-rich Roma Norte neighborhood.

Tlecan’s cocktail menu is a nod to Mexico’s agave culture and lesser-known spirits like bacanora, pox and raicilla. The 50 Best highlights the paloma blanca, made with clarified grapefruit juice, and a piña colada variation using pulque.

Beyond the 50 Best

Mexico’s presence doesn’t end with those four names. The extended list features Form + Matter (No. 59) and Licorería Limantour (No. 63) in Mexico City; and Arca in Tulum (No. 67).

Mexico News Daily

World.title: MND Local BCS: Historic ‘Cabo to Cabo’ running of the Baja 1000 announced for November
World.content:
Before the recent announcement by SCORE (Southern California Off-Road Enthusiasts) International, the sanctioning and governing body of the world’s longest-running and most legendary off-road race, that the Baja 1000 would feature a unique “Cabo to Cabo” routing for its 59th edition this November, Cabo — shorthand for either the municipality of Los Cabos or its most populous city, Cabo San Lucas — had been included on the course map on only two previous occasions: in 2000 and 2007, when the race started in Ensenada and concluded in Cabo San Lucas.

That makes this year’s race — scheduled for Nov. 9 to 15 — a historic one, and not just because the race will start for the first time in Los Cabos; specifically, on Avenida Centenario in San José del Cabo, where the 964.66-mile competition sponsored by BF Goodrich Tires will both start and finish. This will also mark the first time the Baja 1000 has been run entirely within the state of Baja California Sur.

The course map for 2026

An estimated 250 teams representing 15 countries are expected to participate in the 2026 Baja 1000. Teams (generally two drivers or a driver and navigator, along with support crew) compete across several classes determined by age and vehicle type — from trucks, cars and buggies to motorcycles, quads and UTVs — vying not only for cash prizes, but also coveted points in the SCORE World Desert Championship, for which the Baja 1000 is the season’s finale.

The Baja 1000 has no set route. Ensenada has hosted the starting line for 49 of the 58 previous races, and the finish line for 31; hence, the city’s nickname as the “Desert Racing Capital of the World.” La Paz, Baja California Sur’s capital, has also been a popular terminus, serving as the finish line 22 times.

However, new and “innovative” routes are regularly included in the course rotation.

Going ‘Transpeninsular’

“Every three years, we aim to hold a ‘Transpeninsular’ version,” notes Juan Tintos Funcke, General Manager of Score International, per El Imparcial. “The most recent one was in 2023 and ran from south to north. Normally, the route goes from Ensenada to La Paz, but that year it went from La Paz to Ensenada. That is how we constantly seek innovation and offer different challenges in our races — we adjust the logistics to keep the events appealing.”

The “Cabo to Cabo” route in 2026 will certainly be that, winding its way up the East Cape from San José del Cabo, passing La Paz and then Loreto before making a turn to head back down the Pacific Coast, skirting Todos Santos and El Pescadero on the return loop to San José del Cabo.

In total, four of the five municipalities in Baja California Sur will see action along the race route (Comondú, La Paz, Loreto and Los Cabos are included; Mulegé is not).

The birth of the Baja 1000 and its enduring popularity

Southern California hot rod pioneer Don Francisco and race vehicle builder Bill Stroppe were key links between Mexico’s legendary Carrera Panamericana — the world’s longest and most dangerous race held lengthwise across Mexico between 1950 and 1954 — and the Baja 1000. Francisco had helped Stroppe and Clay Smith prepare Lincolns for the Carrera Panamericana, experience with epic-scale routing that no doubt came in handy when he aerially surveyed the inaugural route for the Baja 1000, which was run under the auspices of NORRA (National Off-Road Racing Association), founded by Ed Pearlman, Francisco and others in 1966. NORRA organized the first six Baja 1000 races between 1967 and 1972.

Although the Carrera Panamericana supplied the precedent for an internationally promoted, grand-scale Mexican endurance race, the Baja 1000 grew directly from the timed record runs of the 1960s … inspired by the 1962 durability demonstration of Honda CL72 Scrambler motorcycles, which Dave Ekins and Bill Robertson Jr. drove from Tijuana to La Paz, navigating a network of dirt tracks, washes and trails in just under 40 hours. The 950 miles they traversed were very close to the total later covered by the Baja 1000, and 40 hours is still the time limit for teams to complete the race.

Baja’s timeless off-road allure

The challenges of the Baja California peninsula’s rugged terrain have been attracting those thirsty for adventure ever since, first from those seeking to beat Ekins and Robertson’s time, and later, during the six-decade heyday of the Baja 1000, from everyone from professional drivers to rock stars (Ted Nugent) and Hollywood movie stars like Steve McQueen, James Garner and Paul Newman (who also became a professional race car driver and completed his last Baja 1000 just before he turned 80).

Parnelli Jones, who famously described the Baja 1000 as a “24-hour plane crash,” was among the first of the crossover auto racing stars to embrace the event. After winning the Indianapolis 500 in 1963, he claimed overall Baja 1000 titles in 1971 and 1972 in his famed Dick Russell and Stroppe-built Ford Bronco, “Big Oly.” A host of Formula 1, NASCAR and IndyCar champions followed, including Robby Gordon, Jimmie Johnson, Rick Mears and Alexander Rossi.

However, following the OPEC Oil Crisis in 1973, NORRA’s permits were revoked, and the Baja Sports Committee organized that year’s race before the 1974 event was canceled, and the Mickey Thompson-founded SCORE took over in 1975 — an association that to date has lasted more than 50 years.

What’s at stake this year?

The Baja 1000 brings with it tangible economic benefits: about US $35 million is expected to flow to municipalities statewide. Additionally, the race and its run-up — pre-running begins Oct. 24 — bring excitement as high season ramps up in Los Cabos during what has been a disappointing year for tourism. International arrivals, for example, have thus far been down 8.4% in 2026, and tourism as a whole down 5.6%.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by SCORE International (@scoreinternational)

There’s a lot on the line for racers, too. San Diego’s Luke “The Luke” McMillin, for example, is attempting to complete a rare full-season sweep of the 2026 SCORE calendar, having already logged Trophy Truck class wins in the San Felipe 250, Baja 500 and Baja 400. Tyler Lynn, Carter Klein and their SLR (Slam Life Racing) Honda team, meanwhile, are attempting to go that feat one step better, aiming at a second consecutive Motorcycle class season sweep.

Chris Sands is a writer and editor for Mexico News Daily, and the former Cabo San Lucas local expert for the USA Today travel website 10 Best and writer of Fodor’s Los Cabos travel guidebook. He has also contributed to numerous other websites and publications, including The San Diego Union-Tribune, Marriott Bonvoy Traveler, Forbes Travel Guide, Porthole Cruise and Travel, and Cabo Living.

COLOMBIA · SAFETY

Key Facts The country Colombia, a close US security partner in South America, is led by President Abelardo de la Espriella.

What happened A 51-year-old British cancer doctor who lived in the United States died on Monday, 12 October, after falling ill at a Medellín music festival.

The festival EDC, a brand of the US company Insomniac, held its first Colombian edition on 10 and 11 October at Medellín’s main sports complex.

Earlier death A Costa Rican man died early on Sunday, 11 October, after falling ill on the festival’s opening night.

Medical cases Medellín’s health department counted 193 medical cases at the festival, 107 of them linked to intoxication, and seven hospital transfers.

Cause of death No official cause has been published for either man, and forensic results are still pending.

Power Index Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 51.9 points (October 2026 edition).

A 51-year-old British cancer doctor living in the US has died after falling ill at EDC, a Medellín festival of electronic music in Colombia. He is the second foreigner to die after the Medellín festival, held on 10 and 11 October by a US festival brand.

Colombian outlets including El Espectador and La FM reported on Tuesday, 13 October, that he died the previous afternoon in a clinic. Local media have linked his death to drug and alcohol use, but no official cause of death has been published.

What Happened to the Doctor

El Tiempo reported the death early on Tuesday, describing the man as an English oncologist based in the United States who specialised in prostate cancer. El Espectador and Vanguardia later said he had co-founded a prostate cancer institute in Arizona in 2002.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Colombia ranks 6th of 14 with 51.9 points. Strongest pillar: military means (91); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (28). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB-); 26 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.8 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

He fell ill at the Medellín festival on Sunday, 11 October, and was taken to the El Rosario clinic, Publimetro and Vanguardia report. He died there at about 5 p.m. on Monday, 12 October, a public holiday in Colombia.

La FM reported that Medellín’s security department linked his condition to a high intake of amphetamines and alcohol. El Espectador stressed that the exact circumstances are still under investigation and that the official cause must await the relevant procedures.

The paper also cautioned that drug use inside the Medellín festival should not be assumed without official information to back it up. Colombia’s state forensic institute, known as Medicina Legal, normally establishes the cause of death in such cases.
