The First Death on Opening Night

The first victim was a Costa Rican man who fell ill on the festival’s opening night, Saturday, 10 October. El Colombiano, Publimetro and Vanguardia report that he was found unconscious and died early on Sunday at the Pablo Tobón Uribe hospital.

Investigators are looking into a possible overdose, which has not been confirmed. His father has told El Colombiano and Noticias Caracol that his son was not an addict.

The Rio Times reported the Costa Rican’s death on 11 October, when it was the only death linked to the Medellín festival. Authorities have not said whether the two deaths are connected.

What Medellín’s Health Department Reported

Natalia López, the city’s health secretary, reported 193 medical cases at the Medellín festival’s care points over the two days. Of those, 107 were linked to some kind of intoxication, and seven people were taken to hospitals in the city.

López urged people at large events to look after their health and to use the medical points when they need help. “Above any celebration is life,” she said, according to Telemedellín and La FM.

A Stabbing After the Festival

In a separate case, an Australian man staying in Medellín’s Laureles district was found with 25 stab wounds early on Sunday, 11 October. El Colombiano and Semana both reported the attack, and El Colombiano said he had likely attended the festival that night.

El Colombiano said investigators were reviewing security cameras and treating robbery as one line of inquiry, with no arrests reported. The Rio Times covered the attack on 12 October, and nothing published so far ties it to the two deaths.

Medellín’s Big Night Out

EDC, short for Electric Daisy Carnival, is a large electronic dance music festival brand owned by the US events company Insomniac. The Rio Times previewed the Colombian debut before the event.

The festival used the Atanasio Girardot sports complex, home to the city’s main football stadium, in the Laureles-Estadio area. The two deaths and the stabbing all came during the long holiday weekend of the Medellín festival.

What It Means for You

The US State Department rates Colombia at Level 3, “Reconsider travel,” in an advisory issued on 31 March 2026. It lists drugging among the crimes visitors face and warns: “Never leave food or drinks unattended at a bar or restaurant.”

At any big Medellín festival or night out, stay with friends, watch your drink and find the medical point when you arrive. Carry insurance that covers emergency hospital care abroad, and read The Rio Times guide to staying safe in Colombia.

What Is Not Known

No official cause of death has been published for either man, and no public forensic report backs the drug findings described in the press. It is also not known what, if anything, either man took inside the festival grounds.

Authorities have not said whether the two deaths are linked or where any drugs were obtained. It is also not known whether Medellín will change its rules for future large festivals at the sports complex.

More: Colombia news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who died after the EDC Medellín festival?

Two foreign visitors died: a Costa Rican man who fell ill on the opening night and a British cancer doctor who lived in the US. The doctor, 51, died on Monday, 12 October, a day after he fell ill at the festival.

What caused the deaths?

No official cause has been published for either death. Press reports point to drug and alcohol use, and the authorities are investigating both cases.

How many people needed medical help at the festival?

Medellín’s health department reported 193 medical cases at the festival’s care points, 107 of them linked to intoxication. Seven people were taken to hospitals in the city.

Is Medellín safe for US travellers?

The US State Department advises Americans to reconsider travel to Colombia and warns of drugging and robberies, including through dating apps. Travellers should watch their drinks, stay with people they trust and avoid meeting strangers alone.

COLOMBIA · ECONOMY

Key Facts The country Colombia is Latin America’s fourth-largest economy, and the United States took 28.3% of its exports from January to August 2026.

What happened The International Monetary Fund (IMF) cut its Colombia growth forecast for 2026 to 2.2%, from 2.3% in April, in its October World Economic Outlook.

Next year The IMF now sees growth of 2.3% in 2027, down from 2.5%, and unemployment rising from 8% in 2025 to 10% in 2027.

Inflation The IMF expects average consumer prices to rise 6% in 2026 and 5.7% in 2027, well above the central bank’s 3% target.

Prediction markets Polymarket gives a 65.5% chance Colombia’s central bank holds its 12.25% rate in October (14 October, 4:08 a.m. ET).

Power Index Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 51.9 points (October 2026 edition).

Still open The finance ministry has not yet published its planned debt law, and the terms of any IMF support are not known.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has cut its Colombia growth forecast to 2.2% for 2026, just below the 2.3% it expects for Latin America. The Washington-based lender set out the figures in its October World Economic Outlook this week and lowered its 2027 forecast to 2.3%.

For US investors in Colombian bonds and shares, the cut follows a rise in the central bank’s key rate from 9.25% to 12.25% this year. The IMF also expects inflation to average about 6% this year, twice the central bank’s 3% target.

What the IMF Forecast Says

The IMF now expects Colombia’s economy to grow 2.2% in 2026 and 2.3% in 2027, after growth of 2.6% in 2025. In its April outlook, the IMF’s Colombia growth forecast was 2.3% for this year and 2.5% for next year.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Colombia ranks 6th of 14 with 51.9 points. Strongest pillar: military means (91); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (28). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB-); 26 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.8 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The new Colombia growth forecast comes with a worse inflation picture. The IMF sees average consumer prices rising 6% in 2026 and 5.7% in 2027, up from 5.9% and 5.2% in April.

Unemployment is expected to climb from 8% in 2025 to 9% this year and 10% in 2027, the same path the IMF drew in April. The fund also sees the current-account deficit, the gap in Colombia’s trade and income with the world, widening to 3.4% of economic output in 2027.

Portafolio, a Bogotá business daily, reported the figures early on Tuesday, 13 October. It noted that growth in 2027 would be only 0.1 percentage point faster than this year.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

How Colombia Compares With the Region

The IMF expects Latin America and the Caribbean to grow 2.3% this year and 2.5% in 2027. Its Colombia growth forecast of 2.2% puts the country level with Brazil and ahead of Mexico at 1.5% and Chile at 0.6%.

Peru, its Andean neighbour, is forecast to grow 3% this year, while the United States is seen at 2.3%. Colombia’s inflation forecast of 6% for 2026 is higher than the IMF’s figures for Brazil, Mexico, Chile and Peru.

That mix of slow growth and stubborn prices keeps borrowing costs high for families and companies. It also makes it harder for the central bank to cut rates soon.

Debt, Interest Rates and the Talks With the IMF

Colombia’s central bank, the Banco de la República, raised its benchmark rate by a quarter point to 12.25% on 30 September. The rate stood at 9.25% at the end of 2025, according to the Bogotá daily El Tiempo.

Annual inflation reached 6.29% in September, the national statistics office DANE reported on 7 October. Governor Leonardo Villar said inflation may not return to the bank’s 3% target until 2028, El Tiempo and the news site Valora Analitik reported.

Deputy finance minister Juan Sebastián Betancur told a Senate committee the government will present its “rescue law” on debt within days, El Tiempo reported. Its aim, he said, is to make sure “the bathtub does not overflow with debt”.

The IMF’s own tables show general government debt rising from 59.5% of economic output this year to 62.9% in 2027 and 65.1% in 2028. It puts the overall government deficit at 6.9% of output in 2026.

The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella, a conservative in office since August, asked the IMF in late September to review the economy. A finance ministry team led by Betancur was due to meet the fund in Washington on 6 October to seek financing, Valora Analitik reported.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, bettors give a 65.5% chance that the central bank holds its 12.25% rate in October (14 October, 4:08 a.m. ET). They put a quarter-point hike at 31.5% and a half-point hike or more at 5%.

About US$35,900 has been bet on that market, and the quarter-point hike gained one point over the past day. On Kalshi, which is regulated in the US by the CFTC, a hold is priced at 62% and a quarter-point hike at 28%.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for You

For US holders of Colombian bonds, slower growth and rising debt keep the focus on the government’s coming rescue law and any IMF deal. Both will show how far the new government is willing to cut spending or raise revenue.

For travellers and expats paid in dollars, the official exchange rate was about 3,182 pesos to the US dollar on 14 October. Local prices keep rising, with restaurants and hotels up 9.44% in the year to September, according to DANE.

For US companies that buy Colombian coffee, flowers or oil, the lower Colombia growth forecast changes little in the short term. Harvests, the peso and US trade policy matter more for those prices than a 0.1-point change in growth.

What Is Not Known

The IMF report gives no specific reason for trimming its Colombia growth forecast. The finance ministry has not published the text of the rescue law or listed the cuts it will contain.

It is not known what form any IMF financing would take or how large it could be. The central bank’s next rate decision is due on Friday 30 October and will depend on inflation data still to come.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the IMF’s new Colombia growth forecast?

The IMF expects Colombia’s economy to grow 2.2% in 2026 and 2.3% in 2027. In April it had forecast 2.3% and 2.5%.

Why are interest rates so high in Colombia?

Annual inflation was 6.29% in September, more than double the central bank’s 3% target. The bank raised its benchmark rate to 12.25% on 30 September to bring prices down.

Is Colombia asking the IMF for money?

The government asked the IMF in late September to review Colombia’s economy, and officials planned financing talks in Washington on 6 October. The form and size of any IMF support have not been announced.

What does the forecast mean for the Colombian peso?

The official rate was about 3,182 pesos to the US dollar on 14 October. A weaker growth outlook and high debt can weigh on the currency, while high interest rates tend to support it.

PERU · SECURITY

Key Facts The country Peru is an Andean nation on South America’s Pacific coast and a leading exporter of copper and gold.

What happened Police broke up an alleged Tren de Aragua extortion cell in Puente Piedra, a district on Lima’s northern edge, and detained six Venezuelans.

The suspects Six Venezuelans aged 23 to 32, including a 28-year-old named as the alleged leader; all are presumed innocent.

What was seized A mini Uzi, a rifle, a hand grenade, 85 rounds of ammunition, six phones, a car and four motorcycles.

The alleged scheme A seized notebook allegedly lists four bus companies and a fee of 80 soles (about US$23) a vehicle each week.

The US angle Washington has listed Tren de Aragua as a Foreign Terrorist Organization since 20 February 2025.

Power Index Peru ranks 5th of 14 in Peru ranks 5th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 54.7 points (October 2026 edition).

Police in Peru have broken up an alleged Tren de Aragua extortion cell in Lima and detained six Venezuelans. Tren de Aragua, a gang born in a Venezuelan prison, has been on the US list of terrorist organizations since February 2025.

Peru’s Interior Ministry announced the raid on Tuesday, 13 October, in Puente Piedra, a district on Lima’s northern edge. Officers seized a mini Uzi, a rifle, a grenade and a notebook that allegedly lists weekly payments demanded from bus companies.

What Police Found in Puente Piedra

The raid targeted a house in the Villa Los Olivos housing association that police say served as the gang’s base of operations. RPP, a leading Peruvian radio network, quoted General José Antonio Zavala, head of the police’s criminal investigation directorate, saying so.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Peru ranks 5th of 14 with 54.7 points. Strongest pillar: military means (71); weakest: future resources (37). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The six detained Venezuelans are aged 23 to 32, the Interior Ministry said. Police name Iam Gael León Díaz, 28, as the alleged leader of the group.

The group calls itself “Los Remanentes del Tren de Aragua”, Spanish for “the Tren de Aragua Remnants”. The unit that made the arrests specialises in extortion and organised crime cases.

Officers seized a mini Uzi submachine gun, a rifle, a hand grenade, three magazines and 85 unfired rounds of 9 mm ammunition. A police bomb squad destroyed the grenade in a controlled blast outside the house, RPP reported.

Police also took six mobile phones, a white Chevrolet car, four motorcycles and four licence plates. They found construction-worker uniforms and clothing bearing the logos of several companies.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What the Six Venezuelans Are Accused Of

The six are under investigation for extortion, membership of a criminal gang and crimes against public safety. The ministry says investigators must still identify possible victims and the full scope of the alleged extortion.

The seized notebook allegedly records Tren de Aragua extortion payments from public transport companies on the Puente Piedra route. It names four bus firms, including El Chino and Virgen de la Puerta.

General Zavala said the suspects acknowledged in preliminary statements that they extorted public transport and construction workers, according to RPP.

“According to their own words, they say they have to go and put pressure,” Zavala said. He also said all six appear to have entered Peru irregularly, RPP reported.

Correo, a national daily, reports that the uniforms are under examination because detectives want to know whether the gang extorted other businesses. The phones will be examined for threats, demands for money and messages between gang members.

Why Tren de Aragua Matters to the United States

Tren de Aragua began as a prison gang in Venezuela, with its base in Tocorón prison, and now also operates in Colombia, Peru and Chile. The US State Department lists it as a Foreign Terrorist Organization, with a listing date of 20 February 2025.

That label makes it a crime for anyone in the United States to knowingly give the gang material support, including money. US banks that find funds in which the gang has an interest must also freeze them and report them to the Treasury.

On Friday, 12 June 2026, President Donald Trump announced that a US military strike had killed the gang’s leader, Héctor Guerrero Flores. Washington and Caracas called it a joint operation against “Niño Guerrero”, as he was known, and Venezuela confirmed his death that night.

El Comercio, a leading Lima daily, reported in May that the US Justice Department had charged more than 260 members and associates since January 2025. The department said many suspects in one of those operations were undocumented migrants from Venezuela, Colombia and Honduras.

Lima’s Extortion Wave Hits Transport Workers

The Puente Piedra raid fell under the Unified Command for the Fight Against Crime, which Peru’s conservative president, Keiko Fujimori, launched on 7 October. It brings Peru’s armed forces and the National Police under one command to confront criminal organisations.

On Sunday, 11 October, motorcycle-taxi drivers blocked the Pan-American Highway North in Puente Piedra after one of their colleagues was attacked. They told RPP that four gangs had extorted them since May, and one driver said threats demanded 50,000 soles (about US$14,500).

On Monday, 12 October, prosecutors and police broke up another Lima gang that allegedly charged informal shared taxis 120 soles (about US$35) a week. The raids took place in the Rímac and San Juan de Lurigancho districts, according to the Public Ministry, Peru’s prosecution service.

On Saturday, 10 October, the Interior Ministry announced seven arrests in an alleged Tren de Aragua extortion case against traders in Piura, northern Peru. In one case, the suspects allegedly demanded 100 soles (about US$29) a week from a trader.

The government is also setting up a committee with banks and the telecom regulator to fight extortion. Prime Minister Luis Galarreta announced it on Monday, 12 October, to give investigators faster access to information in extortion and illegal mining cases.

What It Means for You

The US State Department rates Peru at Level 2, “Exercise increased caution”, in its current travel advisory. It warns that crime is common in Peru and that muggings and other violent crime often happen even in daylight.

Puente Piedra lies on Lima’s northern edge, far from Miraflores and Barranco, the seaside districts popular with visitors. The gangs in these cases target bus operators, motorcycle-taxi drivers, traders and builders, according to officials and the drivers themselves.

For US readers, the case shows groups using the Tren de Aragua name still active in Lima after the June strike on its leader. Companies with partners in Peru’s transport or construction trades should note that Tren de Aragua extortion in this case allegedly targeted exactly those sectors.

What Is Not Known

The Interior Ministry has not said on which day the raid took place or how many bus operators paid the cell. Police have also not said how much money the group allegedly collected in total.

It is not yet known whether prosecutors will ask a judge to hold the six in pretrial detention. Investigators have not shown whether this Tren de Aragua extortion cell takes orders from the gang’s wider leadership or only uses its name.

No court has ruled on the case, and all six suspects are presumed innocent. The ministry says the investigation will continue with the competent authorities to establish each suspect’s role.

More: Peru news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Tren de Aragua?

Tren de Aragua is a criminal gang that began in a Venezuelan prison and now operates in several Latin American countries. The United States listed it as a Foreign Terrorist Organization on 20 February 2025.

Who was arrested in Puente Piedra?

Police detained six Venezuelans aged 23 to 32, including a 28-year-old they describe as the cell’s alleged leader. All six are presumed innocent until a court rules otherwise.

How much did the gang allegedly demand?

A notebook seized in the raid allegedly lists Tren de Aragua extortion fees of 80 soles (about US$23) a vehicle each week. Police have not said how many vehicles paid or how much money was collected.

Is Lima safe for American visitors?

The US State Department asks visitors to exercise increased caution in Peru, its Level 2 rating, because crime is common. The extortion cases in this story targeted local transport workers, traders and builders.

Key Facts — The forecast Economists in the central bank’s Focus survey expect Brazilian inflation of 5.22% in 2026 and 4.30% in 2027, and 3.79% in 2028 (published 13 October 2026).

What the Central Bank Projects

The Copom, the central bank’s Monetary Policy Committee, cut the Selic from 14.00% to 13.75% on Wednesday, 16 September 2026. It was the fifth cut of 0.25 points this year, and Brazilian media report the vote was unanimous.

The Copom’s own projection for inflation is 5.2% for 2026 and 3.9% for 2027, based on its reference scenario. For the first quarter of 2028, the horizon the bank cares most about, it projects 3.2%.

The bank said risks to inflation remain higher than usual, with an upward bias, and described a scenario of unanchored expectations that calls for caution. Unanchored means that economists no longer trust inflation to return to the 3.0% goal on its own.

In its quarterly report of 24 September, the central bank put the chance that inflation ends 2026 above the 4.5% ceiling at 90%, up from 79% in the previous report. That figure is not the chance of missing the target, which requires six months in a row outside the band.

The next Copom meeting is on 3 and 4 November 2026, with the decision on the evening of 4 November. It will be the first rate decision after the presidential runoff on 25 October.

Latest Inflation Data: The IPCA for September

The IPCA rose 0.82% in September 2026, the statistics agency IBGE reported on Friday, 9 October. That is the biggest monthly rise since March, against 0.48% in September 2025.

Prices rose 4.58% over the 12 months to September, up from 4.22% in August, and 3.95% since the start of the year. The 12-month rate is back above the 4.5% ceiling after two months inside the band.

Housing was the biggest driver, with a rise of 2.31%, as household electricity bills jumped 7.98% when a credit on Itaipu hydropower bills ended. Airfares rose 9.66%, and food and drink prices rose 0.83% after three months of decline.

IPCA, 12-month rate · IBGE May 2026 4.72% June 2026 4.64% July 2026 4.44% August 2026 4.22% September 2026 4.58%

Brazil’s Inflation Target and Tolerance Band

Brazil’s inflation target is 3.0%, with a tolerance of 1.5 percentage points either side, so the band runs from 1.5% to 4.5%. The National Monetary Council set it in Resolution 5,141 of 26 June 2024, and since January 2025 it is a continuous target.

A continuous target is judged every month, not only in December. The target counts as missed when the 12-month rate stays outside the band for six months in a row, and then the central bank governor must write an open letter to the finance minister.

That happened once, in June 2025, when inflation was above 4.5% for a sixth straight month, and Governor Gabriel Galípolo published his letter on 10 July 2025. The rate returned to the band in November 2025.

In 2026 the rate has been above 4.5% in May, June and September, but never for six months in a row. We found no new letter this year.

What Brazilian Inflation Means for Foreigners

Rents are the first place readers feel it. Brazilian leases are adjusted once a year with a price index, usually the IGP-M or the IPCA, and the IGP-M, a general price index published by the Fundação Getulio Vargas, rose 1.57% in September after three months of decline.

The real is the second. On 13 October one US dollar bought R$5.03 (EODHD closing rate), and Focus analysts expect R$5.15 at year-end, so they see a slightly weaker real by December.

Interest rates are the third. With the Selic at 13.75% and inflation expected at 5.22%, the gap between the two is about 8.5 percentage points, our own simple calculation, so savers in reais earn a high return above inflation.

For a foreign resident paid in dollars or euros, higher Brazilian inflation erodes the exchange-rate advantage over time. Prices of food, power and flights are rising faster than the central bank wants.

The headquarters of the Banco Central do Brasil, the country’s central bank, in Brasília. File photo, 2010. (Photo: Banco Central do Brasil, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

What Prediction Markets Say

Prediction markets let traders buy contracts that pay US$1 if an outcome happens, so a price of 47 cents reads as a 47% chance. On Polymarket, the market “Brazil Annual Inflation 2026” (US$162,609 traded) gave 48.5% to a 2026 rate of 5.00% to 5.49%, 21.9% to 5.50% to 5.99%, and 20.6% to 4.50% to 4.99%.

A second Polymarket market on the Brazilian central bank’s November decision, listed there as “Bank of Brazil” (US$57,027 traded), gave 89.5% to a cut of 0.25 points and 4.8% to no change. Prices were read on 14 October 2026 at 03:50 Eastern time, and they are bets, not forecasts.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Dates to Watch

Brazil inflation calendar · EODHD economic calendar Monday, 19 October: Focus survey next forecasts Friday, 23 October: IPCA-15 for October (forecast: 0.4% in the month) mid-month IPCA Wednesday, 4 November: Copom decision, 282nd meeting Selic Tuesday, 10 November: minutes of the Copom meeting Ata Thursday, 12 November: IPCA for October (forecast: 0.3% in the month) IBGE

The IPCA-15 is a preview of monthly inflation that covers prices from about mid-month to mid-month. IBGE normally publishes both IPCA figures at 9 a.m. Brasília time.

What Is Not Known

No one yet knows if the September jump in electricity prices is a one-off or the start of a longer rise. The end of the Itaipu credit explains part of it, and the next IPCA releases will show whether food and flights follow.

The runoff for president on 25 October 2026 adds a second unknown, because markets may move with the result. We do not forecast how the vote will change inflation expectations.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Brazil’s inflation forecast for 2026?

The central bank’s Focus survey of 13 October 2026 puts 2026 inflation at 5.22%, from 5.01% a week earlier. The Copom’s own projection is 5.2% for the end of 2026.

What is Brazil’s inflation forecast for 2027?

The Focus median for 2027 is 4.30%, which is inside the 1.5% to 4.5% target band but above the 3.0% goal. The Copom projects 3.9% for 2027.

What is the IPCA and what is the Focus survey?

The IPCA is Brazil’s official consumer price index, published monthly by the statistics agency IBGE. The Focus survey is the central bank’s weekly poll of economists, and its median is the standard market forecast.

What is Brazil’s inflation target?

The target is 3.0% with a tolerance of 1.5 percentage points either side, so inflation should stay between 1.5% and 4.5%. It counts as missed after six straight months outside that band.

Will the Brazilian central bank cut interest rates again?

The Selic is 13.75% after a cut on 16 September, and Focus economists expect 13.25% by December. Polymarket traders gave 89.5% to a further 0.25-point cut at the 4 November meeting, and these are bets, not forecasts.

PERU · TRADE

Key Facts The country Peru , on South America’s Pacific coast, has had a free-trade agreement with the United States since 2009.

What happened Ica, Peru’s main grape region, opened its 2026-27 export season with a first US cargo, announced on Tuesday 13 October.

Where grapes grow Ica on the southern coast supplies about half of Peru’s grape exports, ahead of Piura in the north with 35% and Lambayeque with 5%.

Last season Peru exported more than 690,000 tonnes of grapes in 2025-26, worth about US$2 billion, and the United States took about half.

World rank Peru led the world in fresh table grape exports in 2024-25, and China was forecast to draw level with it in 2025-26.

Power Index Peru ranks 5th of 14 in Peru ranks 5th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 54.7 points (October 2026 edition).

Still open The first cargo’s sailing date, port and exporters are not public, and growers expect a 9% drop in exports this season.

Ica, the desert region behind about half of all Peru grape exports, has sent its first cargo of the 2026-27 season to the United States. Peru’s agriculture ministry announced the shipment on Tuesday 13 October, and SENASA, the national farm health service, certified the fruit.

The news matters to American shoppers, because the United States buys about half of all Peru grape exports. Peru vies with China as the world’s top table grape exporter and competes with Chile for American buyers.

What Peru’s Agriculture Ministry Announced

Peru’s Ministry of Agrarian Development and Irrigation, known by its Spanish initials Midagri, said Ica had officially opened its grape export campaign for 2026-27. The first shipment of the new season from Ica went to the United States, the ministry said in a statement on Tuesday 13 October.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Peru ranks 5th of 14 with 54.7 points. Strongest pillar: military means (71); weakest: future resources (37). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The cargo was certified by SENASA, Peru’s national farm health service, which inspects fields and packing plants against the rules of each buying country. With that system in place, Peruvian growers can sell their grapes in 98 foreign markets, the ministry said.

Farmers in the Ica valley grow 50 grape varieties, Midagri said, among them Sweet Globe, Autumn Crisp, Ivory, Timpson, Sweet Celebration and Candy Dreams. Provid, the association of Peru grape growers, told the Lima business daily Gestión that licensed, proprietary varieties made up 87% of exports.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why Ica Leads Peru’s Grape Exports

Ica accounts for about 50% of Peru’s grape exports, followed by Piura in the north with 35% and Lambayeque with 5%, according to Midagri. In the last campaign, SENASA certified 351,304 tonnes of grapes from Ica for 44 foreign markets.

That fruit came from 614 farms, mainly in the province of Ica, with 9,921 hectares (about 24,500 acres), and in Pisco, with 1,418 hectares. Smaller vineyards lie in Chincha, with 182 hectares, and Nasca, with 104 hectares.

The north is the other pillar of the Peru grape season. SENASA said on 29 September that Piura, Lambayeque, La Libertad and Áncash exported more than 319,000 tonnes in 2025-26, about 46% of the national total.

North and south are diverging this season, according to Provid’s latest forecast, reported by the farm news site Agraria.pe on 9 October. Provid expects northern shipments to drop 28% after an early harvest and smaller berries, while the south, led by Ica, should grow 6%.

Peru’s Place in the World Grape Trade

Midagri calls Peru the world’s leading grape exporter, ahead of Chile, the United States and Italy. The US Department of Agriculture’s December 2025 world outlook listed Peru as the top table grape exporter in 2024-25, with 690,000 tonnes.

The same report forecast that China would draw level with Peru at 770,000 tonnes in 2025-26, on growing sales to Southeast Asia. Peru and Chile, by contrast, ship mostly to North America and Europe, where they compete with each other, the USDA said.

Midagri puts Peru grape exports in the 2025-26 campaign at 729,000 tonnes, mainly to the United States, the Netherlands, Mexico, Britain, China, Canada and Spain. Provid valued the season’s grape exports at US$2.07 billion, up 1% on the season before.

Provid’s figures, reported by Gestión in May, showed volume up 4% at 86.4 million boxes of 8.2 kilos, with 52% going to the United States. Europe took 22%, and Provid’s general manager, Luis Miguel Vegas, called it a more price-sensitive market.

Table grapes rank with blueberries, avocados and coffee among Peru’s most emblematic farm exports, Midagri said. They give a farm leg to an economy better known abroad for the mining that dominates Peru’s natural resources.

What It Means for You

For US shoppers, the Peru grape season means a steady flow of imported grapes into American stores over the coming months. The United States is the world’s largest table grape importer and bought a record 909,000 tonnes in 2024-25, the USDA said.

Supply could be tighter this time, because Provid expects Peru grape exports to fall 9% to 78.7 million boxes, or about 645,000 tonnes. Growth in Peru’s farm exports has already slowed on fears of El Niño this year.

Since 24 July, Washington has charged an extra 12.5% tariff on many Peruvian goods in a forced-labour trade case, the official gazette El Peruano reported. Goods worth 45% of US imports from Peru are exempt, but the Peruvian trade site Infomercado listed fresh grapes among those left out.

The US measure does not find that Peru exports goods made with forced labour, Peru’s trade ministry said, but faults its import controls. The ministry said in July it would push for a review of the US forced-labour tariff on Peruvian goods.

What Is Not Known

Midagri did not say on which day the first cargo sailed, from which port, or which companies shipped it. It also gave no value for the shipment and no forecast for the whole season.

The weather is the biggest unknown, because El Niño, a periodic warming of the Pacific, tends to bring heat and heavy rain to Peru’s coast. Vegas told the farm news site Agraria.pe in August that planted area will grow, but volume may not rise in step because of hotter weather.

Provid said its forecast could still change, because some vineyards have not started picking yet. It is also unclear whether Washington will revise the extra tariff, as Peru’s trade ministry wants.

Frequently Asked Questions

When does the Peru grape season start?

Peru’s table grape season usually runs from early October to late March, Provid says, and warm weather brought this year’s harvest forward. Ica, the main growing region, opened its 2026-27 export season with a first cargo to the United States, announced on 13 October 2026.

Where do Peru’s grapes come from?

About half of Peru grape exports come from Ica, a desert region on the southern coast, according to the agriculture ministry. Piura in the north supplies about 35% and Lambayeque about 5%.

Is Peru the world’s biggest grape exporter?

Peru’s agriculture ministry calls it the world’s leading grape exporter, and the USDA listed it as the top table grape exporter in 2024-25. The USDA expects China to draw level with Peru at 770,000 tonnes in 2025-26.

How many Peruvian grapes go to the United States?

The United States took 52% of Peru grape shipments in 2025-26, according to Provid, the growers’ association. Provid put the season’s total at 86.4 million boxes of 8.2 kilos, or about 708,000 tonnes.

Do US tariffs apply to Peruvian grapes?

Since 24 July, the United States has charged an extra 12.5% tariff on many Peruvian goods in a forced-labour trade case. Fresh grapes are not on its exemption list, according to the Peruvian trade site Infomercado, and Peru’s trade ministry wants the measure reviewed.

MEXICO · TELECOMS

Key Facts The country Mexico, the United States’ southern neighbour, has a mobile phone market long led by Telcel, the carrier controlled by tycoon Carlos Slim.

What happened AT&T agreed on Tuesday 13 October to sell its Mexican wireless business to a venture owned equally by Grupo Televisa and Fintech Holdings.

The price US$2 billion, subject to adjustments, paid with cash and up to US$1.4 billion of debt secured on the business, not its owners.

The business AT&T Mexico is the country’s second-largest mobile operator, with about 24.7 million wireless subscribers at the end of 2025.

The buyers Grupo Televisa is a Mexican cable, satellite TV and broadband group listed in New York; Fintech Holdings belongs to investor David Martínez.

What comes next Mexico’s competition authority and other regulators must approve, and the buyers expect to close in the first quarter of 2027.

Power Index Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 71.4 points (October 2026 edition).

AT&T has agreed to sell AT&T Mexico, its mobile phone business south of the border, for US$2 billion. The buyer is a 50-50 venture of Grupo Televisa, a Mexican cable and satellite TV group, and Fintech Holdings, owned by investor David Martínez.

For American investors, the deal would end AT&T’s 11-year push into Mexico and free money for fibre and mobile broadband at home. For Televisa, whose shares trade in New York, it is a big step into mobile phones in a market where Carlos Slim’s Telcel still leads.

What Televisa and Fintech Are Buying

Televisa announced the AT&T Mexico deal on Tuesday 13 October in filings to the Mexican Stock Exchange and the US Securities and Exchange Commission. Its board of directors approved Televisa’s part in the purchase a day earlier, on Monday 12 October.

AT&T Mexico had about 24.7 million wireless subscribers at the end of 2025, and Televisa’s filing counts 7.1 million contract customers in early 2026. It runs its own nationwide network on roughly 233 MHz of radio spectrum, under concessions from the Ministry of Infrastructure, Communications and Transport.

In 2025 the unit booked consolidated revenue of 85.4 billion pesos (about US$4.7 billion) and operating income of 1.4 billion pesos (about US$76 million). Those figures are converted at about 18.36 pesos to the US dollar on 14 October 2026.

Televisa and Fintech will each own half of the business through a holding trust. Televisa will book its stake as a joint venture, so AT&T Mexico’s revenue will not be added line by line to Televisa’s own accounts.

How the US$2 Billion Is Paid

The buyers plan to pay with cash on hand and non-recourse secured debt, which is backed by the acquired business, not by Televisa or Fintech. Televisa’s filing puts that debt at up to US$1.4 billion, split into a US$1.2 billion term loan and a US$200 million credit line.

BBVA México, the Mexican arm of the Spanish bank BBVA, is expected to provide the loans. Televisa itself plans a cash contribution of about US$400 million, and the purchase is not conditional on the financing.

Fintech Holdings is a Delaware company wholly owned by David Martínez Guzmán, a Mexican investor with interests in Telecom Argentina, that country’s main telecom group. A vehicle called Fintech Latam also bought some of the convertible bonds Televisa issued in June 2026, money that will partly finance Televisa’s stake.

Once those bonds convert in June 2027, Fintech Latam will hold a direct and indirect 22.3% of Televisa, which the filing calls a passive investment. El Economista, a Mexican business daily, reports that Martínez’s Fintech has bought into Televisa and raised its stake.

Why AT&T Is Leaving Mexico

AT&T built AT&T Mexico between 2014 and 2015 by buying two local carriers, Iusacell and Nextel México. El Economista puts the cost of those purchases at US$4.375 billion, plus another US$3 billion for a 4G network.

AT&T said in its own announcement from Dallas that the sale sharpens its focus on fibre and 5G networks in the United States. Chief executive John Stankey said “the AI future will run on converged networks with dense fiber assets” and that AT&T will invest at home.

AT&T added that the new owners are well placed to lead the Mexican unit’s next phase of growth. El Economista cites high spectrum fees, regulatory uncertainty and slow-acting rules on the dominant carrier as further reasons for the exit.

Telcel, owned by Carlos Slim’s América Móvil, remains the clear leader in Mexican mobile phones. Televisa already sells mobile plans under its Izzi cable brand, and Izzi and Megacable have taken 1.2 million phone lines from rivals, including AT&T.

Who Must Approve the AT&T Mexico Deal

The sale needs regulatory approval before it can close, and Televisa’s filing names the National Antitrust Commission (CNA), Mexico’s competition authority. El Economista and El Financiero both report that the Telecommunications Regulatory Commission (CRT), Mexico’s telecom regulator, must also sign off.

The buyers expect to complete the purchase in the first quarter of 2027. El Economista expects few regulatory hurdles because AT&T is not dominant in spectrum, and it sees financing as the bigger challenge.

What It Means for You

AT&T shareholders swap a low-margin foreign unit, whose operating income was under 2% of revenue in 2025, for US$2 billion before adjustments. Holders of Televisa’s New York-listed shares, ticker TV, gain exposure to mobile phones through a half-owned venture that carries its own debt.

AT&T says the announcement has no impact on service for its US customers, including those travelling to Mexico. It will report AT&T Mexico as held for sale in its third-quarter filing with the SEC, the US markets regulator.

According to DPL News and Expansión, two Mexican tech and business outlets, AT&T Mexico says customers keep their lines and plans for now. Expansión adds that outstanding balances stay due and that any change will be sent to customers’ registered contacts.

What Is Not Known

The filings do not spell out the price adjustments, the penalty if the deal collapses or the contingent benefits AT&T expects. The shareholder agreement that will govern the partnership between Televisa and Fintech has not yet been signed.

Televisa’s filing lists intellectual-property agreements with AT&T but does not say whether the AT&T name will stay on Mexican stores. AT&T has not detailed the roaming arrangements for its US customers once the network changes hands.

Regulators have not said whether they will attach conditions to their approval. The loans are not final either, since the commitment letter with BBVA México is still expected rather than signed.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is buying AT&T Mexico?

A consortium owned 50% by Grupo Televisa and 50% by Fintech Holdings is buying the business. Fintech Holdings belongs to Mexican investor David Martínez Guzmán.

How much is the AT&T Mexico deal worth?

The purchase price is US$2 billion, subject to adjustments. The buyers will pay with cash and up to US$1.4 billion of debt secured on the business.

When will the sale close?

The buyers expect to close in the first quarter of 2027. Mexico’s competition authority and the telecom regulator still have to approve it.

What happens to AT&T Mexico customers?

AT&T Mexico says customers keep their lines and plans for now, and outstanding balances remain due. Any change will be sent to the contact details customers have registered.

Does the sale affect AT&T customers from the US who travel to Mexico?

AT&T says the announcement has no impact on service, including for customers travelling to Mexico from the United States. It has not yet detailed roaming arrangements for after the sale closes.
