World.title: 1 Million Coral Embryos Return to a Costa Rica Reef in a National First
World.content:
Researchers on Costa Rica’s southern Caribbean coast have raised coral larvae in a laboratory for the first time here, returning nearly 1 million fertilized embryos to the reef at Manzanillo. The work was led by the conservation group Raising Coral Costa Rica and the Scripps Institution of Oceanography at the University of California San Diego.

The team set up a temporary lab at the visitor center of the Gandoca-Manzanillo National Wildlife Refuge in August and September. Corals spawned heavily on the nights of Sept. 3 and 4, releasing clouds of eggs and sperm into the water. About 20 people collected the spawn using nets placed over the colonies, and the researchers cross-fertilized eggs and sperm from different colonies. The species included elkhorn coral, which is critically endangered, and knobby brain coral.

Beyond the embryos released onto the reef, the team reared tens of thousands of larvae in the lab. Hundreds settled into young coral polyps and were moved to Manzanillo’s coral nursery, and the remaining larvae were released at the end of the season. The method matters because fragmenting existing corals, the technique behind most nursery work, produces clones. Breeding corals from spawning mixes genetic material from different parents, and the project said that diversity may help new corals withstand disease and warming oceans.

José Andrés Marín Moraga, who directs Raising Coral’s Caribbean program, said reefs have sustained South Caribbean communities for generations and that helping young corals settle could mark a turning point in their recovery. Emily North, the Scripps researcher who co-directed the field and lab work, said the health of Manzanillo’s coral populations impressed her after seven years working in the Caribbean.

The milestone comes three years after Raising Coral documented the first recorded spawning of elkhorn coral in Costa Rica at the same site in September 2023. The hardest step is getting larvae to settle and survive. The team is studying naturally occurring reef bacteria that may trigger settlement, and plans to embed them in hydrogels that can coat surfaces on natural reefs and restoration structures.

Local residents were part of the effort, including the Manzanillo community development association, refuge staff, the National System of Conservation Areas (SINAC), boat captains, dive instructors, educators, coral farmers and volunteers. Students from a Manzanillo school visited the lab and helped release larvae into the sea.

Mirna Cortés Obando of Cahuita National Park, who took part in the project, said it gave her new hope for the region’s reefs. The three-year research project is funded by the Coral Research and Development Accelerator Platform (CORDAP). It will continue for two more spawning seasons, with experiments aimed at improving how many larvae settle and grow into colonies.

The work adds to other efforts to study the earliest life stages of marine species along Costa Rica’s coasts, including renewed research on fish eggs and larvae.

World.title: Rents in Costa Rica Outpace Inflation Nearly 10 to 1 but Leases Cap the Hit
World.content:
Rents in Costa Rica are climbing almost 10 times faster than prices in general. If you are partway through a lease, though, the law limits how much of that your landlord can pass on to you. Housing rents rose 3.27% in the 12 months through September, according to consumer price data from the National Institute of Statistics and Census (INEC). Overall inflation over the same period was just 0.34%, and prices are down 0.39% so far this year.

Rents rose 0.43% in September alone, making them one of the five items that pushed the monthly index up, according to an analysis by the Center for Financial and Real Estate Business Studies (Cenfi). Cenfi expects rents to end the year 3.54% higher. That projection is not what you will pay if you already have a lease.

Cenfi executive director Melizandro Quirós said the market figure applies to people looking for a new rental or renewing an expired contract, not to the yearly adjustment inside an existing one. If your rent is set in colones, your landlord can raise it once a year, on the lease anniversary, by no more than inflation over the previous 12 months. The latest figure is 0.34%, so on a ₡300,000 monthly rent the most you can be charged is about ₡1,020 more, or roughly $2.

Your landlord can also choose a smaller increase or none at all, and any increase above the legal limit is void. While 12-month inflation was negative, as it was for 16 straight months until August, landlords could not raise colón rents at all, though the law does not require them to cut rent when prices fall.

If your rent is set in dollars, it cannot go up at all during the contract. The law fixes dollar rents for the full term because the currency already does the adjusting, and any change requires both you and your landlord to agree in writing. You can also pay a dollar rent in colones at the Central Bank’s reference sell rate on the day you pay. With the dollar near ₡450, that means a fixed dollar rent currently costs fewer colones than it did a year ago.

The real exposure comes at renewal as housing leases run for at least three years under the law, and if your contract has no automatic renewal clause, your landlord must tell you in writing at least three months before it ends what the rent will be if you stay. That is when market prices come into play. Using Cenfi’s projection, a ₡300,000 rent would rise to about ₡310,620, which is ₡10,620 more per month, or ₡127,440 a year (about $23 a month and $280 a year).

Before you sign a renewal, compare the new figure with similar listings nearby. Quirós said actual prices depend on location, size, number of bedrooms and local supply and demand, so some households will see increases well above the average. More than 361,000 homes in Costa Rica are rented, housing roughly 1.5 million people, according to the latest housing sector report by the Federated College of Engineers and Architects (CFIA) and the University of Costa Rica. The share of households that rent rose 19% between 2020 and 2024.

INEC publishes the consumer price index every month, and the Ministry of Housing and Human Settlements uses it to set the maximum yearly adjustment for colón leases.

World.title: Organization of American States investigate Guatemalan airspace incursion
World.content:
Organization of American States investigate Guatemalan airspace incursion

By Zoila Palma: Minister of Foreign Affairs Francis Fonseca says that the Organization of American States has launched an inquiry into the Guatemalan airspace incursion on September 24, 2026.

“We protest very strongly. We reach out and engage directly with the Guatemalan government, but we also engage with all of our friends and partners to make sure that they are briefed on what is happening. So, we engage with the OAS, for example; in this case, we have activated the OAS. They are working now on a full inquiry into this latest incident. With the GAF plane entering our airspace, they are doing… are going to do an investigation, an independent inquiry into that matter,” Minister Fonseca told 7news.

In addition, he said that Belize is working with CARICOM, SICA, Commonwealth and friends of Belize on this matter.

“And of course, we also bring it to the attention, through our legal team, to the attention of the court, so that they understand what is taking place. So, we… we respond as a peaceful nation; we are committed to peace. And that’s the way we should respond, you know, a very, very professional, principled way. That is how we resolve these issues,” he added.

Minister Fonseca stressed that no country has the authority to authorize anyone to fly into Belize’s airspace except Belize.

“It is our airspace. So, no, no other country has that authority,” he said.

World.title: Belize thanks U.S. for condemning China’s sanctions, seeks support from CARICOM and allies
World.content:
Belize thanks U.S. for condemning China’s sanctions, seeks support from CARICOM and allies

By Zoila Palma: Minister of Foreign Affairs Francis Fonseca told 7news that Belize is grateful for the statement issued by the U.S. State Department condemning China’s attempt to coerce Belize.

“We’re grateful for the statement put out by the U.S. State Department, you know, condemning this attempt to coerce Belize into taking a position in terms of our own foreign policy. So we certainly welcome that statement,” Fonseca said.

In addition, Minister Fonseca said that Belize is also engaged with partners in the Caribbean Community and SICA.

“We are also engaged with our friends and partners in CARICOM, in SICA, the OAS-we’re, you know, briefing them on what has taken place. And we’re looking forward to… to their support as well,” he added.

World.title: Foreign Affairs Minister says “coercive measure” by China is interference with Belize’s right as sovereign nation
World.content:
Foreign Affairs Minister says “coercive measure” by China is interference with Belize’s right as sovereign nation

By Zoila Palma: Minister of Foreign Affairs Francis Fonseca says that he was shocked when he found out that China had announced sanctions against him.

Fonseca says that while the sanctions do not affect him personally because he does not have any assets in China, it should be treated with seriousness since it appears to be a “coercive measure” by China.

“It doesn’t affect me personally. And obviously, I do not have any assets in… in China. But it is a very serious matter, and I think we should treat it with absolute seriousness. I think, you know, the fundamental issue is, you know, the right of small states like Belize to determine our own foreign policy-who we establish diplomatic relations with, who are our friends.

In this case, as you all know, Belize has had diplomatic relations with Taiwan for 37 years. Across political administrations, we have maintained those diplomatic relations because we believe, I think across party lines, that that relationship with Taiwan has been in the national interest of the people and country of Belize. So, we as a government have determined that we want to continue to have diplomatic relations with the People’s Republic of China, Taiwan, and that is our sovereign right to do so, to… to forge our own foreign policy. And so, this is an act, really, of interference with our right or sovereign right as a nation to chart our own course,” Fonseca explained.

Fonseca said that this coercive measure that they have placed on him as an individual who is currently the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Belize has no impact on Belize or Belizeans, since it noted that Belizeans can still travel to China.

World.title: Belize stands firm with Taiwan despite pressure from China
World.content:
Belize stands firm with Taiwan despite pressure from China

By Zoila Palma: Minister of Foreign Affairs Francis Fonseca has reiterated Belize’s support for Taiwan following sanctions announced by China this week.

During an interview with 7News, Minister Fonseca said that Belize’s relationship with Taiwan remains strong.

“Our relationship with Taiwan continues to be very, very strong. As you know, you know, we… we just recently received the Foreign Minister of Taiwan on an official visit to Belize. During that visit, we signed a number of new agreements. We are currently, you know, negotiating a new economic cooperation agreement. So our relationship is very, very strong,” he said.

In addition, Minister Fonseca said that the Ministry received a note from the Chinese embassy in Jamaica which referenced the recent visit of Taiwan’s Foreign Affairs Minister to Belize.

“Clearly, we have, you know, the Prime Minister, as I said, delivered a very strong, forceful statement at the UN General Assembly speaking in support of Taiwan and their right to self-determination. And then, as you said, most recently, we had the visit of the Foreign Minister. So, you know, I think in their note-because they sent a note, we received today a note from… from their embassy in Jamaica to our protocol office… officer in Belize-it talked about that, you know, it referenced that… that visit and our receiving the Foreign Minister,” Fonseca explained.

World.title: International News: TikTok CEO warns against giving AI agents too much access
World.content:
International News: TikTok CEO warns against giving AI agents too much access

By Zoila Palma: TikTok Chief Executive Officer Shou Zi Chew is urging users to better understand artificial intelligence (AI) agents before allowing them to carry out tasks on their behalf.

Chew warned that people may be granting these tools broad permissions without fully understanding what they are authorized to do, Business Insider reports.

Chew explained that AI agents given access to credit card information could make unintended purchases while attempting to fulfill a user’s request. He noted that some agents may be overly eager to complete tasks, potentially resulting in actions that go beyond what users intended. He emphasized the importance of understanding the limits of these tools and being mindful of the permissions granted to them.

The TikTok chief also revealed that the company is training employees on the type of information they should avoid sharing in public AI chats, including trade secrets and privileged legal information. During the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference, which focused on using AI to create value across Asia, Chew also discussed his personal use of AI for tasks such as diet coaching and answering medical questions.

AI agents have gained popularity for their ability to automate everyday activities, including bookings, audits and purchases.

However, reports of unintended actions have raised concerns about their reliability and security.

World.title: International News: Jamaica receives first group of U.S. third-country deportees
World.content:
International News: Jamaica receives first group of U.S. third-country deportees

By Zoila Palma: Jamaica received its first group of third-country nationals deported from the United States on Tuesday, October 13, marking the start of a closely scrutinized bilateral agreement that will allow the Caribbean nation to serve as a transit point for migrants being returned to their home countries or transferred elsewhere.

The group consisted of 22 adults, including seven women, who arrived at Kingston’s Norman Manley International Airport and were quickly processed before being transported by bus under police escort to an undisclosed location, NBC reports.

Jamaican authorities did not allow media access to the arrivals, but said procedures were being followed to ensure the arrangement is implemented in a “safe, orderly and lawful manner.”

The programme operates under a memorandum of understanding signed between Jamaica and the United States in June 2026.

Under the agreement, Jamaica will accept a maximum of 25 migrants every two weeks, with the International Organization for Migration (IOM) responsible for coordinating housing and logistics through its Assisted Voluntary Return programme. Jamaican authorities maintain that the arrangement will not be funded by the government and that individuals with criminal backgrounds will not be permitted to transit through the country.

However, the agreement has sparked political controversy, with opposition figures and transparency advocates questioning why the memorandum was not presented to Parliament and demanding greater disclosure of its terms.

World.title: Ministry of Economic Transformation highlights Climate Change initiatives at Statistics Week 2026 exhibition
World.content:
Ministry of Economic Transformation highlights Climate Change initiatives at Statistics Week 2026 exhibition

By Zoila Palma: The Ministry of Economic Transformation (MET), through its Green Climate Fund (GCF) Readiness 14 Project, participated in the Statistics Week 2026 Public Exhibition hosted by the Statistical Institute of Belize (SIB) on October 13, 2026, at the University of Belize Gymnasium in Belmopan.

Held under the theme “Harmonizing Data, Strengthening Resilience,” the exhibition brought together students, stakeholders, government agencies, and members of the public to learn about initiatives supporting Belize’s national development.

The event also provided a platform for organizations to share information and highlight the importance of reliable data in planning and decision-making.

Through its booth, the GCF Readiness 14 Project highlighted ongoing efforts to strengthen Belize’s capacity to address climate change. Among the initiatives presented was support for a feasibility study exploring the potential establishment of master’s and Ph.D. programmes in climate change at the University of Belize.

The ministry noted that the exhibition provided an opportunity to raise awareness of the project and engage with the public on climate-related initiatives.

World.title: Minister of Economic Development represents Belize at high-level Finance roundtable in Bangkok, Thailand
World.content:
Minister of Economic Development represents Belize at high-level Finance roundtable in Bangkok, Thailand

By Zoila Palma: On October 13, 2026, Minister of Economic Development Osmond Martinez represented Belize at the Xingu Finance Talks High-Level Roundtable in Bangkok, Thailand.

“I highlighted how climate disasters increase borrowing needs while debt obligations limit the resources available to build resilience in Small Island Developing States.

Our Farmers in Corazon, Dolores, Machakila have been significantly affected by climate change, just as our coastal communities such as Monkey River, Punta Gorda and Barranco keep eroding and affected by the Sargassum, our people in Bella Vista, Trio and San Pablo affected with flooding and damage to crops,” Minister Martinez said.

Minister Martinez stressed the importance to reaffirm the need for accessible climate finance that responds to national priorities, protects vulnerable communities and supports long-term development.

World.title: IC WANTS SPENDING CHECK
World.content:
The scene in Black River after the town took a direct hit from Hurricane Melissa last October.

THE Integrity Commission (IC) has called for full documentation and independent review of 476 Government contracts valued at $5 billion that public bodies identified as related to Hurricane Melissa recovery, raising questions about how the spending will be reviewed as Jamaica rebuilds after the disaster.

The contracts were awarded in the final quarter of 2025, with most using emergency or single-source procurement methods.

In its special report to Parliament titled ‘Public Procurement in Jamaica: Key Trends and Issues — Contract Awards in 2025, with Trends from 2006 to 2025’, tabled in the House on Tuesday, the commission said 182 of the recovery-related contracts, valued at $3.9 billion, were awarded through emergency procurement.

Another 262 were awarded through single- source procurement, while 32 were awarded through restricted bidding. “These awards warrant full documentation and independent review by the relevant authorities, and will be examined further in the commission’s report on its special monitoring programme, which is ongoing,” Director of Investigation Kevon Stephenson wrote in the report.

The findings come against the background of a sharp rise in emergency contracting last year, as public bodies responded to urgent needs, including those arising from the hurricane. The commission reported that emergency contracts for the year totalled $16.3 billion across 588 contracts, a 63 per cent increase in value over 2024.

Of that amount, $10.5 billion, covering 331 contracts, was awarded in the final quarter of 2025. The report said $9.7 billion of that fourth-quarter spending, across 278 contracts, was awarded on or after October 28, 2025, when Hurricane Melissa struck Jamaica.

Stephenson acknowledged in the report the necessity for emergency procurement, but said the circumstances created heightened risks that required scrutiny. “The DI (director of investigations) recognises that emergency procurement was necessary to preserve life and to restore essential services.

However, the period following the hurricane was one of heightened procurement risk, by reason of the scale of emergency contracting, the size of certain individual awards, the use of emergency methods for contracts other than those identified as related to recovery, and the exemption of emergency procurement from the ordinary rules,” he wrote.

The report also raised concerns about how some hurricane-related contracts were recorded. It identified 360 single-source awards in 2025, valued at $840 million, whose descriptions referred to a hurricane but which were recorded as ordinary single-source contracts.

Of those, 337 were made in the final quarter of the year. The commission cautioned that some of these awards might already be included among the 262 single-source contracts identified as related to recovery. However, the report said the records indicated that emergency spending may have been understated and that the identification of disaster-related contracts was incomplete.

The findings do not establish that the recovery contracts were improperly awarded or that the spending involved wrongdoing. Rather, the commission is calling for the relevant authorities to examine the awards and the records supporting them. The report also recommends stronger checks after emergency spending.

These include requiring public bodies to report on their procurement activities following a declared disaster and improving oversight of emergency contracts, including checks on whether the Government received value for money.

The commission’s special monitoring programme remains under way, with further examination of procurement connected to the hurricane response and recovery expected to be addressed separately.

World.title: ‘A wish list’
World.content:
Opposition spokesman on health Dr Alfred Dawes responding to an announcement in Parliament on Tuesday by Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton that the Government will construct four new public hospitals. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

Opposition spokesman on health Dr Alfred Dawes has described as a “wish list” an announcement by Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton that the Government will construct four new public hospitals which will nearly double the bed capacity of the facilities they are replacing.

The facilities to be constructed are a new 250-bed Black River Hospital in St Elizabeth, a 250-bed Falmouth General Hospital in Trelawny, a 150-bed Noel Holmes Hospital in Hanover, and a 720-bed Kingston Public Hospital Campus at Orange Street, downtown Kingston.

“I must tell the honourable minister, that is indeed a very well put-together wish list,” Dawes said sarcastically as he rose to respond to Tufton’s 20-minute-long statement in the House of Representatives on Tuesday in which the minister told his fellow parliamentarians of the plans to construct the new facilities.

“We can rarely call it anything more than such because the weight of Cabinet approval is not a budget item,” Dawes added.

Tufton told the House that Cabinet had approved a partnership between his ministry and the National Reconstruction and Resilient Authority (NaRRA) for the works to be carried out.

It is being done in collaboration with the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB).

Dawes, the Member of Parliament (MP) for St Catherine South Eastern, told the Parliament that all Jamaicans want better, safer, and more resilient hospitals.

“The challenge we have consistently had is that whenever this Government is tasked with delivering, we don’t know the cost, we don’t know the completion time, and we don’t know who is going to staff it.

And we have seen that happen over and over again, Dawes said.

He reminded the legislature that in the early 1990s under an IDB-funded project to improve hospitals, there was a special implementation unit in the Ministry of Health.

“This project to rehabilitate and construct major hospitals is going to be lumped with the Montego Bay Hip Strip development, the Vernamfield development, and any other NaRRA project that they deem fit,” he said.

The first-term MP pointed to the continued rising costs associated with the Cornwall Regional Hospital redevelopment project and argued that patients in western Jamaica continue to suffer.

“In fact, patients all across Jamaica are suffering [and] the staff, they’re protesting almost weekly at this point.

And every time there is a protest or concern on social media we’re treated to tours of hospitals to come,” he said.

“This cannot be the status quo; we cannot continue to suffer while we hear about what is to come.

This Government has had 10 years to deliver and now they are delivering promises to come,” Dawes argued.

He said that the Opposition accepts that money must be spent on the hospitals that are being rebuilt, but said, “We would like to know how much money is going to be spent on the abandoned Black River Hospital, how much money are we sinking into these buildings that the minister has, quite honestly, said are unfit for inhabitation and occupation.” Dawes also argued that a hospital is not just a building and a bed, not [just] something to lie on.

“A hospital is service.

A bed without a nurse is a mattress,” he declared.

He lamented that there was nothing in Tufton’s presentation about a staffing plan and pointed out that by the health ministry’s own numbers Jamaica was experiencing an attrition rate of 500 nurses each year.

Dawes said the 47 nurses who arrived from Ghana recently are a welcome addition but that is a mere drop in the bucket.

In his statement, Tufton repeated that the climate-resilient facilities will be reconstructed and modernised by NaRRA.

He did not give a cost or timeline for construction.

“Together these projects will deliver some 1,370 beds inside modern, climate-resilient hospitals.

The three rural hospitals alone will raise beds from 260 today, to 650 beds, more than doubling the facility,” said the minister.

World.title: Jamaica Music Atlas active!
World.content:
Johnathon Kelly

Eager to share his enthusiasm for reggae music, Johnathon Kelly launched the Jamaica Music Atlas in August.

The website (jamaicamusicatlas.com) looks at the history of Jamaican music in 12 countries, among them the United Kingdom, United States, and Canada — home to some of the largest Jamaican Diaspora communities.

An information technology expert, Kelly used AI to gather data for the portal which he regularly updates.

It comprises almost 4,000 songs, 280 locations, and over 150 stories. “The response so far has been extremely encouraging.

What has been particularly rewarding is seeing interest come from well beyond Jamaica. Some of our strongest engagement and feedback has come from the United States and Europe, which really reinforces the fact that Jamaican music has a truly global audience,” Kelly told the Jamaica Observer.

“We have heard from music fans, members of the Jamaican Diaspora, researchers, and people who simply want to understand more about the history, culture, and stories behind the music.” Visitors to the website can discover reggae’s roots in each country featured.

For example, the first venues that played Jamaican music in the UK, the record labels, sound systems, artistes and producers who put reggae on the map there. There is similar comprehensive data for The Netherlands, Belgium, Germany, Spain, Panama, Japan, Brazil, Cote d’Ivoire, and Nigeria.

“A major part of the vision is to make Jamaican music history accessible to different kinds of audiences.

Some visitors may want to do deep research, while others may want to explore a story, follow a musical journey or play a game,” Kelly explained. “The site is gradually becoming a much broader digital experience around Jamaican music rather than simply a collection of information.” In the two months since jamaicamusicatlas.com was activated Kelly has consistently added stories and features.

“We never intended Jamaica Music Atlas to be a static archive, so we have been steadily adding new ways for people to explore and interact with the material,” he said.

World.title: KSAMC urges water party restraint
World.content:
Patrons at a recent water party (File Photo)

THE Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation (KSAMC) has urged water party organisers to carefully consider the timeliness and appropriateness of staging such events, as drought conditions persist and water restrictions threaten to become more stringent.

Speaking at the KSAMC’s monthly meeting on Tuesday, Deputy Mayor Lorraine Dobson, in the absence of Mayor Swaby, acknowledged the concerns of residents surrounding the issuance of licences for water parties.

She appealed to promoters to consider the plight of residents across the Corporate Area who are experiencing water shortages and have been urged to conserve, arguing that seeing water used for recreational purposes could cause frustration and distress.

“I therefore wish to make a direct appeal to the promoters of these events to act responsibly and with sensitivity to the circumstances confronting our residents.

I ask that they carefully consider the timing and manner in which these events are staged and ensure that their activities do not undermine the national call for water being experienced by members of our community,” said Dobson.

Water restrictions have been instituted by the National Water Commission (NWC) across Kingston and St Andrew, St Thomas, St Mary, Portland, St Ann, and St Catherine to protect depleted reservoirs amid an ongoing severe drought.

As of October 11, 2026, the Mona reservoir is at 36.3 per cent capacity, while Hermitage dam stands at 44.9 per cent capacity, leaving both critical facilities severely depleted despite recent rainfall.

Under the legal mandate, residents are strictly banned from using NWC-supplied water for any non-essential or unusual activities.

Prohibited actions include watering lawns, gardens, and farms; refilling swimming pools or ponds; washing vehicles with a hose; and washing down outdoor surfaces like roadways, pavements, or garages.

With no signs of the drought ceasing soon, Water Minister Matthew Samuda recently suggested that stricter regulations could be implemented.

Against that backdrop, Dobson explained that the KSAMC issues permits only to event planners who can provide evidence of a private water source.

However, she said the corporation recognises residents’ frustration and takes the responsible use of the increasingly scarce resource seriously.

“As an authority responsible for granting of permits for events within the municipality, we recognise the importance of exercising our regulatory responsibilities, responsibly in keeping with the national purpose to conserve water.

The KSAMC should not knowingly facilitate and even involve in the use of water supplied by the National Water Commission for recreational purposes in circumstances where such is prohibited,” she said.

“We have also taken note that the minister’s clarification that the current water prohibition order applies specifically to water supplied by the NWC and that promoters of water-based events are required to provide evidence of their water source where privately sourced water is being used,” added Dobson.

World.title: Central Kingston MP highlights big drop in murders
World.content:
Kingston Central Member of Parliament Donovan Williams making his contribution to the State of the Constituency Debate in Parliament on Tuesday. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

What was for a long time one of Jamaica’s most politically volatile constituencies, Kingston Central, which saw up to 50 murders per year, has recorded just four homicides since the start of 2026, Member of Parliament (MP) Donovan Williams has shared.

Williams, a second-term Jamaica Labour Party Government MP, spoke to the issue in the House of Representatives on Tuesday during his contribution to the 2026/27 State of the Constituency Debate.

“Major crimes are down, gang conflicts have plummeted, our murder rate is the lowest it has been when compared to previous years,” said Williams.

He pointed to the introduction of a zone of special operations (ZOSO) in the Parade Gardens community, noting that it has had an immediate impact.

“There was a time in Central Kingston when we were experiencing 50 murders per year across both police divisions that serve the constituency.

So far this year we recorded four murders across the entire constituency,” Williams said.

Highlighting that some communities were doing exceptionally well, he singled out Franklyn Town which, for the past two years, has had no murders.

He said that one murder has been recorded in the Allman Town community, one in Parade Gardens, and two in Rose Gardens.

The Rae Town community recorded a single murder in 2025 and none in 2026.

Williams’ report was specific to the constituency as Jamaica Constabulary Force data show that the Central Kingston Police Division, which expands beyond the riding, has reported eight murders so far this year, compared to 15 over the same period last year.

Williams told the Parliament that other major crimes have also plummeted.

“We still have some issues, we are working through them, but for the most part, we are doing exceptionally well,” he noted.

Our churches are open; our parties are in full swing.

Nightlife has returned to Central Kingston.

Our children are playing in the parks and in the streets and we intend to keep it that way,” he added.

“This is not the Central Kingston that we are accustomed to, this is not the Central Kingston I came and saw in September 2020,” Williams gushed.

He acknowledged the leadership of National Security Minister Dr Horace Chang, Commanding Officer Mishka Forbes of the Kingston Central Police Division, Commanding Officer Michelle Campbell of the East Kingston Police Division, and their predecessors who, he said, helped to lay the foundation of peace which now exists.

Williams also acknowledged the civic organisations that are playing their part in community engagement and peace initiatives such as Yard Empire, Social Development Commission, Project Star, Heavenly Culture, World Peace, Restoration of Light (HWPL), a UNESCOaffiliated non-governmental organisation, as well as the churches.

On the matter of the ZOSO, the two-term MP said the Jamaica Social Investment Fund has advised that an integrated infrastructural development plan has now been crafted for the zone and submitted to the Ministry of Finance for approval by the Public Investment Appraisal Branch (PIAB).

Williams said he was optimistic that the PIAB will approve the plan, especially given that the joint command has recommended the zone enters its build phase.

World.title: CHEQUES STILL COUNT
World.content:
THE Small Business Association of Jamaica (SBAJ) is calling for an extension of the timeline to phase out paper cheques as it warned that the pace of the transition could place additional pressure on micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) that still rely on the payment instrument for day-to-day business transactions.

Speaking in an interview with the Jamaica Observer this week, SBAJ President Garnett Reid said members across the association’s network of more than 700 businesses have raised concerns about the planned elimination of cheques — arguing that they need more time to adjust and access affordable alternatives before the payment method is completely withdrawn.

“Since the announcement of the phasing out, a number of our members have continued to ask us what will happen to those who use cheques. Right now, more than 20-30 per cent of them use cheques to settle transactions,” Reid told the Business Observer.

“We are not against the move to modernise Jamaica’s financial system, but the current schedule is too aggressive, particularly for a large number of small operators who lack the resources, digital infrastructure, and training needed to transition smoothly. What we are therefore calling for is an extension of the time frame by even a year,” he said, while noting that the extension would give businesses more time to adapt while the banking sector and other stakeholders strengthen the systems needed to support digital transactions.

Under the schedule established by the Bank of Jamaica (BOJ) and the Jamaica Bankers Association (JBA), the phased reduction in cheque clearing began on September 1, 2026, with cheques valued at $1 million or more no longer being accepted or processed. The threshold is scheduled to fall to $500,000 on March 1, 2027 and then $100,000 by September 1, 2027, before a complete elimination of cheques takes effect on March 1, 2028.

The BOJ, which has noted the phase-out as part of efforts to reduce systemic risks, said it will also encourage the settlement of high-value transactions through electronic channels, including the Real-Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system and Automated Clearing House (ACH) infrastructure.

Cheque usage locally, which has continued to decline steadily over the last two decades, saw volumes processed in 2025 falling 12.6 per cent to 2.4 million, as total value also declined 6.9 per cent to $444 billion. This compares with more than 8.4 million cheques valued at approximately $2.3 trillion processed in 2010.

Despite the decline, Reid said cheques remain important to some small businesses and as such, the transition must account for those that continue to depend on the instrument.

“Forcing micro-merchants into alternative routes like RTGS drives up ad valorem fees and transactional overheads that strip away the razor-thin profit margins of small businesses. We cannot strip a trusted financial instrument from the economy when the digital infrastructure remains broken,” he said.

SBAJ’s call comes amid recent legal challenges to the phaseout, which has seen at least two church groups stepping out recently to seek judicial review of the decision. The groups, in accusing the central bank of exceeding its legal authority, also said the planned phasing breaches the right of Jamaicans to equitable treatment. They have also similarly indicated that their members frequently use cheques to conduct business, pay bills, and settle debts.

The SBAJ said its concerns were further compounded by what has been a slow roll-out of the central bank digital currency JAM-DEX, which was introduced to support a more efficient and accessible payment system.

Reid said the pace of adoption, which has left some small businesses without practical alternatives to the payment methods they currently use, has also widened the digital divide between the push for financial modernisation and the readiness of merchants on the ground.

“We are in a digital era and SMEs are told every day to grow their digital footprint and increase digital acceptance… but I don’t think we’re all ready yet,” he said, pointing to the need for more training and support for business owners unfamiliar with digital payment platforms and online banking.

Highlighting gaps in the digital payment infrastructure, including limited access to compatible point-of-sale systems and digital wallets, the association further said these pose significant challenges for businesses seeking to make and receive digital payments across their supply chains. It stressed that merchants must be able to collect payments from customers, pay suppliers and purchase inventory using accessible and affordable options and in cases where digital currency is not widely accepted businesses will have to rely on alternative electronic transfers that usually attract higher transaction costs.

“We are modernising the top tier of the economy while leaving our grass roots businesses stranded. Right now, point-of-sale (POS) integration for JAM-DEX is incomplete and there are far too few active wallet providers in the market. Expecting a micro-merchant in rural Jamaica to instantly shift away from paper cheques to high-fee commercial options when they cannot even spend or accept JAM-DEX at local wholesalers is fundamentally unrealistic,” Reid said.

As part of the response, he urged the BOJ, commercial banks, and other stakeholders to work together to strengthen digital payment infrastructure, expand merchants’ access to digital wallets, and provide practical training to help business operators understand and use available payment options.

“Small businesses represent the backbone of the Jamaican economy. Modernisation should lift us up, not lock us out. We stand ready to collaborate with the central bank, but we will not sit quietly while our members are forced out of the financial system by an unforgiving timeline,” Reid said while stressing that the transition cannot be treated simply as a change in banking policy, but as a broader shift that must take account of the financial and technological realities facing small businesses.

World.title: BUTLER CRIES SHAME!
World.content:
Mona High Head Coach Craig Butler reacts during the rescheduled ISSA Walker Cup semifinal match against Jamaica College at Stadium East on October 10, 2026. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

WHILE expressing happiness that Mona High will be playing in the ISSA Walker Cup final, Head Coach Craig Butler has called for serious intervention in Jamaica College’s football programme which he believes is being undermined by a “must-win” mentality.

Butler’s team was granted a place in the urban area knockout final against Kingston College after the competition’s governing body, ISSA, removed Jamaica College (JC) from the tournament after using Reggae Boy Jamone Lyle who was found to be a professional player.

ISSA’s rules state professional athletes are barred from participating in ISSA-run competitions.

Lyle played in last Saturday’s semi-final in which JC beat Mona 4-3 on penalties after a 3-3 draw in regulation and extra time.

After Mona lodged an official complaint, ISSA investigated and it was confirmed that the 17-yearold signed a professional contract in August with Jamaica Premier League club Waterhouse.

ISSA’s disciplinary committee met and ruled JC’s semi-final win null and void which meant Mona will play in Friday’s final.

JC issued a statement early Tuesday afternoon, saying it “had no knowledge of Lyle having entered into a professional contract” while also seeking clarity on the application of ISSA’s rules.

The school, however, stressed that it “remains committed to working respectfully with ISSA and other stakeholders” to uphold the integrity of schoolboy football and support the development of Jamaica’s young sporting talent.

However, Butler who played Manning Cup for JC during his high school days, told the Jamaica Observer that he’s concerned about the direction that the school has been heading in and is urging past students to step in and provide guidance.

“I’m disappointed in the way that I see my school, JC, that I love and how they have allowed the boys to just basically do whatever they want and it has to change at some point and I hope that this is a wake-up call,” he said.

“I hope that the past students, Kit and Kirk Kennedy, Chris Williams — all of the past students that came from our era will go back into the school again and start to contribute in terms of mentorship and make sure the boys know what life is about.

Because guess what? This little football thing that we’re playing, it’s going to go and after that, what happens? Where are these boys being left? What are they being left with? Are they being left with some education? Are they being left with social education? Are they being left with integrity?” Butler, though, says he has nothing personal against Lyle but believes rules must be followed.

“I think that’s a disservice to the player because he’s young and malleable and he’s going to listen.

I don’t, in any shape or form, blame the kid.

I really like him as well.

After the game was over, I hugged him and told him, great game,” he said.

“But to know that the player is ineligible and still use him is something that for me questions Jamaica College’s ethos.

When I went to JC, there was a lot of ethics and a lot of honour in how they did things.

We didn’t need to win at all costs.

We wanted to give good contributors to society and to use football as a vehicle to teach boys how to be men and to lead.

I think this winning at all costs mentality has to stop and I think that JC needed this wake-up call.” Butler says more of his compatriots need to be vocal about JC’s situation before it gets worse.

“Unfortunately, I’m a brave man so I go and ask the questions.

I’m not going to be like my friends that sit down and say ‘yeah, Bullhead, you’re right’ but when the time comes, they keep quiet,” he said.

“I’m not going to keep quiet because guess what? That could have been me when I was a kid.

When Jimmy Sinclair and all of my mentors back then who coached at the school told me the right way to carry myself and behave.

Of course, there have been many times that I have not listened and many times that I have got myself in trouble but I at least knew what was the right thing to do.

I was able to come back to the nuclei of that.

So, I love Jamaica College and because I love Jamaica College, I want them to wake up and who don’t like it, I don’t give a damn.”

World.title: IC says 69% of Gov’t contracts awarded without competition
World.content:
STEPHENSON... the extent of single-source procurement could not be explained simply by the type of goods or services being purchased

Nearly seven in every 10 Government contracts recorded in 2025 were awarded through single-source procurement, while hundreds of same-day awards to individual contractors collectively exceeded the applicable award limits, according to the Integrity Commission (IC).

The findings are contained in the commission’s special report to Parliament titled ‘Public Procurement in Jamaica: Key Trends and Issues — Contract Awards in 2025, with Trends from 2006 to 2025’, which was tabled in the House on Tuesday.

The report found that 23,234 of the 33,583 contracts reported by public bodies in 2025 were awarded through single-source procurement, including emergency contracting.

The contracts were valued at $91.8 billion, representing 27.3 per cent of the total $336.4 billion awarded during the year.

By comparison, open competitive bidding — which allows eligible suppliers to compete for Government contracts — accounted for just 4.1 per cent of contracts by number, although it represented 19 per cent of their total value.

The commission said the figures reflected a long-standing pattern, with single-source procurement accounting for about two-thirds of Government contracts by number every year since 2017.

Under single-source procurement, a public body awards a contract without inviting competing bids through an open tender.

The method is permitted in certain circumstances, but the Public Procurement Act makes open competition the general rule.

Director of investigation at the IC, Kevon Stephenson, said the extent of single-source procurement could not be explained simply by the type of goods or services being purchased.

“Legal services, software licences and subscriptions, and specialised professional services such as forensic, audit and advisory work account for only 7.6 per cent of single-source awards, and training for a further 2.3 per cent.

About 88 per cent are routine purchases of goods, services and works, of which 88.5 per cent were each valued at $3 million or less; the remainder are emergency contracts,” he wrote in the report.

“The prevalence of single- source procurement is therefore not explained by the nature of the requirements, but by the routine use of the method for purchases of lower value,” he added.

The commission’s concerns extend beyond the overall use of the method to the way some contracts were awarded.

It identified 1,618 instances in which two or more single- source contracts were awarded to the same contractor on the same day.

These involved 4,317 contracts valued at $11.5 billion.

In 416 of those instances, the combined value of the same-day awards exceeded the applicable single-source limit, even though each individual contract was within that limit.

Those cases involved 1,619 contracts valued at $2.9 billion.

The commission said the pattern was spread across all four quarters of 2025 and was not therefore explained by Hurricane Melissa, which left extensive damage across sections of Jamaica last October.

Stephenson said the findings required closer examination but did not establish that the contracts had been improperly divided.

“Such patterns may reflect legitimate arrangements, including the issue of separate purchase orders for discrete work packages and the urgent engagement of contractors after an emergency.

They may equally indicate the division of a single requirement into smaller contracts so as to remain within the limits for single-source procurement, which section 25G of the Public Procurement Act prohibits.

These instances warrant examination by the appropriate authorities,” Stephenson wrote.

The report also identified 3,052 single-source awards worth $51.6 billion that exceeded the applicable single- source threshold in force when they were awarded.

Under the law, single-source procurement above the threshold is permitted only in specified circumstances.

However, the commission said the quarterly reports submitted by public bodies did not state which legal grounds had been relied on for those awards, meaning their compliance could not be assessed from the records alone.

The thresholds changed during 2025.

Until May 15, the single-source limits were $1.5 million for goods and services and $2 million for works.

They were subsequently increased to $3 million for goods and services and $5 million for works.

The commission stressed that being within a threshold does not mean a public body must use single-source procurement.

More competitive methods remain available where practical.

In its recommendations, the report calls for public bodies to seek competing quotations for lower-value purchases wherever possible and to record the reasons when they choose single-source procurement despite competition being practicable.

It also recommends that the Ministry of Finance and the Public Service evaluate the effect of the 2025 changes to procurement thresholds and approval limits after a full year of operation, with the results reported to Parliament or otherwise published.

For awards above the relevant approval limit, the commission recommends stronger documentation of the legal reasons for using single- source procurement and greater scrutiny by the bodies responsible for reviewing and approving contracts.

The report’s overall conclusion was that the system was falling short of the law’s objectives in key areas.

“Taken together, these conclusions indicate that the public procurement system, as it operates, falls short of the objects of the Public Procurement Act in respect of competition, value for money, participation and transparency,” the report stated.

The commission’s findings are based on quarterly contract award reports submitted by public bodies and assess contract awards in 2025 alongside trends from 2006 to 2025.

The report calls for changes in both procurement practices and policy to strengthen competition and accountability in the spending of public funds.

World.title: Ukrainian officers warn Starlink slowdown ‘comparable to a nuclear strike against us’
World.content:
“Since last night, all Starlink and Starshield terminals used by our forces have been subject to a speed limit of 100 kilometers per hour,” the officer said.

POLITICO talked to three frontline soldiers, who all spoke on condition of being granted anonymity, as well as a Ukrainian defense ministry spokesperson and the EU's top defense official.

The reported restrictions have revived a question Ukrainian commanders have worried about for years: how much of the country’s battlefield communications can rely on a service controlled by a U.S. company.

Ukrainian soldiers say the restrictions have halted some medium-range drone strikes over Ukraine, disrupting attacks on Russian logistics and leaving frontline Ukrainian troops with less support. The scale of the disruption — and whether it was deliberate — remains unclear.

The restrictions have brought “all medium-range strike operations to a complete halt,” the officer said, including those using mesh-based systems. These rely on a single Starlink-equipped UAV to receive and relay signals to other drones connected through a mesh network, allowing them to strike targets deep inside Russian-held territory or in areas heavily protected by Russian electronic warfare systems.

Such targets include the Donetsk region, the strategically important Novorossiya highway linking Russia to Crimea, the Crimean Peninsula itself, the Kerch area and the Black Sea.

World.title: Deadly drone strikes in NATO waters raise stakes for Black Sea trade
World.content:
Russia has been attacking Ukrainian ports and cities in the area since the start of its full-scale invasion. But the recent strikes have brought the spillover into NATO territory. If they continue, EU leaders will face pressure to protect Black Sea shipping and keep Ukrainian trade moving.

Those questions will be top of mind at Thursday’s European Council summit. According to draft conclusions obtained by POLITICO, leaders are expected to discuss the “immediate restoration of safe passage for grain cargo ships.”

A wider problem

Russia is not the only country using naval drones in the Black Sea. Ukraine has also used them against Russian-linked shipping. In June, a Ukrainian sea drone exploded in Romania’s Constanța port after Kyiv said it had veered off course because of Russian electronic interference.

“The Black Sea situation is quite dangerous because attacks are coming from both [sides],” said an EU shipping representative, who was granted anonymity to speak freely. “You have to worry about both.”

Attribution can also be difficult. Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said Wednesday that investigators still have not proven that Russia is behind the strikes — although some have attributed his reticence to his broadly softer approach toward the Kremlin.

Drone operations by both Russia and Ukraine are likely to continue as long as each has the money and production capacity to sustain them, said Cristian Vlas, assistant research manager for Eastern Europe at the think tank ACLED.

World.title: NGO: Brussels confirms Czech PM’s agri business conflict of interest
World.content:
Babiš has been under renewed scrutiny over Agrofert — a large agro-chemical conglomerate and a major recipient of EU funds — as well as other companies since his return to power last year. Babiš placed the company in a trust fund in a bid to avoid a conflict of interest, but the arrangement has raised questions from both the Commission and the Czech opposition, partly because his children would benefit from it after his death.

Babiš has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing. “I don’t own Agrofert, I never will again and I don’t benefit from it in any way. I don’t know what else I’m supposed to do,” he told Czech media last month. “Apparently, even if I shot myself, it still wouldn’t be enough.”



Babiš’ office did not immediately reply to POLITICO’s request for comment about the contents of the letter.



Werner warned in the letter that Brussels would take all necessary steps to protect EU funds, “including the possible interruption of payment deadlines, suspension of payments or application of financial corrections,” according to TI Czechia.



TI Czechia Executive Director David Kotora told POLITICO that he received the letter in September. A follow-up letter from Werner dated Oct. 5 gives the NGO permission to share the contents of the letter without publishing it.

The conflict-of-interest dispute echoes Babiš’ first term as prime minister, when a Commission audit found he still controlled Agrofert. That left Czech taxpayers to foot the bill for EU subsidies deemed to be erroneously paid.



History could now repeat itself as Brussels last month froze €3.18 million in reimbursements to the Czech state for farm subsidies paid out to Agrofert. That followed its earlier May decision that it would not reimburse any paid-out subsidies until doubts about his involvement in the business could be put to rest.



Commission spokesperson Louise Bogey confirmed it had sent a letter to TI Czechia in September, but would not comment on its content. However, she pointed to her remarks at a Sept. 8 midday briefing, during which she said Babiš was in a “potential conflict of interest” and that “the Commission considers the trust fund set up by Mr. Babiš does not sufficiently mitigate this situation.”



Czechia’s agricultural paying agency, which earlier decided that the conglomerate is eligible for EU subsidies despite the Commission’s warning, said Tuesday it had sent clarifications to the Commission this week.



Agrofert spokesperson Pavel Heřmanský said neither Agrofert nor any of its subsidiaries were involved in the communication between the Commission and Czech authorities.



“The cited letter from DG AGRI expresses the opinion of one of the European Commission’s departments. It does not constitute an official position of the European Commission,” said Heřmanský in a statement, adding that “only the Court of Justice of the European Union can provide a binding interpretation of European Union law.”

He added: “We remain convinced that we have received and continue to receive subsidies in compliance with both Czech and European law.”

World.title: UK rolls out King Charles to welcome Zelenskyy after Trump rift
World.content:
Charles hosted Zelenskyy at Sandringham in March 2025, days after Trump and Vice President JD Vance publicly berated the Ukrainian leader in the Oval Office, and at Windsor Castle earlier this year after Ukraine, the U.K., France and Germany published a joint statement calling for a “just and lasting” deal to end the war with Russia.

Zelenskyy will get a ceremonial guard from No.12 Company The Irish Guards when he arrives at Downing Street Wednesday afternoon, which a No. 10 spokesperson said is believed to be unprecedented.

The latest visit comes amid fresh strains over Trump’s approach to Russia and Ukraine, after he criticized Zelenskyy’s leadership and struck a deal with Moscow to lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports.

It will be the first visit to a European capital by the Ukrainian president since Trump made the announcement last Friday, and his second meeting with Burnham.

Burnham has so far refused to condemn the U.S. president for making a deal with Russia, telling MPs Wednesday he wants to “try and repair bridges so that the support comes back.”

In an overnight statement issued by No. 10 ahead of the visit, Burnham said: “Our rock-solid support to Ukraine is vital for keeping us safe here in the UK and ensuring those on the frontlines have the equipment they need to push back Russia.

World.title: Palantir settles dispute with Sadiq Khan
World.content:
A full trial was expected in January but on Wednesday both sides agreed to “settle their differences” and drop the allegations without admitting liability. They will each cover their own legal costs.

In an agreed statement, the two sides said MOPAC’s decision to block the Palantir contract was “not based on Palantir’s values or ethics or any wider reporting about the company,” though MOPAC said it “recognizes Palantir’s concerns that media reporting of a statement from the Mayor's spokesperson before the decision was taken could have incorrectly created the impression that an assessment of the company’s values had been a factor in that decision.”

“MOPAC’s consideration was based upon its statutory role of examining spend proposals, against the appropriate legal tests and the relevant guidance on procurement, governance, affordability and ensuring value for money for Londoners and in doing so it focussed on the available information at the time,” the statement said.

The settlement also notes that MOPAC is working with Metropolitan Police Service to re-run a competitive procurement for the relevant service, which Palantir will be eligible to bid for.

“MOPAC does not have, and has never had, any policy of not contracting with Palantir,” the statement confirms, while noting the mayor’s duty is to ensure “all procurements are lawful, fair, transparent and deliver value for money.”

“London is the technology capital of Europe, and I am proud that leading software firms choose the city as their home. Palantir makes a significant contribution to jobs and investment in the capital, employing a large number of Londoners whose services have been procured legally by organizations across the U.K. and beyond,” Khan said.

World.title: Burnham rules out partnership with Greens after Zionism row
World.content:
On the motion, he said: “It is wrong. It is antisemitic, and this side of the house will have nothing to do with it.”

Burnham currently has a House of Commons majority, but a seat model by YouGov published last month suggests Labour would be the largest party in a hung parliament at the next general election — not due until the middle of 2029.

The Greens currently have five MPs in the Commons after winning their first by-election in Greater Manchester from Labour in February. Zack Polanski, the Green Party leader, failed to take the Holborn and St Pancras constituency from Labour in a by-election early this month, days after the party conference motion was passed.

A Labour party official was unable to immediately clarify what Burnham’s stance means for local government partnerships between Labour and the Greens.

Polanski said he wouldn’t have supported the motion but did not vote because he was campaigning in the contest. Senior party figures, including former leaders Caroline Lucas and Adrian Ramsay and Westminster leader Ellie Chowns, opposed the motion. Co-Deputy Leader Mothin Ali supported the motion.

In a joint statement after the vote, Polanski, the co-deputy leaders and party MPs said the Green Party “will never tolerate any form of discrimination or harassment.” It said, “there is no conflict between supporting the rights of Palestinians and the rights of Jewish people.”

World.title: France’s Mélenchon sees Spain’s Sánchez as inspiration for fixing public finances
World.content:
Polls show Mélenchon neck and neck with center-right candidate Édouard Philippe in the race to qualify for a second-round runoff against Marine Le Pen, the far-right frontrunner who presented her own budget plans last week.

Under Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, Spain has significantly reduced its budget deficit, while public debt is projected to fall below 100% of GDP in 2026. His government has raised the minimum wage and supported investment in green energy, alongside other sectors. Although inflation is a major concern and economic growth is expected to moderate in 2027, Spain remains one of Europe’s fastest-growing major economies, with the IMF on Tuesday forecasting 2.5% growth in 2026.

Spanish deficit fell significantly under Sánchez, and became one of the Eurozone’s fastest-growing economies after the pandemic.

Spain’s debt-to-GDP ratio dropped below 100% — while France’s raised to 119% — as the government invested heavily in sectors such as green energy and raised the minimum wage. But the cost of living remains a major concern in the country, particularly housing — one of the issues that led Sánchez to call a snap election earlier this month.

More money, less problems?

Mélenchon wants to boost growth by increasing purchasing power through higher salaries — including a higher minimum wage, a 10% raise for public-sector workers and a nationwide round of collective bargaining — as well as higher benefits for welfare recipients and a monthly payment of €1,337 for every French student intended to lift them above the poverty line.

Together, these measures form what his campaign calls an €82 billion “emergency spending” package.

World.title: Siegmunds Machtplan in Gefahr
World.content:
Share on LinkedIn

Ein geheimes Abendessen bringt das Bündnis Sahra Wagenknecht in Erklärungsnot: Fünf BSW-Abgeordnete speisen mit der AfD und dem rechtsextremen Publizisten Jürgen Elsässer. Während die BSW-Spitze tobt, wittert die AfD ihre Chance für die Ministerpräsidentenwahl in Sachsen-Anhalt. Wie ein raffinierter CDU-Plan den AfD-Kandidaten Ulrich Siegmund stoppen soll, offenbart einen beispiellosen Machtkampf.

Abseits der Ränkespiele eskaliert ein Streit um das Gedenken an den Terroranschlag von Halle. Jüdische Studenten verwehren dem Landtagsvizepräsidenten Hans-Thomas Tillschneider den Zutritt zur Synagoge – ein Eklat, der den AfD-Umgang mit Antisemitismusvorwürfen offenlegt. Zugleich spürt die Partei wirtschaftlichen Gegenwind, als BMW dem Landtagspräsidenten Tobias Rausch den Dienstwagen verweigert.

Auch beim Parteinachwuchs rumort es gewaltig: Im Bundesvorstand der „Generation Deutschland“ wirft Helmut Strauß nach wenigen Monaten hin. Der Grund sind Großmachtfantasien und eine gepostete Landkarte, die selbst in AfD-Kreisen als zu radikal gilt. Ein tiefer Einblick in die ideologischen Grabenkämpfe der Parteijugend, der zeigt, wo die rote Linie der AfD verläuft.

„Inside AfD“ ist der POLITICO-Podcast über die umstrittenste Partei des Landes. Trotz Radikalisierung und Beobachtung durch den Verfassungsschutz wächst die AfD weiter. Wie ist das möglich? Was treibt ihre Anhänger, Strategen und Gegner an? Wie funktioniert das Innenleben der Partei? Und was bedeutet ihr Aufstieg für das politische System Deutschlands?

Antworten liefern immer mittwochs Pauline von Pezold von POLITICO und Frederik Schindler von WELT — unaufgeregt, aber kritisch.
