World.title: Thousands of supermarket fridges still exposed after cyberattack
World.content:
French investigators are searching for the hackers who took over refrigeration units at at least 350 supermarkets, forcing staff to throw away spoiled meat and frozen food.

 

Stores belonging to Carrefour, Monoprix, Intermarché and Coopérative U were among those hit when attackers manually overrode fridge temperatures. The affected stores are a small fraction of France’s supermarkets.

The lack of a ransom demand or claim of responsibility has puzzled investigators, according to a source with knowledge of the probe cited by Reuters. Criminal and hacktivist groups usually move quickly to profit from or publicise their attacks.

France’s cybersecurity agency said the breach affected fridges running software from Danish firm Danfoss, as well as Copeland and Dixell systems.

Reuters reported it found at least 4,500 Danfoss interfaces visible online on Tuesday, and scanning firm Onyphe said outdated versions were "still widely represented among publicly accessible interfaces".

Danfoss said many affected units had "reached end of life and no longer receive software or security updates" or were "running outdated firmware". Serious flaws in older versions of its firmware were detailed in August by security firm Claroty and have since been patched.

Copeland, which owns Dixell, acknowledged the "vulnerability", saying: "We are currently working with impacted customers to mitigate the risk."

"This is about basic cyber hygiene," Ken Munro, a partner at British firm Pen Test Partners, told Reuters. "Get it wrong and you get a smelly mess of defrosted food."

He said the attack could be "kids messing around". "If this was a nation state, why affect only a subset of French fridges? There are plenty of other nations with fridges on the internet," he said.

Dutch disruption

In the Netherlands, Ahold Delhaize, which owns Albert Heijn, said it had begun a controlled restart of systems after a cybersecurity incident that started on Sunday. The Dutch cybersecurity watchdog NCSC said it saw no link to the French attack.

Dutch broadcaster NOS reported that Albert Heijn had identified servers in the US, Poland, Moldova and Turkey used in the attack. NOS stressed this reveals nothing about where the hackers are, as traffic is easily routed through other countries.

Security specialist Pim Takkenberg told NOS the servers were probably used to scout the systems or try to steal data.

NOS also reported that the incident exposed how thin food stocks are. Shops and distribution centres hold around six days’ supply between them, replenished continuously by just-in-time IT systems that can fail and depend on the power grid.

A report by Clingendael and Erasmus University last month advised households to keep eight days of emergency food rather than three. It found that severe weather combined with a major power and IT outage could take two weeks to recover from.

World.title: Mont Blanc rises by almost two metres, now standing at 4,807.47 metres
World.content:
Mont Blanc has grown higher. The tallest peak in Western Europe now stands at 4,807.47 metres, almost two metres more than in 2023.

 

An altitude that "is close to the historical value" recorded at the end of the 19th century, according to expert surveyors in Haute-Savoie who have been regularly measuring the summit since 2001.

However, they are urging caution: this "one-off" reading does not allow any conclusions to be drawn about the effects of global warming. Mont Blanc's elevation varies with the weather, in particular precipitation and winds that shift and redistribute the snow at the summit.

"Today, the summit is really shaped by the force of the winds and by precipitation, even though this year has been particularly dry," explains Mathieu Dragon, a chartered surveyor in Haute-Savoie.

A new technique to study the summit

This year, to refine their observations, the surveyors used ground-penetrating radar to map the ice cap and the rocky peak beneath it.

The data collected will help refine their measurements and track how the roof of Western Europe changes over the coming years.

World.title: One person killed and 20 others injured in overnight Russian attacks on Kyiv
World.content:
At least one person was killed and more than 20 others injured in a Russian attack on Ukraine’s capital Kyiv overnight into Wednesday.

 

A large fire broke out in a residential building after it had come under Russian shelling.

The strikes targeted a key power plant in the city, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Zelenskyy noted that the Darnytska CHP-4 plant, which supplies the capital with heating and electricity, was targeted by a ballistic missile.

The attack comes just days after US President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, halting attacks on energy targets.

Since then, the Kremlin’s nightly attacks have nevertheless continued to target energy sites, according to Zelenskyy.

What 'energy ceasefire'?

The attacks also come at a dire time for Ukraine, currently grappling with a crisis which has seen more than 600,000 people lose power in various strikes on energy grids.

"Energy facilities in Kyiv and the surrounding region have come under a massive ballistic missile strike. There are power disruptions in the capital," Mayor Vitali Klitschko wrote on Telegram.

The Ukrainian President accused Moscow of disrespecting US President Donald Trump and his "energy ceasefire".

"The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale –- Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States", Zelenskyy wrote on X.

Meanwhile Russia said it had shot down 900 Ukrainian drones overnight, including 180 near Moscow.

Zelenskyy has previously noted that Ukraine is prepared to abide by Trump’s truce if Russia reciprocates, a plea the Kremlin did not acknowledge.

World.title: Mont Blanc: new French measurements, summit 'grows' to 4,807m
World.content:
The idea of a mountain growing may sound strange, but that is exactly what happens. Its height can even change in just a few years, as has occurred with Mont Blanc which, according to measurements released in France on Wednesday, now reaches 4,807.47 metres above sea level, almost two metres more than in 2023.

 

The new calculations were carried out on 17 September by experts from the Haute-Savoie Departmental Chamber of Surveyors, whose territory includes part of the mountain shared by France and Italy.

The results were officially presented on Wednesday in Saint-Gervais-Mont-Blanc, on the French side of the massif, showing an increase of 1.88 metres in three years, reversing the trend of previous years, when the summit had been lower.

Presenting the results, the president of the Chamber of Surveyors, Jean des Garets, recalled that "the summit is in constant motion".

Why Mont Blanc's altitude changes over time

The apparent "growth" is not due to movements of the mountain itself but to variations in the snow and ice cap that covers the top.

The height of Europe's second-highest peak changes according to the accumulation and redistribution of snow, influenced by wind, precipitation, temperature, sunshine and seasonal weather conditions.

For this reason, the periodic measurement campaigns produce different results. Between 2000 and 2010 the height was repeatedly measured at around 4,810 metres. Afterwards, a gradual decrease was recorded.

In 2021 Mont Blanc reached 4,807.81 metres, while in 2023 it dropped to 4,805.59 metres, the lowest figure in recent years. The 2026 measurement, by contrast, puts the mountain back above 4,807 metres.

The Alps' highest peak rises back above 4,807 metres

The new survey confirms that Mont Blanc remains a summit in constant evolution. Compared with the historic figure from 1894, its current altitude is around 27 centimetres higher.

For experts, the succession of measurements is also a useful tool for monitoring the effects of weather and climate conditions on the Alpine environment.

World.title: FBI arrest Saudi OpenAI employee for allegedly planting recording device in office
World.content:
OpenAI said it has alerted the FBI after it found a hidden recording device in an executive conference room in its San Francisco office, which led to the firing of an employee.

 

The suspect was identified as employee Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national, who was arrested on October 9, about a week after OpenAI discovered the surveillance device. He made an initial appearance in a US court on Tuesday.

He was charged with using or endeavouring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. Alfozan joined OpenAI as an engineer in July 2025.

Prosecutors said the device was wrapped in toilet paper and inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room.

He was allegedly spotted near the executive conference room in CCTV footage on multiple dates before the device was discovered, according to the Justice Department.

Conversations in the conference room "frequently involved discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information," the Justice Department said.

The allegations come as the US and China race to become the leader in AI, which the Trump administration has pushed to be rebranded as "superintelligence".

“We discovered a sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices. We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier,” OpenAI said in a statement posted on X.

The ChatGPT maker said it had “no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data”.

If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (€200,000) fine, followed by three years of supervised release.

World.title: Croatia's wartime grievances threaten Montenegro's hopes of joining EU by 2028
World.content:
Croatia has warned that a series of unresolved disputes with neighbouring Montenegro, including wartime abuses, property claims and contested borders, could stand in the way of the country's ambition to join the European Union by 2028.

 

In a document sent to other EU governments on Monday and seen by Euronews, Zagreb set out eight demands it wants Montenegro to address before completing its accession to the bloc.

Montenegro is widely regarded as the frontrunner among countries seeking EU membership, with hopes of becoming the bloc's 28th member by 2028. But its long-running disputes with Croatia, many dating back to the breakup of Yugoslavia in the 1990s, threaten to derail that timetable.

“Croatia sincerely wishes to turn the page on this painful chapter of shared history and build a forward-looking relationship with Montenegro. Yet mutual trust and genuine, lasting reconciliation cannot be built without resolving these issues,” the document reads.

Montenegro made further progress towards EU membership on Monday, completing negotiations in three more policy areas – statistics, economic policy and employment – bringing the total to 21 out of 33.

However, Croatia is blocking progress in four other areas, covering transport, foreign relations, fundamental rights and home affairs. Because every existing EU member has a say over the accession process, Zagreb has considerable leverage over its neighbour's membership bid.

The document expands on grievances previously outlined by Croatia's Foreign Ministry in July, many rooted in the wars that accompanied Yugoslavia's collapse.

Among the most sensitive is Zagreb's demand for compensation for around 300 Croatian nationals detained and mistreated at the Morinj prison camp in Montenegro between October 1991 and August 1992. Croatian civilians and prisoners of war were forcibly transferred to the camp during the conflict.

Croatia also wants a memorial plaque at the former camp to remain permanently visible. A large metal frame was installed around it following protests by Montenegrin nationalist groups.

Another demand concerns the fate of 14 people still missing from Croatia's war of independence. Zagreb wants Montenegro to help locate their remains, describing the issue as a “major humanitarian issue that has yet to be resolved.”

A further point concerns war crimes: Croatia wants command responsibility for the crimes against civilians committed at Morinj to be considered in the cases of already convicted war criminals.

Croatia also expects Montenegro to resolve long-standing property disputes dating back to the early 1990s, involving Croatian families unlawfully deprived of their property without adequate compensation.

The paper points out that a 2021 law enabled the restitution of land in a region predominantly inhabited by the Albanian minority, “raising concerns about unequal treatment in comparable cases.”

Zagreb is also calling for the return of the Jadran, a sail training ship which has been under Montenegrin control since Yugoslavia dissolved in 1991.

Finally, Croatia wants the territorial disputes with its neighbour settled, over both the land and maritime border, in line with the Arbitration Commission of the Conference on Yugoslavia.

Croatia itself has an unresolved border dispute with Slovenia, although this did not prevent it from joining the EU in 2013.

“Croatia has consistently encouraged Montenegro to resolve outstanding bilateral issues while actively supporting its EU accession,” the paper continues. “Despite Croatia’s sustained efforts and constructive approach, none of the outstanding issues has yet been resolved.”

World.title: Todd Haynes at Lumière Festival: 'It is a time to remember how important it is to protect our freedoms'
World.content:
One of the guests of honour this year at Lyon’s Lumière Film Festival is none other than Todd Haynes, one of the most important and singular voices in contemporary American cinema.

 

The celebrated director and screenwriter of Far From Heaven, I’m Not There, Carol, and May December is known for his pioneering work associated with the New Queer Cinema movement of the early 90s. He then gained acclaim for his films exploring the emotional repercussions of social repression and the unspoken desires revealed by marginalized experiences.

He attends the Lumière Film Festival to present the restored versions of his directorial debut Poison (1991), a provocative exploration of AIDS-era perceptions. He also presents the Julianne Moore-starring psychological drama Safe (1995), marking the first time that these two films have screened in French cinemas since their initial releases.

Euronews Culture sat down with Todd Haynes during the festival to discuss the enduring timeliness of Poison and Safe, his thoughts on the evolving Hollywood ecosystem, as well as his upcoming film De Noche.

Euronews Culture's David Mouriquand with Todd Haynes Euronews Culture

Euronews Culture: How does it feel to be at the Lumière Film Festival in Lyon, the birthplace of cinema?

Todd Haynes: Pretty thrillingly natal! No, really, it's a festival I've been hearing so much about for so long. And it really is such a celebration of movies of all kinds, of every genre, of every era. Restorations are presented, artists are attributed, and it's a really remarkable place and atmosphere, and it's so much about just the filmmaking and the films.

There's a retrospective of your films, including two newly restored versions of Poison and Safe. How do you look back on these films, and how do you feel about the fact that there are going to be audiences at this festival who are seeing these two films for the very first time?

I was there for the introduction of Poison. People were asked in the theater who were seeing it for the first time and almost every hand went up! And it was a completely full theatre, so that just demonstrates a kind of interest and curiosity about what's being shown in Lyon, and an audience that is very enthusiastic about it.

So, it's incredibly meaningful. These are my first two features. They are very, very different. Poison came out in the height of the AIDS era and it was among the first couple of films that would join other films in being categorised as the New Queer Cinema. None of which, I don't think, would have been possible outside of that political and socio-economic crisis - the public health crisis of AIDS. In certain times, those kinds of conditions make creating film and documentary, and protest and organised resistance, essential. They drive a kind of urgency that we don't always feel in our medium or our market. That was absolutely true for Poison. And then I made a film [Safe] that also is, in my mind, inconceivable without the AIDS era as a framework. It's a film that takes the place about as far away from the battlefield, if you will, but still engaged. A lot of the themes and issues deal with illness, and the body, and feeling alienated from the world around you...

I had the pleasure of re-watching both films, and that sense of isolation in Safe still feels incredibly prescient.

That’s always surprising and encouraging to hear. I understand how that might be what people could say about Safe. The film was watched again during Covid. There was a lot of discussion about the film and articles that came out were sent to me. And sadly, these issues remain relevant when we're hit by things that are overwhelming and that challenge every single aspect of the way we lead our lives, and the assumptions about how to live our lives that we take for granted.

Todd Haynes Euronews Culture

One does feel at times like we’re in a replay, if not crashing backwards in battles we’ve fought. Battles around reproductive rights, around tolerance and acceptance over queer communities and trans communities. Todd Haynes

Both explicitly and implicitly about the AIDS crisis, do you find it heartening or disheartening that Poison and Safe still feel timely? After all, Poison was made at a specific time, and there are many members of the gay, trans, queer communities who continue to feel threatened and continue to express fears...

Absolutely. One does feel at times like we’re in a replay, if not crashing backwards in battles we’ve fought. Battles around reproductive rights, around tolerance and acceptance over queer communities and trans communities. Poison in particular addressed very much that sense of vulnerability that the community was feeling under the siege of AIDS and HIV.

Jean Genet, who's a writer and thinker and poet and playwright who I've always loved - but also derived a certain energy from his attitude about how important it is to remember that being defined marginal... The goal to that is not necessarily to find your way back to the table and become just like everybody else. For him, his queerness, it came out of a criminal background. He liked that homosexuality had this criminal aspect to it. He used that as a way of weaponising his critique of dominant culture. Poison was made at the very end of the 80s and we needed a voice like that.

I'm heartened to see that some of Jean Genet’s books are displayed next to DVDs of your films at the Lumière marketplace...

Oh, I didn’t see that. That’s awesome!

Todd Haynes in conversation with Euronews Culture Euronews Culture

It's distressing when you see the conglomeration of huge media organizations that one might imagine would provide enough revenue and foundation for risk-taking to still occur. But sadly, that is rarely what you end up seeing. Todd Haynes

From a European perspective, when you look at present day Hollywood, it’s hard not to see a sense of regression. For instance, to take a recent example, the Paramount-Warner merger feels like it threatens the financing of films from a plurality of voices. What are your thoughts on the evolution of the studio system and Hollywood at the moment?

It's distressing when you see the conglomeration of huge media organizations that one might imagine would provide enough revenue and foundation for risk-taking to still occur. But sadly, that is rarely what you end up seeing. I don't feel it, particularly in the moment, among some of the big streaming companies. There's a sense of wanting to repeat what worked the last time, and keep replicating what the audiences seem to crave. And that's tough.

For my last couple films, we've really gone elsewhere. I mean, we did sell May December, my last feature, to Netflix - and they were a fantastic company, full of incredibly smart people who really believed in the film. But the way we made the film was through the limited amount of investment that we absolutely had to have to get it done so we could all retain our creative freedom and identity. That's how we put together the financing for my current film that I'm finishing now, De Noche. And in that case, I really do want a company fully committed to theatrical release.

Todd Haynes Euronews Culture

Germany has a unique, specific, and at times contradictory attitudes or laws around how we discuss Israel, for instance. Todd Haynes

Discourse around film and the creation of film feels in jeopardy at the moment. For example, we saw it this year at the Berlinale with the controversy surrounding Tricia Tuttle and the pro-Palestinian speeches made by invited filmmakers. Do you fear or foresee that cultural institutions will become increasingly threatened by political pressure, like in Berlin?

Sure. I think Germany has a unique, specific, and at times contradictory attitudes or laws around how we discuss Israel, for instance. There's this happening on the one hand where speech is kind of being watchdogged and limited, and people have a hard time of just saying that it doesn't have to be about Jewish people to have problems with the policies of Netanyahu, or whoever it may be.

But at the same time, the AfD is rising in Germany... So you have that complete sort of disconnect between these two forces - one trying to make remedy after an incredibly horrific past in history, and then all of a sudden, wanting such extreme change to come into place from completely the opposite direction.

So, Germany is a unique case, but I think we're feeling similar things about a crackdown on content and what is called ideology or point of view in the United States. It's targeted at the media, it's targeted at the news industries, and it's targeted at universities... So it is a time to remember how important it is to protect our freedoms, and our ability to speak freely.

Todd Haynes at the Lumiere Film Festival Euronews Culture

To temporarily move away from the doom and gloom, I wanted to share with you that the first film of yours that I saw was Velvet Goldmine (1998), which had a profound impact on me. I remember seeing the trailer for the first time, watching Brian Slade in his feather outfit on stage, hearing the gunshot followed by the needle drop of T. Rex’s '20th Century Boy', and... it still gives me goosebumps.

(Laughs) Awww....

The film turns 30 very soon... How do you look back on Velvet Goldmine and please tell me there’ll be a resotration?

Oh, it's another film that sort of realised or completed a phase of my creative life that was very profound and deep in that whole era of music and the early 70s. And the very interesting relationship between the UK and the US in how that music came to be. Criterion Collection is working on the release of Poison that will coincide with that 30th anniversary. I'm very, very excited about that.

Todd Haynes Euronews Culture

I think seeing a movie on the big screen for the first time can't be overstated. Todd Haynes

Music plays a big part in your filmography – whether it’s Karen Carpenter, Bob Dylan, The Velvet Underground... I read somewhere that you’re working on a documentary about The Cure...

You know, that was news to me! (Laughs) Somebody brought it up... I mean, I love The Cure and they were formative in my life. Their music and evolution as a band from record to record... But no, it's not something I'm doing, and I'm not exactly sure where that came from! (Laughs)

Can you blame people for trying to manifest this project into existence?

(Laughs) Exactly!

Well, glad we got that cleared up! You mentioned your upcoming film, De Noche... You’ve wrapped, right?

We've wrapped the film and we're in post-production. We're moving from the picture cut to the sound. The whole production was based in Mexico. And this film was a particular struggle to get to this place, so I'm very proud of it.

You mention struggles...

Oh well, it began with the relationship with an actor [Joaquin Phoenix] who came to me for it and we moved forward. We got very close to production two years ago, and then he had a very abrupt or unexpected change of heart and walked away. And so De Noche 1 fell apart. But it was remarkable how the financiers and the investors who were there for that version came back, and demonstrated loyalty to the project and a film that means so much to all of us.

I’m glad De Noche 2 happened, with Danny Ramirez and Pedro Pascal starring. You also worked with Jon Raymond, who you’d previously collaborated with on the miniseries Mildred Pierce. I’m a huge fan of his work with Kelly Reichardt, especially on Old Joy and First Cow, which is a masterpiece in my book.

I couldn't agree more. Jon is a novelist first and has become a screenwriter. I’m so proud to have played even the smallest part in introducing Jon to Kelly when I moved to Portland, Oregon. They met each other, and they really hit it off. Many of his short stories were the first places that she went to in order to resuscitate a career in feature filmmaking that she had kind of put aside. And amazingly, well before she ended up even settling down in the Pacific Northwest, she and Jon really became the chroniclers of that region, its history, of Portland and beyond. So that unexpected move in my life to Portland from New York City... There have been so many rewards from it. And Jon is one of my dearest, closest friends. He's the most fabulous human being.

Todd Haynes at Lumiere Film Festival Euronews Culture

Sometimes the simplest technology remains the best and the most profound. Todd Haynes

I can't wait to see De Noche. Is there anything else you can tell us about the film?

I don't know if I've ever quite seen anything like it before as a concept. It sort of begins as a detective story in the late 30s in a very corrupt Los Angeles, and through circumstances and the corruption that these two characters have become embroiled in, they're forced to leave Los Angeles and flee to Mexico. A very inexplicable, unexpected relationship begins to form between the two of them. To get to that point, a lot of dynamics of divisions between them in terms of power and race are overcome bit by bit, step by step, through the exploration of each other as lovers. It ultimately becomes a love story that that leaves you, I hope, longing and wondering what will happen between these two men.

To wrap up, at the opening ceremony of the Lumière Festival, you shared with me that the first film that had a profound impact on you was Mary Poppins. What was it about that film that marked you?

For one thing, it was the sort crown jewel of the Disney experiment, in terms of the films that came out of Disney at that time. The score is so exquisite, the two actors who take the leads are just perfection, it's so beautifully produced... I think for a three-year-old's imagination, there’s something about a maternal subject who comes with unique powers, and also discipline. Just a curious combination of various aspects of that character. I think seeing a movie on the big screen for the first time can't be overstated. The sheer power of that... I think all of those things conjoined to make it a sort of escapable moment of introduction to this medium.

This year has been a very good one in terms of cinema attendance and that being mirrored at the box office. Still, there are cinemas struggling and many fears expressed about the threat that artificial intelligence represents for the creative arts. As broad a question as this is, are you optimistic about the future of cinema?

I have to be optimistic. Because it's a medium I just love. I wasn't able to shoot De Noche on film, as we couldn't afford it, but it will always be my starting point on any film that I make. And what you are seeing among young people is an incredible desire to go out of their houses and leave their home screens and their phones behind and join in the experience of watching a movie on the screen.

You know how we all thought vinyl was going to go away with the introduction of CDs and MP3 and there was a sort of counter movement that was like ‘No, I want to hold it in my hand'... The desire to actually experience it and the warm resonance of hearing vinyl play with a needle on... Sometimes the simplest technology remains the best and the most profound. I hope that continues and I hope we can see that still being played out. It is about younger people and exposing them to what that experience means, and what that's like to share communally in a theatre in the dark.

Todd Haynes Euronews Culture

On that note, Mr Haynes, thank you very much for your time.

The Lumière Film Festival takes place until 18 October in Lyon, France. The restored versions of Todd Haynes' Poison and Safe are being screened, as well as Far From Heaven and I'm Not There. Safe is out now on Criterion 4K UHD Blu-ray.

Todd Haynes' new film, De Noche, finished shooting in April 2026. No release date has yet been announced.

World.title: Turkish police raid Halk TV in Istanbul, sparking outrage over media freedom
World.content:
Financial crime investigators searched the building, forcing a temporary suspension of broadcasts. Prosecutors accused the channel's chairman, Cafer Mahiroglu, of bid rigging, bribery and money laundering. Of the 17 people sought by investigators, 11 were detained.

 

Mahiroglu, who lives abroad, rejected the allegations, calling the takeover politically motivated.

Outside the building, supporters gathered to defend the channel's journalists, while opposition politicians and press freedom organisations condemned the intervention.

The case has raised fresh concerns about media freedom in Turkey, where independent news outlets face longstanding political pressure.

Halk TV is known for its critical coverage of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's government. It has also reported extensively on the legal troubles of Ekrem Imamoglu, Istanbul's jailed mayor and one of Erdogan's main political rivals.

Opposition MP Ali Mahir Basarir warned against taking control of media organisations simply because they criticise the government. Amnesty International called for the broadcaster's independence to be restored.

Turkey stands 163rd out of 180 countries in Reporters Without Borders' press freedom ranking.

World.title: India urges Russia, Ukraine to protect Black Sea shipping
World.content:
New Delhi wants Moscow and Kyiv to ensure safe commercial shipping in the Black Sea amid attacks that put Indian seafarers at risk.

India has urged both Russia and Ukraine to ensure safe passage for commercial shipping through the Black Sea, as attacks on merchant vessels put Indian seafarers at risk and threaten to disrupt vital food and energy supplies.

New Delhi says discussions with both sides are under way.

"The targeting of commercial shipping and seafarers in the region must end, and free and unimpeded navigation and commerce through the international waterways must be restored at the earliest," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said last week.

India accounts for more than 12% of the global seafaring workforce, with 311,936 maritime professionals, according to a 2026 industry report. And attacks on commercial vessels in and around the Black Sea in recent months have highlighted the risks facing civilian crews.

The Turkish-owned MV Royad Mammadov, a cargo ship carrying grain from Ukraine, caught fire and sank following an attack on Monday, killing two crew members. The three Indian nationals aboard the vessel survived, but sustained injuries and were taken to Romania to receive medical treatment.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blamed Russia for launching the strike.

The Defense Ministry in Moscow separately said it had struck two Ukrainian cargo vessels in the Black Sea but did not specifically identify the ships.

The Liberian-flagged oil tanker Aframax Rio was also recently attacked by unmanned vessels off Russia's Black Sea coast near Sochi, according to Russian authorities. The vessel was carrying 23 Indians, but all of them were rescued.

How India has become Russia's trade lifeline To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Can diplomacy deliver safety?

Anil Wadhwa, a former Indian diplomat, said India's proposal to halt attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea covered energy infrastructure, safe passage for grain and energy exports, and an end to strikes on merchant vessels.

"Securing an ironclad guarantee depends entirely on a broader cessation of hostilities between Russia and Ukraine in the maritime theater," Wadhwa told DW.

India's close relations with Russia and expanding engagement with Ukraine give New Delhi access to both sides, but do not guarantee either will honor a shipping arrangement.

Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has described India's proposal for a possible ceasefire with Russia as the "broadest" of the four offers Kyiv has received.

Russia has not publicly endorsed a binding safe-passage deal proposed by India, despite welcoming New Delhi's peace efforts.

Rajan Kumar of the Center for Russian and Central Asian Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University said India could use its diplomatic leverage with Moscow to help bring the two sides towards an agreement.

"India could play a constructive role in facilitating dialogue between Russia and Ukraine, particularly on the issue of ensuring the safety of commercial shipping in the Black Sea," Kumar told DW.

How Ukraine fights in the Black Sea without a navy To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Working with other powers to reach a deal

He argued that India should also work with other influential countries from the Global South, particularly China, Brazil and South Africa.

"A coordinated approach with these countries could enhance their collective diplomatic leverage and strengthen their capacity to persuade both parties to adopt mutually acceptable arrangements for maritime security," said Kumar.

India's initiative comes as US President Donald Trump announced an "energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine over the weekend, although its scope and implementation mechanism remain unclear.

Harsh Pant, vice president of the New Delhi-based think tank Observer Research Foundation, said Trump's intervention could help India's efforts but might produce a narrower agreement that fails to address New Delhi's wider concerns.

"The energy ceasefire could be an initial confidence-building measure, whereas a Black Sea shipping arrangement requires additional commitments on attacks against merchant vessels, ports, maritime routes and the security of commercial traffic," Pant told DW.

"India need not compete with Washington for the public credit of mediation. It could instead press for the inclusion of broader maritime provisions in any US agreement,” he added.

Will India face a higher import bill?

Wadhwa said the proposed energy truce could also benefit Indian seafarers if it secured safe passage for energy cargoes.

"Although Ukraine alleges that the Russians have already breached this so-called truce, there will be pressure on both sides to allow energy cargoes safe passage. India is bound to gain as far as its crews are concerned in such a scenario," he said.

The disruption to Black Sea shipping also has other implications for India such as delays in shipments of key commodities and higher transport costs.

"A prolonged Black Sea disruption would elevate India's import bill mainly via higher freight on Russian crude and constrained soft oil supplies, with the strongest near-term transmission to domestic edible oil prices and food inflation," said Lekha Chakraborty, professor at the National Institute of Public Finance and Policy.

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

World.title: Germany's far-right AfD forges a pro-Russia alliance with the BSW
World.content:
In Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD and BSW are joining forces to push for negotiations with Moscow. What is driving this rapprochement?

The state parliament of the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt is calling for an immediate end to all German financial and military aid to Ukraine. The motion was passed during a special parliamentary session with the votes of the far-right populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW) which combines left-leaning economic positions with right-wing populist positions on immigration.



Both parties are urging Saxony-Anhalt's current state premier Sven Schulze of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), to advocate in the Bundesrat, Germany's upper house representing the federal states, for peace negotiations with Russia.

However, as the federal states have no specific powers in the field of foreign policy, the motion will have no direct impact on Germany's Ukraine policy.

Speaking on behalf of the BSW in the state parliament, legislator Claudia Wittig called on the premier to take action: "It is your responsibility to finally use every available avenue to work for peace."

The proposal drew sharp criticism from all other parties. "Anyone who demands a ceasefire only from the side that has been attacked is not calling for peace, but for capitulation," said CDU lawmaker Stefan Ruland.

What next after far-right AfD win in regional election? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

AfD and BSW bonding over Russia

The special session took place against the backdrop of ongoing negotiations over the formation of a new state government in Saxony-Anhalt. The AfD had emerged as the clear winner of the September 2026 election, securing just under 44% of the vote. However, it fell short of an absolute majority in the state parliament and will need the support of other parties if it is to govern.

The BSW, which narrowly secured representation in the state parliament, is the only party willing to hold formal talks with the AfD on forming a government. Because the AfD is classified by the security authorities in the eastern German state as a "confirmed right-wing extremist" party, all other parties have ruled out any cooperation.

Observers view the joint motion by the AfD and BSW as a sign of closer and potentially enduring cooperation between two parties rooted in very different ideological traditions.

"Their common ground lies in their rejection of the political establishment, their pro-Putin stance, and their criticism of Germany's support for Ukraine," political scientist Armin Pfahl-Traughber of the University of Applied Administrative Sciences of the Federation said in an interview with DW.

The BSW was founded in 2024 as a breakaway from the socialist Left Party. Its founder, Sahra Wagenknecht, after whom the alliance was originally named, had long been a controversial figure on the German left and advocated far-reaching changes to Germany's economic policy. She was the Left Party's most prominent representative of the so-called "Communist Platform", which maintained close ties to Russia.

Over time, however, her socially conservative positions and criticism of Germany's immigration policy came under increasing scrutiny within the party. These growing tensions ultimately led to her departure from the Left Party and the founding of the BSW.

The AfD, too, has repeatedly expressed sympathy for Putin's system. Shortly after the start of Russia's war against Ukraine, Björn Höcke, the influential AfD state chairman in Thuringia, described Russia as a "champion of a world of free and sovereign states."

Historic parallels

The growing rapprochement between the two parties made headlines following a meeting in early October. At the invitation of a far-right publishing house, representatives of the AfD and BSW met in Saxony-Anhalt for what was described as a confidence-building dinner. Also in attendance were controversial figures from both the far right and the dogmatic left. According to their own accounts, participants from both sides explored the possibility of closer cooperation in a cordial atmosphere and in a spirit of mutual trust.

Far left? Far right? What is Germany's BSW? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Jürgen Elsässer, the host of the event and editor-in-chief of the right-wing magazine Compact, has for years promoted the idea of a so-called "cross-front" alliance (Querfront) between the far left and the far right in opposition to Germany's political establishment. He has long sought to build bridges between the two camps.

The historical model for this idea dates back to the 1930s, shortly before Adolf Hitler and the National Socialists came to power in Germany. At the time, national-conservative forces sought cooperation with elements of the political left in an effort to secure a majority of their own. As political scientist Armin Pfahl-Traughber explained in an interview with DW: "The aim, however, was not to save democracy from the National Socialists, but merely to establish an authoritarian political order without them." The idea failed. What followed were twelve years of terror under Nazi rule and World War II.

Pfahl-Traughber does not regard the cooperation between the AfD and BSW as a "cross-front" alliance: "I am not even sure that the BSW can still be classified as part of the political left." While the party's founder, Sahra Wagenknecht, has her roots on the left, she and her allies position themselves on the economic left but the cultural right, the political scientist argues.

AfD lawmaker elected speaker in Saxony-Anhalt To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Are both AfD and BSW reactionary?

The prominent German historian and author Ilko-Sascha Kowalczuk likewise does not consider the BSW as a left-wing party. In an interview with DW, he argued: "The BSW was never left-wing; it was always reactionary."

Kowalczuk considers both the AfD and the BSW a threat to democracy: "The BSW and the AfD are two sides of the same coin. Both are mouthpieces for the Kremlin, both pursue similar domestic political objectives, and both seek a comparable anti-democratic transformation of the state into an authoritarian system."

Although the recent resolution passed by the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament is unlikely to have any immediate impact on Germany's policy towards Ukraine, Kowalczuk warns of its broader implications: "For now, the AfD and BSW remain isolated, but with positions like these they are appealing to large sections of society, particularly in eastern Germany. The erosion of solidarity with Ukraine will continue and will soon spread to larger segments of both the SPD and the CDU," he told DW.

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: Albania: Fire at Education Ministry as students protest
World.content:
Riot police deployed in the Albanian capital Tirana on the second day of student protests. The sudden outbreak seemed at least somewhat reminiscent of the widespread demos in France courting international attention.

Albania's Education Ministry caught fire on Wednesday in a second day of student protests over corruption and education.

The scenes were at least somewhat reminiscent of the protracted student demonstrations in France in recent weeks.

They are probably the most violent outburst of low-level anti-corruption protests against Prime Minister Edi Rama's government and the main opposition led by Sali Barisha that started in May this year.

Many of the demonstrators wore face coverings Image: Florion Goga/REUTERS

What happened in Tirana's student protests?

Police deployed riot police and used tear gas and water cannons to disperse crowds in the capital Tirana.

Thousands of protesters gathered in front of the Education Ministry on Wednesday, many obscuring their faces. Some threw bricks at the building, damaged barriers on the sidewalks and overturned trash cans.

A bank near the Education Ministry also caught fire, according to the Reuters news agency citing a witness.

The demonstration started on Tuesday with a peaceful gathering of several hundred people outside the Education Ministry but quickly escalated and turned violent in places.

Police early on Wednesday reported around 40 detentions and 13 people injured, including six police officers. Unrest continued long after these figures were issued.

Police used tear gas and water cannons on demonstrators in parts of Tirana Image: Florion Goga/REUTERS

Government says demonstrations degenerated into 'orchestrated violence'

Deputy Prime Minster Albana Kociu posted a video of demonstrations on Facebook saying it was "disheartening to see the culture of protest degenerate into orchestrated violence."

She said that the attacks on institutions and police and the "senseless destruction of public property" were "not the language through which the youth should express themselves." Instead, she said they were reminiscent of the "old habits of those who use young people to mask their own political incompetence."

In another post, Kociu called on students who believe in the right to protest to "distance" themselves from "violence and vandalism."

Student organizers say the protests revolve around conditions at universities, higher education costs, financial support and employment prospects after graduation.

More generally, Albania has faced a series of demonstrations this year sometimes referred to as the "Flamingo Revolution." These were at least partly prompted by a controversial construction project on the Adriatic Coast in a protected area where flamingos live.

But these partly environmental protests have also had a more general theme of dissatisfaction with Albania's dominant political forces. PM Edi Rama's Socialists and Sali Barisha's right-wing Democrats have alternated in government for more than 30 years, ever since the post-Cold War democratic transition in the former communist country.

Albania: Europe's new billionaire playground To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The timing is also conspicuous, with the demonstrations starting amid prominent international coverage of widespread school and student protests in France in recent weeks leading to similarly restless scenes.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

World.title: Climate change and drone attacks exacerbate the humanitarian crisis in war-torn Sudan
World.content:
Aid groups warn of an imminent collapse of the health system as fighting continues to displace civilians amid the planting season. The UN has extended an arms embargo, but only for Darfur.

In Sudan, clashes between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have intensified in North Kordofan and parts of Blue Nile state. The fighting has forced thousands of civilians to flee amid the planting season.

Since war broke out between the two factions and their allied militias in April 2023, both sides have fought for power. However, neither has managed to establish control over the entire country.

The SAF, the nation's official army, is in control of Sudan's north and center, including the capital, Khartoum, while the RSF maintains its presence in the western Darfur region and parts of the south.

The brutal war has plunged Sudan into one of the world's worst humanitarian and displacement crises, according to the United Nations and international aid organizations. The estimated death toll ranges from 40,000 to 250,000 people as reliable figures remain difficult to obtain amid the ongoing fighting. More than 12.4 million Sudanese have also been displaced, both within Sudan and to neighboring countries.

Fighting between the RSF and SAF is prompting thousands of civilians to flee from their homes amid the planting season Image: Faiz Abubakr/Middle East Images/IMAGO

This week, the aid organization Action Against Hunger sounded the alarm.

"24.6 million people are experiencing high levels of acute food insecurity," Jan Sebastian Friedrich-Rust, executive director of the German section of the NGO, told DW.

Friedrich-Rust added that an estimated 825,000 children younger than 5 suffer from severe acute malnutrition in 2026, while a total of 4.2 million children and pregnant or breastfeeding women are thought to be acutely malnourished.

In October, the Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) — which monitors food insecurity and uses the internationally recognized Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) system — also warned that several areas including camps for internally displaced people in Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan, are expected to face Catastrophe (IPC Phase 5), the most severe classification of acute food insecurity.

"The situation in Sudan continues to deteriorate and humanitarian needs are growing, even as the resources to respond are shrinking," Fabrizia Falcione, the Sudan representative of the United Nations Population Fund, the UN agency for sexual and reproductive health, said.

"I recently visited the displacement camp Tawila and I am still struggling to find the words to describe what I witnessed," Falcione told DW. "Imagine a population larger than that of Frankfurt, Germany, forced to flee their homes and seek refuge in one place in less than three years."

She added that more than 700,000 people there rely on just one hospital capable of performing Caesarean sections.

Despite repeated warnings about the deteriorating humanitarian situation, the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, which calls for $2.9 billion (€2.59 bn), is just 41% funded, with $1.2 billion (€1.07 bn) received from international donors so far.

Community kitchen fights hunger in Sudan's Tawila camp To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Climate shocks exacerbate Sudan's humanitarian crisis

The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) recently warned that extreme heat and heavy flooding are worsening the crisis in Sudan.

"This year, a massive heatwave brought power cuts of up to 12 hours per day in some regions," Hager Ali, a Sudan researcher at the German Institute for Global and Area Studies (GIGA), told DW. "Riverbeds and dried-out fields are barren, which comes on top of the damage from combat, the RSF's scorched-earth tactics and environmental destruction."

While the drought is affecting roughly half the country, heavy rains and localized flooding have worsened conditions in other areas of Sudan.

"As if that wasn't enough, there is also a massive shortage of fertilizer and diesel," Ali told DW.

Sudan relies on imported fertilizer and diesel shipped from the Persian Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. However, amid the wider Iran war, Iran has been blocking shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, while the Iran-aligned Houthi rebels in Yemen have threatened and at times disrupted shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

"Fertilizer supply collapsed from 450,000 metric tons to only about 50,000" in 2026, Ali said, adding that a similar diesel shortage and the soaring cost of diesel compound the situation in two ways.

"Agricultural equipment uses diesel and the transportation of humanitarian and agricultural goods within the country is getting a lot more expensive," Ali said.

In October, the International Food Policy Research Institute warned that staple food- and fuel prices in Sudan rose sharply in September 2026.

Al-Harith Idriss Al-Harith Mohamed, Sudan's permanent representative to the United Nations, opposed an extension of the arms embargo across Sudan, citing disadvantages for the Sudanese Armed Forces Image: Luiz Rampelotto/EuropaNewswire/Sipa USA/picture alliance

Limited arms embargo curbs hope for an end to the war

Observers have long pointed out that the war in Sudan will not end until foreign backers stop supplying arms. The SAF is officially supported by Egypt, Turkey, Russia and Iran while the United Arab Emirates is alleged to be the RSF's main backer, a claim Abu Dhabi denies.

However, in October, the UN Security Council extended the existing arms embargo only on Sudan's Darfur region until December 11, dropping calls for a nationwide embargo.

"To expand the UN embargo across Sudan would have included drones in particular," Hager Ali said, noting that Sudan is one of the biggest theaters for drone warfare: As of 2026, the leading cause of civilian casualties in Sudan are drone strikes.

She also told DW that Al-Harith Idriss al-Harith Mohamed, Sudan's permanent representative to the United Nations, opposed the extention of the embargo over concerns that it would disproportionately limit the Sudanese Armed Forces on the battlefield.

"An arms embargo would deter potential backers from cooperating with the Sudanese Armed Forces, whereas the Rapid Support Forces don't necessarily source their weapons through official ways," Hager Ali said.

"The RSF rely on trafficking with other militias, private military contractors and traders in the region," she said, adding that because the RSF obtains supplies from numerous sources and actors, it is difficult to target the group through a single embargo.

Sudan's civil war — the limits of humanitarian aid To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: Indonesian VIP prison scandal exposes inequality across Southeast Asia
World.content:
Luxury accommodation uncovered at an Indonesian prison has reignited concerns about preferential treatment for wealthy convicts across Southeast Asia.

Air-conditioned apartments, flat-screen televisions and even a golf simulator are hardly what most people would associate with life behind bars. Yet these luxuries were among the facilities uncovered last month at Indonesia's Cibinong Prison, near Jakarta, during a surprise inspection by the country's Ombudsman.

Investigators discovered more than 10 apartment-style units equipped with refrigerators, sofas and private living areas. A gym was also reportedly under construction.

The revelations prompted an investigation into whether inmates had paid for preferential treatment.

Five prison officials were initially suspended, while the prison's warden was dismissed on October 5. Authorities demolished 10 unauthorized buildings and took further disciplinary action against prison staff.

It wasn't Indonesia's first luxury prison scandal. In 2018, investigators from the Corruption Eradication Commission discovered that wealthy inmates at Sukamiskin Prison in Bandung enjoyed accommodation resembling private apartments.

Similar controversies have emerged elsewhere in Southeast Asia. Last November, authorities in Thailand investigated allegations that Chinese prisoners at Bangkok Remand Prison received special privileges, including access to an executive lounge.

In Malaysia, allegations of preferential treatment for politically connected prisoners have repeatedly surfaced. The latest Indonesian scandal prompted renewed calls for independent inspections of Malaysian prisons.

Why do VIP prison scandals in Southeast Asia keep recurring?

"Just like in the outside world, money and influence act as capital within the prison system. Powerful inmates generally do not lose their wealth and often maintain strong connections with influential people," Iwa Maulana, a senior researcher at Indonesia's Center for Detention Studies (CDS), told DW.

"When certain inmates receive different treatment based on their resources and influence, it demonstrates that, much like in the outside world, a person's identity affects how they are treated, even within prison walls," he added.

Overcrowded and poorly resourced prison systems also create opportunities for corruption.

Indonesia's detention facilities held approximately 279,000 people in late September, despite having an official capacity of around 154,000, according to government data.

Thailand's prisons are also severely overcrowded. At the end of 2025, they held approximately 301,000 inmates, around 21% above official capacity, according to the World Prison Brief.

Corruption within prison administrations also reflects wider governance problems, with Southeast Asian states routinely appearing at the bottom of Transparency International's annual Corruption Perceptions Index.

Where bribery and patronage already influence public services, prison officials may face similar incentives to exchange preferential treatment for money or favors.

"Corruption and political interference may explain particular cases," Nasrul Ismail, senior lecturer in criminology at the University of Bristol, who recently conducted a major study of prison governance in Malaysia, Thailand and the Philippines, told DW.

"When decisions are made behind closed doors, with limited transparency about who receives what and why, there are opportunities for personal connections and financial resources to influence treatment."

Life of child prisoners in Indonesian jails To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

However, he argues the problem extends beyond a relatively small number of wealthy inmates enjoying extraordinary privileges.

Across Southeast Asia, many prisoners depend on financial support from their families for everyday necessities that prison administrations do not provide.

Ismail said poorer inmates often rely on money deposited by relatives into prison canteen accounts to purchase food, clean water and hygiene products.

"This is distinct from wealthy prisoners receiving luxury accommodation, but both illustrate how broader inequalities can be reproduced within prisons through different institutional arrangements. Where minimum standards are not consistently guaranteed, access to decent conditions becomes dependent on the resources and connections prisoners possess," Ismail told DW.

"The fundamental issue is not simply whether wealthy prisoners receive special privileges, but why access to basic welfare and humane treatment can be so unequal in the first place."

Can prison systems be reformed?

Repeated scandals suggest that dismissing officials and demolishing unauthorized facilities achieve little without broader institutional reforms.

Independent inspections are one possible solution. The UN's Nelson Mandela Rules call for regular internal inspections and external monitoring by bodies independent of prison administrations.

Greater transparency over inmate accommodation, transfers, medical treatment and disciplinary decisions would also make preferential treatment harder to conceal.

Reducing overcrowding, improving staff training and protecting whistleblowers could further limit opportunities for corruption.

But CDS researcher Maulana believes meaningful reform requires a more fundamental change in how criminal justice systems operate.

Philippines' largest prison holds mass burial for inmates To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"The current system primarily treats imprisonment as the main form of punishment, leading law enforcement to frequently resort to incarceration for all types of legal violations," which leads to overcrowding and creates opportunities for corruption.

"It is essential to intensify efforts to implement non-custodial penalties and alternatives to detention," Maulana said.

Although prison authorities cannot eliminate the social inequalities outside their walls, Ismail argued that Southeast Asian governments have previously shown a "considerable capacity" to respond to emergencies inside prisons.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, governments quickly contained outbreaks in detention facilities and prevented infections from spreading into the wider population. Yet such interventions rarely translate into lasting improvements in prisoners' living conditions.

Ismail described this as "selective state capacity," whereby "governments demonstrated considerable ability to act when prison outbreaks threatened public health beyond prison walls, yet failed to sustain comparable improvements in prisoners' everyday welfare."

A similar pattern emerges whenever luxury prison scandals attract public attention.

"Investigations are announced, officials may be suspended or dismissed, and new procedures introduced. All of these measures can be necessary and important, but they do not necessarily change the institutional arrangements that enabled preferential treatment," said Ismail.

"The danger is that prison systems become better at responding to scandals than preventing the conditions that allow them to recur."

Edited by: Karl Sexton

World.title: Trump's diesel deal with Russia is unlikely to significantly lower global fuel prices despite expectations of rapid relief
World.content:
As the world's largest diesel exporter, the US benefits from high prices. At home, however, consumers are feeling the strain of rising living costs. Why Donald Trump's deal with Russia is unlikely to change that.

With or without a deal with Russia, diesel prices on global markets are unlikely to fall significantly anytime soon.

That is the assessment of experts interviewed by DW regarding the latest fuel-supply agreement between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

"The main reason for high diesel prices is the war in Iran and the simultaneous disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait," said Samina Sultan, a foreign trade expert at the German Economic Institute (IW) in Cologne.

The situation has led to production outages and made fuel shipments "more expensive, less secure and more difficult," she said.

Trump's deal with Russia also has an additional geopolitical dimension, Sultan said: "It causes the wars in Ukraine and Iran to become completely intertwined."

Wars reducing refinery output

Things are looking up, though. Roughly 13.5 million barrels of crude oil are once again flowing through the Strait of Hormuz a day, according to shipping and commodities analytics firm Kpler.

But for refined products such as diesel, volumes remain far lower at around 677,000 barrels per day, compared with 3.6 million barrels before the war.

Carsten Fritsch, a commodities analyst at Commerzbank, also attributes the price increases to the wars.

"If nothing changes in Ukraine and the Middle East, I see very few ways to resolve these supply bottlenecks," he said.

Trump expects prices to fall at record speed

In a social media post on October 9, Trump announced that he would temporarily suspend some sanctions on Russia and begin importing Russian diesel.

He wrote "diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" in a mix of lowercase and all caps.

Russia confirmed the arrangement. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state news agency TASS on October 13 that supplying diesel fuel was "in the interests of Russia, the United States and global energy markets."

Diesel prices in the US and many EU countries have risen sharply over the past 12 months.

According to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), prices in the US have climbed by about 60% and now stand at $6.30 per gallon, equivalent to $1.66 (or €1.49) per liter of diesel.

Diesel — Made in the USA

But even if Russia were able to flood global markets with cheap diesel, prices would not fall nearly as much as they recently rose, something all of the experts contacted by DW agree on.

Many refineries around the Gulf region have suffered disruptions or damage, while transporting fuel via shadow fleets and securing insurance remains costly, cumbersome and risky.

Another key shift is that Russia is no longer the world's largest diesel exporter. In fact, it is facing its own fuel shortages at home.

The US is now the world's biggest diesel exporter. In 2025, it exported an average of 1.26 million barrels of diesel per day, accounting for roughly 15.4% of global diesel exports.

At the same time, Russia fell to second place with a 9.5% share, and that was before major Ukrainian drone attacks on its refineries.

Debates over export restrictions continue

Besides the new US-Russia diesel agreement, Trump also recently floated the idea of US diesel export restrictions. But the idea was abandoned because it could lead to even higher diesel prices in the country, according to Samina Sultan.

"There simply is not enough diesel storage capacity in the United States," Sultan said. "Production would have to be reduced, and then prices would rise again."

Trump, Russia and Ukraine: Has the US changed sides again? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

If the US were to impose export restrictions on diesel, buyers in Latin America and the European Union would be hit particularly hard. Since Russia invaded Ukraine, EU countries have increasingly imported diesel from the US instead of Russia because of sanctions.

"An export ban merely redistributes the shortage; it does not solve it," said ING chief economist Carsten Brzeski.

"Global prices would continue to rise, while refineries would scale back production as margins shrink," he added.

Limited impact on US diesel demand

Export restrictions aside, few people consider that the US-Russia diesel deal will have any big impact.

According to calculations by the platform The World Data , the promised shipment of 2.2 million barrels of diesel from Russia would not even cover a single day's US diesel demand of roughly 4 million barrels.

Even if all of the diesel volumes announced by Trump were combined, totaling 35.8 million barrels, they would only cover about nine days of US domestic demand.

"I CANNOT OVERSTATE HOW MUCH OF A NOTHING BURGER THIS IS," Canadian oil market analyst Rory Johnston wrote in an all-caps post on X shortly after the announcement.

Russia would normally export almost 10 times that volume if its refinery fleet was not being targeted by Ukrainian drone attacks, he added.

Canada also supplies diesel to the United States. Roughly 80% of all US diesel imports come from its northern neighbor.

Given Trump's verbal attacks on Canada and the ongoing trade dispute, analysts view the prospect of Canada supplying significantly more diesel to the US as highly unlikely.

This piece was originally published in German.

10/14/2026 October 14, 2026 Nord Stream defendant's lawyers challenge war crime charge

Supporters of Ukraine gather ahead of the trial of Serhii Kuznietsov, a Ukrainian accused of involvement in the 2022 Nord Stream pipeline explosions Image: Markus Scholz/dpa/picture alliance

Lawyers for the Ukrainian man accused of organizing the Nord Stream pipeline attack have challenged the evidence and the war crime charge as his trial opened in Hamburg.

Serhii Kuznietsov, a 50-year-old former Ukrainian special forces officer, is accused of planning and supervising the September 2022 sabotage. Prosecutors say the attack targeted civilian infrastructure using prohibited methods of warfare.

Defense lawyer Jes Meyer-Lohkamp said there were no fingerprints, DNA traces or witness statements placing his client aboard the Andromeda, the yacht allegedly used in the operation.

Prosecutors allege Serhii Kuznietsov. boarded the vessel on the German island of Rügen with six accomplices: a skipper, an explosives expert and four divers. The group allegedly attached four explosive devices fitted with timers to the pipelines.

His lawyers argued that Russia used the pipelines as a weapon of economic pressure, making them a legitimate target. They also said Italy had approved his extradition on sabotage allegations, rather than a war crime charge, and sought dismissal of the case.

The defense sought to have the case dismissed, also arguing that military secrecy obligations prevented Serhii K. from discussing potentially exonerating evidence, even with his lawyers.

The explosions ruptured three of the system's four pipelines near Denmark's Bornholm island. Russia had already halted supplies through Nord Stream 1, while Nord Stream 2 had never entered service.
