A potential ban would therefore cause some financial losses, but the company does not expect serious damage.

Margvelashvili also notes that the company exports to markets with strict quality standards, while the Russian side has provided no detailed information about any specific violations.

Energy dependence: a more powerful lever than wine

Roman Gotsiridze, an opposition politician and former head of Georgia’s National Bank, has highlighted natural gas imports in the context of the current developments.

According to figures he cited, Russia accounted for 1.7% of Georgia’s natural gas consumption in 2018. That share rose to 20% in 2023 and 25% in 2024. Estimates put it at around 28% in 2025.

Gotsiridze believes this growing dependence gives Russia an additional lever for economic pressure.

Unlike wine exports, natural gas supplies directly affect energy security, industrial operations and people’s everyday needs.

Gotsiridze has therefore warned the government about possible scenarios involving more severe pressure from Russia.

Could Russia expand the embargo?

Mamuka Pipia, leader of the openly pro-Russian party Solidarity for Peace, says the ban on Georgian beverages represents only the first wave of restrictions.

In his view, further measures will target other companies and product categories.

His prediction deserves particular attention because Pipia represents a political force that takes a favourable view of Russia.

Teona Akubardia also points to an earlier statement by Pipia. She notes that he mentioned a list of Georgian companies accused of supporting anti-Russian activity as early as June.

If such a list did exist, it would be important to establish whether the companies named on it overlap with those now facing restrictions.

Georgian experts also consider it possible that Russia will expand its measures.

Gia Khukhashvili believes Moscow could use new restrictions to pressure Georgian businesses into exercising political caution. Giorgi Rukhadze suggests that the initial decision may be intended to demonstrate Russia’s capacity to exert economic pressure.

These assessments point to several possible scenarios. The restrictions could remain limited to the seven companies and be lifted following negotiations. They could spread to other producers. Alternatively, Russia could make the use of trade restrictions a permanent instrument of pressure.

How is Georgian Dream responding, and has its strategy worked?

The Georgian government insists that maintaining economic ties with Russia serves the country’s interests and that businesses should not give up profitable markets for political reasons.

Georgian Dream also argues that other countries have economic leverage over Georgia.

Commenting on Russia’s latest restrictions, parliamentary speaker Shalva Papuashvili also raised the risks associated with trade relations with the European Union. He pointed to issues involving sanctions, tariffs and the port of Kulevi.

The Georgian Dream government justified its decision not to join international sanctions against Russia by arguing that it needed to protect the Georgian economy. Kobakhidze described the decision as correct and pragmatic.

However, Georgian Dream’s opponents ask what additional security Georgia has gained by maintaining economic ties with Russia.

The restrictions introduced on 9 October have shown that economic relations with Russia do not guarantee Georgian companies unrestricted access to the Russian market. Moscow continues to demand the establishment of so-called state borders with the occupied regions. At the same time, Russia’s sanitary watchdog has restricted imports of products from Georgian companies.

Opposition politician Shalva Kereselidze, a member of the For Georgia party founded by Giorgi Gakharia, links the situation to Georgian Dream’s foreign policy. He argues that the government has damaged relations with the European Union while failing to protect Georgia’s economic and political interests in its dealings with Russia.

“Do not think that the more you concede to Russia, the more favourably it will view you or the sooner it will take your interests into account. No — the outcome will be even worse,” he said.

World.title: Man who killed Russian tourist in Abkhazia could face life sentence but serve just eight years
World.content:
Abkhazia: sentence in Russian tourist’s murder case

The man accused of murdering Amina Bikbova, a Russian tourist in Abkhazia, will not be treated as a repeat offender, despite having previously been convicted of a serious sexual assault. The reason is that Edgar Abukhba was a minor at the time. Said Gezerdava, a lawyer and member of the NGO Centre for Humanitarian Programmes, told Caucasian Knot.

It remains unclear what sentence the court will impose.

“Part one of Article 99 of Abkhazia’s Criminal Code, which covers murder, provides for a maximum sentence of 12 years in a high-security prison. Part two is significantly harsher: it provides for a prison term of between eight and 15 years, life imprisonment or the death penalty.

“However, there is a complication when it comes to calculating prison terms. On paper, the sentence could be 12 or 15 years. But under Abkhazia’s system for calculating prison terms, he may serve only eight years,” Said Gezer­dava said.

The lawyer added, however, that judges he had spoken to said the court would have information about the previous crime and would take it into account when determining the sentence.

The 26-year-old woman from Orenburg, Russia, was on holiday in the Abkhazian city of Gagra, where she met Edgar Abukhba, a 25-year-old local fruit seller. They exchanged messages on their phones for a couple of days. Then, on 24 September, Abukhba invited her for coffee, according to Amina’s friend. No one has seen her since, and she stopped contacting her family. Concerned about their daughter’s disappearance, her parents contacted Abkhazia’s Interior Ministry. A day later, the ministry announced that police had arrested a suspect in the Russian tourist’s murder. The suspect was Edgar Abukhba. On 27 September, reports emerged that Abukhba had been detained on suspicion of murdering Amina Bikbova, a 26-year-old tourist from Russia’s Orenburg region who had not contacted her family for three days. According to investigators, Abukhba confessed to killing her. On 29 September, a court in Gagra ordered him to be held in custody.

In July 2019, Abukhba committed a crime against another Russian tourist. He raped and brutally beat her, leaving her incapacitated. He also stole her phone, money and jewellery. In 2021, a court sentenced him to nine years in prison, but he was released as early as February 2024.

Abukhba has been charged with intentional murder. On 7 October, reports emerged that the case had been transferred from the district prosecutor’s office to the Investigative Department of Abkhazia’s Prosecutor General’s Office.

Amina Bikbova’s father told Caucasian Knot that the Abkhazian authorities had helped the family transport Amina’s body. They buried her on 2 October. According to her father, the authorities in Russia’s Orenburg region provided no assistance.

Conflicts involving tourists have occurred repeatedly in Abkhazia. The most recent incident to come to light took place on 26 August near Lake Ritsa, where tourists clashed with local residents. According to Abkhazia’s Interior Ministry, two tourists suffered soft-tissue injuries and concussions, while police took three Abkhazian residents to a police station.

On 2 August, a woman from Cherkessk who was visiting Abkhazia on holiday was attacked in Sukhumi. She was taken to hospital with a concussion and other injuries.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Georgia to raise pensions for under-70s by 45 lari instead of 20
World.content:
Pension increase in Georgia

From 1 January 2027, the Georgian government will increase pensions for people under 70 by 45 lari instead of the planned 20 lari. Their monthly pension will therefore rise to 415 lari (around $160). Meanwhile, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze argues that setting a minister’s salary below 12,000 lari encourages officials to engage in corruption.

As of August 2026, 905,000 people in Georgia received an old-age pension. Of these, 420,000 were under 70, while 485,000 were aged 70 or older. The initial draft budget for 2027 allocated up to 5.6bn lari (around $2.16bn) for pensions. The announced change will increase this amount by 128m lari (around $49.4m), bringing the total to 5.7bn lari. Under the law, an ordinary member of parliament’s salary, before tax, should rise by 1,080 lari, from 12,800 to 13,880 lari (around $5,359). The Georgian Dream party may decide not to implement this increase.

Kobakhidze said the indexation mechanism under current legislation would have increased pensions by just 20 lari. However, the government decided to raise payments further. The change does not apply to pensioners living in mountainous settlements, where different rules govern pension supplements.

Implementing the decision announced today will require an additional 128m lari in state budget spending.

What did Irakli Kobakhidze say?

According to the prime minister, social spending accounts for more than 33% of the state budget. Available figures show that the government allocated more than 5bn lari for old-age pensions in 2026, while 540m lari went towards co-financing the funded pension system. For comparison, Kobakhidze noted that pension spending totalled 1.065bn lari in 2012.

Kobakhidze said further increases in social spending carry fiscal and macroeconomic risks. He stressed that social spending had already reached the upper limit recommended by international financial institutions. Exceeding that threshold, he warned, could slow economic growth, fuel inflation and undermine Georgia’s access to international financing.

Nevertheless, he promised that the Georgian Dream government would continue looking for ways to increase pensions for people under 70 beyond the statutory indexation rate in the coming years. He added, however, that any increase must remain within acceptable budgetary limits.

Alongside the pension announcement, Kobakhidze addressed public sector pay, linking low ministerial salaries to potential corruption risks.

“Paying a minister less than 12,000 lari means pushing them towards corruption,” he said, explaining that new figures put a minister’s take-home salary at around 12,000 lari.

Kobakhidze argued that a private sector role with comparable responsibilities and workload could pay between 50,000 and 100,000 lari a month. He rejected the suggestion that 12,000 lari was a high salary for a minister.

“Given the work a minister does and the responsibilities they bear, they would earn at least 50,000–100,000 lari in a comparable private sector role. Yet we are expected to accept that 12,000 lari is a high salary for a minister. Is that reasonable? Is it really that high?” Kobakhidze said.

He noted that ensuring public officials receive decent salaries forms part of the government’s anti-corruption policy. In this context, he recalled the previous government’s time in office, saying that Bidzina Ivanishvili, the founder of Georgian Dream, had used his own money to pay salary supplements to public servants. Kobakhidze presented this practice as a measure to combat corruption.

How much will the pension increase cost Georgia’s budget?

Paata Kvizhinadze, chairman of the parliamentary Finance and Budget Committee, said that raising an MP’s salary by 1,080 lari would cost the state budget 1–1.3 million lari. By contrast, increasing the old-age pension by just 1 lari would require 11 million lari.

“MPs’ salaries are not set to increase under the initial draft budget. Even if the increase had been included, it would have added only slightly more than a million lari to budget expenditure — around 1.3 million lari. Meanwhile, raising pensions by 10 lari requires 111 million lari, while an increase of just 1 lari costs 11 million lari. Therefore, we should not link MPs’ salary increases to pension increases,” Kvizhinadze said.

Highlighting the historical ties between Azerbaijan and Vietnam, Vo Thi Anh Xuan said that the adoption of a Joint Statement on the establishment of a strategic partnership during To Lam’s visit to Azerbaijan had played an important role in elevating bilateral relations to a new level.

World.title: Russell Brand a 'ruthless, calculated sexual predator', court hears
World.content:
A "ruthless, calculated and manipulative sexual predator". That is how the Crown Prosecutor has described British entertainer Russell Brand in her opening address at his trial for multiple sex offences on Wednesday.

For almost two decades, Brand was a stand-up comedian, popular TV and radio presenter, and eventually, a Hollywood movie star.

The 51-year-old is now in the dock at London's Southwark Crown Court, accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault, and one count of indecent assault relating to six women over a 10-year period from 1999. He has pleaded not guilty to all seven charges.

Barrister Riel Karmy-Jones KC spent about two hours laying out the prosecution's case against the world-famous defendant on Wednesday morning, local time.

She told the court the women who will give evidence during the trial "did not know each other, have never met each other, and came forward independently of each other".

"Their paths all crossed the defendant's either through their employment, social events through work, or through attending gigs where he was performing," she said.

Ms Karmy-Jones told the jury of eight men and four women that each of the alleged victims' experiences occurred when Brand's career "was beginning to flourish".

She told the court Brand had met the women in different settings; one at a political conference, three in various media-industry settings (including radio stations), one at a London bar and one in the foyer of a venue where he was performing.

"Offending took place in a number of locations: a hotel room, workplaces, a toilet cubicle, in a bar, and at his home address," Ms Karmy-Jones told the court.

"Some of the women involved protested and said no, others had no opportunity to protest, but it mattered not to the defendant.

"Regardless of who they were and what they said or did, Russell Brand was not deterred. His desire, his strong desire, for some form of sexual contact was indiscriminate and voracious."

Russell Brand and his wife Laura Gallacher make their way past the cameras on Wednesday. (Reuters: Corey Rudy)

The Crown Prosecutor told the jury graphic details of the alleged sexual assaults the "demanding" and "entitled" Brand had inflicted on women who were left feeling "stupid" and "ashamed".

"To the defendant, women were simply a means to an end," Ms Karmy-Jones told the court, pointing out Brand was a much-younger man at the time of his alleged crimes.

"Over the years he may have changed both physically and as a person, however, despite that passage of time, his responsibility for wrongs done, and crimes committed at a younger age remain," she told the court.

The court heard Brand had declined to answer questions when police interviewed him about the allegations, but did provide written statements.

In these statements, Ms Karmy-Jones told the court, Brand claimed he did not remember the alleged incidents, had never engaged in non-consensual sexual activity, and that his accusers' accounts may have been "re-imagined".

The first prosecution witness called was Mark Pinheiro, who performed with Brand in cabaret shows on the sidelines of the 1999 Labour Party Conference, at which the first alleged victim claims she was raped.

Pinheiro told the court that in the car on the way from London to Bournemouth — where the conference was held — Brand had said "he hoped one day he would have slept with 5,000 girls".

Pinheiro also told the court several months after the conference, Brand told him he had sex with a woman while they were in Bournemouth and that "things got a little bit heated and a little bit out of hand".

During cross examination, Brand's barrister Ian Winter KC challenged Pinhero's evidence as inconsistent.

The trial before Mr Justice Joel Bennathan is expected to run for at least six weeks. Mr Brand's barrister Ian Winter KC will have the chance to set out the defence case later in the trial, which is the subject of significant global interest.

During proceedings Brand sat up straight in the dock and listened intently to what was being said.

Earlier, as he arrived for his trial with is wife Laura Gallacher, Brand told reporters he felt "blessed".

"I feel, of course, concerned but hopeful that this process will lead to good outcomes for everybody involved, that's my prayer," Brand said outside Southwark Crown Court.

The trial continues.

World.title: Zelenskyy says partners not warning Ukraine of incoming ballistic missiles
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he received no early warning from international partners about incoming Russian ballistic missile strikes on civilian infrastructure in Kyiv.

Russian forces struck the Ukrainian capital with ballistic missiles on Tuesday, killing two people in a high-rise apartment, then hitting a critical thermal power plant in the second attack in 24 hours.

"Once again, no advance warning from our partners. The main target was energy infrastructure, specifically thermal plant No. 4," Mr Zelenskyy said in a post on Telegram.

Mr Zelenskyy said it was unfair that Kyiv was enduring attacks without warnings from partners.

"According to our intelligence, the Russians are preparing further ballistic missile launches.

"The facts show that the Russians do not consider themselves bound to abide by what the president of the United States said," he added, referring to US President Donald Trump's announcement of an energy ceasefire at the weekend.

"And it is certainly unfair that they are destroying our energy infrastructure while Ukraine is not even receiving warnings about ballistic missile launches."

Kyiv relies heavily on US intelligence for early warnings of missile strikes.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy (left) said it was unfair for Ukraine to operate without warning of strikes from its partners. (Supplied: Ukrainian Presidential Press Service)

Mr Zelenskyy had earlier said Ukraine had again received no warning from Western partners before a previous overnight attack on the capital.

Mr Trump said Washington was still sharing intelligence, even as he pressured Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian refineries.

Reuters and other media have reported that US officials have threatened to cut off intelligence sharing and weapons sales to Ukraine unless it stops attacking Russian refineries.

Starlink limited in Ukraine

On Wednesday, Ukrainian officials confirmed SpaceX had introduced a limit on some Starlink services in Ukraine, disrupting combat drone missions that rely on the technology.

The satellite internet terminals from Elon Musk's company are crucial in guiding Ukraine's longer-range drone strikes in occupied southern and eastern Ukraine, which have assisted in disrupting Russian logistics.

"Our defence forces did not receive a warning about this limitation, and this led to the disruption of several missions," presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram.

Beskrestnov said SpaceX had stopped the operation of its military-grade version above 100 miles per hour (160 km/h).

Ukraine's 7th Rapid Reaction Corps, deployed in the south-east, said units had been forced to cancel some missions.

"According to our observations, during flights, the connection could drop for 10-20 seconds at speeds of just 110-120 km/h. The drones kept moving, but these interruptions made them harder to control," the Rapid Reaction Corps said in a statement.

SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside regular US business hours.

Although it was not immediately clear why Starlink's service was throttled, the move comes as Washington pressures Kyiv to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries.

Starlink does not work inside Russia, and the Ukrainian drones hitting Russia's oil industry use other means of communication.

Two killed in struck apartment

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the strike on a nine-storey building had killed two people and injured 21. Sixteen people were being treated in hospital, and four were in serious condition.

Emergency crews were battling fires in apartments throughout the building, and residents were being evacuated.

Russia ignoring 'energy ceasefire': Zelenskyy The Ukrainian president says if Moscow wants Kyiv to stop targeting Russian oil refineries, as demanded by Donald Trump, then it should stop hitting key infrastructure.

Ukrainian authorities confirmed on Wednesday morning that the hours-long missile and drone attack that unfolded overnight, primarily targeting Kyiv and Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city, had damaged 30 energy facilities.

At least 600,000 people were left without power, according to Mr Zelenskyy.

Unconfirmed energy ceasefire

Mr Trump, who lifted sanctions on Russian diesel last week in a bid to lower politically sensitive fuel prices, has said that both sides agreed to halt strikes on energy infrastructure.

Neither Moscow nor Kyiv confirmed this.

Vladimir Putin did not confirm whether the energy ceasefire had been agreed upon. (AP: Dmitri Lovetsky)

"The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States," Mr Zelenskyy wrote on X.

"Russia does not consider the American president's statements strong."

Russia's defence ministry said on Wednesday it had struck four power plants in and around Kyiv and two in Kharkiv, among other targets.

Reuters

World.title: Cracking firetrucks, $1b funding shortfall identified in Victorian audit
World.content:
Victoria's auditor-general has found more than $1 billion in extra investment is needed to provide critical upgrades to the state's fleet of aging fire trucks.

A report released by the auditor-general on Wednesday examined whether the fleet of more than 3,000 fire trucks were fit to meet the state's firefighting needs.

The audit found almost 60 per cent of Country Fire Authority (CFA) and Fire Rescue Victoria (FRV) trucks were more than 15 years old, despite FRV internal documents recommending fire trucks be replaced at that age.

Auditor-General Andrew Greaves found $1.5 billion in investment was needed between 2024-25 and 2033-34 to maintain and replace the trucks that make up the multi-agency firefighting fleet.

He found only $390.4 million — about a quarter of what was needed — had been allocated in grant and budget funds so far, an investment shortfall of more than $1 billion.

"It clearly shows that we have more work to do," Premier Ben Carroll said.

Cracking issue put crews 'at direct risk'

A recent Labor election promise to deliver 150 new fire trucks by 2030 was not considered in the audit, but United Firefighter Union boss Peter Marshall said that offer was only a fraction of what was needed.

He said the report demonstrated what firefighters had been saying for a long time.

"Those persons responsible for the budget cutting, the cost cutting, allowing firefighters to use equipment that was just not suitable and dangerous, they should be made accountable," Mr Marshall said.

The audit also found a widespread cracking issue among trucks managed by the Department of Energy, Environment and Climate Action (DEECA) had "put firefighters at direct risk".

The cracking problem became so widespread DEECA had to suspend more 54 per cent of its own fleet — nearly 350 trucks — ahead of the 2025-26 summer.

The audit found DEECA, the lead agency for bushfire prevention on public land and state forests, continued to use fire trucks with known cracks and also operated trucks over safe weight limits.

Treasurer knocked back funding requests

Former state treasurer Jaclyn Symes was forced to defend her record after the report pointed out that the FRV and CFA shrunk recent funding requests in response to the treasurer's instructions to limit asks in line with the government’s fiscal strategy.

The audit said FRV initially requested almost $160 million in fleet capital in 2024-25, which it found would have covered just over half of the investment required.

FRV's actual funding proposal was reduced to just $14 million, less than five per cent of what the audit calculated was needed.

Ms Symes said fiscal responsibility was necessary and that there was no "special treatment" for some organisations in need of state funding.

"[All government agencies] are asked to make sure that they bid for what they need, not necessarily everything that they want, because it's difficult decisions that need to be made," she said.

CFA fire trucks and volunteers fight fires in regional Victoria as well some outer-suburban growth areas. (ABC News: Kate Ashton)

Opposition Leader Jess Wilson said the restrictions on Victorian fire services was proof the current government had "not managed the finances."

But Emergency Services Shadow Minister Danny O'Brien acknowledged the investment required was "a very big figure".

Mr O'Brien did not say if a Liberal-National government could commit to reaching the $1.5 billion investment the auditor said was needed, but said the opposition would have further announcements on this topic soon.

"We have been working on this for sometime, to trying to work out how we can afford to modernise our firefighting fleet," he said.

World.title: Michelin Guide dishes out first Australian stars to array of SA restaurants
World.content:
A spread of South Australian restaurants has achieved distinguished culinary honours by becoming the first venues in the nation to receive stars from world-renowned guide Michelin.

At a glitzy, red-carpet ceremony at the Adelaide Convention Centre on Wednesday evening, Michelin dished out one-star ratings to 10 SA eateries.

It also delivered a single, coveted two-star rating to Magill Estate Restaurant, which overlooks Penfolds Magill Estate.

The one-star winners are Anvers Restaurant, Maxwell Restaurant, Botanic, Arkhé, Esmay, Aurora at ILA, Hentley Farm, LVN Restaurant at Bird In Hand, Aptos and Skillogalee Barrel House.

"Tonight marks an historic milestone — the first time the Michelin Guide has recognised restaurants in Australia," Michelin Guide international director Gwendal Poullennec said.

"To every restaurant recognised tonight — congratulations.

"They are all putting South Australia on the world culinary map."

World-renowned Michelin Guide stars have been distributed to SA restaurants. (Reuters: Christian Hartmann)

The winners come from across some of South Australia's premium produce districts, including McLaren Vale, the Adelaide Hills and the Barossa Valley.

Magill Estate Restaurant chef Scott Huggins could barely contain his delight, saying it was a "dream that's come true".

"We looked at opening restaurants in France to achieve a Michelin star — that's how crazy it can be," he said.

"It's come to South Australia, so extremely lucky and honoured to be the first restaurant in Australia to achieve two stars.

" It's like buying a lottery ticket — just not knowing until the number's been read out how it's going to land. "

The Michelin Man at the Adelaide Convention Centre. (ABC News)

Dozens of other venues and individual chefs were recognised in various ways, with Shobosho chef Shakaan Abillion winning the inaugural young chef award.

"We now have 77 different venues being recognised by Michelin," SA Premier Peter Malinauskas said.

Esmay chef Alanna Sapwell said the honour of a star rating would fill her colleagues with pride.

"I just walked out and my whole team's just in tears, and I think I was just a little bit in shock before," she said.

"I would really love to see this spread throughout Australia because it should be inclusive."

Esmay chef Alanna Sapwell hopes the recognition spreads across the industry nationally. (ABC News)

Aptos chef Justin James, who hails from the US, likened the achievement to the Super Bowl and the Oscars, while Jake Kellie from Arkhé said SA was currently the envy of the national culinary scene.

"I was very fortunate [to be] in Sydney last night speaking with a lot of industry folk, and they're all very jealous that we've got this amazing opportunity to put South Australia on the world map," he said.

'This is life-changing'

The awards have been hyped for their potential to lure international tourists to South Australia.

The awards ceremony represents the first time Michelin has rated Australian restaurants in its guide, after entering a commercial agreement with the SA government.

The government said the price it paid was confidential for commercial reasons.

Mr Malinauskas said the recognition bestowed by the awards was "worth its weight in gold" and described the ceremony as a "special night for the hospitality industry" in Australia.

"Every restaurant represented here tonight, every chef, should be brimming with pride."

Australian food advocate Mandy Hall says the awards are "life-changing". (ABC News)

Earlier in the night, Australian food industry advocate Mandy Hall said achieving a Michelin star was "life-changing — there's no question".

"We already have global recognition — but to actually have the Michelin stamp and that star next to your name is amazing," she said.

"These people decide very early on in their life that they want to dedicate their life to this career — and when I say 'dedicate', they really do; they give it everything, they have relationships with all their producers, so this is life-changing."

World.title: India's 'cockroach' movement leaders detained for five days
World.content:
Two leaders of India's "cockroach" youth movement will serve five days in jail after being detained during a protest.

Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das were among a dozen people detained by police on Tuesday after they climbed over barricades to enter a historic site popular for protests in New Delhi.

Police said this week that the site, Jantar Mantar, was no longer an official protest venue and accused Das and Ranka of trespassing.

The arrests follow a sweeping police crackdown over the weekend aimed at preventing mostly young Indians from gathering to demand the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

The Cockroach Janta Party is demanding the resignation of the chief election commissioner. (AP: Manish Swarup)

Police briefly detained thousands of demonstrators.

"Jantar Mantar belongs to the people of India. We will reclaim it," opposition leader Rahul Gandhi wrote on X.

Protests intensify

Protests have intensified over an ongoing nationwide revision of voter lists that has removed more than 130 million names since last year.

India releases 'cockroach' leaders as movement calls for more protests In a social media post after his release, the founder of the movement said PM Narendra Modi was "an embarrassment to India."

Critics say the exercise is politically motivated and could disenfranchise millions of eligible voters.

The Election Commission and Prime Minister Narendra Modi's administration say the revision is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries.

Abhijeet Dipke, the "cockroach" movement's founder, criticised Modi in a post on X.

"If you're so determined to crush dissent, have the courage to officially declare an Emergency instead of hiding behind these cowardly tactics," he wrote.

The "cockroach" movement began as an online satirical campaign this summer after India's chief justice compared unemployed young people to parasites.

Many young Indians embraced the remark, adopting the cockroach as a symbol of resilience.

Protests led by the group forced the resignation of Modi's education minister in July, a rare setback for the prime minister, who has been in power for more than 12 years.

AP

World.title: The boldness Australia needs has no political home right now
World.content:
This year's Boyer Lecture series explores the opportunities and challenges of Australia's engagement with Asia in the 21st century. Keynote speaker Sam Roggeveen, director of the Lowy Institute's International Security Program, gave his lecture Four Forces: Australia in the New Asia this evening. This is an edited extract.

The biggest change to Australia's region since World War II is underway. Three forces are reshaping Asia and Australia's place in it: the decline of one empire, the rise of another, and the emergence of a powerful neighbour on Australia's doorstep.

Amid this regional shift, a fourth potent force is at play: an unmistakeable change in the character of Western liberal democracy, including in Australia.

These four forces present a challenge not just to our place in the world, but to our politics and identity; we are a Western nation perched alongside Asia as it enters a post-Western era.

We can't stop these international forces, but we have a choice to make about how we meet the challenge, a choice about whether we leave our fate in the hands of others or take the harder road towards self-reliance.

The 'material dethroning of the West'

It doesn't take much persuading these days to convince Australians that China is an important part of their future, because it is already so conspicuous in our daily lives. It is a major source of immigrants, students and consumer products, our largest trading partner, and it is credited with keeping Australia out of recession during the global financial crisis.

There is no mistaking the change in character of Western liberal democracy, Sam Roggeveen says. (Supplied)

But what China means to Australia is a fraction of what it means to the world. China is the largest trading partner to around 120 other countries, too. Roughly a third of all the physical objects produced in the world today are made in China. Its economy is now at least four-fifths the size of America's and may even be the largest in the world, depending on how you measure.

For the economic historian Adam Tooze, China's rise represents nothing less than "the material dethroning of the West as the central driver of world history".

Until not so long ago, China's economic rise was only good news. It was lifting hundreds of millions of its own people out of poverty, producing cheap goods for the world, and creating wealthy consumers for our goods and services. But China's rise was always going to create problems, including for our ally, the United States.

When the Cold War ended, the US became Asia's uncontested leader. The hope, at the time, was that China would simply go along with that arrangement. The plan in Washington was that even as China became richer, it would remain subordinate to the US. China would become something like Japan or Germany — economic powerhouses with no big independent foreign policy ambitions.

Clearly, that's not how things are turning out. China is building the world's biggest navy and quadrupling the size of its nuclear arsenal. It punishes American allies, including Australia, by imposing trade restrictions. Its behaviour in the South China Sea, where it has built artificial islands based on dubious legal claims, can be fairly described as territorial expansion. China is clearly not going to become a super-sized version of Germany or Japan.

We should assume China wants to lead in the region, and that means subordinating the US and its allies, and even pushing Washington out of Asia altogether. That's not because China is communist or because it's a dictatorship. It is those things, and that makes China harder to deal with. But this is a simple question of scale. China is big and big countries demand leadership.

Now, nothing up to this point would perturb any mainstream foreign policy commentator. But here's where I swerve off the beaten path. Because the consensus in Australia is that, whatever challenge China presents to us, the Americans will help us face it. In fact, our entire national defence is built upon this premise.

No previous US president could have prevented China's ascent, and no future US president is going to enter a competition with China that could lead to war. (Reuters: Kylie Cooper)

The US is weaker in Asia

China's rise has made America's position in Asia unsustainably weak. It used to be easy for America to make lavish promises to defend its partners and allies in Asia because no other country was strong enough to challenge it. That's not true anymore. It would now be incredibly costly for the US to meet the commitments it has made.

It is still assumed, on the Korean Peninsula and in Taiwan, and even in Japan and Australia, that the US will be willing to risk the lives of thousands of its troops, and perhaps even nuclear attacks on its own cities, to defend us. But the US simply has no vital reason to accept such risks. The sacrifice would not be worth it.

Now, it's important to stress: saying that America's position in Asia is weak is not the same as saying that America itself is weak. In fact, the United States has a reasonable claim to being the strongest and most secure nation in the history of the world. But that's part of our problem.

America has the world's biggest military, a huge economy, thousands of nuclear weapons, and is separated from China by a vast ocean. It is so secure that it simply doesn't need to be Asia's leader. It's nice to have, but not essential. So, when a challenger as big as China comes along, we should not assume that the US will bear the burden of resisting it.

If this is jarring, it's because it has happened relatively quickly. One of my predecessors as Boyer Lecturer, the distinguished Australian foreign policy thinker Owen Harries, titled his first address And Then There Was One, because in 2003 the US was the only superpower in the world. It's worth adding that Owen did not assume this would be a permanent condition.

You will note I haven't mentioned President Trump so far, who is so often the focus of our alliance concerns. And why not? He has threatened to annex Greenland, make Canada the 51st state, and throw Ukraine under the bus. Still, it's a mistake to focus on Trump because it invites us to believe that he was the cause of the power shift I am describing, and that things will return to something like "normal" after he leaves the world stage. They won't.

No previous US president could have prevented China's ascent, and no future US president is going to risk their nation's safety and prosperity by entering a competition with China that could lead to war.

So no, this is not a Trump phenomenon. It is a permanent shift.

The AUKUS deal came at exactly the moment when American reliability went into permanent decline.

AUKUS hits a jarring note

This is why AUKUS is such a jarring note in our national life. The agreement to supply Australia with eight nuclear-powered submarines, announced by the Morrison government in 2021 and now supported by the Albanese government, represents the biggest change to our alliance in its history. Yet it comes at exactly the moment when American reliability goes into permanent decline.

AUKUS is an illustration of one of the least attractive aspects of our national character: an insatiable desire to win the approval of Americans. Of course, the Americans sense this and they exploited it when we proposed AUKUS, which involves not just our biggest ever military purchase but billions of Australian dollars invested in US shipyards.

Listen to the Boyer Lecture Series on ABC listen Featuring distinguished speakers from across Australia, Singapore and Indonesia, this year's Boyer Lecture series explores the opportunities and challenges of Australia's engagement with Asia in the 21st century.

In the 1930s, America built the gambling mecca of Las Vegas, an entire city in the desert dedicated to fleecing gamblers. If AUKUS demonstrates anything, it is that the Americans still have a talent for separating fools from their money.

Australia should be sceptical of both China and America as one rises and the other declines. And from this dual scepticism flows an obvious conclusion: we must do more to look after ourselves.

Once we accept that our relationship with the US will become more transactional, the natural instinct will be to find a partner to replace it. But there is no replacement.

The sheer scale of the Asia Pacific counts against an alliance-like security partnership with Tokyo. Japan is pre-occupied with security threats far closer to home, and lacks the military capacity and ambition to be a significant power in our part of Asia.

What about India? It is in a slightly different category because of its size and still untapped potential — one day, it will likely surpass the US in GDP terms. But India is also too far away from Australia to be a close security partner. It is difficult to imagine that any security threat to Australia would ever be so vital to India that New Delhi would offer us help, and the same is true for Australia in its dealings with India.

There is one nation which, although it will never replace the US, does have vital interests that align with ours. It is close to Australia and has vast economic potential, enough to resist being pulled into China's orbit.

Today, Indonesia is South-East Asia's leader and soon its economy will surpass ours. (ABC News: Mitch Woolnough)

A great power on our doorstep

Indonesia matters to Australia because it is big and it is near.

Two hundred and ninety million people dispersed across an archipelago that covers Australia's northern approaches, and boasting consistent growth that will see it enter the top five economies in the world by the middle of the century.

Australia is about to have a great power on its doorstep.

For Australia's security, Indonesia ranks above every other nation. If we get this relationship wrong, the dangers are immense. Soon, Indonesia will be wealthy and strong, and we will not want it as an enemy.

We've had an antagonistic relationship with Jakarta before and even faced off against Indonesian troops in the so-called Konfrontasi of the early 1960s. But Indonesia was a poor country then, with little military power or influence on the regional stage. Today, Indonesia is South-East Asia's leader and soon its economy will surpass ours. From there, the gap will only widen.

For Australia, then, the stakes in the relationship continue to grow. The more powerful Indonesia becomes, the less we can afford a breach with Jakarta.

But if we get this relationship right, Indonesia offers a natural barrier against threats from third countries. And the good news is Canberra and Jakarta share one crucial interest: neither Australia nor Indonesia wants China to dominate our region. Right there is the kernel of a deeper partnership with Jakarta. It can be something like an alliance dedicated to ensuring that no outside power ever dominates the region we share.

Of course, that ambition remains distant and Jakarta may never be the partner we would like it to be. But with that vital interest in common, many barriers can be overcome, including the fact that Australia and Indonesia do not share what our politicians call "shared values".

If that sounds coldly transactional, then so be it. We Australians cherish our political traditions, but we've never insisted that our regional partners adopt our ways.

Only a 10th of Brits say Brexit has made their life better. (Reuters: Neil Hall)

Lessons from the UK

The United Kingdom is, like us, a liberal democracy and an island lying just off a powerful continent. Ten years ago, the UK comprehensively sabotaged its own economy and its relationship with its neighbours.

I don't need to dwell on the damage Brexit has done over the past decade: according to The Economist magazine, it has taken at least 2.5 per cent, or maybe as much as 8 per cent, off Britain's GDP. Only a tenth of Brits now say Brexit has made their life better.

Why did it happen? We're told it was about xenophobia and anti-European sentiment. Yet despite some truly ugly outbreaks of racial violence, Britain remains a fundamentally liberal and tolerant society. And don't forget, the defining message of the Brexit campaign was not about keeping foreigners out, it was about taking back control.

That slogan — take back control — is a clue to what's really going on, not just in the UK but in every Western democracy touched by the rise of right-wing populism, including ours. I think the lesson of Brexit is not that British voters were xenophobic, but that they distrusted their own elites.

In every Western democracy, the gap between voters and their political leaders has widened to a chasm because the connective tissue between voter and government has withered and decayed. That connective tissue is the political party.

The decline of the big centre-right and centre-left parties that dominated Western democratic politics in the second half of the 20th century is the signature political phenomenon of our time. Those parties represented well-defined constituencies. The centre-left clustered around unions and the working class. The centre-right around business, small and large, and the middle class. But every force that once tied big political parties to a defined constituency — unionism, manufacturing, religion, class and even race — has withered.

The effect on the big parties has been catastrophic. It was the weakening of the Conservative Party at the hands of its own Eurosceptics and Nigel Farrage's UKIP that triggered the Brexit referendum. Major parties have declined all over Europe too, creating openings for new political forces.

In Australia, the collective membership of the Labor and Liberal parties couldn't fill the MCG. At the 2007 federal election, 43 per cent of us put Labor first. By 2025, even though Labor won the election convincingly, that figure was 33 per cent. The trends are roughly the same for the Coalition. Our primary votes are now split an even three ways, with independents and small parties also getting roughly one third.

The result is that modern Australian governments achieve power whilst never really feeling that they are in charge.

If a government doesn't feel it has a mandate, it sets about trying to manufacture one. Perhaps you've noticed that the term "social licence" has crept into our political vocabulary — that's an implicit acknowledgement of the democratic deficit I'm describing.

Our governments launch endless enquiries and establish expert bodies to make decisions that were once considered to be within their own remit. These are all signs of governments desperately searching for new indicators of public approval and devising mechanisms to work around its absence. No truly confident government would feel the need.

The Howard government was the last under the old two-party settlement. Not coincidentally, that was also when Australia had its last major economic reform. If we have indeed become a timid nation, as Paul Keating argues, then I think this is why.

The missing piece is a sense of authority arising from democratic legitimacy. That's what instils courage and policy boldness in governments.

Our future without a powerful regional ally

For the first time in our history, we face a future without a powerful ally committed to regional supremacy.

We face a future in which Asia will be led by an Asian superpower, one that has interests and ambitions that clash with ours. And we face a future in which our close neighbour, Indonesia, will have greater national power than us. All of this in a political environment undergoing its biggest realignment since the creation of the Liberal Party in 1944.

The changes to our region demand not just a new defence strategy or a new foreign policy, but an ambitious national reform agenda dedicated to creating a truly self-reliant Australia.

Yet our domestic political malaise is frustrating our ability to meet the regional challenges. The major parties are exhausted and fragile; they lack the energy and authority to embark on such a journey. The last big wave of Australian reform, in the 1980s and 90s, was built on consensus between our major parties. If there is to be another wave of reform it will need to be built on the ashes of the two-party system.

Right now, the boldness Australia needs has no political home. The far right offers nostalgia for a wholly imagined monoculture. The left is pre-occupied with conservation and flirts with de-growth. The major parties offer technocratic tinkering. There is not a single political force in Australia today focused squarely on building Australia's wealth and strength.

The most telling evidence is that Labor, the Coalition and One Nation are now all, to one degree or another, retreating from immigration.

Loading

Immigration retreat also one from Asia

Given the temper of our immigration debate, perhaps the least popular argument one can make right now is for Australia to get bigger. But immigration is our national superpower, and we do multiculturalism better than any country on earth.

Although many factors go into producing a strong nation, sheer size is vital. When Singapore got rich in the 1970s, the world applauded. When China got rich in the 2000s, the world shook. The difference is scale.

Australia should recommit to immigration not because "diversity is strength", to use the prime minister's anodyne phrase, but because scale is strength. Retreating from immigration will make us materially weaker. It will also raise the drawbridge to talented and industrious Asians who want to make Australia home. It will cut us off from our region. A retreat from immigration is a retreat from Asia.

Yet our politicians now propose to take us to the precipice. If the political mood against immigration holds until the next election, voters will be invited to consign Australia to a shrunken, inward looking, future — our own version of the Brexit referendum.

But Australia can't afford to turn its back on Asia the way the UK turned its back on Europe. Creating the conditions for an Australia that stands strong and independent in Asia begins with a simple act of recognition: we must look after ourselves.

If that sounds confronting, then I would close by reminding you that Asia is a source of immense opportunity, as well as risk. Although we in the West are passing through a moment of profound cultural pessimism, in Asia the future is still a source of optimism. And no wonder — the people living in its gleaming new cities are, in some cases, only one generation removed from rural poverty.

Young Australians are travelling freely around the region and imbibing its culture. They see Tokyo's urbanism, China's cityscapes, Singapore's garden-city infrastructure. These cities evoke a sense of promise.

Australia should want to capture the spirit of progress that animates those places, to be a country where the future feels exciting and abundant, maybe even a little glamorous.

Let that sense of optimism guide Australia as we navigate the difficult choices ahead.

Sam Roggeveen's keynote lecture will be on ABC TV and iview at 3:25pm October 17 and iview. This lecture and others from Louisa Lim, Mari Pangestu and Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong will air on consecutive Sundays from October 18 on ABC Radio National's Sunday Extra program, at 8:05am.

World.title: Woman charged over crash that claimed life of 11yo girl
World.content:
A woman has been arrested over a two-car crash in which an 11-year-old girl was killed in Adelaide's south last month.

South Australia Police said the woman was driving a Nissan sedan in which the girl was a passenger when it was involved in a collision with a Subaru station wagon at Moana on September 22.

Emergency services were called to the scene on Commercial Road about 6:45pm.

The 35-year-old Christie Downs woman was taken to hospital in a serious condition, but the girl died at the scene.

The 37-year-old Seaford Meadows man who was driving the Subaru was also taken to hospital with minor injuries and was later discharged, police said.

Police said the driver of the Nissan was arrested today and was charged with aggravated causing death by dangerous driving and aggravated causing harm by dangerous driving.

The woman, who has lost her licence, was bailed to appear in the Christies Beach Magistrates Court in November.

Police said major crash investigators were continuing to examine the circumstances of the crash.

World.title: Shots fired in Tullamarine linked to road rage incident, police say
World.content:
Police are investigating reports of gunshots being fired in Melbourne's north-west in a confrontation investigators believe may be linked to an earlier road rage incident.

Emergency services were called to reports of a collision between two vehicles and gunshots in Tullamarine just after 3pm today.

No injuries have been reported.

Investigators believe the incident occurred after an earlier road rage incident involving the occupants of an Isuzu utility and a Hyundai SUV.

Police said the victims in the Isuzu made their way to Broadmeadows Police Station, while the alleged offenders ditched the Hyundai and fled in a getaway vehicle.

Police have established two crime scenes, one on May Street and one on Dawson Street.

Aerial footage shows the white Hyundai appears to have been crashed and abandoned, with detectives on the scene collecting evidence.

World.title: Contending, rebuilding or stuck in limbo: What AFL trade period says about your team’s flag hopes
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 Contending, rebuilding or stuck in limbo: What AFL trade period says about your team’s flag hopes Andrew Wu and Marc McGowan October 15, 2026 — 1:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

This year’s AFL trade period did not have as many blockbuster moves or as many cliffhanger deals to complete in the final day, but there was still plenty enough to maintain our interest. Among the players to switch teams were the league’s games record-holder, a dual Brownlow medallist, a seven-time club champion, one of the competition’s best on-ballers, an All-Australian defender, a No.1 draft pick, and a Coleman medallist. We graded every club’s performance through the free agency and trade period to find the best- and worst-performed in this year’s player movement window. Trade moves: (from left) Zak Butters, Zach Merrett and Nick Blakey. Photos: Jason South, Hawthorn Football Club, Nathan John/North Melbourne FC. Artwork: The Age Hawthorn



In: Zach Merrett (Ess/trade), Ben King (GC/free agency), Josh Goater (NM/trade), pick 107, R2 2027 (GC), R1 2028 (GC), R2 2028 (GC)

Out: Aidan Schubert and Sam Butler (GC/trade), Finn Maginness (WB/trade), Bodie Ryan (Mel/trade), picks 17 and 27, R1 2028 (Haw), R2 2028 (Haw)

Draft picks: 29, 37, 71, 94, 107, 112

Trade rating: 10/10 Are the Hawks closer to a flag after this trade period? You betcha. Adding King and Merrett to a team already overflowing with talent was a home run for the brown and gold, and Goater was worth the punt in a cheap-as-chips trade. Hawthorn rated Schubert highly, but he was a mile down the key-forward pecking order, while Butler and Maginness were also surplus to demands and Ryan had been delisted. Bringing in readymade talent is worth far more than picks to the Hawks, given where they are – and even then, they didn’t give much up – so this was a ragingly successful fortnight. Western Bulldogs In: Jordon Butts (Ade/free agency), Zak Butters (PA/free agency), Finn Maginness (Haw/trade), Hudson O’Keeffe (Carl/trade), picks 42, 53, 83, 89, R2 2027 (PA), R3 2027 (Mel), R4 2027 (PA), R2 2028 (PA), R3 2028 (PA), R3 2028 (GC), R4 2028 (Melb)

Out: Picks 14 and 33, R3 2027 (GC), R1 2028 (WB)

Draft picks: 42, 53, 55, 83, 89, 91, 109

Trade rating: 9.5/10 The Bulldogs could hardly be happier. They beat Geelong and others to secure Butters’ prized signature in a major coup, as well as adding fellow free agent Butts to shore up their defence and added O’Keeffe for ruck depth. They played ball in a five-club mega deal that was largely designed to appease Port Adelaide for losing Butters and avoid them matching their restricted free agency offer. Butters and Marcus Bontempelli instantly become arguably the best duo in the AFL, and they will spearhead the Dogs’ premiership assault. They also took a cheap flyer on ex-Hawk Maginness.



Geelong In: Toby Greene (GWS/free agency), Jordan Ridley (Ess/trade), Rowan Marshall (StK/trade), Pick 62, R3 2028 (StK), R4 2028 (Ess)

Out: Jack Bowes (Ess/trade), Pick 16, R1 2027, R2 2028

Draft picks: 36, 57, 62, 75, 93, 111

Trade grade: 8.5/10 The Cats have gone all-in to win a flag while they can still get decent footy from Patrick Dangerfield and Jeremy Cameron. They have strengthened every third of the field. Veteran match-winner Greene, who came for nothing, provides a star-studded forward line with even more firepower and can also add to their secondary midfield rotations. If they can get the best out of the injury-plagued Ridley, who turns 28 next week, they have a topline defender to bolster their intercept game. In Marshall, the Cats land a ruckman who can match the best rucks around the ground. The latter pair, though, have come at the cost of two firsts and a second, leaving the Cats without a pick until 36 in this year’s draft. They also ran out of picks to seriously get into the race for Nick Blakey – but with three high-class players to come into their best 23, the Cats should start next season one of the flag favourites. Rowan Marshall in the Cats’ famous hoops. AFL Photos Melbourne



In: Zane Duursma (NM/trade), Will McLachlan (BL/trade), Bodie Ryan (Haw/trade), Picks 4, 14, 48, 52, R2 2027 (BL), R2 2027 (WC), R4 2027 (WC), R2 2028 (WC)

Out: Trent Rivers and Jack Viney (WC/trade), picks 12, 49, 87, 107, R1 2027 (Mel), R2 2027 (Mel), R3 2027 (Mel), R2 2028 (Mel), R4 2028 (Mel)

Draft picks: 4, 14, 48, 52

Trade rating: 8.5/10 No club is better at accumulating draft picks and rising in the order than the Demons. Duursma was a bust at North Melbourne as the No.4 selection three years ago, but Melbourne present him with a second chance without the same risk (effectively pick 33). They also brought in Lions forward Will McLachlan for pick 45, which came in the deal that sent Viney and Rivers to West Coast. Melbourne encouraged ex-skipper Viney to explore his options after he fell behind younger midfield options. The Demons pulled another surprise when they traded pick 107 for delisted Hawks defender Ryan. He’s done it again: Melbourne list boss Tim Lamb. Getty Images Richmond In: Kieren Briggs (GWS/free agency), Nathan O’Driscoll (Frem/trade), pick 5

Out: Pick 63, R1 2027 (Rich), R2 2027 (Rich), R4 2027 (Rich)

Draft picks: 2, 5, 44, 99

Trade rating: 8.5/10



Take a bow, Blair Hartley. The Tigers’ shrewd list boss enjoyed an outstanding free agency and trade period. Ruckman Briggs filled a position of need and arrived for free, while wingman O’Driscoll cost them only pick 63. But they saved their best work for last in being the successful applicant for Port Adelaide’s No.5 pick, giving them two top-five choices. Richmond secured that coveted selection for a second-rounder this year, as well as first-, second- and fourth-round picks in the Tasmania-compromised 2027 draft. Factor in that Tassie have already pre-listed seven of the best players from that draft class, and this is terrific business from the Tigers. North Melbourne In: Nick Blakey (Syd/trade), picks 33, 49, R3 2027 (PA), R3 2028 (Syd)

Out: Zane Duursma (Mel/trade), Josh Goater (Haw/trade), picks 6, 47, R2 2027 (NM), R1 2028 (NM), R2 2028 (NM)

Draft picks: 33, 49, 66, 74, 84, 102

Trade rating: 8/10 The Kangaroos intended for contracted Crows key defender Nick Murray to be their No.1 target until Blakey suddenly became available. The ex-Swan delivered the type of recruiting coup that has eluded them for decades, but they certainly paid for it. Blakey joins on an eight-year deal worth up to $12 million, and will be expected to perform an integral role in North climbing the ladder. However, the failure to secure Murray from Adelaide is an obvious disappointment because the Roos still lack a reliable lockdown option for rival tall forwards. It was not for a lack of trying, but they ran out of assets and could not secure the top-20 pick the Crows demanded. Duursma and Goater left for worse returns than they were drafted. View post on X



Carlton In: Joel Amartey (Syd/free agency), Lachie Whitfield (GWS/trade), Picks 31, 50, R3 2028 (Coll), R4 2028 (PA)

Out: Hudson O’Keeffe (WB/trade), Flynn Riley (Coll/trade), Picks 25, 26, 2028 third-round pick

Draft picks: 13, 18, 31, 50, 61, 72, 90, 108

Trade grade: 8/10 After a busy and successful trade period last year, the Blues were again extremely active. They filled two of their three main list needs, landing key forward Amartey from Sydney to provide support for Harry McKay and bringing in veteran Whitfield from the Giants to add to their speed and ball use off half-back. Equally important, they achieved their gains with minimal loss of draft capital. Amartey came as a free agent, while Whitfield cost pick 25 and minor pick slides in the draft. Their ruck stocks need replenishing after the exits of O’Keeffe and Riley, though neither was in their best 30. The big question now surrounds how the Blues will acquire son of a gun Cody Walker, who would fulfil the third list aim of future-proofing their midfield. Their current picks of 13 and 18 can match a bid no earlier than three. Amartey, Whitfield and Walker will be strong additions to a team that bowed out in the elimination final. View post on X Collingwood



In: Lachie Neale (BL/free agency), Jesse Hogan (GWS/free agency), Flynn Riley (Carl/trade), pick 65

Out: Scott Pendlebury (GC/trade), Pick 77, R3 2028

Draft picks: 11, 30, 67, 68, 70, 88, 106

Trade grade: 7.5/10 The Pies don’t believe in rebuilding – and showed it at the trade table, landing a 33-year-old (Neale), a 31-year-old (Hogan) and almost a third veteran over 30 in Richmond’s Jayden Short. The Pies had an offer in front of Short, who was keen to become a Magpie, but could not meet the Tigers’ demands. It may prove a blessing in disguise for the Pies, who are already well stocked for half-back flankers and need more youth. Operating alongside Nick Daicos, Neale will significantly strengthen the Pies’ clearance game while also lowering their midfield age profile after Pendlebury’s departure. Hogan, with only 25 games in the past two seasons due to injuries, comes with risk, but his best is still top class – as he showed in the state game. Riley is a project ruck who, ideally for the club, will not be needed often at senior level. With two list spots available, the Pies may need to delist and redraft a youngster like Harry DeMattia or Tew Jiath to their rookie list. A solid exchange period for the Pies, who kept their first two picks while bolstering their best 23. St Kilda In: Sam Marshall (BL/trade), picks 16 and 41

Out: Rowan Marshall (Geel/trade), R1 2027 (StK), R3 2028 (StK)

Draft picks: 10, 16, 41, 51, 69, 87, 105

Trade rating: 7.5/10 The Saints were far quieter on the trade front than a year ago, but what they did was pretty good. They demanded a first-round selection from Geelong for Marshall – and that is exactly what they got despite the Cats’ initial reluctance. That said, the only reason Marshall wanted out for the second year in a row is because they spent oodles of money recruiting fellow ruckman Tom De Koning. St Kilda targeted and secured fringe Lion Marshall for their first-round selection next year, while also gaining Brisbane’s second-rounder this year. With his running capacity, Marshall should immediately become a senior regular under Ross Lyon.



Essendon In: Jack Bowes (Geel/trade), Keidean Coleman (BL/trade), Picks 17, 25, R1 2027 (Geel), R2 2028 (Haw), R2 2028 (Geel)

Out: Zach Merrett (Haw/trade), Jordan Ridley (Geel/trade), Picks 27, 62, R4 2028 (Ess)

Draft picks: 1, 17, 25, 80, 98

Trade grade: 7/10 The rebuilding Bombers stripped back their list even further by finally biting the bullet on club great Merrett and letting star defender Ridley leave for a fresh start – but it has given the Dons more picks to build their next successful era. They currently hold four picks in the first 27, not including the likely compensation pick at the start of the second round, and bolstered their future draft hand. Merrett leaves a huge hole in their midfield, but getting a future first for Ridley, who played just 26 games in his past three seasons, is good business, even if it will expose them to more short-term pain. The Bombers added experience through midfielder Bowes and Lions playmaker Coleman, both of whom will play in round one if fit. They had a crack at Gryan Miers and were disciplined not to part with a pick in the top 20, and wanted Nick Blakey but were never in the hunt. West Coast



In: Trent Rivers and Jack Viney (Mel/trade), R2 2028 (Mel)

Out: Pick 45, R2 2027 (WC), R4 2027 (WC), R2 2028 (WC)

Draft picks: 3, 23, 58, 64, 73, 82, 100

Trade rating: 7/10 The Rivers and Viney deal with the Demons went down to the wire, despite the Eagles not having much to do in this period. There was a lot of talk about West Coast’s pick 23 this year, but it did not feature in the final trade. They also picked up Melbourne’s 2028 second-rounder, while handing over pick 45, second-round selections the next two years and a 2027 fourth-rounder. The ex-Demons duo will slot straight into the senior side, with Viney adding valuable experience and leadership and Rivers a local product. Fremantle In: Pick 63

Out: Nathan O’Driscoll (Rich/trade)

Draft picks: 19, 40, 60, 63, 78, 96, 114

Trade grade: 6/10 The Dockers are hard to mark. After coming so close to an historic flag, their confidence in their list was reflected in their quiet trade period. Freo’s list boss David Walls did little but what he did was astute. Wingman O’Driscoll, who was not in the club’s grand final team, was traded for a late pick to Richmond. They filled his spot with a cheaper option, securing Dom Bedendo as a delisted free agent who can provide wing depth and play immediately if needed. They retain a full suite of picks in 2027 and 2028, and can add a decent player with their first-round selection.



Gold Coast In: Scott Pendlebury (Coll/trade), Aidan Schubert (Haw/trade), Sam Butler (Haw/trade), Pick 8, R3 2027 (GC), R1 2028 (Haw)

Out: Ben King (Haw/free agency), Pick 67, R2 2027, R1 2028, R2 2028

Draft picks: 8, 81, 85, 103

Trade grade: 6/10 This is not the trade period that Damien Hardwick thought he would have been sitting through after his second season at the helm. They salvaged something out of a bad situation by turning sharpshooter King into the promising but untested key forward Schubert, and Butler. Though King did not finish in the top-10 of the Suns’ best and fairest this year, their forward line is significantly weaker after his departure. Pendlebury will provide much-needed leadership on and off the field. Pick eight gives them a presence in a strong top end of the draft, but the Suns start 2027 further back than where they finished 2026. GWS



In: Picks 20, 26, 59, 77, R3 2028 (Carl)

Out: Toby Greene (Geel/free agency), Jesse Hogan (Coll/trade), Kieren Briggs (Rich/free agency), Lachie Whitfield (Carl/trade), Pick 31

Draft picks: 9, 20, 26, 59, 77, 86, 104

Trade grade: 6/10 Related Article AFL 2026 How side deals, mega bucks and a rare breakout of honest and rational negotiating ruled trade period The outs are concerning, but the Giants still have the talent to play finals next year. The departures of Greene and Whitfield all but mark the end of an era for the Giants, who did not let sentiment get in the way of doing business. They wanted to keep Greene but were pragmatic with two-time club champion Whitfield, who would arguably be on the podium for their greatest players. Whitfield would likely have become the expansion club’s first 300-gamer next year but the resetting Giants wanted to get more now than in 12 months’ time if he left as an unrestricted free agent. Greene’s departure leaves Stephen Coniglio as the sole foundation Giant remaining. They backed in the future with Max Gruzewski over 2024 Coleman medallist Hogan, and did not offer a contract to local product Briggs, a ruckman not suited to the new ruck rules. With picks nine and 20, they should have the points to secure academy prospect Ethan Matthews and end up with another pick in the early 20s. Brisbane Lions In: Picks 21, 27, 28, 45, R1 2027 (StK), R2 2027 (WB), R2 2027 (Mel)

Out: Lachie Neale (Coll/free agency), Sam Marshall (StK/trade), Will McLachlan (Mel/trade), Keidean Coleman (Ess, trade), Picks 20, 53, 59, R2 2027 (BL)

Draft picks: 21, 27, 28, 45, 79, 97, 115

Trade grade: 5.5/10



Equalisation did its thing with the Lions. Even if he did not have a big grand final, Neale is a big loss to their midfield, as seen by his third in the best and fairest. Marshall and McLachlan are younger types who left for more senior action, as did talented playmaker Coleman, who missed all three flags due in large part to injury. Their departures will hurt the Lions’ depth, though the picks received for McLachlan and Coleman will help them secure the points to match a bid for academy prospect Caylen Murray, a medium-sized defender. Port Adelaide In: Luke Pedlar (Ade/trade), picks 7, 12, 22, 34, R1 2027 (Rich), R1 2027 (Melb), R2 2027 (Rich), R4 2027 (Rich), R1 2028 (WB)

Out: Zak Butters (WB/free agency), picks 4, 32, 46, 83, R2 2027 (PA), R3 2027 (PA), R4 2027 (PA), R2 2028 (PA), R3 2028 (PA), R4 2028 (PA)

Draft picks: 7, 12, 22, 24, 34, 46, 65, 101

Trade rating: 5.5/10 The Power made the most of a bad situation, but it was bad nevertheless. You can never truly be pleased with a trade period where your best player – Butters – leaves for a new club, particularly when you wanted to keep him. The five-club mega deal Port Adelaide was a central figure in, completed purely to avoid the Power matching the Dogs’ Butters offer, was proof of how farcical the free agency system has become. They came out of that with a strong haul of picks, and knew they had enough draft points to match Essendon’s impending No.1 bid on academy rising star Dougie Cochrane. That meant they could offload the No.5 pick to Richmond to strengthen their draft hand next year to do more matching of father-son and academy prospects. Pedlar is a solid, but unspectacular, addition.



Look away, Port fans: Zak Butters in Western Bulldogs colours. Getty Images Adelaide In: Picks 32 and 35, R4 2027 (Rich)

Out: Jordon Butts (WB/free agency), Luke Pedlar (PA/trade), pick 34

Draft picks: 15, 32, 35, 43, 56, 92, 110

Trade grade: 5/10 Surprisingly, for a club in a “win-now phase”, as their list boss Jarryd Roughead put it, the Crows did not strengthen their list for the final season of Matthew Nicks’ contract. If anything, they are worse off, losing depth in their key defensive post. Butts is off to the Western Bulldogs though they held firm in keeping Nick Murray, who was desperate to get to North Melbourne. Murray’s disappointment at not securing a trade will disappear if he can break his way into the Crows 23 for a finals campaign. The Crows traded out fringe half-forward Pedlar to climb up two places in this year’s draft. They will be busier next year in their chase for St Kilda superstar Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera, who is out of contract at the end of 2027. Out the door: Joel Amartey left the Swans for the Blues. Sitthixay Ditthavong



Sydney In: Picks 6, 39, 47, R2 2027 (NM), R1 2028 (NM), R2 2028 (NM)

Out: Joel Amartey (Carl/free agency), Nick Blakey (NM/trade), Pick 52, R3 2028 (Syd)

Draft picks: 6, 38, 39, 47, 54, 76, 95, 113

Trade rating: 4.5/10 Key forward Amartey walked to Carlton, who significantly outbid the Swans, 12 months after Sydney traded for Blues star Charlie Curnow. That hurt, and delivered only pick 39 as compensation, but the hammer blow was still to come when Blakey requested a trade to North Melbourne after meeting with a bevy of clubs. That followed a major breakdown in relations between Blakey and the Swans. Sydney list boss Chris Keane set about returning maximum value once it became obvious Blakey emphatically wanted out. On that front, Keane and the Swans did well to gain the No.6 pick this year and a 2028 first-rounder among the more expansive package. But Sydney’s list won’t be as strong next year. World.title: Russell Brand behaved as a ‘ruthless’ sexual predator, prosecutors allege
World.content:
Graphic content WorldEuropeCourts Russell Brand behaved as a ‘ruthless’ sexual predator, prosecutors allege Jill Lawless Updated October 15, 2026 — 12:37am ,first published 10:34pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Warning: Graphic content Russell Brand behaved as a “ruthless” sexual predator when he assaulted six women over the course of a decade, a prosecutor alleged as she opened the rape and sexual assault case against the actor-comedian. Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault. The charges involve six women and alleged offences between 1999 and 2009. Russell Brand arrives at Southwark Crown Court on Wednesday for his trial. Getty Images Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones told jurors at Southwark Crown Court in London on Wednesday (local time) that the six women, who do not know each other, were assaulted in “a hotel room, workplaces, a toilet cubicle in a bar and at his home address”.



She said that at the time Brand had an “indiscriminate and voracious” desire for sexual contact, and “women were simply a means to an end”. The prosecutor said Brand could be funny and charming, “a flirt with a huge sexual appetite – childlike in his expectation that his every desire should be met”. “He was ruthless, he was calculating, he was manipulative. And, the prosecution say, he was a sexual predator,” Karmy-Jones said. Brand listened intently from the dock as the prosecutor described each of the alleged incidents, including the earliest, in which Brand allegedly raped a woman in a hotel room during the Labour Party’s annual conference in 1999. Brand, then a rising stand-up comedian, was performing in a cabaret on the fringe of the conference in the English seaside town of Bournemouth. Two years later, another woman alleges, Brand tried to drag her into the men’s toilet at the office building where she worked.



“There can be little doubt as to what Mr Brand’s intention was,” Karmy-Jones said. A third woman alleges that in 2004 Brand orally raped her in the toilets of a London bar, telling her “Don’t be a spoilsport” when she asked him to stop. Related Article Courts What to know about Russell Brand’s rape and sexual assault trial The prosecutor said that the other charges relate to a woman who says Brand kissed and groped her at a London radio station in 2004 or 2005, leaving her feeling “dirty and disgusting”; a then-21-year-old fan who says Brand anally raped her at his home after she met him at one of his shows in 2009; and a woman who says Brand demanded a massage and pressed his face into her groin during the recording of an  in 2009. Karmy-Jones told the jury that none of the alleged victims reported the alleged assaults at the time due to guilt, shame and concern that they would be blamed.



She said that jurors would hear from the women later in the trial, and “I have no doubt you will find their evidence compelling”. Brand denies all the charges. In police interviews, he denied ever engaging in non-consensual sexual activity. A court artist sketch of Brand during jury selection. Elizabeth Cook/PA via AP Brand is on bail and arrived at court on Wednesday to a crowd of photographers and video journalists. He said he felt “blessed”. “I feel, of course, concerned but hopeful that this process will lead to good outcomes for everybody involved,” Brand said. “That’s my prayer.”



Known for risqué stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, Brand rose to prominence in the early 2000s, hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him to the Greek. In recent years he has moved away from mainstream media, relocated to Florida and built a large online following with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion. The Associated Press doesn’t name victims of alleged sexual violence, and British law protects their identities from the media for life. AP Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.
