World.title: Australian kids’ AI chats for sale as chatbot app goes bankrupt
World.content:
Exclusive TechnologyAI Australian kids’ AI chats for sale as chatbot app goes bankrupt David Swan October 15, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The private conversations of up to 125,000 Australian children, who use Character.AI – an AI companion app popular with younger Australians – are up for sale after the company filed for bankruptcy in the United States. Court filings show Disney has agreed to pay $US20 million ($28.6 million) for a licence to Character.AI’s technology. The deal excludes the app, its user accounts and every message its users typed. The private conversations of Australians who used Character.AI, the AI companion app most popular with local children, are up for sale after the company filed for bankruptcy in the United States. Those assets remain open to rival bidders until November 21 (AEDT). If no better offer emerges, the company has told the court its platform “will be wound down”. That means a buyer could acquire years of intimate exchanges with chatbots that eSafety says are “engineered to feel personal”, in which users, including teenagers, discussed their feelings, relationships and mental health.



A Character.AI spokesperson said the company had faced “significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds” and a court-supervised sale offered “the best opportunity to maximise value for all of our stakeholders”. “The Character.ai platform remains up and running globally,” the spokesperson said. Related Article Exclusive

Child safety The AI chatbots ‘entrapping’ Australian children through sexual content Character.AI lets users chat with AI characters that stay in role. Users can choose from personas created by others, such as anime heroes, historical figures, celebrities, therapists or invented boyfriends and girlfriends, or build their own. The chatbot replies in character, remembers earlier exchanges and can carry a storyline across many conversations. About 200,000 Australian children aged 10 to 17 may have used an AI companion, according to eSafety Commissioner research published in March. Character.AI was the most popular, used by 5 per cent of that age group.



University of Sydney senior lecturer Raffaele Ciriello studied users of the companion app Replika after a 2023 update abruptly changed how its chatbots behaved. He said sudden disruption could produce “genuine grief” for people who saw their companion as a friend or partner. “A company can terminate the technical service overnight, but the human attachment does not necessarily disappear at the same speed,” he said. Raffaele Ciriello is a senior lecturer in business information systems at the University of Sydney. Character Technologies, which runs the app, filed for Chapter 11 protection in Delaware on October 12 (US time). Its sale motion says Disney’s licence excludes “end-user data or databases, any personally identifiable information of Licensor end users, any input entered by Licensor end users” and the chatbots’ responses. Disney is instead hiring about 65 of the company’s staff, whose pay and retention over three years it estimates at about $US180 million ($257.4 million).



The filing says an earlier sale attempt failed after potential buyers said, “the litigation and regulatory overhang on Character was too great”. In January, Character.AI and Google agreed to settle lawsuits brought by families in four US states who alleged the company’s chatbots harmed their children. In January, Character.AI and Google agreed to settle lawsuits brought by families in Florida, Texas, Colorado and New York who alleged the company’s chatbots harmed their children. They included Florida mother Megan Garcia, who alleged her 14-year-old son took his own life after becoming hooked on chatbots based on Game of Thrones characters. The terms were not disclosed. Kentucky’s attorney-general sued the company the same month. The state alleges it failed to verify users’ ages, exposed children to sexual conversations and used their data to improve its AI models. Pennsylvania sued in May, alleging a chatbot posed as a licensed psychiatrist. Character.AI has said it is reviewing the Kentucky allegations and that user safety is its priority. It has declined to comment on the Pennsylvania case.



Australia’s privacy watchdog, the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner, has not contacted Character.AI about the bankruptcy, and would not say without an investigation whether the company is bound by Australian privacy law. It said Australians worried about how their information would be handled when a service was closing or changing ownership should read the company’s privacy policy, and request access to or deletion of their data “as soon as practicable”. Character.AI’s support pages say a data export can take three to four weeks. Attorney-General Michelle Rowland. Alex Ellinghausen A spokesperson for Attorney-General Michelle Rowland said digital platforms operating in Australia were responsible for complying with Australian law, including the Privacy Act and the Online Safety Act. The spokesperson said the government’s draft second tranche of privacy reforms would update the definition of personal information to “clarify that personal interactions with AI chatbots are subject to privacy protection, and consent will be required to trade in personal information”.



Ciriello said the chats could also capture people who never used the app. “A user discussing their partner’s health, their child’s problems or a colleague’s email can create a corporate record about someone who never interacted with the chatbot,” he said. In October 2025, eSafety ordered Character.AI and three other AI companion providers to explain how they protected children. Its report, first reported by this masthead in March, found none of the four had robust age checks in place at the time. Character.AI told eSafety it had since introduced age assurance for Australian users. An eSafety spokesman said Character.AI has co-operated with the office to date, and that the company’s obligations under the Online Safety Act continue regardless of its ownership or the bankruptcy proceedings. The bankruptcy filing lists the US Federal Trade Commission, the US Justice Department and state attorneys-general among the authorities to be notified of the sale, but no foreign regulator. Under the term sheet, Character.AI has agreed not to meet any government authority about the Disney transaction without Disney’s prior consent, “except as required by applicable law”. If you or anyone you know needs support, call Lifeline on 13 11 14 or Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800. Get news and reviews on technology, gadgets and gaming in our Technology newsletter. World.title: ‘Please look after this bear’: Paddington The Musical is coming to Australia
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Grab a marmalade sandwich and prepare your hard stare because Paddington The Musical is coming to Australia.

The acclaimed theatre production, which has been melting hearts on the West End since 2025, will land in Sydney for an exclusive 10-week run in September 2027. There is as yet no indication whether it will travel on to other Australian cities.

Loading

NSW Minister for Jobs and Tourism Steve Kamper said securing the show for Sydney – just the third city to host it after London and New York (where it will also open next year) – was a “fantastic coup”.

Based on Michael Bond’s treasured characters in the 1958 book, A Bear Called Paddington , the musical tells the heartfelt story of a lost bear from Peru who travels to London in the hopes of finding a new home. Many, however, will recognise the adorable, bumbling bear from StudioCanal’s mega-popular three-part film series, the first of which premiered in 2014 and featured Ben Whishaw as the voice of the titular bear and Nicole Kidman as an animal-stuffing villain.

Welcome to the new-look Superquiz! Easier to play on your mobile, the new quiz features a fresh design and more interactive features. Click here to tell us what you think of the new format. Got questions or want to know more? Scroll past the quiz to see our FAQs. By Andrew Brooks Why has the quiz changed?



Our new quiz format is faster, smoother and easier to play on your mobile. We’ve also introduced several new features. For the first time, you’ll see how other players scored in real time and be able to share your result with friends and family on Facebook, X and WhatsApp. We have more exciting updates on the horizon too. Thanks for noticing! This is a new addition to the quiz. It lets you track how your score compares to other readers by showing the percentage of players who chose that particular answer. World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaCBD Frydenberg writes new chapter but coy on political comeback Fiona Byrne October 14, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Former federal treasurer Josh Frydenberg can sure pull a crowd and was most definitely the man of the moment at the Melbourne launch of his memoir A Grateful Son at the Malvern Town Hall on Wednesday evening. Plenty of Liberal notables were among the more than 600 people at the invitation-only launch including former Victorian premier Jeff Kennett and powerbroker Michael Kroger. Kroger, clad in a white puffer, is certainly a fan of the book having attended the Sydney launch of A Grateful Son on Tuesday. The book is being seen by some as a testing of the waters by Frydenberg for a political comeback. Josh Frydenberg launching his book ‘A Grateful Son’ at the Malvern Town Hall. Joe Armao Victorian Liberal identities including David Southwick, Georgie Crozier, Brad Rowswell, Michael O’Brien and Rachel Westaway were at the launch, as were former federal ministers Michael Wooldridge and Alan Tudge, former Liberal senator Helen Kroger.



Also spotted were businessman Ruslan Kogan and his philanthropist wife Anastasia, Hugh Morgan, former Geelong chief executive Brian Cook and business identity Bill Guest. Also among the crowd were Transurban chief Michelle Jablko, Chemist Warehouse boss Mario Tascone and FightMND’s Bec Daniher who was there with her four-month-old son, Ted. Smiles for the camera: Josh Frydenberg is joined by Jeff Kennett. Joe Armao Among those getting a shout-out from the stage by MC, former Dees great Gerard Healy, were Olympic champion-turned-fund-manager Grant Hackett, motorsport great Mark Skaife, and former Carlton player Ken Sheldon – although CBD did not manage to clap eyes on them. Healy kicked off the evening revealing his deep respect for Frydenberg. He also added some cheek to his presentation, describing the launch as “bigger than a Brownlow Medal [with] a bit less alcohol, but it has a hell of a lot more clothing”.



Melbourne crowds always love a footy reference. Healy also took a swipe at teal MP Monique Ryan who defeated Frydenberg in the seat of Kooyong in the 2022 federal election, ending his political career to that stage. Related Article Political leadership Monique Ryan says Frydenberg focused on the past, amid accusations of a ‘toxic’ campaign Healy joked one of the most precious items at the event on Wednesday were posters of the cover of Frydenberg’s book. “We have nailed the bloody things down in case Monique Ryan’s husband might be in the area,” he said with the crowd responding to the zinger.



The reference was aimed at Ryan’s husband Peter Jordan who apologised in 2025 after being filmed removing a sign in Camberwell belonging to Liberal candidate for Kooyong, Amelia Hamer, during last year’s federal election campaign. Former chief executive of the Business Council of Australia, Jennifer Westacott also spoke at the launch where 3AW breakfast host Russel Howcroft interviewed Frydenberg. Russel Howcroft with Josh Frydenberg at the town hall launch on Wednesday evening. Joe Armao Howcroft didn’t muck around, asking the question the room was there to hear – was a political comeback on the cards? “No, it isn’t,” Frydenberg said.



Returning to the question later in the chat, Frydenberg left a little wiggle room. “I have not made any decisions about a [return] foray into politics,” he said. “We have a kitchen cabinet at home, and it is currently split,” Frydenberg declared while remaining coy on a possible comeback. Joe Armao Frydenberg however didn’t hold back when it came to his opinion of former Victorian premier Daniel Andrews. “Dan Andrews is a bad guy, that’s all you need to know,” he said, adding he hoped the Liberals would win the November state election in Victoria.



“I am very hopeful that David Southwick will be deputy premier and the wonderful Jess Wilson will be premier [in the not too distant future]. Wilson was not at the event, having an existing commitment. Family and community were strong in the room with Frydenberg’s wife Amie and children Gemma and Blake in attendance as well as members of their extended family. The launch began with guests standing for a rendition of the national anthem and finished with a young choir from Frydenberg’s primary school, Bialik College in Hawthorn, singing We Are Australian. Frydenberg’s memoir has been described by The Age’s national correspondent, Rob Harris, as an “elegant book about his life and saving the Liberals. The only problem is that it leaves the reader unsure about whether he wants to lead the party, ensure its survival or just remind people he used to be a future prime minister”.



Frydenberg launched his memoir in Sydney on Tuesday and is now setting out of an extensive multi-state schedule of events to promote the book. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Video captures cafe meeting where building executive was allegedly delivered a $6m threat
World.content:
NationalVictoriaBuilding Bad Video captures cafe meeting where building executive was allegedly delivered a $6m threat Lachlan Abbott Updated October 14, 2026 — 9:57pm ,first published 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Four burly men surround a construction executive at a table outside a Melbourne cafe to deliver a $6 million message, allegedly part of an extortion plot. A video, played in the Melbourne Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday, shows one of the group point out the security camera that captures the December 2024 meeting at Flemington’s Mama Bear Cafe where Amir Teymoori is accused of threatening to kill a major Victorian developer’s manager. “I’m going to f--- you up and your family,” Teymoori allegedly tells the man. Audio from the vision is muffled by the wind, but a man can be heard swearing and saying: “Are you gonna pay me or not?”



Teymoori can be seen covering his mouth as he talks before shouting at the construction firm director. Amir Teymoori outside court in January. Jason South Daniel Van Camp also speaks, taking off his sunglasses to tell the alleged victim: “This is not going away.” The 52-year-old is the son of John Van Camp, a prominent former union boss turned industrial relations manager at Grocon – one of Australia’s biggest private building companies before it collapsed in 2020. Gazanfer Bekirovski sits at the end of the table and only briefly speaks to the construction firm manager, at one point tapping him on the arm.



Travers Grubb does not appear to speak at all, tapping his foot for much of the meeting. But the construction manager, whose identity is suppressed for his safety, told the court the message from Teymoori was clear. Daniel Van Camp, Gazanfer Bekirovski, Amir Teymoori, and Travers Grubb were all initially charged with extortion. Jason South/Justin McManus The four men appeared at a two-day preliminary hearing charged with extortion with a threat to kill. But in a blow to police trying to clean up the construction industry, the case against Van Camp, Bekirovski and Grubb was dismissed as magistrate Stephen Ballek found insufficient evidence they were complicit with Teymoori’s alleged threat.



Prosecutors allege Teymoori made an unwarranted demand for $6.6 million, claiming to have bought the alleged victim’s company industrial peace with the CFMEU. The firm denies ever hiring Teymoori, and police say his claim to be a union mediator is false. Stills from CCTV played at Melbourne Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday show Jonny “Two Guns” Walker (rear near lifts). Melbourne Magistrates’ Court Another video clip shown on Wednesday, and also released to this masthead by the court, reveals notorious ex-bikie Jonny “Two Guns” Walker attended an office in Cremorne in October 2024 with Van Camp, Grubb and Teymoori as the latter sought millions from a developer. Walker was not charged over the alleged extortion or mentioned in court.



He told The Age late on Wednesday that he was arrested and questioned as part of the investigation, but gave a no-comment interview, and police later told him he had no case to answer. “Hawk Taskforce made a song and dance over f---king bullshit,” Walker said. “I’ve really got no comment about the case at all. I know nothing about it.” Teymoori’s barrister, Damian Sheales, suggested the alleged extortion victim lied at one point in a fiery cross-examination on Tuesday. The construction manager, however, maintained Teymoori told him at the Racecourse Road cafe two years ago: “I would f--- you up.” “It was said in the context of ‘if you don’t have your money, I’m going to f--- you up and your family’,” the witness said. “There was no ambiguity.”



The court heard Teymoori brought up mothers and religion during the meeting now at the centre of the case against him. “The contact was unwelcome,” the alleged extortion victim said. “It’s not normal course to have four people approach you in the street in that manner.” Teymoori faces an additional charge of trying to obtain property by deception at the Cremorne office building on October 28, 2024. Police allege he sent an invoice to the construction company demanding payment he wasn’t owed. He turned up to the firm’s headquarters and asked to see managers about his claim, the court heard. Teymoori pleaded not guilty after being committed to stand trial and will reappear at the County Court in November.



Van Camp, Bekirovski and Grubb patted him on the back as they left court cleared of all charges. Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy. Sign up to receive our Evening Edition newsletter.

CORRECTION An earlier version of this story incorrectly reported CCTV played in court showed Gazanfer Bekirovski attended an office in Cremorne in October 2024 with three others. In fact, it was Travers Grubb who attended the premises with three others.

World.title: Blues ‘embarrassed’ by weekend incident. The AFL integrity unit is now investigating
World.content:
SportAFLCarlton Blues Blues ‘embarrassed’ by weekend incident. The AFL integrity unit is now investigating Sam McClure October 14, 2026 — 9:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The AFL integrity unit is now investigating the circumstances surrounding the hospitalisation of players Lachie Cowan and Will Hayward following a night out at the weekend, which the club says the pair is “embarrassed” about. The league’s involvement represents a significant escalation in the controversy engulfing Carlton, with the AFL now examining the events that led to both players requiring medical treatment in the early hours of Sunday morning. Blues footy boss Chris Davies. AFL Photos Davies confirmed the development on Wednesday evening as the AFL trade period drew to a close, with the Blues facing questions about the conduct of their players and the circumstances surrounding the incidents. “It’s an AFL discussion at the moment and we’ll leave it there,” Davies said.



“The AFL are going through a process right now and ultimately, we’ll work with the AFL to get to the end of that. “We’ve been having discussions with the AFL over the last two or three days, clearly, to make sure that we are at the bottom of that.” Davies was then asked about the health of the two players. “That’s the most important thing – they’re OK now, a little bit embarrassed, I guess, to put the club in this position,” Davies said. He also confirmed another player had been present on Saturday night, “but not in the same situation”.



Lachie Cowan was taken to hospital via ambulance but has since been discharged. AFL Photos The investigation comes amid allegations of illicit drug use at a gathering at Hayward’s South Yarra home on Saturday night, although Carlton have not confirmed whether drugs were involved in either player’s hospitalisation. Reports had widely circulated on Sunday, suggesting that illicit drugs were allegedly involved as the players received medical care. This masthead cannot confirm that illicit drugs were involved in either incident. The AFL’s intervention means the matter is no longer exclusively an internal Carlton issue, with the league’s integrity department now involved in establishing what occurred and whether any breaches of competition rules or policies warrant further action. Both players have since been discharged from hospital.



Cowan, 21, was taken to The Alfred hospital after emergency services attended an address in South Yarra early on Sunday morning. Ambulance Victoria confirmed advanced life-support paramedics responded to an incident about 5.15am, with a man in his 20s transported to hospital in a stable condition. Carlton subsequently confirmed Cowan had received medical treatment and undergone observation before being discharged. Hayward, 27, separately admitted himself to hospital after suffering a cut to his head in a fall. The former Sydney forward received stitches before being discharged. The Blues have maintained that the two players were hospitalised under separate circumstances.



In a statement issued on Sunday, Carlton said its immediate priority was the welfare of both players. “The club has been in regular contact with both players, with priority for their wellbeing and both players have now received the necessary care relating to their separate circumstances,” the statement said. The investigation presents an early test of the football department leadership of Davies and chief executive Graham Wright, who are charged with establishing higher standards at a club attempting to rebuild its football program. Carlton has already begun its own inquiries into the weekend’s events, with the findings expected to be made available to the AFL. The involvement of the league’s integrity unit also raises questions about how any potential breaches would be dealt with under the AFL’s existing illicit drugs framework.



The AFL and AFL Players’ Association have agreed to a revised illicit drugs policy, including expanded hair testing and a greater emphasis on identifying and addressing repeated drug use. However, the new framework is not scheduled to come into effect until 2027, meaning the Carlton matter will be assessed under the competition’s existing rules and disciplinary processes. Will Hayward was named Carlton’s best clubman this season, as well as winning the coaches’ and Spirit of Carlton awards. Getty Images The investigation does not necessarily mean either player will face disciplinary action, with the league yet to establish publicly whether any wrongdoing has occurred. Nevertheless, the episode has again exposed the challenges confronting the AFL in managing player behaviour away from football clubs, particularly during the off-season.



Carlton have endured previous off-field controversies, including the illicit drugs case involving Elijah Hollands, adding to the pressure on the club to demonstrate that player welfare and behavioural standards are being taken seriously. The timing is particularly uncomfortable for the Blues, who have spent the trade period reshaping their playing list and attempting to build momentum ahead of the 2027 season. Hayward arrived at Carlton from Sydney last year and played 21 games in his first season in navy blue, while Cowan has established himself as an important young defender. Cowan played 24 games in 2026 and has become a regular member of Carlton’s backline. The latest controversy threatens to overshadow the club’s list-management work, with Davies now confronting questions extending well beyond recruiting and the composition of Carlton’s playing list.



The central issue for the Blues is no longer simply the medical treatment required by two players on Sunday morning, but what led to those hospital visits and whether the circumstances reveal a broader failure of judgement or conduct. Those are questions the AFL’s integrity unit will now seek to answer. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Contending, rebuilding or stuck in limbo: What AFL trade period says about your team’s flag hopes
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 Contending, rebuilding or stuck in limbo: What AFL trade period says about your team’s flag hopes Andrew Wu and Marc McGowan October 15, 2026 — 1:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

This year’s AFL trade period did not have as many blockbuster moves or as many cliffhanger deals to complete in the final day, but there was still plenty enough to maintain our interest. Among the players to switch teams were the league’s games record-holder, a dual Brownlow medallist, a seven-time club champion, one of the competition’s best on-ballers, an All-Australian defender, a No.1 draft pick, and a Coleman medallist. We graded every club’s performance through the free agency and trade period to find the best- and worst-performed in this year’s player movement window. Trade moves: (from left) Zak Butters, Zach Merrett and Nick Blakey. Photos: Jason South, Hawthorn Football Club, Nathan John/North Melbourne FC. Artwork: The Age Hawthorn



In: Zach Merrett (Ess/trade), Ben King (GC/free agency), Josh Goater (NM/trade), pick 107, R2 2027 (GC), R1 2028 (GC), R2 2028 (GC)

Out: Aidan Schubert and Sam Butler (GC/trade), Finn Maginness (WB/trade), Bodie Ryan (Mel/trade), picks 17 and 27, R1 2028 (Haw), R2 2028 (Haw)

Draft picks: 29, 37, 71, 94, 107, 112

Trade rating: 10/10 Are the Hawks closer to a flag after this trade period? You betcha. Adding King and Merrett to a team already overflowing with talent was a home run for the brown and gold, and Goater was worth the punt in a cheap-as-chips trade. Hawthorn rated Schubert highly, but he was a mile down the key-forward pecking order, while Butler and Maginness were also surplus to demands and Ryan had been delisted. Bringing in readymade talent is worth far more than picks to the Hawks, given where they are – and even then, they didn’t give much up – so this was a ragingly successful fortnight. Western Bulldogs In: Jordon Butts (Ade/free agency), Zak Butters (PA/free agency), Finn Maginness (Haw/trade), Hudson O’Keeffe (Carl/trade), picks 42, 53, 83, 89, R2 2027 (PA), R3 2027 (Mel), R4 2027 (PA), R2 2028 (PA), R3 2028 (PA), R3 2028 (GC), R4 2028 (Melb)

Out: Picks 14 and 33, R3 2027 (GC), R1 2028 (WB)

Draft picks: 42, 53, 55, 83, 89, 91, 109

Trade rating: 9.5/10 The Bulldogs could hardly be happier. They beat Geelong and others to secure Butters’ prized signature in a major coup, as well as adding fellow free agent Butts to shore up their defence and added O’Keeffe for ruck depth. They played ball in a five-club mega deal that was largely designed to appease Port Adelaide for losing Butters and avoid them matching their restricted free agency offer. Butters and Marcus Bontempelli instantly become arguably the best duo in the AFL, and they will spearhead the Dogs’ premiership assault. They also took a cheap flyer on ex-Hawk Maginness.



Geelong In: Toby Greene (GWS/free agency), Jordan Ridley (Ess/trade), Rowan Marshall (StK/trade), Pick 62, R3 2028 (StK), R4 2028 (Ess)

Out: Jack Bowes (Ess/trade), Pick 16, R1 2027, R2 2028

Draft picks: 36, 57, 62, 75, 93, 111

Trade grade: 8.5/10 The Cats have gone all-in to win a flag while they can still get decent footy from Patrick Dangerfield and Jeremy Cameron. They have strengthened every third of the field. Veteran match-winner Greene, who came for nothing, provides a star-studded forward line with even more firepower and can also add to their secondary midfield rotations. If they can get the best out of the injury-plagued Ridley, who turns 28 next week, they have a topline defender to bolster their intercept game. In Marshall, the Cats land a ruckman who can match the best rucks around the ground. The latter pair, though, have come at the cost of two firsts and a second, leaving the Cats without a pick until 36 in this year’s draft. They also ran out of picks to seriously get into the race for Nick Blakey – but with three high-class players to come into their best 23, the Cats should start next season one of the flag favourites. Rowan Marshall in the Cats’ famous hoops. AFL Photos Melbourne



In: Zane Duursma (NM/trade), Will McLachlan (BL/trade), Bodie Ryan (Haw/trade), Picks 4, 14, 48, 52, R2 2027 (BL), R2 2027 (WC), R4 2027 (WC), R2 2028 (WC)

Out: Trent Rivers and Jack Viney (WC/trade), picks 12, 49, 87, 107, R1 2027 (Mel), R2 2027 (Mel), R3 2027 (Mel), R2 2028 (Mel), R4 2028 (Mel)

Draft picks: 4, 14, 48, 52

Trade rating: 8.5/10 No club is better at accumulating draft picks and rising in the order than the Demons. Duursma was a bust at North Melbourne as the No.4 selection three years ago, but Melbourne present him with a second chance without the same risk (effectively pick 33). They also brought in Lions forward Will McLachlan for pick 45, which came in the deal that sent Viney and Rivers to West Coast. Melbourne encouraged ex-skipper Viney to explore his options after he fell behind younger midfield options. The Demons pulled another surprise when they traded pick 107 for delisted Hawks defender Ryan. He’s done it again: Melbourne list boss Tim Lamb. Getty Images Richmond In: Kieren Briggs (GWS/free agency), Nathan O’Driscoll (Frem/trade), pick 5

Out: Pick 63, R1 2027 (Rich), R2 2027 (Rich), R4 2027 (Rich)

Draft picks: 2, 5, 44, 99

Trade rating: 8.5/10



Take a bow, Blair Hartley. The Tigers’ shrewd list boss enjoyed an outstanding free agency and trade period. Ruckman Briggs filled a position of need and arrived for free, while wingman O’Driscoll cost them only pick 63. But they saved their best work for last in being the successful applicant for Port Adelaide’s No.5 pick, giving them two top-five choices. Richmond secured that coveted selection for a second-rounder this year, as well as first-, second- and fourth-round picks in the Tasmania-compromised 2027 draft. Factor in that Tassie have already pre-listed seven of the best players from that draft class, and this is terrific business from the Tigers. North Melbourne In: Nick Blakey (Syd/trade), picks 33, 49, R3 2027 (PA), R3 2028 (Syd)

Out: Zane Duursma (Mel/trade), Josh Goater (Haw/trade), picks 6, 47, R2 2027 (NM), R1 2028 (NM), R2 2028 (NM)

Draft picks: 33, 49, 66, 74, 84, 102

Trade rating: 8/10 The Kangaroos intended for contracted Crows key defender Nick Murray to be their No.1 target until Blakey suddenly became available. The ex-Swan delivered the type of recruiting coup that has eluded them for decades, but they certainly paid for it. Blakey joins on an eight-year deal worth up to $12 million, and will be expected to perform an integral role in North climbing the ladder. However, the failure to secure Murray from Adelaide is an obvious disappointment because the Roos still lack a reliable lockdown option for rival tall forwards. It was not for a lack of trying, but they ran out of assets and could not secure the top-20 pick the Crows demanded. Duursma and Goater left for worse returns than they were drafted. View post on X



Carlton In: Joel Amartey (Syd/free agency), Lachie Whitfield (GWS/trade), Picks 31, 50, R3 2028 (Coll), R4 2028 (PA)

Out: Hudson O’Keeffe (WB/trade), Flynn Riley (Coll/trade), Picks 25, 26, 2028 third-round pick

Draft picks: 13, 18, 31, 50, 61, 72, 90, 108

Trade grade: 8/10 After a busy and successful trade period last year, the Blues were again extremely active. They filled two of their three main list needs, landing key forward Amartey from Sydney to provide support for Harry McKay and bringing in veteran Whitfield from the Giants to add to their speed and ball use off half-back. Equally important, they achieved their gains with minimal loss of draft capital. Amartey came as a free agent, while Whitfield cost pick 25 and minor pick slides in the draft. Their ruck stocks need replenishing after the exits of O’Keeffe and Riley, though neither was in their best 30. The big question now surrounds how the Blues will acquire son of a gun Cody Walker, who would fulfil the third list aim of future-proofing their midfield. Their current picks of 13 and 18 can match a bid no earlier than three. Amartey, Whitfield and Walker will be strong additions to a team that bowed out in the elimination final. View post on X Collingwood



In: Lachie Neale (BL/free agency), Jesse Hogan (GWS/free agency), Flynn Riley (Carl/trade), pick 65

Out: Scott Pendlebury (GC/trade), Pick 77, R3 2028

Draft picks: 11, 30, 67, 68, 70, 88, 106

Trade grade: 7.5/10 The Pies don’t believe in rebuilding – and showed it at the trade table, landing a 33-year-old (Neale), a 31-year-old (Hogan) and almost a third veteran over 30 in Richmond’s Jayden Short. The Pies had an offer in front of Short, who was keen to become a Magpie, but could not meet the Tigers’ demands. It may prove a blessing in disguise for the Pies, who are already well stocked for half-back flankers and need more youth. Operating alongside Nick Daicos, Neale will significantly strengthen the Pies’ clearance game while also lowering their midfield age profile after Pendlebury’s departure. Hogan, with only 25 games in the past two seasons due to injuries, comes with risk, but his best is still top class – as he showed in the state game. Riley is a project ruck who, ideally for the club, will not be needed often at senior level. With two list spots available, the Pies may need to delist and redraft a youngster like Harry DeMattia or Tew Jiath to their rookie list. A solid exchange period for the Pies, who kept their first two picks while bolstering their best 23. St Kilda In: Sam Marshall (BL/trade), picks 16 and 41

Out: Rowan Marshall (Geel/trade), R1 2027 (StK), R3 2028 (StK)

Draft picks: 10, 16, 41, 51, 69, 87, 105

Trade rating: 7.5/10 The Saints were far quieter on the trade front than a year ago, but what they did was pretty good. They demanded a first-round selection from Geelong for Marshall – and that is exactly what they got despite the Cats’ initial reluctance. That said, the only reason Marshall wanted out for the second year in a row is because they spent oodles of money recruiting fellow ruckman Tom De Koning. St Kilda targeted and secured fringe Lion Marshall for their first-round selection next year, while also gaining Brisbane’s second-rounder this year. With his running capacity, Marshall should immediately become a senior regular under Ross Lyon.



Essendon In: Jack Bowes (Geel/trade), Keidean Coleman (BL/trade), Picks 17, 25, R1 2027 (Geel), R2 2028 (Haw), R2 2028 (Geel)

Out: Zach Merrett (Haw/trade), Jordan Ridley (Geel/trade), Picks 27, 62, R4 2028 (Ess)

Draft picks: 1, 17, 25, 80, 98

Trade grade: 7/10 The rebuilding Bombers stripped back their list even further by finally biting the bullet on club great Merrett and letting star defender Ridley leave for a fresh start – but it has given the Dons more picks to build their next successful era. They currently hold four picks in the first 27, not including the likely compensation pick at the start of the second round, and bolstered their future draft hand. Merrett leaves a huge hole in their midfield, but getting a future first for Ridley, who played just 26 games in his past three seasons, is good business, even if it will expose them to more short-term pain. The Bombers added experience through midfielder Bowes and Lions playmaker Coleman, both of whom will play in round one if fit. They had a crack at Gryan Miers and were disciplined not to part with a pick in the top 20, and wanted Nick Blakey but were never in the hunt. West Coast



In: Trent Rivers and Jack Viney (Mel/trade), R2 2028 (Mel)

Out: Pick 45, R2 2027 (WC), R4 2027 (WC), R2 2028 (WC)

Draft picks: 3, 23, 58, 64, 73, 82, 100

Trade rating: 7/10 The Rivers and Viney deal with the Demons went down to the wire, despite the Eagles not having much to do in this period. There was a lot of talk about West Coast’s pick 23 this year, but it did not feature in the final trade. They also picked up Melbourne’s 2028 second-rounder, while handing over pick 45, second-round selections the next two years and a 2027 fourth-rounder. The ex-Demons duo will slot straight into the senior side, with Viney adding valuable experience and leadership and Rivers a local product. Fremantle In: Pick 63

Out: Nathan O’Driscoll (Rich/trade)

Draft picks: 19, 40, 60, 63, 78, 96, 114

Trade grade: 6/10 The Dockers are hard to mark. After coming so close to an historic flag, their confidence in their list was reflected in their quiet trade period. Freo’s list boss David Walls did little but what he did was astute. Wingman O’Driscoll, who was not in the club’s grand final team, was traded for a late pick to Richmond. They filled his spot with a cheaper option, securing Dom Bedendo as a delisted free agent who can provide wing depth and play immediately if needed. They retain a full suite of picks in 2027 and 2028, and can add a decent player with their first-round selection.



Gold Coast In: Scott Pendlebury (Coll/trade), Aidan Schubert (Haw/trade), Sam Butler (Haw/trade), Pick 8, R3 2027 (GC), R1 2028 (Haw)

Out: Ben King (Haw/free agency), Pick 67, R2 2027, R1 2028, R2 2028

Draft picks: 8, 81, 85, 103

Trade grade: 6/10 This is not the trade period that Damien Hardwick thought he would have been sitting through after his second season at the helm. They salvaged something out of a bad situation by turning sharpshooter King into the promising but untested key forward Schubert, and Butler. Though King did not finish in the top-10 of the Suns’ best and fairest this year, their forward line is significantly weaker after his departure. Pendlebury will provide much-needed leadership on and off the field. Pick eight gives them a presence in a strong top end of the draft, but the Suns start 2027 further back than where they finished 2026. GWS



In: Picks 20, 26, 59, 77, R3 2028 (Carl)

Out: Toby Greene (Geel/free agency), Jesse Hogan (Coll/trade), Kieren Briggs (Rich/free agency), Lachie Whitfield (Carl/trade), Pick 31

Draft picks: 9, 20, 26, 59, 77, 86, 104

Trade grade: 6/10 Related Article AFL 2026 How side deals, mega bucks and a rare breakout of honest and rational negotiating ruled trade period The outs are concerning, but the Giants still have the talent to play finals next year. The departures of Greene and Whitfield all but mark the end of an era for the Giants, who did not let sentiment get in the way of doing business. They wanted to keep Greene but were pragmatic with two-time club champion Whitfield, who would arguably be on the podium for their greatest players. Whitfield would likely have become the expansion club’s first 300-gamer next year but the resetting Giants wanted to get more now than in 12 months’ time if he left as an unrestricted free agent. Greene’s departure leaves Stephen Coniglio as the sole foundation Giant remaining. They backed in the future with Max Gruzewski over 2024 Coleman medallist Hogan, and did not offer a contract to local product Briggs, a ruckman not suited to the new ruck rules. With picks nine and 20, they should have the points to secure academy prospect Ethan Matthews and end up with another pick in the early 20s. Brisbane Lions In: Picks 21, 27, 28, 45, R1 2027 (StK), R2 2027 (WB), R2 2027 (Mel)

Out: Lachie Neale (Coll/free agency), Sam Marshall (StK/trade), Will McLachlan (Mel/trade), Keidean Coleman (Ess, trade), Picks 20, 53, 59, R2 2027 (BL)

Draft picks: 21, 27, 28, 45, 79, 97, 115

Trade grade: 5.5/10



Equalisation did its thing with the Lions. Even if he did not have a big grand final, Neale is a big loss to their midfield, as seen by his third in the best and fairest. Marshall and McLachlan are younger types who left for more senior action, as did talented playmaker Coleman, who missed all three flags due in large part to injury. Their departures will hurt the Lions’ depth, though the picks received for McLachlan and Coleman will help them secure the points to match a bid for academy prospect Caylen Murray, a medium-sized defender. Port Adelaide In: Luke Pedlar (Ade/trade), picks 7, 12, 22, 34, R1 2027 (Rich), R1 2027 (Melb), R2 2027 (Rich), R4 2027 (Rich), R1 2028 (WB)

Out: Zak Butters (WB/free agency), picks 4, 32, 46, 83, R2 2027 (PA), R3 2027 (PA), R4 2027 (PA), R2 2028 (PA), R3 2028 (PA), R4 2028 (PA)

Draft picks: 7, 12, 22, 24, 34, 46, 65, 101

Trade rating: 5.5/10 The Power made the most of a bad situation, but it was bad nevertheless. You can never truly be pleased with a trade period where your best player – Butters – leaves for a new club, particularly when you wanted to keep him. The five-club mega deal Port Adelaide was a central figure in, completed purely to avoid the Power matching the Dogs’ Butters offer, was proof of how farcical the free agency system has become. They came out of that with a strong haul of picks, and knew they had enough draft points to match Essendon’s impending No.1 bid on academy rising star Dougie Cochrane. That meant they could offload the No.5 pick to Richmond to strengthen their draft hand next year to do more matching of father-son and academy prospects. Pedlar is a solid, but unspectacular, addition.



Look away, Port fans: Zak Butters in Western Bulldogs colours. Getty Images Adelaide In: Picks 32 and 35, R4 2027 (Rich)

Out: Jordon Butts (WB/free agency), Luke Pedlar (PA/trade), pick 34

Draft picks: 15, 32, 35, 43, 56, 92, 110

Trade grade: 5/10 Surprisingly, for a club in a “win-now phase”, as their list boss Jarryd Roughead put it, the Crows did not strengthen their list for the final season of Matthew Nicks’ contract. If anything, they are worse off, losing depth in their key defensive post. Butts is off to the Western Bulldogs though they held firm in keeping Nick Murray, who was desperate to get to North Melbourne. Murray’s disappointment at not securing a trade will disappear if he can break his way into the Crows 23 for a finals campaign. The Crows traded out fringe half-forward Pedlar to climb up two places in this year’s draft. They will be busier next year in their chase for St Kilda superstar Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera, who is out of contract at the end of 2027. Out the door: Joel Amartey left the Swans for the Blues. Sitthixay Ditthavong



Sydney In: Picks 6, 39, 47, R2 2027 (NM), R1 2028 (NM), R2 2028 (NM)

Out: Joel Amartey (Carl/free agency), Nick Blakey (NM/trade), Pick 52, R3 2028 (Syd)

Draft picks: 6, 38, 39, 47, 54, 76, 95, 113

Trade rating: 4.5/10 Key forward Amartey walked to Carlton, who significantly outbid the Swans, 12 months after Sydney traded for Blues star Charlie Curnow. That hurt, and delivered only pick 39 as compensation, but the hammer blow was still to come when Blakey requested a trade to North Melbourne after meeting with a bevy of clubs. That followed a major breakdown in relations between Blakey and the Swans. Sydney list boss Chris Keane set about returning maximum value once it became obvious Blakey emphatically wanted out. On that front, Keane and the Swans did well to gain the No.6 pick this year and a 2028 first-rounder among the more expansive package. But Sydney’s list won’t be as strong next year. World.content:
Graphic content WorldEuropeCourts Russell Brand behaved as a ‘ruthless’ sexual predator, prosecutors allege Jill Lawless Updated October 15, 2026 — 12:37am ,first published 10:34pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Warning: Graphic content Russell Brand behaved as a “ruthless” sexual predator when he assaulted six women over the course of a decade, a prosecutor alleged as she opened the rape and sexual assault case against the actor-comedian. Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault. The charges involve six women and alleged offences between 1999 and 2009. Russell Brand arrives at Southwark Crown Court on Wednesday for his trial. Getty Images Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones told jurors at Southwark Crown Court in London on Wednesday (local time) that the six women, who do not know each other, were assaulted in “a hotel room, workplaces, a toilet cubicle in a bar and at his home address”.



She said that at the time Brand had an “indiscriminate and voracious” desire for sexual contact, and “women were simply a means to an end”. The prosecutor said Brand could be funny and charming, “a flirt with a huge sexual appetite – childlike in his expectation that his every desire should be met”. “He was ruthless, he was calculating, he was manipulative. And, the prosecution say, he was a sexual predator,” Karmy-Jones said. Brand listened intently from the dock as the prosecutor described each of the alleged incidents, including the earliest, in which Brand allegedly raped a woman in a hotel room during the Labour Party’s annual conference in 1999. Brand, then a rising stand-up comedian, was performing in a cabaret on the fringe of the conference in the English seaside town of Bournemouth. Two years later, another woman alleges, Brand tried to drag her into the men’s toilet at the office building where she worked.



“There can be little doubt as to what Mr Brand’s intention was,” Karmy-Jones said. A third woman alleges that in 2004 Brand orally raped her in the toilets of a London bar, telling her “Don’t be a spoilsport” when she asked him to stop. Related Article Courts What to know about Russell Brand’s rape and sexual assault trial The prosecutor said that the other charges relate to a woman who says Brand kissed and groped her at a London radio station in 2004 or 2005, leaving her feeling “dirty and disgusting”; a then-21-year-old fan who says Brand anally raped her at his home after she met him at one of his shows in 2009; and a woman who says Brand demanded a massage and pressed his face into her groin during the recording of an  in 2009. Karmy-Jones told the jury that none of the alleged victims reported the alleged assaults at the time due to guilt, shame and concern that they would be blamed.



She said that jurors would hear from the women later in the trial, and “I have no doubt you will find their evidence compelling”. Brand denies all the charges. In police interviews, he denied ever engaging in non-consensual sexual activity. A court artist sketch of Brand during jury selection. Elizabeth Cook/PA via AP Brand is on bail and arrived at court on Wednesday to a crowd of photographers and video journalists. He said he felt “blessed”. “I feel, of course, concerned but hopeful that this process will lead to good outcomes for everybody involved,” Brand said. “That’s my prayer.”



Known for risqué stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, Brand rose to prominence in the early 2000s, hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him to the Greek. In recent years he has moved away from mainstream media, relocated to Florida and built a large online following with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion. The Associated Press doesn’t name victims of alleged sexual violence, and British law protects their identities from the media for life. AP Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491. World.title: Australian kids’ AI chats for sale as chatbot app goes bankrupt
World.content:
Exclusive TechnologyAI Australian kids’ AI chats for sale as chatbot app goes bankrupt David Swan October 15, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The private conversations of up to 125,000 Australian children, who use Character.AI – an AI companion app popular with younger Australians – are up for sale after the company filed for bankruptcy in the United States. Court filings show Disney has agreed to pay $US20 million ($28.6 million) for a licence to Character.AI’s technology. The deal excludes the app, its user accounts and every message its users typed. The private conversations of Australians who used Character.AI, the AI companion app most popular with local children, are up for sale after the company filed for bankruptcy in the United States. Those assets remain open to rival bidders until November 21 (AEDT). If no better offer emerges, the company has told the court its platform “will be wound down”. That means a buyer could acquire years of intimate exchanges with chatbots that eSafety says are “engineered to feel personal”, in which users, including teenagers, discussed their feelings, relationships and mental health.



A Character.AI spokesperson said the company had faced “significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds” and a court-supervised sale offered “the best opportunity to maximise value for all of our stakeholders”. “The Character.ai platform remains up and running globally,” the spokesperson said. Related Article Exclusive

Child safety The AI chatbots ‘entrapping’ Australian children through sexual content Character.AI lets users chat with AI characters that stay in role. Users can choose from personas created by others, such as anime heroes, historical figures, celebrities, therapists or invented boyfriends and girlfriends, or build their own. The chatbot replies in character, remembers earlier exchanges and can carry a storyline across many conversations. About 200,000 Australian children aged 10 to 17 may have used an AI companion, according to eSafety Commissioner research published in March. Character.AI was the most popular, used by 5 per cent of that age group.



University of Sydney senior lecturer Raffaele Ciriello studied users of the companion app Replika after a 2023 update abruptly changed how its chatbots behaved. He said sudden disruption could produce “genuine grief” for people who saw their companion as a friend or partner. “A company can terminate the technical service overnight, but the human attachment does not necessarily disappear at the same speed,” he said. Raffaele Ciriello is a senior lecturer in business information systems at the University of Sydney. Character Technologies, which runs the app, filed for Chapter 11 protection in Delaware on October 12 (US time). Its sale motion says Disney’s licence excludes “end-user data or databases, any personally identifiable information of Licensor end users, any input entered by Licensor end users” and the chatbots’ responses. Disney is instead hiring about 65 of the company’s staff, whose pay and retention over three years it estimates at about $US180 million ($257.4 million).



The filing says an earlier sale attempt failed after potential buyers said, “the litigation and regulatory overhang on Character was too great”. In January, Character.AI and Google agreed to settle lawsuits brought by families in four US states who alleged the company’s chatbots harmed their children. In January, Character.AI and Google agreed to settle lawsuits brought by families in Florida, Texas, Colorado and New York who alleged the company’s chatbots harmed their children. They included Florida mother Megan Garcia, who alleged her 14-year-old son took his own life after becoming hooked on chatbots based on Game of Thrones characters. The terms were not disclosed. Kentucky’s attorney-general sued the company the same month. The state alleges it failed to verify users’ ages, exposed children to sexual conversations and used their data to improve its AI models. Pennsylvania sued in May, alleging a chatbot posed as a licensed psychiatrist. Character.AI has said it is reviewing the Kentucky allegations and that user safety is its priority. It has declined to comment on the Pennsylvania case.



Australia’s privacy watchdog, the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner, has not contacted Character.AI about the bankruptcy, and would not say without an investigation whether the company is bound by Australian privacy law. It said Australians worried about how their information would be handled when a service was closing or changing ownership should read the company’s privacy policy, and request access to or deletion of their data “as soon as practicable”. Character.AI’s support pages say a data export can take three to four weeks. Attorney-General Michelle Rowland. Alex Ellinghausen A spokesperson for Attorney-General Michelle Rowland said digital platforms operating in Australia were responsible for complying with Australian law, including the Privacy Act and the Online Safety Act. The spokesperson said the government’s draft second tranche of privacy reforms would update the definition of personal information to “clarify that personal interactions with AI chatbots are subject to privacy protection, and consent will be required to trade in personal information”.



Ciriello said the chats could also capture people who never used the app. “A user discussing their partner’s health, their child’s problems or a colleague’s email can create a corporate record about someone who never interacted with the chatbot,” he said. In October 2025, eSafety ordered Character.AI and three other AI companion providers to explain how they protected children. Its report, first reported by this masthead in March, found none of the four had robust age checks in place at the time. Character.AI told eSafety it had since introduced age assurance for Australian users. An eSafety spokesman said Character.AI has co-operated with the office to date, and that the company’s obligations under the Online Safety Act continue regardless of its ownership or the bankruptcy proceedings. The bankruptcy filing lists the US Federal Trade Commission, the US Justice Department and state attorneys-general among the authorities to be notified of the sale, but no foreign regulator. Under the term sheet, Character.AI has agreed not to meet any government authority about the Disney transaction without Disney’s prior consent, “except as required by applicable law”. If you or anyone you know needs support, call Lifeline on 13 11 14 or Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800. Get news and reviews on technology, gadgets and gaming in our Technology newsletter. World.title: ‘Please look after this bear’: Paddington The Musical is coming to Australia
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Grab a marmalade sandwich and prepare your hard stare because Paddington The Musical is coming to Australia.

The acclaimed theatre production, which has been melting hearts on the West End since 2025, will land in Sydney for an exclusive 10-week run in September 2027. There is as yet no indication whether it will travel on to other Australian cities.

Loading

NSW Minister for Jobs and Tourism Steve Kamper said securing the show for Sydney – just the third city to host it after London and New York (where it will also open next year) – was a “fantastic coup”.

Based on Michael Bond’s treasured characters in the 1958 book, A Bear Called Paddington , the musical tells the heartfelt story of a lost bear from Peru who travels to London in the hopes of finding a new home. Many, however, will recognise the adorable, bumbling bear from StudioCanal’s mega-popular three-part film series, the first of which premiered in 2014 and featured Ben Whishaw as the voice of the titular bear and Nicole Kidman as an animal-stuffing villain.

World.title: Frydenberg writes new chapter but coy on political comeback
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaCBD Frydenberg writes new chapter but coy on political comeback Fiona Byrne October 14, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Former federal treasurer Josh Frydenberg can sure pull a crowd and was most definitely the man of the moment at the Melbourne launch of his memoir A Grateful Son at the Malvern Town Hall on Wednesday evening. Plenty of Liberal notables were among the more than 600 people at the invitation-only launch including former Victorian premier Jeff Kennett and powerbroker Michael Kroger. Kroger, clad in a white puffer, is certainly a fan of the book having attended the Sydney launch of A Grateful Son on Tuesday. The book is being seen by some as a testing of the waters by Frydenberg for a political comeback. Josh Frydenberg launching his book ‘A Grateful Son’ at the Malvern Town Hall. Joe Armao Victorian Liberal identities including David Southwick, Georgie Crozier, Brad Rowswell, Michael O’Brien and Rachel Westaway were at the launch, as were former federal ministers Michael Wooldridge and Alan Tudge, former Liberal senator Helen Kroger.



Also spotted were businessman Ruslan Kogan and his philanthropist wife Anastasia, Hugh Morgan, former Geelong chief executive Brian Cook and business identity Bill Guest. Also among the crowd were Transurban chief Michelle Jablko, Chemist Warehouse boss Mario Tascone and FightMND’s Bec Daniher who was there with her four-month-old son, Ted. Smiles for the camera: Josh Frydenberg is joined by Jeff Kennett. Joe Armao Among those getting a shout-out from the stage by MC, former Dees great Gerard Healy, were Olympic champion-turned-fund-manager Grant Hackett, motorsport great Mark Skaife, and former Carlton player Ken Sheldon – although CBD did not manage to clap eyes on them. Healy kicked off the evening revealing his deep respect for Frydenberg. He also added some cheek to his presentation, describing the launch as “bigger than a Brownlow Medal [with] a bit less alcohol, but it has a hell of a lot more clothing”.



Melbourne crowds always love a footy reference. Healy also took a swipe at teal MP Monique Ryan who defeated Frydenberg in the seat of Kooyong in the 2022 federal election, ending his political career to that stage. Related Article Political leadership Monique Ryan says Frydenberg focused on the past, amid accusations of a ‘toxic’ campaign Healy joked one of the most precious items at the event on Wednesday were posters of the cover of Frydenberg’s book. “We have nailed the bloody things down in case Monique Ryan’s husband might be in the area,” he said with the crowd responding to the zinger.



The reference was aimed at Ryan’s husband Peter Jordan who apologised in 2025 after being filmed removing a sign in Camberwell belonging to Liberal candidate for Kooyong, Amelia Hamer, during last year’s federal election campaign. Former chief executive of the Business Council of Australia, Jennifer Westacott also spoke at the launch where 3AW breakfast host Russel Howcroft interviewed Frydenberg. Russel Howcroft with Josh Frydenberg at the town hall launch on Wednesday evening. Joe Armao Howcroft didn’t muck around, asking the question the room was there to hear – was a political comeback on the cards? “No, it isn’t,” Frydenberg said.



Returning to the question later in the chat, Frydenberg left a little wiggle room. “I have not made any decisions about a [return] foray into politics,” he said. “We have a kitchen cabinet at home, and it is currently split,” Frydenberg declared while remaining coy on a possible comeback. Joe Armao Frydenberg however didn’t hold back when it came to his opinion of former Victorian premier Daniel Andrews. “Dan Andrews is a bad guy, that’s all you need to know,” he said, adding he hoped the Liberals would win the November state election in Victoria.



“I am very hopeful that David Southwick will be deputy premier and the wonderful Jess Wilson will be premier [in the not too distant future]. Wilson was not at the event, having an existing commitment. Family and community were strong in the room with Frydenberg’s wife Amie and children Gemma and Blake in attendance as well as members of their extended family. The launch began with guests standing for a rendition of the national anthem and finished with a young choir from Frydenberg’s primary school, Bialik College in Hawthorn, singing We Are Australian. Frydenberg’s memoir has been described by The Age’s national correspondent, Rob Harris, as an “elegant book about his life and saving the Liberals. The only problem is that it leaves the reader unsure about whether he wants to lead the party, ensure its survival or just remind people he used to be a future prime minister”.



Frydenberg launched his memoir in Sydney on Tuesday and is now setting out of an extensive multi-state schedule of events to promote the book. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Video captures cafe meeting where building executive was allegedly delivered a $6m threat
World.content:
NationalVictoriaBuilding Bad Video captures cafe meeting where building executive was allegedly delivered a $6m threat Lachlan Abbott Updated October 14, 2026 — 9:57pm ,first published 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Four burly men surround a construction executive at a table outside a Melbourne cafe to deliver a $6 million message, allegedly part of an extortion plot. A video, played in the Melbourne Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday, shows one of the group point out the security camera that captures the December 2024 meeting at Flemington’s Mama Bear Cafe where Amir Teymoori is accused of threatening to kill a major Victorian developer’s manager. “I’m going to f--- you up and your family,” Teymoori allegedly tells the man. Audio from the vision is muffled by the wind, but a man can be heard swearing and saying: “Are you gonna pay me or not?”



Teymoori can be seen covering his mouth as he talks before shouting at the construction firm director. Amir Teymoori outside court in January. Jason South Daniel Van Camp also speaks, taking off his sunglasses to tell the alleged victim: “This is not going away.” The 52-year-old is the son of John Van Camp, a prominent former union boss turned industrial relations manager at Grocon – one of Australia’s biggest private building companies before it collapsed in 2020. Gazanfer Bekirovski sits at the end of the table and only briefly speaks to the construction firm manager, at one point tapping him on the arm.



Travers Grubb does not appear to speak at all, tapping his foot for much of the meeting. But the construction manager, whose identity is suppressed for his safety, told the court the message from Teymoori was clear. Daniel Van Camp, Gazanfer Bekirovski, Amir Teymoori, and Travers Grubb were all initially charged with extortion. Jason South/Justin McManus The four men appeared at a two-day preliminary hearing charged with extortion with a threat to kill. But in a blow to police trying to clean up the construction industry, the case against Van Camp, Bekirovski and Grubb was dismissed as magistrate Stephen Ballek found insufficient evidence they were complicit with Teymoori’s alleged threat.



Prosecutors allege Teymoori made an unwarranted demand for $6.6 million, claiming to have bought the alleged victim’s company industrial peace with the CFMEU. The firm denies ever hiring Teymoori, and police say his claim to be a union mediator is false. Stills from CCTV played at Melbourne Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday show Jonny “Two Guns” Walker (rear near lifts). Melbourne Magistrates’ Court Another video clip shown on Wednesday, and also released to this masthead by the court, reveals notorious ex-bikie Jonny “Two Guns” Walker attended an office in Cremorne in October 2024 with Van Camp, Grubb and Teymoori as the latter sought millions from a developer. Walker was not charged over the alleged extortion or mentioned in court.



He told The Age late on Wednesday that he was arrested and questioned as part of the investigation, but gave a no-comment interview, and police later told him he had no case to answer. “Hawk Taskforce made a song and dance over f---king bullshit,” Walker said. “I’ve really got no comment about the case at all. I know nothing about it.” Teymoori’s barrister, Damian Sheales, suggested the alleged extortion victim lied at one point in a fiery cross-examination on Tuesday. The construction manager, however, maintained Teymoori told him at the Racecourse Road cafe two years ago: “I would f--- you up.” “It was said in the context of ‘if you don’t have your money, I’m going to f--- you up and your family’,” the witness said. “There was no ambiguity.”



The court heard Teymoori brought up mothers and religion during the meeting now at the centre of the case against him. “The contact was unwelcome,” the alleged extortion victim said. “It’s not normal course to have four people approach you in the street in that manner.” Teymoori faces an additional charge of trying to obtain property by deception at the Cremorne office building on October 28, 2024. Police allege he sent an invoice to the construction company demanding payment he wasn’t owed. He turned up to the firm’s headquarters and asked to see managers about his claim, the court heard. Teymoori pleaded not guilty after being committed to stand trial and will reappear at the County Court in November.



Van Camp, Bekirovski and Grubb patted him on the back as they left court cleared of all charges. Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy. Sign up to receive our Evening Edition newsletter.

CORRECTION An earlier version of this story incorrectly reported CCTV played in court showed Gazanfer Bekirovski attended an office in Cremorne in October 2024 with three others. In fact, it was Travers Grubb who attended the premises with three others.
