World.title: Blues ‘embarrassed’ by weekend incident. The AFL integrity unit is now investigating
World.content:
SportAFLCarlton Blues Blues ‘embarrassed’ by weekend incident. The AFL integrity unit is now investigating Sam McClure October 14, 2026 — 9:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The AFL integrity unit is now investigating the circumstances surrounding the hospitalisation of players Lachie Cowan and Will Hayward following a night out at the weekend, which the club says the pair is “embarrassed” about. The league’s involvement represents a significant escalation in the controversy engulfing Carlton, with the AFL now examining the events that led to both players requiring medical treatment in the early hours of Sunday morning. Blues footy boss Chris Davies. AFL Photos Davies confirmed the development on Wednesday evening as the AFL trade period drew to a close, with the Blues facing questions about the conduct of their players and the circumstances surrounding the incidents. “It’s an AFL discussion at the moment and we’ll leave it there,” Davies said.



“The AFL are going through a process right now and ultimately, we’ll work with the AFL to get to the end of that. “We’ve been having discussions with the AFL over the last two or three days, clearly, to make sure that we are at the bottom of that.” Davies was then asked about the health of the two players. “That’s the most important thing – they’re OK now, a little bit embarrassed, I guess, to put the club in this position,” Davies said. He also confirmed another player had been present on Saturday night, “but not in the same situation”.



Lachie Cowan was taken to hospital via ambulance but has since been discharged. AFL Photos The investigation comes amid allegations of illicit drug use at a gathering at Hayward’s South Yarra home on Saturday night, although Carlton have not confirmed whether drugs were involved in either player’s hospitalisation. Reports had widely circulated on Sunday, suggesting that illicit drugs were allegedly involved as the players received medical care. This masthead cannot confirm that illicit drugs were involved in either incident. The AFL’s intervention means the matter is no longer exclusively an internal Carlton issue, with the league’s integrity department now involved in establishing what occurred and whether any breaches of competition rules or policies warrant further action. Both players have since been discharged from hospital.



Cowan, 21, was taken to The Alfred hospital after emergency services attended an address in South Yarra early on Sunday morning. Ambulance Victoria confirmed advanced life-support paramedics responded to an incident about 5.15am, with a man in his 20s transported to hospital in a stable condition. Carlton subsequently confirmed Cowan had received medical treatment and undergone observation before being discharged. Hayward, 27, separately admitted himself to hospital after suffering a cut to his head in a fall. The former Sydney forward received stitches before being discharged. The Blues have maintained that the two players were hospitalised under separate circumstances.



In a statement issued on Sunday, Carlton said its immediate priority was the welfare of both players. “The club has been in regular contact with both players, with priority for their wellbeing and both players have now received the necessary care relating to their separate circumstances,” the statement said. The investigation presents an early test of the football department leadership of Davies and chief executive Graham Wright, who are charged with establishing higher standards at a club attempting to rebuild its football program. Carlton has already begun its own inquiries into the weekend’s events, with the findings expected to be made available to the AFL. The involvement of the league’s integrity unit also raises questions about how any potential breaches would be dealt with under the AFL’s existing illicit drugs framework.



The AFL and AFL Players’ Association have agreed to a revised illicit drugs policy, including expanded hair testing and a greater emphasis on identifying and addressing repeated drug use. However, the new framework is not scheduled to come into effect until 2027, meaning the Carlton matter will be assessed under the competition’s existing rules and disciplinary processes. Will Hayward was named Carlton’s best clubman this season, as well as winning the coaches’ and Spirit of Carlton awards. Getty Images The investigation does not necessarily mean either player will face disciplinary action, with the league yet to establish publicly whether any wrongdoing has occurred. Nevertheless, the episode has again exposed the challenges confronting the AFL in managing player behaviour away from football clubs, particularly during the off-season.



Carlton have endured previous off-field controversies, including the illicit drugs case involving Elijah Hollands, adding to the pressure on the club to demonstrate that player welfare and behavioural standards are being taken seriously. The timing is particularly uncomfortable for the Blues, who have spent the trade period reshaping their playing list and attempting to build momentum ahead of the 2027 season. Hayward arrived at Carlton from Sydney last year and played 21 games in his first season in navy blue, while Cowan has established himself as an important young defender. Cowan played 24 games in 2026 and has become a regular member of Carlton’s backline. The latest controversy threatens to overshadow the club’s list-management work, with Davies now confronting questions extending well beyond recruiting and the composition of Carlton’s playing list.



The central issue for the Blues is no longer simply the medical treatment required by two players on Sunday morning, but what led to those hospital visits and whether the circumstances reveal a broader failure of judgement or conduct. Those are questions the AFL’s integrity unit will now seek to answer. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Wellington train crash: Answers will still take many more months
World.content:
Investigators will not say for many more months why a train on Wellington's Johnsonville line ran a red light, resulting in a crash earlier this year.

The Transport Accident Investigation Commission (TAIC) has released an interim report this morning, setting out a timeline of events for the crash between the Box Hill and Khandallah stations on 6 June.

Six people were injured, two seriously.

TAIC chief investigator of accidents Louise Cook said the report laid out only the facts of the event.

"The commission at this stage hasn't made findings or identified safety issues."

The report found the passenger train had gone past a red light, causing the train to be diverted onto a runway line where it hit a concrete stop block.

During diversion, the train lost power as the pantograph - the rods on the roof of a train linked to the overhead powerline - disconnected from the line.

But it remained unknown why there was a red light or why the train continued past it.

Cook told RNZ a stop light had been activated as the signalling system had detected that the track ahead was already occupied.

But she could not confirm whether the track had actually been occupied, or if the system had erroneously activated a stop light.

She said understanding why the driver ran the red light was "all part of the ongoing inquiry".

"Once that inquiry is complete, the final report will set out findings, safety issues and, where appropriate, recommendations to avoid similar accidents in the future."

World.title: Corrections staff missed warnings that may have helped prevent prisoner's suicide - coroner
World.content:
Corrections staff missed warnings that may have helped prevent a prisoner's suicide, and increased his risk by putting him in an isolated cell, a coroner has found.

The understaffed receiving office at Auckland's Mt Eden prison only had 15 minutes to assess each prisoners' mental health risk, and didn't see the previous suicide attempts on his record.

Te Teihana Mackie, 31, was found dead in his cell on 5 November 2019.

He had been remanded in custody following a police chase the previous month.

Coroner Erin Woolley found Corrections staff considered Mackie low-risk despite having attempted suicide multiple times, most recently in January 2019.

"The nurse recorded that Teihana responded appropriately, maintained good eye contact during the assessment and engaged in conversation," Woolley recounted.

"Teihana denied any thoughts of self-harm or suicidal thoughts and the nurse assessed him as not being at risk of self-harm."

Woolley said Mackie should not have been assessed that way.

"The strong reliance placed on demeanour when conducting risk assessments is concerning because neither the health staff nor correction officers had any training in the place of a person's demeanour in that risk assessment," she wrote.

"Some of the mental health nurses also said they had not been trained in how to assess a person's risk of self-harm but had learnt these skills on the job."

Mackie had struggled with mental health issues since his early childhood.

"He was born as an identical twin, with a brother, who died of sudden unexplained death in infancy at four months old. Teihana's medical records note that he struggled to overcome the grief he felt about the loss of his brother," Woolley wrote.

"Teihana's father was not a nice man and was abusive towards his family, including Teihana."

Between 2006 and 2019, Mackie was convicted 34 times - although he only ever spent time in prison while on remand.

Woolley noted that at the time of Mackie's death, Mt Eden prison was processing between 80 and 100 incoming prisoners every day.

"The receiving office corrections officer said she would usually spend about 15 minutes in total on the entire risk assessment process, from the time of reviewing records, speaking to the prisoner and completing the paperwork," Woolley said.

During her evidence, the officer agreed that "the pressure of the workload meant that sometimes it would not be possible for her to spend 15 minutes with each prisoner, and that in 15 minutes, she could only do the most basic of assessments".

Mackie was first put in a "Hotel Unit," but three days later refused to be locked down in his cell, ripped the net off a tennis table and started swinging it at prison staff.

He was then moved to the Management Unit, where he later had a seizure and was moved to the Intervention and Support Unit to be supervised.

But without any room in the typical ISU cells, Mackie was instead put in a "dry cell" with no toilet or shower.

Prisoners can only be placed in dry cells for up to three hours unless authorised, but Mackie was left in the cell for 40 hours without any paperwork to justify it.

Multiple staff did not know why Mackie had been put there.

"The mental health nurse was surprised to find Teihana in a dry cell because he had reviewed Teihana's notes before going to see him and could see that Teihana had been placed in the ISU for medical, not mental health, reasons," Woolley said.

"The custodial staff were unable to explain why Teihana was in a dry cell and would not say who had placed him in the cell."

Despite this, "during the Sunday afternoon handover, the staff discussed why Teihana was in the dry cell and the decision was made to leave him there until Monday when this could be clarified with the full nursing team".

About a week after Mackie was moved out of the ISU and back to the Management Unit, he committed suicide.

"At around 11:20am [on 5 November], Teihana was found unresponsive in his cell. A medical code blue event was called by unit staff but despite full medical resuscitation efforts, Teihana could not be resuscitated," Woolley wrote.

The coroner found both the rushed risk assessment process and his unlawful time in the dry cell had material impacts on his death.

"It is my overwhelming impression that the number of staff assigned to work in the receiving office, when compared to the number of prisoners that are received at Mt Eden each day, resulted in a near impossible workload for the staff to manage," Woolley said.

Woolley recommended that the currently in-development electronic health management system make it mandatory for staff to review a prisoner's most recent records before they're able to complete the assessment.

She also recommended that staffing be increased so assessors had at minimum 20 minutes with each prisoner.

"[And] it is abundantly clear from the evidence that prisoners should not be placed in dry cells unless it is absolutely necessary because of the serious, detrimental effects of spending time in dry cells."

"It is disturbing that these cells are used for overflow purposes. In my view, this practice must cease."

Woolley also recommended that the prison operations manual be amended to state that dry cells should not be used for overflow purposes, and that if there are no ISU beds available the prisoner must remain in their current cell.

Emma Gardner, acting deputy chief executive Pae Ora said Corrections received the final findings from the coroner earlier this month and was working through the recommendations. "But since 2019 we have already made significant improvements to our processes and how we support prisoners with their mental health and wellbeing".

Gardner said when a prisoner arrived, they were screened twice for the risk of self-harm and processes were put in place to ensure follow-up.

A multi-disciplinary team met regularly to support vulnerable prisoners, she said, and the process for segregation forms had been updated.

"We continue to invest in improving mental health support, specialist services for people with mental health and addiction needs, and enhanced training and support for frontline staff," said Gardner. "Corrections has a duty of care to all people in prison and we take this responsibility very seriously. While the causes of self-harm are multifaceted and complex, we are committed to doing everything we can to prevent deaths in custody."

World.title: ASB finance debate gives platform for smaller parties to again show their stuff
World.content:
Analysis - The ASB finance leaders' debate in Queenstown has traditionally been a feisty and unpredictable event, where canny politicians can go off script and feed off the energy of the often-boisterous live audience.

This year's event was another fiery and fun affair to add to the impressive Queenstown debate canon.

However, while there were plenty of zingers, one-liners and fierce exchanges, the debate probably didn't have quite the crazy fizz of past years.

A new, larger venue, with its bigger crowd of 800, mostly in the dark, possibly didn't help when it came to connecting with the debaters.

However, I suspect the stakes and nature of the polls in this election may have also played a part.

Unlike previous elections, we had four minor-party leaders on stage with the two main parties, who were anything but bit players.

And they acted like they knew it too.

ACT's David Seymour, the Greens' Chlöe Swarbrick, the Opportunities Party's Qiulae Wong and New Zealand First's Shane Jones all spoke and debated with a confidence that signalled they expected, and would demand, big roles in shaping the next government.

Green co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick. NICK MONRO / RNZ

None of them looked out of place or diminished alongside National's Nicola Willis and Labour's Barbara Edmonds.

That's not to say Willis and Edmonds were giving them a free run.

Both got stuck in and had clearly honed their attack lines after debating each other repeatedly over recent weeks.

Edmonds appeared to have a strong night. She talked up her skills as a tax lawyer repeatedly and seemed to be full of confidence that I'm not sure was as evident a few years ago.

Interestingly, though, she still felt the need to hammer the point that she would be the next finance minister, not Willis or, indeed, Swarbrick.

The reference to Swarbrick seemed to be a kickback at the Greens' strong polling and the suggestion a week or so back from the Greens'-leader that she was seriously coveting the job.

Willis also appeared assured and was at her best attacking Edmonds over her capital gains tax and the decision to scrap the Investment Boost policy.

ACT leader David Seymour. RNZ / Nick Monro

But then she copped some friendly fire from Seymour, who stressed he would, if elected, try to stop her "nuts" plans to break up the Foodstuffs supermarket chain.

Seymour delivered some good one-liners throughout the night and pushed hard on the need to cut red tape and foster entrepreneurs.

He was hamstrung, to a degree, by the topics, with the party's core issue of debt and the state of the books not featuring strongly.

Wong, meanwhile, looked comfortable enough talking up her land tax proposal and insisting that economic growth and protecting the environment weren't mutually exclusive.

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong. RNZ / Blessen Tom

However, she was more restrained in interjecting than the others and suffered from a lack of airtime as a result.

Jones had no such qualms, butting in with quips about his fast-track legislation and the benefits of mining. His bombastic approach and colourful language won plenty of laughs and cheers from the audience.

At one point, he even seemed to celebrate some rare common ground with Swarbrick on the issue of whether the government should allow councils to impose bed taxes.

Jones begrudgingly said he would join the Greens, Labour and The Opportunities Party in backing bed taxes, as he was so sick of having to debate the issue.

NZ First's Shane Jones. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

For Swarbrick, it was also another focused and disciplined performance, following on from a solid multi-party debate earlier in the week.

The debate didn't deliver any major new revelations or policies.

Although we did learn that New Zealand First is now the only party that would most likely not sign up to an accord on the future of superannuation next term.

World.title: Debate doubts: Does anyone believe the two Chrises?
World.content:
Analysis - One of the few moments of agreement in Wednesday night's NZME leaders' debate came right at the outset, when both men insisted, hand on heart, they'd never told a porkie in politics.

It was about as convincing as the next 90 minutes.

Time and again, National's Christopher Luxon and Labour's Chris Hipkins gave voters little reason to believe them, with one frequently flip-flopping and the other over-committing.

Tuesday night's 1News-Verian poll showed the uphill battle the leaders faced coming in, with their respective parties tied at just 28 percent, evenly matched in their mediocrity.

Both leaders were also stuck on 20 percent as preferred prime minister. In other words, three out of every five voters has someone else in mind.

Moderator Ryan Bridge put the wider predicament to both men bluntly: "Why are you guys doing so poorly?"

Looking for someone to blame, neither looked inwards. Hipkins attributed the malaise to general voter disillusionment, while Luxon noted a "global political problem" where mainstream parties had "failed to deliver" - but not his, he quickly clarified.

Luxon was particularly prone to making sweeping commitments, only to hurriedly retreat from them.

Asked whether he'd increase the minimum wage in line with inflation, he responded: "Yes, and that's what we've more or less been doing."

Christopher Luxon. NZME / Dean Purcell

Except in each of the past three years, the coalition has increased the minimum wage by less than the rate of inflation, as Hipkins noted.

Luxon performed a similar somersault on supermarkets, promising New World and Pak'nSave would be split apart by the end of the next term, "for sure".

This time it was Bridge who reminded him the policy was actually contingent on the Commerce Commission's sign-off.

The parties' fiscal plans also came in for a battering, with Bridge recalling both parties' previous promises to deliver surpluses that never materialised.

"Can we trust either of you?" Bridge remonstrated.

On other matters, the leaders were dubiously definitive.

For the umpteenth time, Luxon was pressed on whether he would pick up the phone to Opportunity's Qiulae Wong if he needed her party's support to form a government.

And for umpteenth time, Luxon insisted: "No, I've ruled them out."

"No way, Qiulae," Bridge quipped. Yes, way.

Moderator Ryan Bridge. NZME / Dean Purcell

Hipkins was also trigger-happy with his permanent pen, perhaps forgetting for a moment that Labour no longer commands the support or sway it once did.

In an in-the-moment captain's call, he ruled out giving key law and order portfolios to any Green or Te Pāti Māori MP, after they posed for photographs with Mongrel Mob members.

No doubt Hipkins is hoping the firm condemnation plays well with middle New Zealand - but the reality of MMP is that numbers matter - and on current polling, the Greens would have a claim on a sizeable wedge of the Cabinet table.

At just 28 percent, Hipkins is hardly in a position of such strength to be dictating terms to his potential partners.

The same applies to his declaration that Greens' co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick could never be Treasurer.

Both men did have their moments to shine.

Hipkins was at his strongest on jobs and pay, pointing out there were 48,000 more people unemployed on the latest figures compared with when Luxon took over as prime minister.

"You celebrate cutting jobs," he chided Luxon. "I want to create them."

Chris Hipkins. NZME / Dean Purcell

And when Luxon accused Labour of failing to properly fund its promise to restore pay equity, Hipkins turned the attack around, delivering an impassioned defence of care and support workers.

"[National] think women should settle for being paid less than men," he said. "I don't."

Luxon, on the other hand, was at his best when making the case for his government's economic management.

Asked to explain why his government had yet to fix the economy, he deployed a killer line: "It's really easy to burn a house down. Takes time to rebuild it."

He also made the most of a near-uninterrupted opportunity to savage Labour's proposed capital gains tax.

"It's going to kill our economy. It's going to add a lot of costs. It's going to slow down and suck out our recovery," Luxon warned.

"But the worst thing I think you're going to do, Chris, is you're going to trash the property market."

Luxon finished by looking straight down the barrel of the camera: "Mark my words, you are going to pay, New Zealand. You are going to pay."

At last, Hipkins fired up, accusing Luxon of lying.

"This is why people don't trust what you say," he said, again bringing the debate back to the question of trust and honesty.

In a lighter moment, the two men were invited to reminisce on their school years, but both refused to divulge the name of their best friend.

"Did neither of you have friends?" Bridge teased.

World.title: National's Nicola Willis and Labour's Barbara Edmonds debate in Queenstown
World.content:
Analysis - National's Nicola Willis and Labour's Barbara Edmonds turned up to Queenstown ready for a bit of rough and tumble on Wednesday evening.

The ASB Great debate featuring cross-party finance spokespeople has a history of getting a bit rowdy, and while it's often the large audience responsible for a lot of that, this year it was the panelists leading the charge.

In addition to Willis and Edmonds the 800-strong southern crowd got served up Act's David Seymour, New Zealand First's Shane Jones, the Greens' Chlöe Swarbrick, and newcomer Qiulae Wong of the Opportunity party.

Stood side-by-side in the middle of the panel of five, Willis and Edmonds scrapped it out about the government's Investment Boost and Labour's plan to scrap it and replace it with a policy that targets small businesses.

Debate moderator TVNZ's Jack Tame asked Edmonds what a business like Coronet Peak, which has benefitted from Investment Boost's tax support for businesses would do without it, Edmonds fired back "I don't have to copy Nicola, we are two very different people" to huge applause from the crowd.

In an unusual twist, Swarbrick and Jones paired up regularly throughout the debate, and were highly amused by the scrap playing out in the middle of the panel, leading Jones to pipe up and suggest the Green co-leader "offer some clarity".

Edmonds held her ground against Willis however, saying in her opening remarks she would be the next finance minister: "Not Chlöe Swarbrick and not Nicola Willis - Barbara Edmonds the MP for Kenepuru will be."

Seymour summarised the Willis and Edmonds showdown saying: "It's like two bald men fighting over a comb in the middle there."

Jones also received some big laughs in his opening remarks when he detailed how slow and clogged up the economy had become, shouting: "Look at my beloved fast-track, it's turned into a constipated beast."

Tax was also a big talking point with Wong, Edmonds, and Swarbrick given a shot at pitching their respective land, capital gains, and wealth tax proposals to the audience.

The debate descended into sledges and lots of shouting as Willis and Seymour took their turns picking holes in them all.

Swarbrick revved up at Willis, who said Labour would introduce a capital gains tax (CGT) and Swarbrick who wants a wealth tax would "kick the door wide open" and expand it.

Given an opportunity to respond, Swarbrick harked back "to a time even I can remember" when National criticised the international visitor levy, only to then increase it when in government.

Seymour was highly amused by that, quipping: "I love how Chlöe said she was old enough to remember something that happened in 2018."

A new coalition also came out of the tax debate when Wong, Edmonds, Jones and Swarbrick were all asked whether they would support a bed tax for Queenstown if in government, and it was a unanimous yes from them all, much to the delight of the crowd.

Another big laugh came when Willis and Seymour were in the thick of a debate on breaking up the supermarkets and Jones interrupted to say: "Now you know what our Cabinet meetings are like."

Seymour - not one to miss an opportunity - replied: "One person has to bring the basic economics to Cabinet, that's exactly what it's like!"

One of the final topics rounding out the debate was the issue of superannuation and how the country will afford it in years to come.

All of the politicians were asked if they supported being part of a cross-party review on the country's retirement future.

Seymour said he would entertain it with a yes, but noted he was disappointed it wasn't a big feature of the debate overall, given what a significant issue it is.

Wong was supportive, saying Opportunity needed to be in Parliament and in the room "to be the broker in a heated environment where people don't agree and have proven not to hold themselves accountable to long-term plans".

Edmonds acknowledged Willis who had agreed to the idea with her at the weekend. Willis returned that and said she too wanted to celebrate Edmonds on that front but added she was disappointed the conversation hadn't happened during this term, which she blamed on Labour.

Swarbrick was also in the 'yes' camp but said the "missing piece" in this election was also talking about investment in climate change adaptation and planning.

World.title: Walters explains choice of Walsh over Tedesco for World Cup opener
World.content:
Kevin Walters has declared the battle for Australia's fullback berth remains wide open despite Reece Walsh winning the nod over James Tedesco to start in the Kangaroos' World Cup opener.

Walters claimed ahead of Thursday night's clash with New Zealand that Tedesco, the captain as Australia lifted the trophy four years ago, would have a chance to prove his worth in the group-stage game against Fiji in Brisbane on October 25.

Walsh, the hero of last year's Ashes whitewash, will don the No.1 jersey at Sydney's Allianz Stadium, but as for whether the Brisbane Broncos star will be first choice later in the tournament, Walters is keeping an open mind.

Less can be more for Rugby League World Cup The Rugby League World Cup exists in a constant state of change but ahead of the tournament opener between Australia and New Zealand the much-maligned tournament can prove less can be more.

The Kangaroos coach indicated he had chosen to rest Tedesco and playmaker halfback Sam Walker following their exploits in the Sydney Roosters' NRL grand final win.

"I feel it's in the best interest of the team they get a spell this week and they'll play next week," Walters said on Wednesday.

"To be honest, I haven't decided that (fullback) position yet, that's why we're here, and they'll both get an opportunity.

"They're both Clive Churchill medallists, the last two, so I look at it that way. I'm very fortunate to have both of them in the team.

"They're different players, but I love what they both bring to the team. Teddy's the more experienced custodian and Reece is on the way up as such."

Walsh has retained his place after his heroics in last year's Ashes. (Getty Images: PA Images/Mike Egerton)

The one drawback to Walsh is his fitness, with Thursday's opener his first competitive match in close to two months after sustaining an ankle injury in clubland.

"He (Walsh) has had a good preparation and there's a few players in that position themselves, so it's good to get them around the group," Walters said.

Walsh will be part of a relatively settled Kangaroos spine, with Cameron Munster at five-eighth and Harry Grant at hooker.

Halfback Mitchell Moses is the only new addition to the key playmaking roles.

Moses was on last year's Ashes tour but didn't take the field, with the Parramatta skipper an understudy to Nathan Cleary, who has missed this World Cup following his compound ankle fracture.

Tedesco last played for Australia in 2023. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

"He's a very influential player, an experienced player, particularly his kicking game around the halves will be invaluable," Walters said.

"He gets his opportunity and I'm sure he's looking forward to taking it as well.

"They (Munster and Moses) are very calm and know what we need to do in different situations."

The Kangaroos have not lost to New Zealand on Australian soil since 2015, and while the Kiwis have a monster forward pack, Walters insists his side have the firepower to match them.

"It's a strong New Zealand side, certainly, but I feel like the guys that we have picked in the Australian squad, they're not mugs," the Kangaroos coach added.

"We've got Origin players, Test players, premiership winners, that's what the World Cup is all about: seeing the best players on the world stage."

AAP

World.title: Afghan batter recreates infamous hamstring injury used against Australia
World.content:
Sediqullah Atal's maiden Test century has led Afghanistan to an epic draw against Bangladesh in a one-off cricket Test.

Afghanistan batted for 142 overs, 92 on the fifth and final day, in its second innings to force a sensational draw on Tuesday. It began the day on a dodgy 132-3, lost five more wickets, but fought on to hold out to stumps at 346-8.

But it was the actions of number nine Qais Ahmad in the dying minutes that drew the most attention in the match's final act.

With the finish line in sight and just two wickets left, Ahmad played a forward defence to spinner Taijul Islam before collapsing to the ground clutching his hamstring.

The Bangladesh team was not impressed, and had commentator Ahmad Farhad Fidai in stitches as he likened it to the actions of Afghanistan's Gulbadin Naib, who suffered a suspicious cramp fielding at slip in their famous 2024 T20 World Cup win over Australia.

"Qais Ahmad does it again. This reminds me of Gulbadin Naib," an amused Fidai said, clearly believing Ahmad's fall to the turf was nothing more than time-wasting antics.

"Oh boy, not again.

"You really don't need to see the replay; we can understand from here what's going on."

Ahmad soldiered on and finished the match with a six over midwicket.

Bangladesh dominated the match after winning the toss and batting first. Bangladesh earned a first-innings lead of 106 runs, then declared its second innings at 7-372 after player-of-the-match Litton Das was out for 102. That gave Bangladesh an imposing lead of 478 and four and a half sessions to bowl out Afghanistan.

But Afghanistan defied the odds despite losing two wickets in the first seven overs on Monday.

First drop Atal, in his third Test, ate up most of the chase as he faced 332 balls over 8.5 hours to score 111. He was caught close to the wicket after tea, the seventh man out.

Afghanistan still had 23 overs with just tailenders left. But 34-year-old Yamin Ahmadzai faced 85 balls for a career-best 19, and Ahmad, who has played franchise cricket in eight countries, faced 80 to finish with an unbeaten career-best 49.

AP/ABC

World.title: Less can be more for Rugby League World Cup
World.content:
The only things that stay the same about the Rugby League World Cup are that it never stops changing and it continually has to justify its own existence.

For the third tournament in a row, there will be a different format and a different number of teams, dropping from 16 to 10, and for the umpteenth tournament in a row, the sceptics will question why it's worth playing a Rugby League World Cup at all and compare it unfavourably to the rugby and football versions.

Those world cups exist in different universes than the league equivalent, even as nation-swapping and diaspora-heavy squads, two hallmarks of the much-maligned international rugby league, become more prevalent in their larger cousins.

The Rugby League World Cup has to prove itself anew every four years. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

Measure the Rugby League World Cup against those that dwarf it in scale and it will always be miles behind. It is playing a different game, one that is carving out a place all its own.

On the back of the rise of Tonga and Samoa over the past 10 years, Test football is at its strongest and most vibrant in years, with the two Pasifika nations emerging as legitimate draws and top-class teams.

Tonga's two matches against Australia in the 2024 Pacific Championships drew crowds of more than 33,000 and 28,000, and both Tonga and Samoa have made their first tours to England since the last World Cup.

When the ancient island rivals went head-to-head in Brisbane last year, more than 40,000 came through the gates, the second-largest non-World Cup final crowd for a Test in Australia in the last half-century.

Samoa creates rugby league magic The passion of the Pacific shines through in Samoa's rugby league team, and the pride the people have is evident on the island.

A similar attendance is expected for the tournament opener between Australia and New Zealand on Thursday night, and if the Sydney Football Stadium can sell out, it'll be the biggest Test crowd in Sydney since 1974.

It marks the beginning of a chance for the Rugby League World Cup to reshape itself a little more permanently and take advantage of the renewed interest by recasting itself as a pinnacle for the game rather than a starting point.

Rugby league had to make a choice whether its World Cup was a beginning or an end, a proving ground for developing nations or a battleground for the best, because it could not be both at the same time.

At the sharp end of recent tournaments, when it's the best teams in the world having it out, the product is reliably compelling, rich and powerful. The problem is it's just taken too long to get there.

In 2022, there was a crackerjack knockout phase, highlighted by Samoa's epic win over Tonga in Warrington, New Zealand sneaking home against Fiji in Hull, and two brilliant semifinals, including a golden point epic that doubles as one of the best games in the tournament's history.

The night a rag-tag group of rugby league Russians took on the world champions Russia might only make one trip to the Rugby League World Cup but the memories forged in the 2000 tournament, especially in their record loss to Australia, are wild enough to last a lifetime.

But the group stage was a forgone conclusion almost all the way. Only two of the 24 preliminary matches were decided by one score or less. There were 10 scores over 60 and two scores over 90.

Australia's 110-4 massacre of Russia in 2000 remained untouched as the most lopsided result in World Cup history, but matches from 2022 fill out the second, third and fourth spots on that list.

Developing nations have their place in the international rugby league and the emotional scenes upon qualification for Jamaica, or Greece's epic tale of playing qualifying matches on the edge of war zones and in undisclosed locations to stay one step ahead of the authorities, are proof of the value developing nations can bring.

But it is hard to see the benefits of England nearly putting 100 points on the Greeks, or a disinterested Australia beating Scotland 84-0.

The trickle-down effects of those games, such as they are, can take decades to rise to the surface, if they ever do at all.

The knockout phase of recent World Cups have been rugby league dynamite. (Getty Images: Gareth Copley)

The game's wholehearted embrace of the set restart rule and the increased speed of play makes it harder for the smaller nations to compete on a physical level, and the perfunctory nature of the group stages makes the tournament even longer.

In a world where fan interest and player fatigue are already being stretched to their limits, it adds even more to an already overstuffed season.

So while it may not please the true believers, the move to 10 teams is a good one. This tournament is leaner and has the potential to be meaner.

The lack of northern hemisphere teams — it's just England, France and Lebanon, with none from the Americas and no other home nations after Scotland and Ireland were demoted to affiliate status and Wales failed to qualify — is regrettable, but exclusivity cuts both ways because less can be more.

This is a tournament with barely any fat on it, and as a result, it's as open at the top as it's ever been.

Australia is still the favourite because such is the largesse of talent available that it's almost impossible to name a Kangaroos team that isn't oozing with class, but it's far from invulnerable.

Its talent pool has been diluted, and there are several squad members who are coming off indifferent or underdone seasons.

Some have made it due to coach Kevin Walters's loyalty to the side that retained the Ashes in a 3-0 whitewash last year, but others are in because there's a lack of other options as the eligibility rules slowly spread the talent around.

Nobody has benefited more from that spread than New Zealand, who welcome Kalyn Ponga to the squad for his belated Test debut as the herald of a new era.

On paper, it's a better side than the one that handed Australia its biggest-ever defeat just three years ago — it has all three middles from this season's Dally M Team of the Year — and a second World Cup title is a distinct possibility.

The bookies have Samoa and Tonga as equal-third favourites to make the final, well ahead of England, and their group-stage clash at Parramatta Stadium has been sold out for months.

Samoa and Tonga have already sold out their group stage match. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

The English have a little more to prove after last year's lacklustre Ashes showing, an embrace of heritage players that has divided their fan base and the controversial exclusion of Leeds halfback Jake Connor from the squad.

Outside the top five, there's still plenty to follow. Write off the perennially underrated Fijians, who beat New Zealand in 2017 and came within six points of doing the same in 2022, off at your peril.

France and Lebanon won't be as dangerous, but the French have 20 homegrown players in their squad and 10 of Lebanon's starting 13 for their first game have NRL experience.

Even the Cook Islands, which will play in front of crowds that dwarf its home's population, will have Cronulla's KL Iro and former Kangaroo Valentine Holmes to call upon.

Another Australian victory is far from a guarantee in this World Cup. (Jan Kruger: Getty Images for RLWC)

Injuries have robbed Papua New Guinea of some of their biggest names, but their group matches against Samoa and Lebanon will be the Kumuls' biggest on home soil since the PNG Chiefs were admitted to the NRL and shape as the first dress rehearsals for what awaits the game in the land where they love it most.

Through it all, this World Cup can have it all. There will still be stories of paupers taking on princes against all odds and of the unbridled passion and pride that has kept international football alive despite the many obstacles.

Those tales and teams will always have their place, but for the most part, this tournament will be collections of top-level rugby league talent crashing into each other in the fast until only the world champions are left to rise from the wreckage.

What the tournament gives up in diversity and novelty, it can win back in quality, because at some point, a World Cup has to be about the best of the best being at their best, and there are more nations who can dream of that than ever before.

Never in the World Cup's 72-year history has the sky seemed so open. Ten teams might not seem like many, but if five have designs on the crown, it can be plenty.

World.title: F1 returns to Africa with Rwanda signing 10-year deal
World.content:
Africa will return to the Formula 1 calendar for the first time since 1993 with Rwanda set to host a grand prix from the early 2030s in a 10-year deal.

Formula 1 last raced on the continent at South Africa's Kyalami Circuit to the north of Johannesburg and has long sought a way back.

The race will be called the African Grand Prix, and held at a circuit that is yet to be built alongside a new international airport under construction at Bugesera, about 40 kilometres south of the capital Kigali.

"Today is a landmark moment for Formula 1," F1 chief executive Stefano Domenicali said at a press conference with Rwandan President Paul Kagame and International Automobile Federation (FIA) head Mohammed Ben Sulayem on Tuesday.

"With Rwanda joining the calendar from the next decade, our sport will race in every inhabited continent, bringing the world championship closer than ever to fans around the globe.

"Africa has always been part of Formula 1's future, and from the beginning we were determined to return in the right way, with the right partner, a long-term commitment and a clear vision for creating meaningful impact."

Kagame announced his landlocked East African country's bid two years ago.

The purpose-built grade one track, designed by Austrian former driver Alex Wurz with long-time F1 architect Tilke also involved, is expected to be completed early in the next decade and be fast and flowing with significant changes of elevation and putting spectators close to the action.

Rwanda Development Board chief executive Jean-Guy Afrika said the track would have a 100,000 capacity and also be a multi-purpose facility with year-round utilisation as a concert and exhibition venue.

"We want to make it bigger than just Rwanda. We want to make it the moment when the sport came back to Africa and then never left," he told a press conference, adding that the initiative would likely be "powered by the private sector and coordinated by the government".

Rwanda will be the third African country to host a round of the championship since the start in 1950, with Morocco putting on a race outside Casablanca in 1958.

Reuters

World.title: De Minaur sets up Shanghai quarterfinal with Zverev
World.content:
Alex de Minaur has taken a giant stride towards clinching another ATP Finals berth after roaring into the last eight of the Shanghai Masters.

Continuing to defy the hip flexor injury that threatened to end his season less than a week ago, de Minaur downed dual grand slam semifinalist Karen Khachanov 6-3, 6-4 to jump to seventh place in the Race to Turin's live standings.

Crucially, Australia's baseline warrior has leapfrogged Novak Djokovic and Frances Tiafoe, who have already been eliminated in China, as he chases more valuable rankings points in the quarter-finals — and potentially beyond.

De Minaur retires injured, handing China Open title to Djokovic Alex de Minaur says he did not want his Beijing campaign to end in the way it did, with injury forcing the Australian to retire early in the second set.

But Alexander Zvererv, who will be the year-end world number one, stands in his way after the German beat Alexander Bublik 7-6(6), 4-6, 7-6(1).

In his fifth encounter against Khachanov, de Minaur knew efficiency was key.

"It was really important for me to serve well and I think I definitely did that, especially down the stretch," he said.

"I got into a little bit of trouble, a couple of love-30 games, and I was able to find some good serves when I needed it."

De Minaur, who reached the semi-finals at the prestigious season-ending tournament last year, cut a forlorn figure after being forced to retire early in the second set of last week's China Open final against Djokovic, when a set down.

His comeback has been nothing short of remarkable.

"Ultimately I've been getting better and better every day," the 27-year-old said.

"Today was by far my best match and I think that I'm only going to get better.

"I know that once I'm fit physically and mentally, I'm the player that I [want to be] and I'm excited to be competing and going to the tail end of these tournaments and feeling great about myself."

Despite a 4-8 record against Zverev, de Minaur prevailed in their past two meetings, both at Laver Cup, including two weeks ago. Zverev has fitness problems of his own.

"My ankle was acting up, unfortunately," Zverev said, who saved three set points against Bublik in the first-set tiebreak.

"It was understandable because I have been playing a lot of tennis, which is kind of a good sign because I have been playing well. I am starting to feel my body more and more but I am happy to get through."

AAP

World.title: Regulator says he would quit over political influence in Man City scandal
World.content:
The chair of English football's regulatory body says he would resign if any political interference affected potential sanctions against Manchester City.

City has been found guilty of widespread breaches of the Premier League's financial rules, which could result in punishments including a massive fine, points deductions or even expulsion from England's top flight.

Separately, the Independent Football Regulator can force club owners to sell and can withhold a license to operate if it deems them unfit.

An independent panel found the United Arab Emirates-backed City had artificially inflated its revenue by more than $1 billion over nearly a decade, circumventing fair-play rules.

Loading...

Football regulator chair David Kogan said it was still awaiting the outcome of City's appeal against the verdict.

The UAE is a big investor in the UK. Asked about the regulator's ability to remain independent given wider relations between the governments, Kogan said: "Any form of political interference in the way we operate is going to result in my resigning from this role, and I stand by that completely.

"We've come under absolutely no political pressure whatsoever on this or any other topic. And I don't expect to in the future," he said.

Kogan's comments came after UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he would be "really concerned" to lose City's current ownership. Mr Burnham also said he would not get "directly involved in the process."

City is accused of providing misleading information about its finances over a nine-year period from 2009-18. During that time, it won three titles and signed some of the world's best players. It went on to enjoy a period of unprecedented dominance of English soccer.

The guilty verdict marks the biggest scandal in Premier League history and raises questions about the club's future, owned by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, deputy prime minister of the United Arab Emirates and a member of Abu Dhabi's royal family.

Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan owns Manchester City. (Reuters: Ameer Al-Mohammedawi/Pool)

The British government established the Independent Football Regulatory Commission last year to set governance standards in English soccer.

Part of that includes the issuing of licenses for clubs to be able to operate, which will begin in November.

Kogan suggested the guilty verdict would not affect issuing a license to City because its appeal is ongoing.

"A verdict once it's gone through an appeal process will certainly be something that we would clearly be taking into account when looking at awarding a license or looking at the owners, directors and senior executives," he said.

Majority of English clubs are loss-making

Kogan was speaking in Manchester about the regulator's "State of the Game" report on English soccer.

The report states that despite the success of English soccer — including the Premier League, the world's richest and most popular league — 94 per cent of clubs across the pyramid are loss-making, and more than a quarter would be unable to survive more than 30 days if owners pulled funding.

It says a major problem is teams spending too much to keep up with rivals.

"At the heart of English football's success is a massive contradiction. While some of our clubs are among the richest and most competitive in the world, others are standing on the edge of financial disaster," Kogan said.

"This lack of resilience can no longer be ignored."

Seventeen clubs "would be loss-making even if their players played for free," the regulator's CEO Richard Monks said.

"Owners in many football clubs will inject the money two or three days before payday and not keep any cash in the club. This is not how most businesses are run, and it's a major issue which we will require football to address."

The regulator has been involved in negotiations between the Premier League and the English Football League regarding what are known as solidarity payments to help develop England's lower leagues. That includes parachute payments to teams relegated from the top flight.

The regulator is proposing to spread those payments more evenly among teams. It is part of a suite of proposals, including measures to help clubs improve financial risk management.

World.title: Why hair tests are still not being used in the AFL's illicit drugs battle
World.content:
The issue of Illicit Drugs Policy (IDP) reform in the AFL remains in limbo after seven months of waiting and increasing scrutiny of the parties involved, and no clear indication of when it might be resolved.

An in-principle agreement for a new policy was announced in March by the AFL in conjunction with the AFL Players Association but is yet to be implemented.

The AFL and AFLPA said it would be the "toughest in Australian sport" and become operational in 2026 once outstanding matters had been resolved.

The policy is in the news now because of allegations of drug use by the so-called "Pullman Five"; five Sydney Swans players involved in the Pullman Hotel scandal in August.

Last weekend, Advanced Life Support paramedics attended a house owned by a Carlton player.

There is no suggestion any of the Carlton players were using illicit drugs.

So what is the current state of play, and what is the plan for the future?

What is the current AFL Illicit Drugs Policy?

The IDP was first established in 2005 and was, according to the AFL, "unashamedly a harm minimisation policy".

Players caught breaching the IDP are subject to a three-strike system.

If a player is caught with drugs in their system for the first time, they are given a suspended $5,000 fine and receive targeted testing and counselling. The club doctor is the only staff member informed of the player's drug use.

A second strike means the player will be named and suspended for four games.

A third strike results in a 12-match suspension. Travis Tuck in 2010 is the only player to have ever recorded three strikes.

Most players who are caught using drugs in public or through social media, such as Bailey Smith (when he was at the Bulldogs), are generally suspended under the AFL's "conduct unbecoming" rules.

Bailey Smith was given a two-match suspension for illicit drug use when he was with the Bulldogs in 2022. (AAP: Hamish Blair)

The policy has come under enormous criticism in the two decades it has been in place, most notably from independent senator Andrew Wilkie, who denounced the policy in a speech to federal parliament in 2024.

What is the proposed new policy?

When the AFL and Players' Association announced the new policy in March, they said it would strengthen "the game's response to illicit drug use across both the AFL and AFLW competitions".

AFL reveals new illicit drug policy The AFL says its new illicit drugs policy, which includes biannual hair-testing of all players, is the most stringent in Australian sport.

The organisations maintained the policy was based on medical advice for players' health and wellbeing.

When in place, the new policy will see all AFL and AFLW players undergo annual education programs and have a hair sample tested twice a year for evidence of drug use.

Hair samples retain evidence of drug use for up to three months, whereas urine samples, which are currently used, may only show evidence of drug use for a handful of days.

It's expected the players will be tested during the pre-season in order to cover the period when they're on leave and then again following their mid-season bye.

If a player tests positive, they will enter a behavioural change program overseen by their club doctor.

If a player records a second positive test, they'll be put on an individual management plan, which will be overseen by an AFL IDP manager.

A third positive test will see the player referred to a Fitness to Play assessment by an independent panel, and at that point, the club president, chief executive and general manager of football would be informed.

Players who use illicit drugs publicly will be suspended for two to four weeks.

So, what's happened?

Seven months after the AFL and Players' Association announced an in-principle agreement on the policy, it still hasn't been put into place.

ABC Sport understands there are still points of disagreement between the two bodies.

The outstanding matters include designing the education program and the behavioural change program for players who are found with drugs in their system, and appointing members to a joint committee to oversee the program.

Until the new program is in place, the old system will continue to operate.

ABC Sport has asked the AFL and the AFLPA why the current policy was not in place, when it's expected to begin and who, if anyone, has been employed to run the program?

The AFL didn't respond to those questions, and the Players' Association declined to comment.

Tech.title: Ukraine claims Starlink is suddenly disrupting service for its military
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Ukrainian officials claim the Elon Musk-owned Starlink put new limits on its service in the area without warning, disrupting the country’s drone operations and missions, according to reports from Reuters and the Financial Times. The move comes just days after Musk wrote on X that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy “has gone too far,” in response to President Donald Trump’s disapproval of Ukraine targeting Russian oil refineries.

“It is clear that this action is not coincidental and is related to the current political situation,” Ukrainian defense tech advisor Serhii Beskrestnov writes on Telegram.

Beskrestnov writes that Starlink has imposed a new restriction that prevents it from connecting to devices traveling at over 100mph. He adds that this has “led to the disruption of several missions,” as reported by Reuters. The limitation is impacting Ukraine’s ability to protect itself from Russian drone strikes as well, Beskrestnov says.

The apparent Starlink restriction has begun to draw criticism from international leaders. Radosław Sikorski, the deputy prime minister of Poland, which pays for Ukraine’s Starlink subscription, issued a warning to Musk on X: “Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again? As your European customers, we are watching you.” SpaceX didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.
